321ef4d0-79f2-4a6d-87d0-fb9f037fe51b.description:
The soil sample was collected during the winter months and kept at 4 degrees C until processing.

This fungus can easily be mistaken for a chytrid, especially species of Catenaria. It is a fast grower, even at cold temperatures. In pure culture, it does not produce aerial sporangia often. Chlamydospores are produced abundantly along the hyphae, which are aseptate. The chlamydospores superficially resemble zoosporangia.
It appears to be homothallic, and produces zygospores with apposed suspensors. One is typically much larger than the other.

Identification is based off morphology and a partial 28s rRNA gene sequence.
It exists as a pure culture in the University of Alabama culture collection.

3e2bb9ab-608b-4a8e-bc61-ee64a0803712.description:
Growth occurred on pine pollen.
Identification is based off morphology and a partial 28s rRNA gene sequence.
It exists as a pure culture in the University of Alabama culture collection.

The original identification was incorrect. I revised it based on a new phylogeny, which placed it with Rhizophydium globosum, and on the number of discharge pores, which is 1-7 placed sporadically on the sporangium as opposed to many evenly spaced discharge pores.

The coloring in the pictures is tolene blue, which was added to help visualize structures.

aedd3615-25d7-4089-b48e-01e7494c0f60.description: Once thought to be a chytrid, it was realized it is not. The anterior, tinsel flagellum places it with the oomycetes. It's similarity to the genus Catenaria yields the specific epithet of catenoides. Recovered off pine pollen.

fc627f3c-1ec9-4e13-aec6-ed0e276a107c.description:
This is one of the most easily recognizable chytrids. It grows on human hair with the lipids removed and can be coaxed from richly organic soils. Cemetaries are a good place to find this chytrid. Its defining feature is the presence of forked spines.
Attempts at bringing this chytrid in to culture have failed.

Phylum Ciliophora: 
Los ciliados son algunos de los organismos unicelulares más extendidos. La mayoría son reconocidos por sus cilios: flagelos cortos dispuestos en filas, grumos, o soldados entre sí para formar estructuras compuestas. Estos pueden ser utilizados para el movimiento, la alimentación, o, a veces la sensación.

Clase Oligohymenophorea: 
Normalmente tienen tres membranelas y una membrana paroral en o cerca de la boca. En algunos esta última se extiende en gran medida, mientras que en otros se reduce. Tipo de vida libre se alimentan principalmente de bacterias y algas pequeñas.

Paramecium caudata:
Tienen forma de sandalia, con una ranura de alimentación prominente que va desde la parte delantera a una boca central. Son nadadores rápidos.

b2807eec-dcbf-437c-a372-116104e1564f.description: The photo doesn't show this species properly. It forms tiers of brackets usually on vertical cut surfaces of wood. If you look hard it will probably be in your garden. The small brackets have a purplish hue. This specimen was unusual because it was growing on broom stems. Microscopically it has rather  obvious balloon-shaped cells below the surface layer.

73e11a03-f19e-4d25-a214-b5676b0aae93.description: This a jelly fungus on barkless fallen logs of pine.  Superficially it looks like a Tremella but the genus Exidia is not related. Exidia tend to be firmer than Tremella. Tremella is also a parasite on other fungi and Exidia is not. Some Exidia have pimples on the surface, and this has a few scattered ones. The real distinguishing features are microscopic. Exidia has elongate spores like bannanas and Tremella are nearly spherical. There are very few species recorded from pine. Originally I thought this was E. saccharina but sequencing says it is nearer to E. japonica and I have resurrected the name E. novozealandicus for it.

67b8c736-5b15-40ca-aa8c-5226a87837e9.description:
A light microscopic image of Ditylum brightwellii (West) Grunow 1883. Class: Mediophyceae, Subclass: Lithodesmiophycidae, Order: Lithodesmidales, Family: Lithodesmiaceae.

Girdle view, showing rectangular outline. Rectangular in girdle view. The shape of the valve, in valve view, is often triangular, though other forms, such as square and circular shapes are observed. A long external process (bilabiate) extends from the centre of each valve. D. brightwellii has a delicately ornamented, continuous marginal fringe (frimbriate) that is slotted (ansulae--like a narrow handle of a cup). Chloroplasts are discoid, small and numerous, occurring when not stressed (easily plasmolysed) or in a resting state spread out along the outside edge of the cell wall. Areolae are elongated around the central area of the valve, and are noticeably larger than those areolae on the valve mantle. 

A common coastal marine diatom, not reported from polar regions. Cells are generally solitary, however they will form chains; chains are easily broken with agitation. 

D. brightwellii and D. sol are the species usually recorded although two more, D. buchanaii and D. pernodii are reported from tropical waters (von Stosch, 1986). 

Collected by net from a coastal plankton sample at Spanish Hills Wharf.

04248868-c53d-4667-bb65-96c09c130e5f.description:
Tripos fusus (Ehrenb. 1834) F. Gómez, comb. nov. (Gómez, F., 2013) 

Also currently named Ceratium fusus (Ehrenberg) Dujardin 1841, as Guiry (2020) regard it a synonym of Tripos fusus (Ehrenberg) F.Gómez (2013).

Class, Dinophyceae; Subclass, Peridiniphycidae; Order, Gonyaulacales; Family, Ceratiaceae; Genus, Tripos

Light microscopic (LM) image of the dinoflagellate Tripos fusus. 

Description: Elongated and spindle-shaped body. Both horns, apical and antapical, approximately equal length. Both horns are gradually tapering and the left horn slightly bent or straight. The right hypothecal horn is very small to an almost non-existent tooth-like form (Steidinger et al.  1997). Widest part of the cell is at the cingulum, medially located. Many yellow-brown chloroplasts. Cells are reported to be 300-600 µm long and 20-30 µm wide (Hoppenrath et al. 2009) and 200-300 µm long by 15-30 µm wide (Al-Kandari et al. 2009). Surface of cell has linear markings on the surface (Horner 2002, Steidinger et al. 1997). Bioluminescence reported. A cosmopolitan species, reported from tropical to temperate marine waters. Can form thick blooms, reported to be toxic (Guiry, 2012).

Methods: Collected by plankton net from Trincomali Channel, N 48º  56.141’, W 123º  30.706’, west side of Galiano Island, Southern Gulf Islands, British Columbia, Canada, July 14, 2005. Live image of the cell on a slide. Imaging with a Swift portable field, FM 31, phase contrast, and a Nikon CoolPix 4500 camera.

Thank you Kiyo Okuda for the boat trips on Trincomali Channel.

A very large motile colony containing between 500 and 60,000 Chlamydomonas like cells on the edge of a shell of mucilage. Phototactic.

Eucampia zodiacus Ehrenberg 1839

A live image of the marine diatom Eucampia zodiacus Ehrenberg 1839. Class, Mediophyceae; Subclass, Chaetocerotophycidae; Family, Hemiaulaceae. E. zodiacus is the type species for this genus (Guiry & Guiry 2021).

Girdle view. Only five species of Eucampia reported (Round et al., 1990,  Guiry & Guiry 2021). Cells often form flattened chains by interlocking the two short apical elevations (horns). The wide apertures between valves may be elliptical, oval, angular elliptical to square in outline. Valves are concave between the two elevations. The labiate process (rimoportulae) is centrally located on the valve. Helical-spiral chains form due to small differences in growth of the valves and girdle. Chloroplasts are round to ovoid bodies (Hendey 1964, Hasle & Syvertsen 1996, Hoppenrath 2009).
Eucampia zodiacus is a cosmopolitan marine centric diatom species, not reported from polar regions. Frequently found in plankton samples from Galiano Island, BC., Canada (Waters 1972, Shim, 1976)

Specimen from surface waters of North Cable Bay, Galiano Island, British Columbia, Canada, July 23, 2004.

86eb5e59-df43-444b-8afb-de00696772df.description:
Light micrograph of the dinoflagellate Dinophysis acuminata Claparède & Lachmann 1859. 

Phylum, Myzozoa; Class, Dinophyceae; Order, Dinophysiales; Family, Dinophysiaceae. 

A marine armoured dinoflagellate; a small species of Dinophysis, with reported cell length of 38-56 microns (Hoppenrath et al. 2009). Cells are oval to elliptical in shape and elongated. Laterally flattened (compressed). Posterior is rounded. Epitheca is much smaller than the hypotheca. The surface is covered by circular areolae each with a small pore (see SEM images). Small protuberances are sometimes present at the posterior end of the cell. The left sulcal list (flange extension of the thecal plates) is developed but narrow and of even width, extending halfway or a little beyond the midpoint of the cell. It is reported that D. acuminata has a range of morphologies, rendering its taxonomic position somewhat uncertain (Plankton*Net and Kraberg and Montagnes 2012). Theca is covered by 19 plates. Some populations are bioluminescent and may cause DSP (diarrheic shellfish poisoning in humans) toxins (okadaic acid). Is mixotrophic; has chloroplasts and is also known to be phagotrophic (uses it's peduncle to extract cell contents of the prey organism).

20 micron net collection from surface waters in Porlier Pass, between Galiano Island and Valdes Island, Southern Gulf Islands, British Columbia, Canada. Aug 5, 2012.

b68ad4c2-817d-4fa7-8354-b5e8c537a238.description: LM image of a silicoflagellate of the Dictyocha genus, species is fibula. Dictyocha is a genus with a small group of reported extant species, however thirty extant species are reported for all the three genera of silicoflagellates. Well preserved fossil record back to the Cretaceous (120 MYA). Presumed only photoautotrophic; golden-brown chloroplast. In only one of three life stages do they form a silica skeleton. Two flagella; one very small, one long. From coastal ocean plankton collected from Spanish Hill Warf, Trincomali Channel, Galiano Island, Gulf Islands, near Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada, January, 20-2005.

f1b41897-3ee8-40c6-939c-613f575ae254.description:
SEM and light micrographs images of the diatom Chaetoceros didymus Ehrenberg 1845. 

Phylum: Bacillariophycophyta, Subphylum: Bacillariophytina, Class: Mediophyceae,  Order: Chaetocerotales, Family: Chaetocerotaceae; Genus: Chaetoceros

Environmental sample. Girdle view. Cells appear rectangular in valve view and colonies are in straight chains. C. didymus has a conspicuous semi-circular protrusion in the centre of a concave aperture between valves. May have fine siliceous hairs on the valve face (EM or high magnification). Setae originate and cross each other very close to the valves, at the corners of the cells (unlike C. protuberans) and are perpendicular to the axis of the chain. The setae are four-sided, have spines and scattered poroids. There is a rimoportula centrally located on the valve with an externally tube-like structure and the valve has small poroids (Shevchenko et al. 2006). Two plate-like chloroplasts per cell. It is likely that C. didymus is a complex of taxa containing many varieties (Hasle and Syvertsen 1997 also see remarks by Jameson and Hallegraeff 2010). 

Methods:

Collected at Spanish Hills Wharf, Trincomali Channel, North Galiano Island, Southern Gulf Islands, British Columbia, Canada, January, 2006 and August 11, 2010.  Live imaging with a Leitz Dialux with darkfield condenser and SEM imaging with a Hitachi s4700 at the UBC BioImaging Facility, 2006.

Rhabdonema arcuatum (Lyngbye) Kützing 1844

Girdle view of the marine diatom Rhabdonema arcuatum  (Lyngbye) Kützing 1844. Class Bacillariophyceae
Subclass Fragilariophycidae
Order  Rhabdonematales
Family  Rhabdonemataceae (Guiry and Guiry 2021). 

A colonial diatom that forms flat ribbon-like bands, most often seen in girdle view. In valve view, elliptical to linear-lanceolate cells. Round (punctate) pores and thickened ribs (costae) on the girdle bands (Hendey 1964, Al-Yamani & Suburova 2019).

Subclass: Rhizosoleniophycidae, Order: Rhizosoleniales, Family: Rhizosoleniaceae. Guinardia delicatula forms colonies that are close set and straight chained, has indistinct bands, flat valves with slight curvature at the edges and one thin external process (use phase contrast) that is neither perpendicular nor parallel to the pervalvar axis. It has a reported length that is 3-5x the diameter (published range of 9-22 μm) of the cell (Hasle et al. 1997:163). G. delicatula cells have 2-8 large chloroplasts (Plankton Net). It is a planktonic and cosmopolitan marine diatom. Net collection from Trincomali Channel, Spanish Hill Wharf (N48˚ 59.688’, W123˚ 35.064’), Galiano Island, Southern Gulf Islands, British Columbia, Canada, surface waters, 10.0˚C water temp at surface, November 29, 2008.
Reported by Shim (1976) as Rhizosolenia delicatula in the Strait of Georgia.

Genus: Cylindrotheca Rabenhorst, 1859, nom. cons. (Guiry & Guiry 2023)

Holotype species: Cylindrotheca gerstenbergeri Rabenhorst 1859: no.81
type species: Cylindrotheca gracilis (Brébisson ex Kützing) Grunow

Taxonomic notes on the genera:

Phylum Bacillariophyta
Subphylum Bacillariophytina
Class Bacillariophyceae
Subclass Bacillariophycidae
Order Bacillariales
Family Bacillariaceae
Genus Cylindrotheca (Guiry & Guiry 2023)

Genus Characteristics:

Needle like, straight or arcuate (shaped like a bow or curved)
Frustules cylindrical, round and narrow: fusiform (tapering at both ends; spindle-shaped)
Apical ends slightly expanded (SEM and LM images, see Round et al. 1990 and personal observation)
Frustules twisted about the apical axis, so valve and girdle follow spiral course around the cell, thus rotating when in motion through sediment (The frustule of C. gracilis is highly twisted)
Very weakly silicified
Striae irregular if present
Raphe subtended by numerous thin, rib-like fibulae
Central raphe ending present or absent, raphe is continuous.
Central endings are straight and very slightly expanded
Girdle bands numerous and narrow, lightly silicified strips
Valves appear to be hyaline in LM
Plastids two (C. closterium) to many
Widely distributed in the marine epsilon of marine habitats, rarely freshwater (C. gracilis)
Only C. closterium is commonly found in the plankton
Small number of species (four), but abundant in coastal waters (Round et al. 1990: 626-627, Hasle & Syvertsen 1996: 293, Spaulding and Edlund 2008, Plinski and Witkowski 2020).
Species:

Cylindrotheca closterium (Ehrenberg) Reimann & J. C. Lewin 1964 (Guiry & Guiry 2021), previously Nitzschia closterium (Ehrenberg) W.Smith 1853 (Hendey 1964: 263, Pl. XXI, fig. 8), Basionym: Ceratoneis closterium Erhenberg.

Characteristics: Valves curved or almost straight, length 30-400 µm (100-150 µm usual range, width 2-8 µm, fibulate fine 12-37 µm) (Hasle & Syvertsen 1996: 293, Bérard-Therriault et al. 1999, Hoppenrath et al. 2009: Fig 46:p & q, Plinski and Witkowski 2020: 121-122, Guiry & Guiry 2021)

Summary:

According to Plinski and Witkowski (2020) the size and width range are similar in both C. closterium and C. gracilis, however the valves of the latter genus are spirally twisted throughout the frustule and more straight than C. closterium. Cylindrotheca closterium is cosmopolitan, planktonic and common on seaweeds, sediments (epipelic) and polar ice (Round et al. 1990, Hasle & Syvertsen 1996).

Location and file names:

Cylindrotheca closterium is common to Salish Sea coastal marine waters (Cupp 1943: 200, Fig. 153, Shim 1976: 188, Pl. 3, Fig. 7, Tynii 1986, Waters et al. 1992: 7, Maher et al. 2010).

Methods:
Collected by 60  µm plankton net from Spanish Hills Wharf, Trincomali Channel, Galiano Island, July 21, 2006.
Live specimens were imaged with a Leitz Dialux or Leitz Diavert with phase contrast or bright-field and Nikon 4500 CoolPix digital camera. Light microscopy, taxonomy and identifications by Mark Webber.

Genus: Detonula F.Schütt ex De Toni, 1894
Taxonomic Classification:

Phylum: Bacillariophyta, 
Subphylum: Bacillariophytina, 
Class: Mediophyceae, 
Order: Thalassiosirales, 
Family: Thalassiosiraceae, 
Genus: Detonula (Guiry and Guiry 2023)

Holotype species: Detonula pumila (Castracane) Gran 1900: 113

Species: 

Detonula pumila (Castracane) Gran 1900. A marine species.

Basionym is Lauderia pumila Castracane as this species was commonly placed under the genus Lauderia, which upon casual observation can look like D. pumila. Cupp (1943) called it Schroederella delicatula (H.Peragallo) Pavillard 1913 and Hasle (1973) suggested that Schroederalla be dropped for Detonula.

SEM and LM images of Salish Sea specimens:

Spanish Hills Wharf, Trincomali Channel, Galiano Isl.: SHW IX-2-Detonula pumila-July 14-2005_m01_2.jpg. Depressed centre, single central fultoportula (single strutted process) in smaller depressed well, 22.8 µm dia., ca. 10 µm pervalvar axis. marginal processes 8 in 10 µm, areolae smaller in centre than toward margin, ca. 32 areolae in 10 µm (centre), decreasing to 26 in 10 µm near margin.

Spanish Hills Wharf, Trincomali Channel, Galiano Isl: Detonula pumula-SHW-stb1-s4700-016-Nov 3-2010_2.tif: Depressed centre, single central fultoportula (single strutted process) in smaller depressed well, 31.4 µm dia., marginal processes 6 in 10 µm, areolae smaller in centre than toward margin, 28 areolae in 10 µm (centre), decreasing to 26 in 10 µm near margin.

Spanish Hills Wharf, Trincomali Channel, Galiano Isl: Detonula pumila-SHW-stb3-6-s4700-21-July 20-2008_2.tif: Depressed centre, single central fultoportula (single strutted process) in smaller depressed well, 22.3 µm dia., 18.2 µm pervalvar axis, marginal processes 6 in 10 µm, areolae smaller in centre than toward margin, 28 areolae in 10 µm (centre), decreasing to ca. 26 in 10 µm near margin.


Description:
Cylindrical cells, 16-46 µm diameter (Hoppenrath et al. 2009, Jameson et al. 2010) in girdle view non-dividing cells are square in outline. Lightly silicified (Hasle and Syvertsen 1997, Horner 2002). Tight junctions between cells and forms straight chains Hoppenrath et al. 2009, Jameson et al. 2010). Occasionally found as single cells. One (occasionally two) central fultoportula (single strutted process) that has a polysaccharide (Round et al. 1990, Horner 2002), thread (Hasle and Syvertsen 1997, Hoppenrath et al. 2009, Jameson et al. 2010) connecting one valve to the next cell; usually conspicuous (Horner 2002). 

Centre of valve is slightly depressed. The valve surface has small areolae; round near the centre and more elongate towards the margin (Round et al, 1990). Radiating costae and near the margin there is one ring of radial ribs (fultoportula), in a zig-zag pattern with flanged extensions linked to the next cell (Round et al. 1990, Hoppenrath et al. 2009). Marginal processes reported as 6-8 in 10 µm. Threads sometimes visible extending from the margin of cells (Horner 2002). A single marginal labiate process is reported (Round et al. 1990, Hasle and Syvertsen 1997). The valve surface has numerous radial bands (copulae) with ligule and numerous small areolae on the bands (Round et al. 1990). 

Discoid shaped plastids. Can be mistaken for Lauderia sp.; Lauderia does not have a valve face central process or linking thread (Round et al. 1990, Hasle and Syvertsen 1997). Reported to be a neritic species from temperate regions, sometimes forming blooms (Round et al. 1990, Hoppenrath et al. 2009, Horner 2002,). Auxospores documented, but not resting spores (Horner 2002, Hoppenrath et al. 2009).

Morphometric characteristics for three species of Detonula:

1.	D. confervacea: 6-20 µm diameter, 15-31 µm pervalvar axis, 10 marginal processes in 10 µm, 30-40 areolae in 10 µm
2.	D. pumila: 16-46 µm diameter, 15-120 µm pervalvar axis, 6-8 marginal processes in 10 µm, ca. 20 areolae in 10 µm
3.	D. moseleyana: 28-120 µm diameter, 60-212 µm pervalvar axis, 8-12 marginal processes in 10 µm, 21-28 areolae in 10 µm (Hasle and Syvertsen 1997: p. 35, Tab. 2, (Bérard-Therriault et al. 1999, Hoppenrath et al. 2009, Lee et al. 2015).

Detonula pumila has often been reported in the Salish Sea and Western Pacific waters by Cupp 1943 (Schröderella delicatula (H. Pér.) Pav.), Shim 1976:123-125, Pl. 5, 2a,b ( Schröderella delicatula (H. Pér.) Pav ), Waters et al. 1992, Horner 2000, Horner 2002, Maher et al. 2002 (Schroederella delicatula). 

Methods: Specimen collected with a 60 μm mesh plankton net, surface to 3m deep sample, from Spanish Hills Wharf (North Galiano Island Wharf, (N48˚ 59.688’, W123˚ 35.064’), Galiano Island, Southern Gulf Islands, British Columbia, Canada, July 14 2005, July 15 & 20, 2008, 2010 or March and April 2020. Isolated D. pumila cells were transferred to the Canadian Centre for the Culture of Microorganisms (CCCM) at UBC, November 2, 2010. Calcofluor White Stain from Millipore-Sigma. Lactphenol Blue from Brunel Microscope in the UK www.brunelmicroscopes.co.uk. Light micrographs: Leitz Dialux, Nikon TE300 and Nikon E800. SEM imaging with Hitachi s4700 UBC, BioImaging Facility and Hitachi s4800 UVIC AMF. Thanks go to Elaine Himphrey for SEM assitance. Collection, prep., imaging and taxonomy by Mark Webber.

9df9e0de-6147-4670-b15c-87f947b452ca.description:
Species identified:

Isthmia nervosa Kützing 1844. 

Genus: Isthmia Agardh, C.A. (1832).
Taxonomic classification:

Phylum: Bacillariophyta, 
Subphylum: Bacillariophytina, 
Class: Mediophyceae, 
Subclass: Chaetocerotophycidae, 
Order: Hemiaulales, 
Family: Isthmiaceae, 
Genus: Isthmia (Guiry & Guiry,  2020). 

Samples from the Salish Sea as part of the Salish Sea Diatom Project (imerss.org)

Genus and species Description for both I. enervis and I. nervosa:

The genus is heteropolar, where one valve is more elevated than the other. Isthmia species are found in both trapezoidal and rombhoidal forms. Valves are oval with no distinct transition from valve to mantle. Isthmia nervosa apical axis 170-240 µm long (Cupp 1943: 166). Both I. nervosa and I. enervis have only one pseudocellus per cell, a bulbous extension in which a cluster of small areolae are seen. The areolae cluster is far more pronounced in I. nervosa than I. enervis: the areolae being smaller in size in I. enervis, and the areolae suddenly reduces in size at the pole of the pseudocellus of I. nervosa. It is proposed that the pores behind the apex of the pseudocellus secrete a mucilage pad by which the cell attaches to the host, though areolae of the pseudocellus may also be involved. The costae (rib-like thickenings) are the distinctive “nerves” of I. nervosa. The cribra (plates with pores) in I. nervosa vary over the valve face unlike I. enervis where the cribra are more regular. 

Both species have a U-shaped notch on the distal end of the girdle band (copula). However, it is far less obvious in I. nervosa, but usually a distinctive feature of the epivalve of trapezoidal cells of I. enervis. Round (1984) notes that on some cells of I. enervis the girdle band notch could not be detected. I. nervosa has very prominent struts supporting the girdle diaphragm, less so for I. enervis. Isthmia, a small genus, and a coastal marine diatom are colonial, and epiphytic on seaweeds. It is both highly silicified and large relative to other diatoms. Many diatom taxonomists have placed Isthmia in the Biddulphiaceae as there are complexities to its characteristics and hard to place in the centric group (Kützing, 1844; W.Smith 1856: Plate 47 Fig. F.; Van Heurck 1880-1881: XCVI, fig. 1-3.; Hendey 1964; Round 1984; Round et al. 1990; Sims (1996); Guiry and Guiry 2020). 

Salish Sea specimens. Images: Isthmia nervosa-Gen Plank Box 009 SHW-Dec 20-2010_TM4000-H-H2O2-Aug 24-2022_Stb 5a MW_22(x250)_3.tif; SHW-Isthmia nervosa-3495-Dec 26-2010.jpg; SHW-Isthmia nervosa-3506-Dec 26-2010.jpg; SHW-Isthmia nervosa-3509_2-Dec 26-2010.jpg; SHW-Isthmia nervosa-9942-July 20-08.jpg; SHW-Isthmia nervosa-9945-July 20-08.jpg; SHW-Isthmia nervosa-9962-July 20-08.jpg.
Morphometric data: 
Frustules are heteropolar, rhomboidal or trapezodial in girdle view. Valves are ovoid without distinction or transition from valve through mantle. Apical axis 164.9-202.2 µm long, intact frustule length 251.0-333.3 µm (SHW SEM and LM specimens). Only one pseudocellus per cell with a distinctive cluster of areolae and the areolae suddenly reduce in size at the pole of the pseudocellus. Valve areolae are round, elliptical to polygonal and have complex thick cribra and simple pores penetrate the framework in various locations. Costae are robust and distinctive leading to the name of the species “nerves”. The U-shaped notch on the distal end of the girdle band is hard to detect in I. nervosa. I. nervosa has very prominent struts supporting the girdle diaphragm. Areolae in the girdle bands of I. nervosa have cribra. Forms branching colonies with large mucilage pads. Discoid chloroplasts. 

Previously reported by Shim (1976) in the Strait of Georgia, Salish Sea and Cupp (1943) for the Pacific West Coast, from San Francisco to Alaska.

Methods:

Net collection from Spanish Hills Wharf, Trincomali Channel, North Galiano Island, Southern Gulf Islands, British Columbia, Canada, July 20, 2008, December 20 and 26, 2010. Live cells imaged in 0.2 µm filtered marine water under a coverslip with either a Leitz Dialux microscope. Fixation by a final concentration of 4% formalin. Cells were prerinsed to remove salts, cleaned in 30% hydrogen peroxide at 100°C for 3 hours and rinsed many times in deionized, sterile and distilled lab grade water to a pH of 6.5-7. Cleaned frustules were pipetted onto aluminum SEM stubs and imaged with a Hitachi TM4000 Plus at the Advanced Microscope Facility (AMF), at University of Victoria (UVIC), B.C., Canada. Many thanks go to Elaine Humphrey of the Advanced Microscope Facility, University of Victoria. Collection, cleaning, preparation of stubs and slides, imaging, and taxonomy by Mark Webber (IMERSS).

e42a921d-62d9-420a-94fb-9d2064e3dd31.description:
Cerataulina pelagica (Cleve) Hendey 1937

SEM image of the centric marine diatom Cerataulina pelagica (Cleve) Hendey 1937. Class  Mediophyceae, Subclass  Chaetocerotophycidae, Order Hemiaulales, Family Hemiaulaceae, Genus Cerataulina.

In light micrographs the wing-like extensions are not very evident, however they are conspicuous in SEM images. Cells of C. pelagica have circular valves, indistinct bands, and the labiate process is central or subcentral on the valve face (the orientation of the labiate process appears to be variable between specimens (MW, GH & ES (1980)). Note the rows of areole oriented towards the process. Cells often form chains, however with SEM preparation the cells are separated.  It is a planktonic, and cosmopolitan marine diatom.

Methods:
Plankton net collection from Trincomali Channel, Southern Gulf Islands,  British Columbia, Canada, surface waters, 150m west of Spanish Hill Warf (N48˚ 59.688’, W123˚ 35.064’) Galiano Island, 4:10 pm., 16.1˚C water temp at surface,  July 11, 2008. Many thanks to Elaine Humphrey for SEM assistance (Hitachi 4700-UBC, BioImaging Facility) .

Tripos lineatus (Ehrenb. 1854) F. Gómez, comb. nov. (Gómez, F., 2013) 

Previously called Neoceratium lineatum (Ehrenberg) F. Gomez, D. Moreira & P. Lopez-Garcia 2010

Class, Dinophyceae; Subclass, Peridiniphycidae; Order, Gonyaulacales; Family, Ceratiaceae; Genus, Tripos

Light microscopic (LM) image of the dinoflagellate Tripos lineatus (taxonomic synonym of Ceratium lineatum (Ehrenberg) Cleve 1899). 

Tripos lineatus looks similar to Tripos furca (Ehrenb. 1834) F. Gómez, comb. nov., but T. lineatum is smaller, the hypotheca between the antapical horns is almost parallel to the cingulum, and the long apical horn emerges distinctively from the epitheca. The body shape is “pentagonal” (Plankton*net 2012), notably the the cingulum area is broad relative to T. furca. The two antapical horns are straight but diverge slightly, the right horn longer than the left. Many yellow-brown chloroplasts. Cells are reported to be 70-180 µm long and 25-45 µm wide (Hoppenrath et al. 2009): this cell is 209 µm long and 63 µm wide.

Methods: Collected by plankton net from Trincomali Channel, N 48º  56.141’, W 123º  30.706’, west side of Galiano Island, Southern Gulf Islands, British Columbia, Canada, January 21, 2006. Live image of the cell on a slide. Imaging with a Leitz Diavert and a Nikon CoolPix 4500 camera.

Many thanks to Dr. Mona Hoppenrath, then at the Dept. of Botany, University of British Columbia (UBC) for confirming the species in this image and taxonomic discussions. Thank you Kiyo Okuda for the boat trips on Trincomali Channel. In collaboration with Dr. Elaine Humphrey, a previous Director of the UBC Bioimaging Facility.

References:

31f3a6d9-cbcf-4127-9be7-b3e7367c8449.description: Valve outline is ovate to narrow ovate, with rounded footpole.  Apical porefield is visible on footpole.  Proximal raphe slightly deflect unilaterally. Striae are arched and radiate near the central area, becoming slightly radiate at the footpole and nearly parallel at the headpole.  Areolae are difficult to resolve, except for a distinct enlarged centermost areolae on the large striae closest to the central area. b524ed9f-0184-4997-a20e-3a44227b9f0f.description:
Scale bar = 10µm.

Valves have highly variable morphology based on size.  In larger specimens valves are elliptic with cuneately rounded apices, and the footpole has a noticeably more narrow point.  In mid-size valves the outline becomes ovate.  The smallest valves may become elleptic and nearly as wide as they are long.  Under light microscope, the only way to distinguish between S. ovalis and S. brebissonii is to look at larger valves: S. ovalis has two cuneate apices, while S. brebissonii has a cuneate footpole and a broadly rounded headpole.  Smaller valves are impossible to differentiate without SEM.  

Striae are not resolvable under light microscopy, but costae at the sternum are 17-21 per 10µm, and marginal fibulae are 4-5 per 10µm.

In this population, small valves (>35µm) were very abundant but only one specimen was found to be large enough to positively identify as S. ovalis.  It is assumed to be representative of the population.  The population's constricted dimunitive size range may be indicative of recent failure to sexually reproduce.

7df9e418-e58d-4c53-9c34-c3be0ce17f3a.description:
Scale bar = 10µm

Valves are wide elliptic to sub-circular and display significant curvature along the apical axis (concave on raphe valve, convex on rapheless valve), making it difficult to view an entire valve face in focus at once.  Frustules are monoraphid, with significant dimorphism between raphe and rapheless valves.  

Raphe valve has straight raphe with enlarged and undeflected proximal ends.  Small central area is circular to rhombic.  Striae are fine but distinctly punctate and uniseriate.  Striae are parallel at the central area and become radiate and strongly arched towards the valve margin.  Rapheless valve has coarse, elongated, and irregular striae.  Striae remain uniseriate.  

Although size ranges and autecology overlap with C. placentula, the two species may be distinguished by the hyaline ring of C. placentula or by the wider, more warped valve face of C. pediculus.

Note: On the plate the two left-most images are of the same frustule, focused through to show both the raphe and rapheless valve.

4e7a5f49-afd3-4bb9-b314-5d5894a21aef.description:
Scale bar = 10µm

In girdle view frustules are bent (image on right), so that in valve view one valve is concave and one is convex.  On the convex valve, raphe extend to the valve center, and central area is small and oval to elliptic (not pictured).  On concave valve, raphe are significantly shortened and end close to the apices; central area is absent (center image).  Striae are 12-14 per 10µm.  Internally, a pseudoseptum is present at both apices (image on left).  Apical pore field is present at footpole, and cells grow on mucilage stalks.

ece96ed7-77a1-4a97-9f03-3ffcb06dac48.description:
Scale bar = 10µm

Valves are large (93-118 µm) and sigmoid with rounded ends.  Central area is elliptical and connects parallel with raphe at each end.  Striae run in a grid pattern along the apical and transapical axes, and are equally distinct in both directions.  Striae are slightly radiate near the central area, and are otherwise strictly parallel and gridlike.  Striae density is nearly identical in both axes (18-19 per 10µm longitudinally, 20 per 10µm transverse).

d11c256f-7385-4562-91a3-8faf74078342.description: A light microscopic image of Ditylum brightwellii (T. West) Grunow 1885. Class: Mediophyceae, Subclass: Lithodesmiophycidae, Order: Lithodesmidales, Family: Lithodesmiaceae, Genus: Ditylum. Girdle view, showing rectangular outline. An environmental sample of three cells. A common coastal marine diatom, not reported from polar regions. Cells are generally solitary, however they will form chains; chains are easily broken with agitation. Width: 11-140 µm (Galiano Island observations), 208 µm recorded in culture: personal observations. Rarely accounts for a high percentage of a diatom population (e.g. as an exception it accounted for 95.8% of all diatoms on November 15, 2008 at Spanish Hill Wharf, Galiano Island, British Columbia-MW). A long external process extending from the centre of each valve. Marginal ridge of the valve is often triangular, though other forms, such as square and circular shapes are observed. Chloroplasts are discoid, small and numerous, occurring when not stressed or in a resting state spread out along the outside edge against the cell wall. D. brightwellii and D. sol are the species usually recorded although two more, D. buchanaii and D. pernodii are reported from tropical waters (von Stosch, 1986). Cells collected with a 60 micron net at Spanish Hills Wharf, North Galiano Island (N48˚ 59.688, W123˚ 35.064), Southern Gulf Islands, British Columbia, Canada. Dark-field with a Leica S8APO stereomicroscope and DigiRetna 16 MP camera.

Ditylum brightwellii (T. West) Grunow 1885.

Class: Mediophyceae, Subclass: Lithodesmiophycidae, Order: Lithodesmidales, Family: Lithodesmiaceae, Genus: Ditylum. 

SEM (Scanning Electron Microscope) images of an intact Ditylum brightwellii cell. Girdle and valve views showing triangular outline.  Environmental sample, no cleaning.  

A common coastal marine diatom, not reported from polar regions. Cells are generally solitary, however they will form chains; chains are easily broken with agitation. Width: 11-140 µm (Galiano Island observations), 208 µm in culture: personal observations. Literature reports that D. brightwellii is cosmopolitan (Horner 2002,  Hoppenrath 2009) and rarely accounts for a high percentage of a diatom population (Round et al. 1990). However, that is not the case in September through December at Spanish Hills Wharf: for example, on November 15, 2008, D. brightwellii accounted for 95.8% of all diatoms (personal observations and by counting chamber). A long external process extending from the centre of each valve. Marginal ridge of the valve is often triangular, though other forms, such as square and circular shapes are observed. Chloroplasts are discoid, small and numerous, occurring when not stressed or in a resting state spread out along the outside edge against the cell wall. D. brightwellii and D. sol are the species usually recorded although two more, D. buchanaii and D. pernodii are reported from tropical waters (von Stosch, 1986). 

Methods: Cells originally collected on November 2019 and 2021 with a 20 and 60 micron net at Spanish Hills Wharf, North Galiano Island (N48˚ 59.688, W123˚ 35.064), Southern Gulf Islands, British Columbia, Canada. Cells prepared for the SEM by Mark Webber. SEM image by Elaine Humphrey, taken with a Hitachi S4800 FE Scanning Electron Microscope (FESEM), and Hitachi TM4000, Advanced Microscope Facility (AMF), University of Victoria, B.C., Canada. 5b294306-2e86-4883-96bf-f06663ad1901.description: Just was found growing on an old baked potato that was indoors. Preparing to a website dedicated to phycomyces, several things appeared to match up. When it grew it did not touch other objects and instead girl away from them. It appears to have different growth stages with the yellow and brown/black globose tips. It's only light source would have been through blue dish soap therefore giving it a blue light to grow with theoretically. The globose sections smeared on my hand when I rubbed against them as if it were a liquid droplet or had a thin membrane separating my hand from the liquid. The stems were fairly sturdy and did not break easily as I would expect for mold. This added to my suspicion of it being fungi. I also posted in several identification groups on Facebook. Many people agreed with phycomyces. Two others suggested Mucor sp. After comparing my photos to those of the Mucor on Google, it appeared that Mucor had a much shorter stem in comparison to my specimen. Newly added photos of microscopic details at 400x rules out Phycomyces microsporus due to spore shape. Edit 7/20/2020: I think it is Phycomyces blakesleeanus based on the spore lengths.. measured 10...got 8, 10, 9, 10, 9, 10, 8, 9, 8, and 9 microns in length.

As part of some undergraduate research following my first year in college, I isolated 2 novel bacteriophages from soil samples in a rainwater basin nearby. I named this one "Conboy", and it infects Arthrobacter bacteria sp. ATCC 20122.

Species Identified:

Coscinodiscus radiatus Ehrenberg 1840

Class: Coscinodiscophyceae, Order: Coscinodiscales, Family: Coscinodiscaceae, Genus: Coscinodiscus. Image of Coscinodiscus radiatus Ehrenberg 1840. 

Cells isolated on December 15, 2009 from Trincomali Channel (TC), Spanish Hills Wharf, Galiano Island, B.C. 

Coscinodiscus radiatus:

A common coastal marine diatom, not reported from polar regions. Cells are solitary. Not abundant, but common throughout the year in our TC samples. Cells flat (coin shaped) or only slightly convex with a shallow mantle and round edge (margin) [Images 1-3]. Diameter range reported as: 13-218 µm (Hasle et al., 1986, Sancetta, 1987, Sar et al., 2010). The plastids are numerous and cocciform. Central rosette of areolae (pores), that may be indistinct, and with a hyaline area ranging from apparent to indistinct. Hyaline lines are absent (Hoppenrath et al., 2009) [Images 1, 4]. The range of areolae in 10 µm is 3.5-6 near the centre, 2-6 in the middle of the valve, and 4-8 at the valve margin [Image 1, 4]. Small rimoportulae are randomly distributed throughout the valve; they are considerably smaller than the valve areolae [Images 1, 4]. Cribra are slightly domed and covers the areolae [Images 1-3]. One ring of marginal rimoportulae [Images 1-2]: there are two macrorimoportulae with a reported angle range of between 129-145 degrees and numerous microrimoportulae 2-4 per 10 µm. Three bands comprise the cingulum  [Images 1-2]. One band has numerous small areolae along striae located on the pervalvar axis [Image 4] reported at 45-50 in 10 µm (Hasle et al., 1996, Sar et al., 2010).

Observations on Trincomali Channel samples and notes on diagnostic features:

Areolae: A central rosette of areolae (pores), that may be indistinct, and with a hyaline area ranging from apparent to indistinct. Hyaline lines are absent (Hoppenrath et al., 2009). The areolae are large for this genus—averaging 0.8 µm in diameter for the TC isolates [Images 1, 4], and generally consistent in diameter with two exceptions; 1) much smaller at the margin (Al-Yamani et al., 2009), and 2) for small cells (Sar et al., 2010). Areolae form in radial rows of decussating (intersecting) arcs. The reported range of areolae in 10 µm is 3.5-6 near the centre, 2-6 in the middle of the valve, and 4-8 at the valve margin (Hasle et al., 1986, Hasle et al., 1996, Sar et al., 2010). This matches the measurements for this isolate: 5-5.5 in 10 µm near the centre, 5-6 in the middle of the valve and 5-6 µm in 10 µm at the valve margin (equivalent to the 2009 TC isolate and clone) [Images 1, 4].

Single opening in the hyaline area: A small opening has been reported on the hyaline area of the exterior valve that does not reach into the interior (Hasle et al. 1986); not reported in Sar et al. (2010), found in one deeply cleaned 2011 TC isolate (Images 19-20); not yet found in our 2019 TC isolate and cleaned clones.

Cribra: Cribra are slightly domed and covers the areolae [Images 1-3]. The areolae have numerous small pores. Pore measurements for other TC isolates derived from SEM images range from 0.4 µm to 1 µm. Unlike C. perforatus—a species easily confused with C. radiatus (Sar et al., 2010)—C. radiatus has no subsidiary perforations around the cribrum; however, in C. radiatus there are noticeably larger poroids circling around the outside of the cribra. The 2019 TC isolate has cribra filled with a range of 86 to 98 pores: Hasle et al. (1986) has images of cribra showing a range of between 54 and 149 (our counts). Hasle et al. (1986) caution on using differences in cribra structure for Coscinodiscus identifications. However, Sar et al. (2010) consider the differences in cribra pattern important, at least for distinguishing C. radiatus from C. perforatus. These differences in Coscinodiscus species require further investigation.

Valve rimoportulae: Scattered across the valve are small rimoportulae, much smaller than the areolae, that may differ in quantity amongst cells and by size of cells (Sar et al., 2010) [Image 1]. Valve rimoportulae in the TC 2011 and 2019 isolates measured 0.3 µm in diameter and exhibit the same variability in distribution noted by Sar et al. (2010).

Marginal rimoportulae: In girdle view, the cells are distinctively coin shaped (discoid) with a narrow perivalvar axis (Hasle et al., 1996, Sar et al., 2010) with one ring of marginal rimoportulae [Images 1-3]. The marginal ring has two macrorimoportulae with a reported angle of between 129-145o (Sar et al., 2010); clone J (2019) has a range of between 124 -137 degrees. By imaging with SEM, the inner macrorimoportulae are seen to be long and tubular with slit like openings. The outer opening is indented on the mantle and is visible with LM. There are regularly spaced smaller microrimoportulae along the marginal ring also visible with a LM, 2-4 per 10 µm [Image 1] (3-4 in Hasle et al., 1986, 4-5 Hasle et al., 1996, 2-3 in Sar et al., 2010), and for this 2009 isolate, 3-4 per 10 µm [Image 1]. Though they have a similar anvil shape, these microrimoportulae are noticeably shorter than the macrorimoportulae (Hasle et al., 1996). For Clone J-2019, the former are 0.55 µm and the latter are 0.9 µm at their widest dimension. The slits of both types of rimoportulae face the same direction, away from the valve centre, though we have occasionally observed microrimoportulae turned in dissimilar orientations. Coscinodiscus radiatus rimoportulae are morphologically different and larger than for C. perforatus, including a larger external opening of the macrorimoportulae (visible with LM) (Sar et al., 2010). Macro and micro rimoportulae are a diagnostic feature for Coscinodiscus species (Hasle et al. 1986).

Cingulum: There are three bands comprising the cingulum (Hasle et al., 1986, Sar et al., 2010) [Images 1-2]. One band has numerous fine areolae along striae located on the pervalvar axis [Image 4] reported at 45-50 in 10 µm (Sar et al., 2010); the 2011 and 2019 TC isolates have 40-43 in 10 µm. 

Methods: 

Coscinodiscus radiatus cells isolated by micro-pipette from a general plankton tow with a 60 micron net at Spanish Hills Wharf, Trincomali Channel, North Galiano Island (N48˚ 59.688, W123˚ 35.064), Southern Gulf Islands, British Columbia, Canada, December 15, 2009. Cells isolated by micro-pipette and cleaned in at least three drops of sterile TC water. Transferred into HESNW growth media provided by the  Canadian Center for the Culture of Microorganisms (CCCM, culture #: SHW-Cg-01) at the University of British Columbia, Vancouver. For SEM, cells preserved with 2% Formalin and washed repeatedly with distilled water through 13 mm plastic filters to remove salts (see complete method used in iNaturalist, Galiano Island, Attheya longicornis). Filters dried and stuck onto aluminium SEM stubs. Stubs sputter coated with gold. The SEM images were taken with a Hitachi S-4700 FESEM at the UBC Bioimaging Facility, University of British Columbia, Vancouver. Many thanks to Elaine Humphrey and Derrick Horne who assisted in sample preparation and the taking the SEM images.

Images:

Image 1: SEM image. Valve view showing flat circular shaped cell. Isolated on December 15, 2009 into f/10 growth media and cloned. Gold sputter coated. SEM image taken with a Hitachi 4700 at the UBC Bioimaging Facility.

Image 1b: SEM image. Valve view showing flat circular shaped cell. Isolated on December 15, 2009 into f/10 growth media and cloned. Gold sputter coated. SEM image taken with a Hitachi 4700 at the UBC Bioimaging Facility.

Image 2: SEM (Scanning Electron Microscope) image. Valve view showing flat, coin shaped cells. Isolated on December 15, 2009 into f/10 growth media and cloned. Gold sputter coated. SEM image taken with a Hitachi 4700 at the UBC Bioimaging Facility.

Image 3: SEM (Scanning Electron Microscope) image. Valve view showing flat, coin shaped cells. Isolated on December 15, 2009 into f/10 growth media and cloned. Gold sputter coated. SEM image taken with a Hitachi 4700 at the UBC Bioimaging Facility.

Image 4: SEM (Scanning Electron Microscope) image. Inner valve view showing flat, coin shaped frustule. Isolated on December 15, 2009 into f/10 growth media and cloned. Gold sputter coated. SEM image taken with a Hitachi 4700 at the UBC Bioimaging Facility.

Tripos fusus (Ehrenb. 1834) F. Gómez, comb. nov. (Gómez, F., 2013) 

Also currently named Ceratium fusus (Ehrenberg) Dujardin 1841, as Guiry (2020) regard it a synonym of Tripos fusus (Ehrenberg) F.Gómez (2013).

Class, Dinophyceae; Subclass, Peridiniphycidae; Order, Gonyaulacales; Family, Ceratiaceae; Genus, Tripos

Light microscopic (LM) image of the dinoflagellate Tripos fusus. 

Description: Elongated and spindle-shaped body. Both horns, apical and antapical, approximately equal length. Both horns are gradually tapering and the left horn slightly bent or straight. The right hypothecal horn is very small to an almost non-existent tooth-like form (Steidinger et al.  1997). Widest part of the cell is at the cingulum, medially located. Many yellow-brown chloroplasts. Cells are reported to be 300-600 µm long and 20-30 µm wide (Hoppenrath et al. 2009) and 200-300 µm long by 15-30 µm wide (Al-Kandari et al. 2009). Surface of cell has linear markings on the surface (Horner 2002, Steidinger et al. 1997). Bioluminescence reported. A cosmopolitan species, reported from tropical to temperate marine waters. Can form thick blooms, reported to be toxic (Guiry, 2012).

Methods: Collected by plankton net from Trincomali Channel, N 48º  56.141’, W 123º  30.706’, west side of Galiano Island, Southern Gulf Islands, British Columbia, Canada, January 21, 2006. Live image of the cell in a glass bottomed culture dish. Imaging with a Leitz Diavert inverted microscope and a Nikon CoolPix 4500 camera.

Many thanks to Dr. Mona Hoppenrath, then at the Dept. of Botany, University of British Columbia for confirming the species for these images and taxonomic discussions. Thank you Kiyo Okuda for the boat trips on Trincomali Channel.

d29671b8-2e59-429c-b48a-c98aeba7b91c.description:
A ciliate that resembles an Easter egg. This one was found in a natural pond intermittently connected to the Gatineau river by a culvert.

The colourful cytoplasm consists mainly of food vacuoles containing cyanobacteria in various phases of digestion. The cytostome (cell mouth) is supported by a cytopharyngeal basket composed of stiff microtubular rods (at the anterior right, from cell's perspective). The cell has numerous spindle-shaped trichocysts, visible here as short black lines.

Species Identified:

Leptocylindrus danicus Cleve 1889

Genus: Leptocylindrus Cleve, 1889

Taxonomic classification:

Phylum Bacillariophyta
Subphylum Bacillariophytina
Class Mediophyceae
Subclass Chaetocerotophycidae
Order Chaetocerotales
Family Leptocylindraceae (Guiry and Guiry 2021)

Type species: Leptocylindrus danicus Cleve, P.T. (1889) (Guiry and Guiry 2023).

Genus Summary: Leptocylindrus frustules are cylindrical elongated cells with adjoining circular valve faces (valves appear flat, concave and convex). They are without conspicuous processes or complex ornamentations. Cells are weakly siliceous and both valve and girdle structures are not visible with light microscopy using water mounts. Both L. danicus and L. minimus have a row of small marginal projections, flap-like (triangular) spines, with smaller ones in between (“blister like markings”; Round et al. 1990) that are found between the valve face and the mantle. Just outside of the annulus is an off-center pore (only seen with SEM). Leptocylindrus commonly forms straight or very slightly curved chains Each cell has numerous small rounded plate like pale chloroplasts (unlike L. minimus that has two elongated plate-like pale chloroplasts or occasionally one chloroplast). Cell diameter for L. danicus is 5-16 μm, 2-10 x longer than wide and for L. minimus - 1.5- 6 μm and pervalvar axis 30-50 μm (Al-Kandari et al. 2009). Morphology of the resting spore can differentiate the two species (Hargraves 1990). L. danicus and L. minimus are commonly found together (Hargraves 1990). It is a planktonic and cosmopolitan marine diatom, forms blooms, though not yet reported from Arctic. AlgaeBase (2023) lists seven species that are accepted as taxonomically valid (Hendey 1964: 280, Round et al. 1990, Hasle & Syvertsen 1996, Bérard-Therriault et al. 1999, Hoppenrath et al. 2009, Jameson & Hallegraeff 2010, Nanjappa et al. 2013, Plinski and Witkowski 2020).

Characteristics: Centric

1.	Valves with radial symmetry (symmetric about a point)
2.	Joined by their valve faces thereby forming filamentous chains 
3.	Valves face convex or concave
4.	a central annulus (off centre pore) 
5.	a group of poroids
6.	Sub-central pore at times present
7.	Poroid areolae in radiating striae.
8.	Mantle curved
9.	Short triangular, often blunt flap-like processes along a ring at the margin between valve face and mantle.
10.	Copulae in the girdle consisting of elongated, nearly trapezoidal half bands, with rows of areolae along their short axis.
11.	Forms blooms
12.	Chloroplasts two or more and variable in shape
13.	formation of resting spores in vitro cultures)(Round et al. 1990, Hasle & Syvertsen 1996, Nanjappa et al. 2013). 

Species: Leptocylindrus danicus Cleve, P.T. (1889) 

References: Hustedt 1930, p. 558-560, Fig. 318-319; Cupp 1943: 78, Fig. 39; Hendey 1964: 140, Pl. 5, Fig. 2, 2a-b; Rivera et al. 2002; Nanjappa et al. 2013: 922-923, Figs. 3 A-I, 4; Hasle and Syvertsen 1997: 93, 95, Plate 14; Snoeijs & Balashova 1998: 61, Pl. 449; Bérard-Therriault et al 1999: 55, Pl. 46b; Plinski & Witkowski 2020: 45, Fig. 152

Description:
Weakly silicified cells, 5.9-7.7 (NZ) 8.7-12.4 (3–13) µm in diameter, 38 (NZ) 30-45 (22–75) µm in pervalvar length, forming short or long cylindrical filamentous chains. Chloroplasts are numerous, pale, lens-shaped or ellipsoidal distributed along the cell edge. Valves circular, either slightly convex or concave with a distinct central annulus delimiting a group of poroid areolae. Sub-central pore generally adjacent to the annulus, 0.14 (NZ) (0.06–0.13) µm diameter with a distinct silica rim. Poroid areolae 13 (NZ) (18–30 in 1 µm) arranged in radiating striae 8 (NZ) (11–16 in 1 µm), the striae run from the annulus fully across the mantle and often split into two half-way within the valve face. Proximally, the mantle curves evenly and continues almost perpendicular to the valve face distally. A circle of triangular flap-like spines, occasionally alternating with lower elevated spines are located at the margin of the valve face. Copulae elongated and nearly trapezoidal and perforated by parallel striae of round areolae which are generally in continuity with areolae of the valve face. Auxospore nearly spherical, smooth, covered with weakly silicified circular plates. Spores semi-globular, composed of two unequal valves bearing spines.

Remarks: 

Leptocylindrus danicus and L. minimus are common to occasionally rare in Salish Sea waters. They can be differentiated by light microscopy (LM) since L. danicus has a larger diameter range and the chloroplasts are numerous and lens shaped, whereas L. minimus has 1-2 elongate chloroplasts (iNat: 50302063). With LM it is possible observe the larger triangular flap-like spines located at the mantle edge. The sub-central pore is absent in L. minimus.

Leptocylindrus danicus from Porlier Pass, Galiano Island: Characteriscs: diameter range 7.2-11.7 µm and max. length 51.5 µm

Live specimens collected with a 20 µm net. Imaged live with a Leitz Dialux microscope, bright-field.

f75aff45-ac43-4451-a754-4638484fefe5.description:
The 1st and 2nd photos are enlargements of sections of the colony when first encountered, i.e, when the cells were only loosely associated.   Photos 3 through 10 capture the relatively rapid aggregation of the cells into a tight cluster; aggregation appeared near maximum within 1.5 minutes after the start of the observation.  I suspect exposure to the focused illumination from the scope somehow triggered the aggregation. 
Amazing to witness!  Interesting (and fast!) signaling biochemistry at play here! ...or is this similar to the coordinated flight of bird flocks, relying on "visual" cues?

774f29b3-3e39-44cd-b0b0-7c71d0430c9d.description:
Eucampia zodiacus Ehrenberg 1839

A live image of the marine diatom Eucampia zodiacus Ehrenberg 1839. Class, Mediophyceae; Subclass, Chaetocerotophycidae; Family, Hemiaulaceae. E. zodiacus is the type species for this genus (Guiry & Guiry 2021).

Girdle view. Only five species of Eucampia reported (Round et al., 1990,  Guiry & Guiry 2021). Cells often form flattened chains by interlocking the two short apical elevations (horns). The wide apertures between valves may be elliptical, oval, angular elliptical to square in outline. Valves are concave between the two elevations. The labiate process (rimoportulae) is centrally located on the valve. Helical-spiral chains form due to small differences in growth of the valves and girdle. Chloroplasts are round to ovoid bodies (Hendey 1964, Hasle & Syvertsen 1996, Hoppenrath 2009).

Eucampia zodiacus is a cosmopolitan marine centric diatom species, not reported from polar regions. Frequently found in plankton samples from Trincomali Channel, Galiano Island, BC., Canada (Waters 1972, Shim, 1976)

Methods:

From marine plankton collected in the Trincomali Channel, Spanish Hill Wharf, North Galiano Island, Gulf Islands, British Columbia, Canada, May 15, 2021. Live sample. Nikon TE300, 40x DIC NA 0.90.

References:

Guiry, M.D. & Guiry, G.M. 2012. AlgaeBase. World-wide electronic publication, National University of Ireland, Galway. http://www.algaebase.org; searched on 16 May 2021. 

Hasle, G.R. & Syvertsen, E.E. (1996). Marine Diatoms. In: Identifying Marine Phytoplankton. (Tomas, C.R. Eds), pp. 173-176, Plate 35, p. 175. San Diego: Academic Press.

Hendey, N.I. (1964). An introductory account of the smaller algae of British coastal waters. Part V. Bacillariophyceae (diatoms). Her Majesty’s Stationary Office, London. pp. 107. Plate VII, fig. 1.

Hoppenrath, M., Elbrachter, M., Drebes, G. (2009) Marine Phytoplankton, Selected microphytoplankton species from the North Sea around Helgoland and Sylt. Schweizerbart’sche Verlagsbunchhandlung, Stuttgart, Germany. p. 98, Figs 42 j-q.

Round, F.E. Crawford, R.M. and Mann, D.G. (1990). The Diatoms, Biology & Morphology of the Genera, pp. 262-263. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, UK.

Shim, J. H. (1976). Distribution and Taxonomy of Planktonic Marine Diatoms in the Strait of Georgia, B.C. Phd. Thesis, UBC. p. 152., p. 224 Plate II. Fig. 2.

Waters, R.E., Brown, L.N. and Robinson, M.G. (1972). Phytoplankton of Esquimalt Lagoon, British Columbia: Comparison with West Vancouver Island Coastal and Offshore Waters. Canadian Technical Report of Hydrography and Ocean Sciences. No. 37. Department of Fisheries and Oceans. p. 7,  Table 2.

Mag. 400x
The additional spines, highlighted in photos 1 & 2, make this specimen distinct from M. rotata.  The pattern and form of the spines and indentations in the semi-cells, to my eyes, most closely resembles images of M. compereana as seen here: http://www.digicodes.info/Micrasterias_compereana.html.  Another possibility is M. papillifera as seen here http://protist.i.hosei.ac.jp/PDB/Images/Chlorophyta/Micrasterias/papillifera/sp_03.html.  Both species have these additional spines.

Similar to *Stentor amethystinus* in habitat, shape and behaviour, but lacks purple pigment granules (see fourth and fifth images).

6308483e-7a64-4a90-9fb6-29a01a6d260d.description: A green species of *Dileptus* was found and described by C.G. Ehrenberg in Berlin, in 1833.  It has not been redescribed since then. The species in Ottawa's Mer Bleue Bog is a true *Dileptus*, with a macronucleus made up >50 scattered nodules (see second image).  Toxic extrusomes (Type I, per Vdacny & Foissner) are rod-shaped and 4-5 μm long (see third and fourth images). Type II extrusomes were not observed, but are probably present. The ciliate occurs throughout the summer at one location, and often blooms very abundantly in September.
6308483e-7a64-4a90-9fb6-29a01a6d260d.place_guess: Ridge Rd, Ottawa, ON K0A 2Y0, Canada

e50bf225-6b06-4843-8b3a-b04ad022b644.description:
Hypophyllous, likely on *Quercus virginiana* leaf. Long, straight chasmothecial appendages with bulbous bases – characteristic of *Phyllacytinia*.
Species ID is difficult without *Taxonomic Manual of the Erysiphales*, which is a bit pricey. *Phyllactinia alnicola* has been reported on *Q. virginiana* in Texas as *Microsphaera alni*, though longer chasmothecial appendages might be expected for that species. 
**Ascospores**
*Range*: 34.5–39.5 μm × (16.8–)17.5–21.5 μm; 1.62–2.23 μm/μm
*Average*: 36.61 μm × 19.77 μm; 1.86 μm/μm
**Asci**
*Average*: ~55 μm × 45 μm
**Conidia**
*Range*: (46–)48–51(–52.7) μm × (15.7–)18–24 μm; 2–2.6(–3.3) μm/μm
*Average*: 49.44 μm × 20.61 μm; 2.45 μm/μm
**Chasmothecia**
*Diameter Range*: 174–224 μm
*Average*: 203 μm
*Appendage Length Range*: 263–321 μm
*Average*: 299 μm
*App. Length/Diameter Range:* 1.32–1.65 μm/μm
*Average*: 1.48 μm/μm

**Images**
Scale bars 10 μm unless otherwise specified. All mounted in either LPCB or Melzer's.
1: Chasmothecia and appendages; top left and bottom right scale bars 100 μm
2-4: Habitus with appendages visible
5. Ascospores and ascus
6. Conidioma and conidia
7. Penicillate structures
8. Overzealous squash
9. Hypha and appressorium(?)
10. Sterigma-like strucutre from penicillate hyphae
11. Appressorium (?)
12. Underside of leaf.
13. More habitus.

6a3e8eaf-acf2-4c90-ac5b-a33187ed1cd2.description:
Hypophyllous on *Modiola caroliniana*. Not easily confusable due to the host; microscopy matches literature anyway. Both teliospores and basidiospores highly variable in size and shape. 

**Measurements**
*Teliospores*
37–80 × 10–21 μm 
*Teliospores in literature*
45–87.5 × 8.0–17.0 µm ([Albu *et al.* 2019](https://doi.org/10.1094/PDIS-02-19-0303-PDN))
31–81(–95) × 10.5–20 (–25) µm ([Aime & Abbasi 2018](https://doi.org/10.3897/mycokeys.39.27378))
*Basidiospores*
9–12.5(–17.8) × 6–9(–10.5) μm 

**Images**
All slides in LPCB, scale bar 100 μm for image 1, 50 μm for image 3, 10 μm otherwise.
1: Cross section of telium, teliospores visible on lower surface
2: Epiphyllous habit
3: Various teliospores
4: Sterigmata, two with attached basidiospores
5: Spent sterigmata
6: Promycelia/metabasidia in various stages of growth from teliospores
7: Basidiospores
8: Notched teliospore apex
9: Hypophyllous spermogonium
10: Early or broken teliospore germ tube
11: Additional habit

Mag. 400
D. archeri?, though I'm confused by the presence of two cell types.  The larger, cyst-like cells appear to be intimately associated with the colony, but do they derive from D. archeri (cysts for long term survival?) or are they parasitic or epiphytic cells exploiting the Diplophrys colony?  I could not find a literature reference regarding the ability of D. archeri to form cysts.
The first 3 images provide a close-up view.  Images 4 - 9 were taken periodically over a ~9 minute interval as the colony consolidated.  The YouTube video spans this same time interval (5, ~15 second videos catenated in a single video): https://youtu.be/ZJ2OV10jLvU.

048ae168-f6d6-41e3-8cb6-6edf9f5b3f0c.description:
Epiphyllous on *Quercus nigra*, creating a dense mat of mycelium. Around 5 or 6 asci per chasmothecium and 6 spores per ascus. Due to the length of the chasmothecial appendages, this should be *Erysiphe extensa* var. *curta* (shorter appendages than *E. extensa* var. *extensa*, but still much longer than the otherwise similar [*E. abbreviata*](https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/101560874)).

**Measurements**
*Ascospores*
22–28.5 × 10.7–13.5 μm
*Asci*
50–70 × 34–43 μm
*Chasmothecial Diameter*
(85–)94–119 μm
*Chasmothecial Appendage to Diameter Ratio*
1.9–2.6
*Chasmothecial Appendage Count*
6–9 (maybe more, many were broken off)

**Description from Literature**
> Mycelium usually epiphyllous, persistent, thin films on the whole surface of leaves, cleistothecia (80–)90–170 μm in Diam., 5–20 appendages, 1–2.5 times as long as the cleistothecial diameter, 3–10 asci, 45–65 × 35–50 μm, 3–8, usually 4–6 spored, 18–28 × 11–18 μm  
 
U. Braun, Mycotaxon 15: 130 (1982).

Gemmule spicule (aka, gemmulosclere) of a freshwater sponge; a single specimen was photographed at different focal planes. 6f1e543d-e05e-4c5d-91b4-9be46538254c.description:
Mag. 100x (1), 400x (2,3)
Dead, empty cell of a relatively large Closterium (375µ x 30µ; L/W = 12.5).  The photos correspond very well with reference images found here http://www.digicodes.info/Closterium_rostratum.html#2011012001.  It is interesting to note that the older semi-cell is much more deeply stained by iron containing compounds such as iron oxide; accounting for the rust-brown color of the longitudinal striations.  (as described here http://cfb.unh.edu/phycokey/Choices/Charophyceae/Desmids/desmid_unicells/placoderms/CLOSTERIUM/Closterium_Image_page.html) The striations, though much less pronounced, are still visible in the younger semi-cell (last photo).  I would love to know if the time-dependent accumulation of iron compounds in the cell wall is active (i.e, energy driven with some resulting benefit) or passive (a byproduct of cell wall chemistry and its ability to snag iron compounds from the water).  What do Closterium need with a Faraday cage!? :o) ...Whatever the reason, it makes the dead cells attractive in their own right!
- A pond edge water sample (freshwater) was taken on 3/6/2022 using a 10 micron dip net to enrich for microorganisms. Air temp. 41C. Sampling area was at the inflow of a small brook that feeds the pond and was ice-free. The pond was predominantly ice covered.

b664985e-3834-42f3-80bc-342f334d98af.description:
Mag. 400x
This is the 3rd, fresh-waterbody in our small town where D. archeri was found.  Initially, the colony formed a single crescent of sluggishly moving cells (photo 1), which separated into 2 independent colonies  that moved well beyond the visible length of their filopodia (photo 2 composite)... a separation of >5 filopodia-lengths :o)... the separated colonies could not be viewed in the same 400x objective field!  I wish I could of hung out to see if the 2 clusters of cells would find each other and reunite (hoping to witness a chemotactic event!)  For a video of the colony before the separation see https://youtu.be/7q87exxS2aY.
- A pond edge water sample (freshwater) was taken on 3/6/2022 using a 10 micron dip net to enrich for microorganisms. Air temp. 41C. Sampling area was at the inflow of a small brook that feeds the pond and was ice-free. The pond was predominantly ice covered.

3168872d-9fbc-4964-b0e0-568ce2db241e.description:
When I first posted this observation, the species had no name and had only been found at one location, a rain-fed bog lake in Ottawa. Since then, I found the species at two sites in Chisasibi, on the the coast of James Bay.  And, with the help of Ferry Siemensma and Michaela Strueder-Kypke, I published a formal description of the species, *Arcella prismatica* Taylor, Strueder-Kypke, Siemensma, 2025.

A full description of the species can be seen on Ferry's site: https://arcella.nl/arcella-prismatica/

289b79b5-1563-4c4e-95bf-0aa43b921480.description:
Found in Rock pigeon (C. livia) and identified at Pelican Harbor Sea Bird Station. Commonly causes a disease called Trichomoniasis which leads to cankers in Columbiformes species. 

The protozoa can easily be detected by the wiggling motion in which they move and by the multiple flagella they use to move. Wish I could post a video to show it better but photo will have to do. 

Note: As per law, PHSS does not take in or treat nonnative species including the one that this was found in. That bird was released back by the individual that brought them in.

Mag. 400x
*Coelastum*, but uncertain regarding the species. The cell-cell connections/junctions are visible.  Optical phenomenology: what appear to be extracellular, purple droplets adjacent to some cell junctions are actually (I think!) unobstructed channels penetrating the coenobium. White light passing through these tiny channels is diffracted; the least diffracted (therefore eventually seen at the eyepiece) will be blue and violet light, while the redder (longer) wavelengths will be most diffracted and out of the visual path to the eyepiece....  Seems like a viable explanation for the purple lights. Yes?

b82beb9b-9801-44a4-b85f-3f8bcefa50e7.description: A pregnant rotifer! I got this sample from the bottom of a lake near the shore. After four days I put the rotifer under the microscope. The stomach indicates that it belongs to the family *Philodinidae*. Because it has four toes, is viviparous, has long and distinctive spurs and did not seem that malleable, I come to the conclusion that this individual belongs to the genus *Dissotrocha*. The problem with the genus is that the integument would have more detail like epidermal pores but this is not visible in this individual. This might be due to the lack of image contrast. Despite that I uploaded one image where I tried to focus on the integument. As I could not make out any humps or spikes on its trunk and the spurs are not that long I am sure that this is *D. macrostyla*.

432479a8-db8b-491c-b01c-1a859bd66cef.description:
Mag. 400x (1), 100x (2)
Not certain of the ID, *P ehrenbergii*, as seen here https://www.algaebase.org/search/images/detail/?img_id=19450. Specimen is long, relatively narrow (~325µ x 15µ). Possesses apical vacuoles containing crystals like Closterium.  The size and shape might suggest *Docidium baculum*, but the semi-cell junction at the isthmus lacks any hint of a crenulated surface https://www.desmids.nl/maand/english/docidium_baculum.html.  I could not determine whether Docidium species have apical, crystal-containing vacuoles.
- A water sample was taken on 09/13/2022 from the shore of Long Pond using a 10µ dip net to enrich for microbes. Air temp. 71°F. (Sample was stored at room temperature and assayed again on 10/1/2022.)

c57af46b-4355-40f4-86af-32aa3ad28e92.description:
Stephanopogon apogon including giant forms from the near shore benthos of a  marine channel connecting Gardiner's Bay and Three Mile Harbor. 

The first one I found was a giant at 125 um, much larger than most of the bloom at 30 to 75 um. I watched as it ingested a diatom and proceeded to go spastic twitching and adhering its mouth to the slide. I realized that smaller individuals were blooming and gathering nearer the edge of the slide.  
I also observed a strange form of conjugation or some other phenomenon.

I sent some pics to my friends Ivan Čepička and Bill Bourland in Prague who informed me that I had a treasure trove of an amazing organism: Stephanopogon.  I am sending them samples for molecular phylogenetic analyses. 

 Stephanopogon closely resembles certain ciliates and was originally classified with them ([1], but is now considered related to heterolobosean flagellates. The cell is somewhat flattened, with multiple smooth flagella arranged in rows running from the front to the back, and has an anterior mouth supported by rods. They feed on bacteria, diatoms, and other smaller organisms. There are 2-16 nuclei, but they are not differentiated into macronuclei and micronuclei as occurs in ciliates. They have a cosmopolitan distribution.

Because nuclear dimorphism is absent, Stephanopogon had been regarded as an evolutionary intermediate between the ciliates and other protozoa, and possibly an ancestor of the animals as well. Corliss and Lipscomb showed that it is not cytologically similar to ciliates, lacking their complex pellicle and infraciliature.[2] Further electron microscopical studies added details to the understanding of the cytological organization of Stephanopogon.[3][4] Yubuki and Leander demonstrated that Stephanopogon is closely related to Percolomonas within the Heterolobosea. The bases of the flagella in both genera are attached to an electron dense cytoskeletal material,[5] but it has been argued that this is not an apomorphy of the clade [6]

It has recently been included as a heterolosean in the class Percolatea, along with Percolomonas.

d979b593-868a-4ead-83b0-9474a529ab19.description:
Cryptopharynx mauritanicus Dragesco 1965. 

From near shore  benthos of the beach at Lion Head Marina on estuary Hog Creek.  I have found and posted (on Facebook) this ciliate previously from other local estuaries but post the latest finding due to its rarity and obscurity and the new location. My measurement of this individual exactly matches Dragesco's description of 110 micrometers.  

Cryptopharynx mauritanicus was first described by Dragesco in 1965  in the fine sands of the Mauritanian beaches (near Port-Etienne).    
There have been no further studies since Dragesco's original description. 

The following is paraphrased from Dragesco's 1965 description in his survey of North African benthic ciliates.  Unfortunately, its scarcity and the inability to make cytology preparations made  the observations somewhat incomplete. Of medium size (L = 110 micrometers), C. mauritanicus shows a certain variability in shape. It is generally a flattened and asymmetrical animal: the right (ventral) side only is ciliated,  flat and very thigmotactic, while the left side (dorsal)  is rather rounded and not ciliated. The mouth is lateral and has a structure very similar to that of Cryptopharynx setigerum Kahl which is the type species for the genus: a spiral oral apparatus rises on the apical side, then turns to the left by more than 360 ° and finally limits a small circular mouth opening, which seems to continue with a outline of pharynx. Long and thick cilia adorn this oral apparatus. 

 Cryptopharynx mauritanicus  has marginal and "dorsal" ornamentation, in fact arranged on the left side which is unciliated. But, in the case which concerns us, this ornamentation presents a curious duality: on all the periphery of the cell and, partially also on the left unciliated side, one notices a great quantity of small cuticular finger-like expansions. In addition, on the entire convex part of the left face, grains of sand adhere to the cuticle through a colorless "mucus".  C. mauritanicus is further characterized by its pulverized macronucleus, made up of some 50 to 70 spheroidal elements, of small size (0 = 3 to 4 i). We have not seen any micronucleus (note,Moreover, that some species of Cryptopharynx seem to lack it).

Brown, shuttle-shaped protrichocysts can be seen, both between the kineties  and on the non-ciliated face. C. mauritanicus is distinguished from other species of the genus by its pulverized nuclear apparatus, the large number of kineties and its double ornamentation of finger-like papillae and grains of sand.

Imaged in Nomarski DIC using Olympus BH2S under SPlan 40x objective plus variable phone cropping on Samsung Galaxy S9+. I also include the sample site and Dragesco's original 1965 drawing.

3b6af396-f7f0-4175-be9b-b2a95b7d49aa.description:
Oncosonderia tubiglia- a sonderiid ciliate from the near-shore benthos of marine estuary Accabonac Harbor. The individual measures 200 um and is imaged in Nomarski DIC using Olympus BH2S under SPlan 40x objective plus variable phone cropping on Samsung Galaxy S9 +. 


The family Sonderiidae includes the genera Sonderia, Sonderiella, Oncosonderia, and Parasonderia (Xu,Shao, Miao, and Song 2013). 

The following is adapted from Modeo et al  Morphology, ultrastructure, and molecular phylogeny of the ciliate Sonderia vorax with insights into the systematics of order Plagiopylida doi: 10.1186/1471-2180-13-40. 

"The genus Sonderia was established by Kahl in 1928 for ciliates collected from Oldesloe salt marshes (Hamburg region, Germany) and later on from the Island of Sylt (North Sea, Germany). These interesting ciliates are ubiquitous and common in the sapropelic environment of salt marshes and in ecologically similar brackish water sites with oxygen deficiency.

Within the genus Sonderia quite conspicuous, ovoid-ellipsoid ciliates are included. These are dorsoventrally flattened, uniformly ciliated, and show a conical, subapical oral cavity. The cell length of genus representatives varies, according to the species, from 80 to 250 μm. Their surface is covered by a distinctive layer of bacteria organized in parallel along the host body axis and plunged in a gelatinous coating between kineties. From a few to numerous long, needle-shaped extrusomes are present in the cortex. Oral kineties extend from somatic ones, both organized as monokinetids, and run perpendicularly to the upper and lower lips of the oral cavity opening. A transversely striated band arises near the right margin of the oral cleft and dorsolaterally runs down".
