e0c27697-b882-4d10-9326-212f968f3a86.description:
Lac Gilbert is a headwater lake in a valley, which protects it from the wind. It has a relatively deep hole (12 m) at one end that allows the bottom water to go anoxic over the course of the summer. The stability of the water column means that distinct bands of different communities develop in layers in the water, and also on the sediments. For instance, above the anaerobic zone that starts at 9 m depth, there is a band of Hydra on the sediments that feeds on migrating zooplankton.
The surface water is pristine and low in nutrients, so phytoplankton abundance is low, allowing light to penetrate deep into the lake. Photosynthetic pigments increase greatly in the anoxic layer, where large populations of anoxygenic photosynthetic bacteria appear. Just above the oxygen-free zone, the sediments develop a dense mat of spiral cyanobacteria, *Arthrospira jenneri*. Their identity is given away by the thickness of the filament relative to coil length. *A. jenneri*, like all cyanobacteria, is facultatively anaerobic. That means it can grow in a zone that is bathed in the nutrients released by anaerobic processes.
These are images from both the water column and the sediment mat.  Some are transmitted light and some are by epifluorescence. Some are unstained and some are stained with a fluorescent dye (DAPI) that makes nucleic acids fluoresce light blue. *Arthrospira* is blue-green by transmitted light, and red by epifluorescence. The red of epifluorescence signals the presence of chlorophyll. Sediment samples will have bright yellow particles. These are granules of polyphosphate that are stored by bacteria and that glow yellow when stained by DAPI. The deep water column samples, without DAPI, contain cyanobacteria, and also photosythetic picoplankton (red dots) that are probably photosynthetic bacteria.
The filament labelled *Oscillatoria* in one of the photos is orange because it contains a fluorescent auxiliary pigment, phycoerythrin. It might be another member of the Oscillatoriales, maybe *Planktothrix*, but there is no large Planktothrix layer in the lake.

58763205-efb1-48fa-b439-2581ef5b1b29.description:
Cantina marsupialis (J.Larsen & D.J.Patterson) Pánek, A.Yabuki, Čepička, Takishita, Y.Inagaki & B.S.Leander 2015, a microaerophilic stramenopile flagellate from a biofilm that formed on a sample of the coarse sand intertidal benthos of marine estuary Acabonac Harbor at Louse Point launching ramp imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100x oil objective with oiled condenser. 

The cells measure from 6 up to 12 um.  The species was originally described as Cafeteria marsupialis by Larsen and Patterson 1990 (1) from Queensland Australia and Rio de Janiero Brazil.  In 2015, Yubuki et al (2), in the first study to include cultures, ultrastructural data and DNA sequences for the species, erected the genus Cantina designating Cafeteria marsupialis as the type species for the new genus after showing that the molecular phylogenetic position of three different “C. marsupialis” isolates was not closely related to the type species of Cafeteria.  We can clearly see all of the described features (1,2) including the beating anterior flagellum creating currents which draw bacteria into the furrow. 

"Cafeteria marsupialis Larsen and Patterson, sp. nov. Diagnosis. Cells 5-15 um(usually 7-10 um) long, both flagella about 10 um. Ventral face of body with a distinct furrow, the attachment flagellum extending along this, and directly behind the cell to attach to the substrate. Description. D-shaped cell body, 5-15 um long, mostly 7-10 um, laterally flattened, some cells greatly distorted. Dorsal face convex, ventral face fiat or concave, with a groove giving the cell the appearance of a pouch (hence the name); with the left face of the cell extending slightly further forward than the other. Two flagella; anterior flagellum 7-10um long, when feeding it extends directly away (normal to) from the furrow and has an asymmetric beat envelope. When swimming, the cell moves jerkily and the anterior flagellum has a more symmetric beat envelope and projects in front of the cell. The posterior flagellum is about 10um long, lies in the furrow, and projects behind the cell with the tip usually attached to the substrate, so that the cell has an aspect of 'standing' on the substratum on a stalk; the posterior flagellum trails behind in swimming cells. Bacteria are drawn into the furrow by the water current created by the anterior flagellum, they enter the cell from the rearmost part of the furrow via a channel which curves towards the dorsal side of the cell.  Remarks. The arrangement and beat pattern of the flagella resembles that of other species in the genus. This species is distinctive because of the furrowing of the ventral surface of the body" (1).

"Cantina marsupialis (NY0206) is a microaerophilic stramenopile with D-shaped cells that are 7.23–12.1 um long (average: 8.55 um, n = 30) and 5.03–9.13 um wide (average: 6.24 um, n = 30).  A lorica is not present. Cells swim with one flagellum oriented forward and one flagellum trailing behind. When attaching to the substrate with the posterior flagellum, the cells beat the anterior flagellum laterally. The anterior flagellum is about 1.5 times longer than the cell length; the posterior flagellum is about 1.2–1.5 times longer than the cell length. Bacteria are ingested within a deep ventral groove. The food vacuoles are located on the middle to posterior part of the cell" (2).

"Cantina gen. nov Diagnosis. Stramenopiles with D-shaped cells possessing a large groove on the ventral side and two flagella; one oriented anteriorly and one oriented posteriorly. Mitochondria with a few tubular cristae. Microaerophilic, living in marine sediments. Type species. Cafeteria marsupialis Larsen and Patterson 1990 (=Cantina marsupialis comb. nov.). Etymology. “Cantina” refers to the English word “canteen”, which has a similar meaning to the previous genus name Cafeteria. Gender feminine" (2). 

1.  Some flagellates (Protista) from tropical marine sediments JACOB LARSEN and  DAVID J. PATTERSON.   JOURNAL OF NATURAL HISTORY, 1990, 24, 801-937 

2.  Morphological Identities of Two Different Marine Stramenopile Environmental Sequence Clades: Bicosoeca kenaiensis (Hilliard, 1971) and Cantina marsupialis (Larsen and Patterson, 1990) gen. nov., comb. nov. Naoji Yubuki, Tomáš Pánek, Akinori Yabuki, Ivan Čepička, Kiyotaka Takishita, Yuji Inagaki, Brian S. Leander.  Journal of Eukaryotic Microbiology 2015, 0, 1–11

83c754ab-3294-4a37-8157-225bef0a4a09.description:
Species identified:

Bacillaria paradoxa J.F.Gmelin

Genus: Bacillaria Gmelin, J.F. (1791)

Holotype species: Bacillaria paradoxa J.F.Gmelin, nom. illeg. 1791: 3903

Taxonomic classification:

Phylum Bacillariophyta
Subphylum Bacillariophytina
Class Bacillariophyceae
Subclass Bacillariophycidae
Order Bacillariales
Family Bacillariaceae 
Genus: Bacillaria (Guiry and Guiry 2023)

Summary:

Bacillaria species are found in marine, brackish and occasionally high conductivity waters. Commonly occurring in coastal plankton, it is assumed to be carried from sediments and other substrates. It was O. F. Muller in 1786 that named the first diatom species, Vibrio paxillifer which was the basis for the type of the first diatom genus described, Bacillaria Gmelin (1791), one of Muller’s animalcula infusoria. Live cells form a unique moving colony whereby individual cells slide back and forth to each other. Shape is linear or linear-lanceolate. Valve face is relatively flat, with very shallow mantles. Apices are slightly rostrate, cuneate or capitate. The striae are distinct and relatively coarse. Striae usually uniserate, more occasionally biseriate. Areolae are round poroids covered by hymenes. Chloroplasts most often two, one near each apex. Bacillaria species have a centrally located raphe within a raised keel along the apical axis, whereas in contrast, Nitzschia has an excentrically located raphe and keel on opposite sides of the frustule (Round et al. 1990, (https://diatoms.org/genera/bacillaria ; https://diatoms.org/morphology/nitzschioid )

Genus Characteristics:

1)	In valve view, linear or linear-lanceolate, with pointed, rounded, cuneate to slightly rostrate apices.
2)	Striae transverse, parallel, usually uniseriate or occasionally biseriate, appearing in LM as simple lines.
3)	Areolae are round poroids, vela exterior.
4)	Raphe is centrally located, continuous along the whole apical axis and slightly keeled, fibulate. 
5)	Raphe sternum often with ridge on one side of raphe externally. 
6)	Fibulae simple, rib-like, arching into the valve, linked longitudinally by ridges.
7)	External polar endings pore like, T-shaped or with hooked terminal fissures.
8)	Girdle bands open. 
9)	Usually two chloroplasts, rarely four, one towards each apice. The central gap between them is where the nucleus lies.
10)	Cells form motile colonies, sometimes linked by interlocking ridges and grooves on the raphe sternum, cells moving along each other (Round et al. 1990, Hasle and Syvertsen, 1997, Jahn and Schmid 2007, Spaulding et al. 2001, Mann et al. 2023)

Species identified:
 
Bacillaria paxillifera (O.F.Müller) T.Marsson 1901: 254 (as 'paxillifer')
Linear, tapering near the valve ends to rostrate apices. Apices of the apical axis are almost identical in morphology and relatively bilaterally symmetrical. Length 60-170 μm, width 4-8 μm. Striae: parallel, 20-25 in 10 μm. The raphe is located approximately in the valve centre, fibulae are unevenly spaced, 5-9 in 10 μm. The raphe is continuous from pole to pole and ends in a t-shaped groove at the apices, internally in a deflected helictoglossa. Striae uniseriate, areolae are poroid and occluded by hymenes type velum. A ridge is on one side of the raphe. Small spines can be visible on the valve margin. Forms motile colonies (Sims et al. 1996, Hasle and Syvertsen, 1997, Witkowski et al. 2000, Jahn & Schmid 2007, Plinski and Witkowski 2020,  Guiry and Guiry 2023, Mann et al. 2023). 

Occassionally found on Z. marina at Montague Harbour Marine Provincial Park (MHMPP), Galiano Island. Collected July 20, 2020, Aug 4, 2020 (SEMs), March 7, 2021 (SEMs & LMs) and November 15, 2020 (LM). Characteristics: Length 78.0-83 µm, width 5.8-7 µm, striae coarse and uniseriate, striae 19-21 in 10 µm, fibulae unevenly spaced 6-8 in 10 µm, raphe is central and extends along the apical axis.

Bacillaria paxillifera has previously reported from the Salish Sea by Cupp 1943 (as Nitzschia paradoxa (Gmelin) Grunow, Shim (1976: 183, Pl. 24, fig. 5., Tynii 1986, McQuoid and Hobson 2001).

Collected by brushing or scrapping leaf sections of Z. marina from MHMPP, August 3, 2020, October 16, 2020, March 7, 2021 and July 2021. Taxonomic classification:

Phylum Bacillariophyta

Class Bacillariophyceae

Order Bacillariales
Family Bacillariaceae

Genus Summary:

Bacillaria species are found in marine, brackish and occasionally high conductivity waters. Commonly occurring in coastal plankton, it is assumed to be carried from sediments and other substrates. It was O. F. Muller in 1786 that named the first diatom species, Vibrio paxillifer which was the basis for the type of the first diatom genus described, Bacillaria Gmelin (1791), one of Muller’s animalcula infusoria. Live cells form a unique moving colony whereby individual cells slide back and forth to each other. Shape is linear or linear-lanceolate. Valve face is relatively flat, with very shallow mantles. Apices are slightly rostrate, cuneate or capitate. The striae are distinct and relatively coarse. Striae usually uniserate, more occasionally biseriate. Areolae are round poroids covered by hymenes. Chloroplasts most often two, one near each apex. Bacillaria species have a centrally located raphe within a raised keel along the apical axis, whereas in contrast, Nitzschia has an excentrically located raphe and keel on opposite sides of the frustule (Round et al. 1990, (https://diatoms.org/genera/bacillaria ; https://diatoms.org/morphology/nitzschioid )

Genus Characteristics:

1)	In valve view, linear or linear-lanceolate, with pointed, rounded, cuneate to slightly rostrate apices.
2)	Striae transverse, parallel, usually uniseriate or occasionally biseriate, appearing in LM as simple lines.
3)	Areolae are round poroids, vela exterior.
4)	Raphe is centrally located, continuous along the whole apical axis and slightly keeled, fibulate. 
5)	Raphe sternum often with ridge on one side of raphe externally. 
6)	Fibulae simple, rib-like, arching into the valve, linked longitudinally by ridges.
7)	External polar endings pore like, T-shaped or with hooked terminal fissures.
8)	Girdle bands open. 
9)	Usually two chloroplasts, rarely four, one towards each apice. The central gap between them is where the nucleus lies.
10)	Cells form motile colonies, sometimes linked by interlocking ridges and grooves on the raphe sternum, cells moving along each other (Round et al. 1990, Hasle and Syvertsen, 1997, Jahn and Schmid 2007, Spaulding et al. 2001, Mann et al. 2023)

Genus: Licmophora C. Agardh (1827) nom. et typ. Cons.

Found on Z. marina. Collected at Montague Harbour Marine Provincial park (MHMPP). Collected Aug. 4, 2020, Collected November 15, 2020, March 7, 2021 and July 2021 (LM and SEM).

Taxonomic classification:

Phylum:	Heterokontophyta
Subphylum:	 Bacillariophytina
Class:	 Bacillariophyceae
Subclass:	 Fragilariophycidae
Order:	 Licmophorales
Family: Licmophoraceae
Genus:		Licmophora (Guiry and Guiry 2023)

Holotype species, synonym(s), etc.: Licmophora argentescens C.Agardh

Summary:

Licmophora is an araphid genus. Species in the genus are cosmopolitan, found in most marine habitats including Arctic, Antarctic, and tropical regions. Cells grow in colonies, often fan shaped on branched mucilaginous stalks or pads, attached to various substrates such as seaweeds, rocks, animals or detached and found singly in the plankton. Frustules are heteropolar. They have a narrow base (sometimes slightly capitate) and broader apex and in valve and girdle view the cell is cuneate (wedge shaped). The valves have a narrow, sometimes indistinct central sternum. Septa present, distinct or indistinct (Plinski and Witkowski 2020), internally around the apical ends and tapering off down each side of the copulae. The areolae are round or elongate and externally covered by a criba. The striae are transapical, uniseriate and parallel, except at the apices where they can become radiate. A rimoportula is present on one valve at the base and on the other valve, or both valves, at the apex. External rimoportula is a circular slit like opening, whereas the internal rimoportula opening is labiate, fan shaped, sometimes stalked and flush with the frustule. Normally, there are two or three rimoportulae per cell. If 2 rimoportulae per frustule, then, one is located at the basal apex, the other at the head apex. If 3 rimoportulae, one is located at the basal apex, one at the head apex of each valve. A series of slits (multiscissura) is present around the base of both valves where mucilage for stalks and pads is secreted. Spines are present at the head apex of some species. Plastids numerous and small. There are five distinguishable girdle bands. Areolae on the copulae (girdle bands) are smaller than those on the valve. Valvocopulae open at the basal apex and maybe a septum at the apex. Relying on identification of species by light microscopy may be problematic due to fine features; SEM and TEM are utilized. AlgaeBase lists 102 accepted species and 10 varieties (Honeywill 1988, Round et al. 1990, Lobhan 2013, Lobhan et al. 2018, Plinski and Witkowski 2020: 56, Spaulding et al. 2021, Guiry and Guiry 2023).

Description of: Licmophora paradoxa (Lyngbye) C. Agardh 1828: 32. Due to the high striae count at both poles, it is likely this specimen is Licmophora tincta (C.Agardh) Grunow 1868: 35, syn. Licmophora_paradoxa var. tincta (Ag.) Hust. It is very similar to L. paradoxa, however the species has higher striae at 33 in 10 µm (Proshkina-Lavrenko 1950: 20, Pl. 6, fig. 11a. b.). Characteristics: distinct septa, 30-140 µm long, 7-18 µm width, sternum distinct, transapical striae fine 23-32 in 10 µm at the basal pole, 27-30 in 10 µm at the head pole. Elongate areolae
near the sternum. (Agardh 1828: 32 (no measurements given), Proshkina-Lavrenko 1950: 20, Pl. 6, fig. 11a. b., Hendey 1964: 168, Sims et. al. 1996: Pl. 123, fig. 3, Honeywill 1998: 239, Witkowski et al. 2000: 67). 

Image files: Licmophora paradoxa_Zm MHMPP-Mar 7-2021 En Box 9-leaf 6-16P overview-TM4000 MW (Feb 22-2022) Licmophora_4(x1.0k)_2.tif; Licmophora cf. paradoxa on ZM MHMPP-T56 9M_B H2O2-TM4000-(MQ-July 29-2021_13 (x1.2k)_2.tif: Characteristics: 50 µm long, 10.9 µm wide, sternum distinct, striae fine: 29 striae in 10 µm in mid. valve, 30 striae in 10 µm at basal pole and 34 striae in 10 µm at head pole, Elongate areolae
near the sternum. Small spine evident at head pole.

Previously reported by Shim (1976) as Licmophora paradoxa (Lyngbye) C. Agardh.

Licmophora species have previously been reported in the Salish Sea and Western Pacific waters. From historic records, four species and one variety of Licmophora have been documented: 

1.	Licmophora abbreviata C.Agardh 1831: 42: 20-110 µm long, 4-8 µm wide, striae at the base of valve 11-12 in 10 µm, in the upper part 14-16 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020) 
2.	L. gracilis (Ehr.) Grun: 40-110 µm long, 10-16 µm wide, striae 20-22 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020)
3.	L. ehrenbergii (Kützing) Grunow 1867: 36: 60-180 µm long, 15-30 µm wide, striae evenly distributed throughout the valve, striae 8-11 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020)  
4.	L. ehrenbergii  f. grunowii (Mereschk.) Hust.
5.	L. paradoxa (Lyngb.) Agardh.: 30-100 µm long, 7-13 µm wide, striate delicate, striae at the foot pole 23-25 in 10 µm, in the head pole 27-30 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020).

Collected by brushing or scrapping leaf sections of Z. marina from MHMPP, August 3, 2020, October 16, 2020, March 7, 2021 and July 2021. e935fde7-d444-43d0-b4af-9420ad8887c9.description:
Kipferlia bialata Kolisko et al 2010  syn Carpediemonas bialata Lee and Patterson 2000, a  Carpediemonas-like organism (CLO), from a biofilm that formed 5 days after sampling the fine sand sulfidic intertidal benthos of marine estuary Acabonac Harbor at Landing Lane. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlanapo 40 0.95 objective and SPlan 100 1.25 oil objective without oiled condenser.  The cells measure 8 um in length.  Thanks to Alastair Simpson for guiding me with the identification that most of these are consistent with Kipferlia bialata admixed with Dysnectes, another CLO.  

Carpediemonas is genus of Metamonada, and belongs to the group Excavata. This organism is a unicellular flagellated eukaryote that was first discovered in substrate samples from the Great Barrier Reef. Carpediemonas can be found in anaerobic intertidal sediment, where it feeds on bacteria. A feature of this species is the presence of a feeding groove, a characteristic of the excavates. Like most other metamonads, Carpediemonas does not rely on an aerobic mitochondrion to produce energy. Instead, it contains hydrogenosomes that are used to produce ATP. This organism has two flagella: a posterior one used for feeding on the substrate, and an anterior one that moves in a slower sweeping motion. Carpediemonas is assigned to the fornicates, where similar Carpediemonas-like organisms are used in researching the evolution within excavates. Although Carpediemonas is a member of the metamonads, it is unusual in the sense that it is free-living and has three basal bodies.

"Carpediemonas-like organisms (CLOs) are important for understanding the evolutionary history of anaerobic excavates (e.g. diplomonads and parabasalids), especially their cytoskeletal traits and the functions of their modified mitochondria (e.g., hydrogenosomes and mitosomes). Kipferlia bialata is probably the most commonly encountered CLO and has an intriguing molecular phylogenetic position within the Fornicata" (1). 

"Kipferlia n. gen. Diagnosis. Free-living, biflagellated and colourless cells with a conspicuous ventral groove. The right margin of the groove is markedly extended by a fine membrane, visible by electron microscopy. The posterior flagellum beats within the groove, and bears a single broad vane, located ventrally. Inhabits low-oxygen marine environments. Similar to Carpediemonas and Dysnectes in typical habitat and general appearance when viewed by light microscopy, but distinct from both in SSU rRNA gene phylogenies" (2). 

"Type species. Kipferlia bialata (Ruinen, 1938) n. comb. Other species. None described Etymology. Kipferln (sing. Kipferl; German) are small crescent-shaped cookies from southern Germany and Austria. The name refers to the shape of the type species. The name Kipferlia is considered to be of feminine gender, in agreement with the species epithet for the type species. Taxonomic assignment: Eukaryota; Excavata; Fornicata Kipferlia bialata (Ruinen, 1938) n. comb. Basionym. Cryptobia bialata Ruinen, 1938 Other synonyms. Carpediemonas bialata (Ruinen, 1938) Lee and Patterson 2000. Comments. Originally described in 1938 as Cryptobia bialata (Ruinen, 1938), this organism was next identified as a distinct morphospecies by Lee and Patterson (2000), who renamed it Carpediemonas bialata" (2). 

"Kipferlia bialata n. gen n. comb. CL6 Bean shaped 2 flagella posterior flagellum 1.5 cell length. Movement very slow, often adheres to surfaces, rapid beating of the anterior flagellum.  Clade CL6, representing the C. bialata morphospecies (here renamed Kipferlia bialata n. gen. n. comb., see below), branches independently as the most basal group of Fornicata, with very weak support (46 bp and 0.91 pp). There is no evidence of a specific relationship between CL6 and CL4 (i.e. Carpediemonas proper)" (2).

"Carpediemonas bialata (Ruinen, 1938 ) Lee and Patterson, n. comb. Description. Cell outline kidney-shaped, 6±14 mm long (mostly, 9±12 mm), not rigid, with a longitudinal ventral groove. A membrane moves down along the groove every 4±6 s. Two flagella emerge from the anterior part of the cell; the anterior flagellum bends backwards, is about the length of the cell and beats over the cell with a slow sweeping motion. The acronematic posterior flagellum beats asymmetrically and is about 1.5 times the cell length. The posterior flagellum may vibrate actively in the groove when not beating. Cells consume bacteria up to 5 mm and food materials are transferred by the moving membrane to the back of the cell. The cells may have many food vacuoles and attach to the substratum with the tip of the posterior flagellum. Cells move slowly by skidding or gliding with the anterior flagellum beating with a flicking motion. Commonly observed in late cultures. Remarks. Ruinen (1938 ) described Cryptobia bialata from Australia as a biflagellated protist with a ventral groove, and with an undulating membrane and symmetrical walls. In respect of general appearance, size and flagellar lengths, the organisms from the present site agree well with Ruinen’s description. Body form, flagellar beating and distribution of this species agree well with C. membranifera, and we here transfer Cryptobia bialata to Carpediemonas. We believe that Carpediemonas bialata has already been described with cells of C. membranifera under the name Percolomonas membranifera in Larsen and Patterson (1990 ) (see Remarks to C. membranifera). This species often co-occurs with C. membranifera.  C. bialata can be distinguished from C. membranifera by its larger size and the cell shape. Carpediemonas bialata resembles Jakoba libera (Ruinen, 1938 ) Patterson, 1990 in general cell shape and the orientation of two flagella, but is distinguished by its acronematic anterior flagellum, the direction of curvature of the anterior flagellum, by the length of the posterior flagellum and by the moving membrane. The moving membrane has been seen in other taxa such Chilomastix cuspidata (Simpson, unpubl. note). We note that those species may be related to each other" (3).

e52bb5e6-aca5-473d-9f64-399bd700180e.description:
Trochilioides tenuis (Deroux, 1976) Chen et al. 2011  from a biofilm that formed on a sample from the fine sand sulfidic intertidal benthos of marine estuary Acabonac Harbor at Landing Lane.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPLANAPO 40 0.90 objective and SPLAN 100 1.25 oil objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S9+.  The cell measures 50 um in length, larger than the reported range but it is well known that size varies among populations.  Nonetheless, all of the other characters seen as well as the infraciliature matches the redescription of Pan et al 2011 below.   It is thought that "Brooklynella, Trochilioides and Microxysma represent transitional genera between Hartmannulidae and Dysteriidae with intellectual morphological characteristics" (2). 

"Genus Trochilioides Chen et al. 2011 Trochilioides tenuis (Deroux, 1976) Chen et al. 2011 (Fig. 2; Table 1) According to Article 13.3.3 of ICZN (1999), Trochilioides Kahl, 1931 is a nomen nudum, so Chen et al. (2011) re-established the genus by fixing T. recta as type species. Trochilioides tenuis was originally reported by Deroux (1976c), based only on its infraciliature. So far no re-description has been attempted, we here redescribe it based on a Qingdao population. Improved diagnosis: Small Trochilioides, 30–40 × 20–35 μm in vivo, body elliptical in outline; consistently three right kineties, four left kineties and seven postoral kineties; single contractile vacuole located at anterior of right side; marine habitat" (1). 

"Description of Qingdao population: Cell size about 30–40 × 20–35 μm in vivo; body usually elliptical in outline with anterior end bluntly rounded and posterior end somewhat tapered. Ventral side flat and dorsal side humped with several longitudinal stripes after protargol impregnation. Usually, rice-like pellicular granules irregularly distributed on dorsal side. Cytostome prominent, oval shaped, ventrally positioned in anterior 1/5 of cell  but nematodesmal rods not detected. Cytoplasm colourless, containing numerous small, greasily shinning globules (2–3 μm across), and food vacuoles (4–8 μm across), which render cells slightly greyish. Single contractile vacuole, about 5 μm in diameter, located at anterior 1/3 of right side. Single oval macronucleus centrally positioned, about 11 × 6 μm in vivo. Podite leaf shaped and 5 μm long, subcaudally located. Cilia 7 μm long. Movement by gliding on the substrate" (1). 

"Infraciliature:   Consistently, three right kineties, seven postoral kineties and four left kineties surrounding the cytostome. Two right-most kineties almost equal in length, extending anteriorly to anterior margin. Posterior ends of right kineties terminating at the same level and a fragment, comprising three or four basal bodies, located on the left of them. Left and postoral kineties very short, the posterior ends of which are progressively shortened from right to left. Equatorial fragment composed of 0–8 basal bodies, and terminal fragment consisting of 2–4 ones. The oral ciliature composed of three dikinetid fragments: two circumoral kineties (Co) arranged in parallel, equal in length; and one preoral kinety, relatively long, obliquely arranged in front of Co. During cell division, the oral primordium of opisthe generated from three sections of postoral kineties" (1). 

1.  Taxonomic Studies on Three Marine Ciliates from China, Including a New Species (Ciliophora, Cyrtophorida).  Hongbo PAN, Honggang MA, Xiaozhong HU, Khaled A. S. AL-RASHEID and Saleh A. AL-FARRAJ.    Acta Protozool. (2013) 52: 25–33  http://www.eko.uj.edu.pl/ap ACTA doi:10.4467/16890027AP.13.003.0831 

2. Historical Review of Studies on Cyrtophorian Ciliates (Ciliophora, Cyrtophoria) from China. Zhishuai Qu, Hongbo Pan, Jun Gong, Congcong Wang, Sabine Filker and Xiaozhong Hu.  Microorganisms 2022, 10, 1325. https://doi.org/10.3390/microorganisms10071325

7f5cfe16-7c4f-4cb6-80e3-9bc03d67dfcd.description:
Condylostoma spatiosum Ozaki and Yagiu in Yagiu, 1944 from from a biofilm that formed on a sample from the fine sand sulfidic intertidal benthos of marine Estuary Acabonac Harbor at Landing Lane.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPLAN 10x, SPLANAPO 20x, SPLANAPO 40 0.95, and SPLAN 100 1.25 oil with oiled condenser all with variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S9+. 

The elongated ellipsoid cell measures 800 um in length when fully extended with a gradually tapered rounded posterior and exhibits contractility and marked flexibility. There is a moniliform macronuclear apparatus chain comprising 14 ovoid nodules beginning at the level of the cytopharynx. There is no contractile vacuole.  There are numerous large food vacuoles. These features correspond to C. spatiosum (see below). 

"Body size of 480-800×80-130 μm, usually about 670×105 μm in vivo. Shape elongated ellipsoidal, dorsoventrally slightly flattened, anterior end truncated and slanted left side, posterior end gradually tapered and narrowly rounded, body margin slightly parallel. Buccal cavity about 25% of body length, oral cavity fairly deep with transversely striated inner wall. Macronucleus aligned usually with the right margin of the body, distinctly nodulated and connected by threads, composed of 11-25 usually 19 nodules with many small nucleoli in impregnated preparations). No contractile vacuole. Cortex very flexible and contractile. Slightly yellowish ellipsoidal cortical granules about 0.5-0.8×0.7-1.5 μm in size and about 1-5 irregular rows in between kineties. Cytoplasm colorless with some small inclusions 4 μm in vivo, lipid-like droplets and large food vacuoles. Movement moderately slow, usually gliding on bottom.

 Somatic kineties arranged longitudinally in 49-74 rows, mostly commenced near the buccal field, formed suture posteriorly, consisted of dikinetids and somatic cilia about 12μm in length in vivo. Frontal cirri near the apical end of right margin, two membrane-like cirri were located, respectively, on outside of the buccal cavity, about 40 μm in length in vivo and on the apical end of the paroral membrane and connected with paroral, about 20 μm in length in vivo. The adoral zone of membranelles which conspicuously covered the left side of the buccal field, occupied 16-40% of the body length, the proximal portion extending spirally into the cytopharynx, consisting of 111-144 adoral membranelles. The paroral membrane located on the inner side of the buccal cavity in impregnated preparations, was conspicuously long and smoothly undulated" (1).

1.  Morphological Redescriptions of Three Condylostoma Ciliates (Heterotrichida: Condylostomatidae) New to Korea Ji Hye Kim, Seok Won Jang, Mann Kyoon Shin.  Anim. Syst. Evol. Divers. Vol. 28, No. 3: 149-160, July 2012

6f9e516b-51df-4e1e-812c-8d53a88940ed.description:
Genus: Nitzschia Hassall, 1845, nom. cons.
Taxonomic classification:

Phylum: Heterokontophyta
Subphylum: Bacillariophytina
Class: Bacillariophyceae
Subclass: Bacillariophycidae
Order: Bacillariales
Family: Bacillariaceae
Genus Nitzschia (Guiry and Guiry 2023)

Type species: Nitzschia sigmoidea (Nitzsch) W.Smith 1853: 38, pl. XIII [13]: fig. 104 (Guiry and Guiry 2023)

Summary: 

Genus Description: A species rich genus of raphid diatoms and widely distrbuted throughout all freshwater and marine habitats. They may be the most abundant group found in coastal waters. Due to the large number of species within the genus, identifications can be problematic, especially with light microscopy, due to the often very fine striae, a raphe hard to discern, large variations in valve outline and in live cells the chloroplasts obscure morphologic details. AlgaeBase lists 886 accepted species names and 234 accepted varieties (Guiry and Guiry 2023). Essentially a nitzschioid symmetery, valves with bilateral symmetry and valves most often symmetrical to both apical and transapical axes. The raphe is positioned near the valve margin (eccentric) and the raphe is enclosed within a canal, often raised onto a keel. Mucko et al (2020) give 7 main diagnostic characteristics for determining species in Nitzschia:
1)	valve shape, 
2)	the position and structure of the raphe, 
3)	presence/absence and shape of the proximal raphe endings and terminal raphe fissures, 
4)	areola structure, 
5)	cell size,
6)	stria and f
7)	fibula density.
In 1990 Round et al. moved Fragilariopsis, Psammodictyon and Tryblionella from Nitzschia. (Round et al. 1990, Trobajo et al. 2012, Shorenkove et al. 2016, Mucko et al. 2020, Mann et al. 2021, Spaulding et al. 2021).

Species Description: 
Nitzschia longissima (Brébisson ex Kützing) Grunow 1862: 581 (basionym: Ceratoneis longissima Brébisson ex Kützing 1849: 891 (Guiry and Guiry 2023). Morphometric data: Valves are spindle shaped, tapering (fusiform) and strongly elongate at both ends. The main body of the cell is about 1/3–1/4 of the total length. 50-840 µm long, 6-10 µm wide, raphe eccentric, fibule 3-7 (average 4.2) in 10 µm, striae in the LM is hardly visible but appears 17 in 10 µm, and 32-38 in 10 µm with SEM. Absence of a hyaline area near the centre (as in N. rectilonga). Numerous rod-shaped chloroplasts throughout the cell (Proshkina-Lavrenko 1948: 340, Pl. 104, fig. 7, Hendey 1964, Witkowski et al. 2000: 391-392, Pl. 207, fig. 6-7, p. 66, Bérard-Therriault et al. 1999: Shorenko et al. 2014, Shorenko et al. 2016, PL 57. Fig d-f, Plinski and Witkowski 2020: fig. 639, pp. 340-341, Guiry and Guiry 2023).

Found on Z. marina leaves. Collected at Montague Harbour Marine Provincial Park (MHMPP), Galiano Island, B.C. Canada. Collected November 15, 2020.

Images: Nitzchia cf. longissima on Z marina-MHMPP-Nov 15-2020-5-NAL-Meth C_3 (FS 0085,.88 &91)_4.tif; Nitzchia cf. longissima on Z marina-MHMPP-Nov 15-2020-5-NAL-Meth C_3_0074_3.tif: Morphometric data: Valves are spindle shaped, tapering (fusiform) and strongly elongate at both ends. The main body of the cell is about 1/3 of the total length. 243.6 µm long, 8.3 µm wide, raphe eccentric, fibule 5-6 in 10 µm, striae in the LM is hardly visible but appears 15-16 in 10 µm. Absence of a hyaline area near the centre. Numerous rod-shaped chloroplasts throughout the cell (undetermined).

Nitzschia longissima was reported by Cupp 1943: 200-201, Shim 1976: Pl. 24, fig. 11 and Waters et al. 1992: 7, in the Salish Sea.

Methods:

Collected by brushing or scrapping leaf sections of Z. marina from MHMPP, August 4, 2020, October 16, 2020, March 7, 2021 and July 20, 2021. Cells were cleaned with concentrated hydrogen peroxide or nitric acid at 100 C for 3-5 hours to remove organics, then rinsed multiple times in ddH20 to a neutral pH. Mounted on SEM stubs or in Naphrax on slides for light microscopy. Imaging with a Nikon TE300 and Tuscen DigiRetna16 MP camera or Nikon E800.
Live specimens were imaged with either a Nikon TE300 or Nikon E800 with either bright-field or DIC.In-situ, environmentally prepared samples were made using minimal contact of 8-10 mm leaf section, soaked in ddH2O to remove salts and dried through an EtOH series (50%-100%) and finished off with 100% Hexamethyldisilane HMDS (Hazrin-Chong and Manefield 2012). Mounted on carbon stickies onto aluminum SEM stubs and imaged with either the Hitachi s4800 or TM4000 at AMF, at University of Victoria, B.C. My thanks to Siobhan Schenk and Laura Parfrey in the Parfrey Lab at UBC for molecular data from the eelgrass and collaboration with IMERSS. Also thanks go to Elaine Humphrey of the AMF, UVIC, imaging by Ron Read, Melanie Quenneville and Arjan van Asselt. LM (Nitzschia longissima) and SEM imaging, taxonomy and identifications by Mark. Webber.

acc0ebfa-ddbb-4967-a2ec-c551079caf06.description:
Plagiopyla ovata Kahl, 1931 from the fine sand sulfidic intertidal benthos of marine estuary Acabonac Harbor at Landing Lane. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPLANAPO 40 0.95 objective and SPLAN 100 1.25 oil objective with slide oiled to condenser plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S9+. 

Several individuals are shown which range from 64 up to 80 um in length.  The cell size and upward curving mid-region of the oral tube with the right side of upper oral lip slightly bulged forming a nose-like structure serve to distinguish the species from its closest congener P. frontata. 

"Body size in vivo about 50–85×33–48µm; length to width ratio about 1.5–2.0:1 in vivo and 1.4–1.9:1 in stained specimens. Body rigid, non-contractile, dorsoventrally flattened, obovate, anterior end widely rounded, posterior end more or less narrowed (Figs 3a, d and 4a–c). Single macronucleus, globular to ellipsoidal, centrally located, about 20–30×15–24µm in vivo and 17–29×12–24µm in stained specimens (Figs 3g and 4d, j). Single micronucleus, globular, about 5µm in diameter in vivo and 4µm in diameter after protargol impregnation, closely associated with macronucleus, i.e. located at edge of, or slightly enveloped by, macronucleus (Figs 3g and 4j). Extrusomes slightly curved, 4–8µm long, distributed uniformly in ectoplasm and randomly in endoplasm (Figs 3a, e and 4e); extruded extrusomes slender needle-like (Figs 3e and 4k). Single contractile vacuole located near posterior end of cell, with two distinct pores located behind dense ciliary rows, pores observable in both living and stained specimens (Figs 3a, b, i and 4d, e)" (1). 

"Striated band on dorsal side, starting at level of buccal cavity and extending anteriorly a short distance, then turning sharply backwards forming a loop about 7–10µm long, extending posteriorly parallel to somatic kineties, and terminating just below mid-body region (Figs 3b, i and 4f, i, o). Distance from anterior end of cell to beginning of striated band about 25% of cell length. In total, striated band about 34µm long, i.e. approximately half of cell length, consisting of numerous transverse ridges, each 2–3µm wide. Locomotion by swimming while rotating about main body axis, always spiralling to left" (1). 

"In total, 56–63 monokinetidal somatic kineties (30–37 on ventral side and 23–30 on dorsal side), kinetids of ventral kineties usually more densely packed than those of dorsal kineties (Figs 3h, i and 4n, o). One or two dense ciliary rows (DC) in posterior region of cell on dorsal side left of cytoproct, about 6–21µm long, composed of 13–22 kinetosomes (for individuals with two DCs, only the left one is counted) (Figs 3b, i and 4o). Somatic cilia 6–10µm long, uniformly and densely distributed on cell surface (Figs 3a, h, i and 4a, n, o). About ten caudal cilia located along left posterior margin of cell, 8–10µm long, straight and oriented in a different direction to somatic cilia (Fig. 3a). Silverlines in irregular-rectangular grid (Figs 3c and 4i)" (1). 

"Oral region formed by two lip-like structures, composed of dense oral kineties. Right side of upper oral lip slightly bulged forming a nose-like structure (Figs 3a and 4h). Slit-like buccal opening located at right-ventral side of cell (Figs 3a, h and 4a). Distance from anterior end of cell to beginning of buccal opening about 25% of cell length (Figs 3a and 4a–c). Tube-like buccal cavity about 85% of cell width, extending transversely to left and curving upwards in mid-region (Figs 3a, f and 4a–d, h). Distance from anterior end of cell to top of buccal cavity about 6–9µm. Oral ciliature more dense than somatic ciliature (Figs 3h and 4n). 53–61 oral kineties on cell surface and extending inwards (Figs 3f, g and 4m, n). Upper oral lip kineties 2–4µm long. Gap between upper oral lip kineties and somatic kineties about 2–3µm (Figs 3a, h and 4g, l, n)": (1).

"The genus Plagiopyla includes nine marine species viz., Plagiopyla binucleata Agamaliev, 1978, Plagiopyla cucullio (Quennerstedt, 1867) Wallengren, 1918, P. frontata Kahl, 1931, Plagiopyla marina Gourret & Roeser, 1886, Plagiopyla minuta Powers, 1933, P. mystax (Lynch, 1930) Nitla et al., 2019, Plagiopyla nyctotherus Poljansky & Golikova, 1959, P. ovata Kahl, 1931, and Plagiopyla stenostoma Alekperov & Asadullayeva, 1996. Among these, P. minuta, P. nyctotherus, and P. mystax are endocommensals of the sea urchin Strongylocentrotus, whereas other species are free-living. Most species of the genus Plagiopyla (including P. ovata) have a single ovoidal to ellipsoidal macronucleus and a single spherical micronucleus. However, two of the known marine species have different nuclear characteristics, i.e. two macronuclei in P. binucleata, and one vermiform macronucleus in P. stenostoma, and thus can be easily distinguished from their congeners" (1). 

"P. frontata differs from P. ovata in having a shorter frontal region section (region between anterior cell margin and upper oral lip) relative to the length of the cell (17% in P. frontata vs. 25% in P. ovata), a straight buccal cavity tube (vs. a buccal tube curving upwards in its mid-region in P. ovata), and the upper oral lip perpendicular to the buccal opening (vs. not perpendicular in P. ovata). P. marina differs from P. ovata in having a shorter frontal region relative to the length of the cell (17–20% in P. marina vs. 25% in P. ovata) and long ovoid (vs. ovate to obovate) body shape" (1).  P. ovata is smaller than P. frontata.  Nitla et al. 2019 emphasized the size range reported by Kahl of P. frontata versus P. ovata 113–174 um vs 73–79 um (2). 

1.  Redescription and SSU rRNA gene-based phylogeny of an anaerobic ciliate, Plagiopyla ovata Kahl, 1931 (Ciliophora, Plagiopylea).  Ran Li, Wenbao Zhuang, Congcong Wang, Hamed El-Serehy, Saleh A. Al-Farraj , Alan Warren and Xiaozhong Hu.  Int. J. Syst. Evol. Microbiol. 2021;71:004936 DOI 10.1099/ijsem.0.004936

2. Critical revision of the family Plagiopylidae (Ciliophora: Plagiopylea), including the description of two novel species, Plagiopyla ramani and Plagiopyla narasimhamurtii, and redescription of Plagiopyla nasuta Stein, 1860 from India VENKATAMAHESH NITLA, VALENTINA SERRA, SERGEI I. FOKIN, LETIZIA MODEO, FRANCO VERNI, BHAGAVATULA VENKATA SANDEEP, CHAGANTI KALAVATI and GIULIO PETRONI.  Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society, 2019, 186, 1–45.

ae7bbfc5-755e-46e5-8b80-6cba6acc5455.description:
Isthmia nervosa Kützing 1844. 

Phylum: Bacillariophyta, Subphylum: Bacillariophytina, Class: Mediophyceae, Subclass: Chaetocerotophycidae, Order: Hemiaulales, Family: Isthmiaceae, Genus: Isthmia (Guiry & Guiry,  2020). 

Light microscopic image, girdle view, of the centric diatom Isthmia nervosa. Specimen from Pebble Beach, east Galiano Island, Strait of Georgia, BC, Canada. Isthmia sp. is colonial, epiphytic on seaweeds and a coastal marine diatom. It is both highly silicified and large relative to other diatoms. 

The genus is heteropolar, where one valve is more elevated than the other. Isthmia spp. are found in both trapezoidal and rombhoidal forms (shown here is a rhomboid form). Valves are oval with no distinct transition from valve to mantle. 

The costae (rib-like thickenings) are the distinctive “nerves” of I. nervosa. The cribra (plates with pores) in I. nervosa vary over the valve face unlike I. enervis where the cribra are more regular. 

Both I. nervosa and I. enervis have only one pseudocellus per cell, a bulbous extension in which a cluster of small areolae are seen. The areolae cluster is far more pronounced in I. nervosa: the areolae being smaller in size in I. enervis, and according to Round (1984) the areolae suddenly reduce in size at the pole of the pseudocellus of I. nervosa. It is proposed that the pores behind the apex of the pseudocellus secrete a mucilage pad by which the cell attaches to the host, though areolae of the pseudocellus may also be involved (Round 1984).

Both species have a U shaped notch on the distal end of the girdle band (copula). However, it is far less obvious in I. nervosa, but usually a distinctive feature of the epivalve of trapezoidal cells of I. enervis (Round 1984). Round (1984) notes that on some cells of I. enervis the girdle band notch could not be detected. I. nervosa has very prominent struts supporting the girdle diaphragm, and less so for I. enervis.

Methods:

Net collection from Pebble Beach, East side of Galiano Island, Southern Gulf Islands, British Columbia, Canada, June 25, 2020. Cell cleaned in 30% cold hydrogen peroxide for 7 days. Brightfield imaging in ddH2O with a Nikon E800, MU2003 20 MP camera and Motic AE31 inverted microscope and an MU 12 MP camera.

abccb3a0-1e3c-42a9-8128-9dc2e3972554.description:
Psammomitra retractilis (Claparède & Lachmann, 1858) Borror, 1972  (syn Psammomitra brevicauda KAHL, 1933) from the intertidal benthos of marine estuary Acabonac harbor at Louse Point launching ramp. The cell measures 120 um in length and is contractile.  There are 5 long frontal membranelles.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPLANAPO 40 0.95 objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S9+. 

The systematics have been confused and convoluted and this confusion is extensively reviewed by Berger (1).  Yi et al (2) showed " by morphological and SSrRNA gene data that Psammomitra branched with Holosticha at a rather deep level, and  Psammomitra should be arranged in an isolated position near the Holostichidae but represent a taxon within the order Urostylida (sensu Berger, 2006) at the rank of family, i.e. Psammomitridae Jankowski, 1979 stat. nov " (2`).  There has also been confusion between the two species described by Kahl under the older genus name Micrometra- M. brevicauda and M. retractilis (4).  Song and Warren feel that Psammometra brevicauda is synonymous with P. retractilis, which they described at the time as Uroleptus retractilis" (1,3). 

"Psammomitra retractilis. This taxon is the sole species of the genus and has been frequently found in marine habitats (for a review, see Berger, 2006). It has an urostylid midventral complex composed of cirral pairs only, and a characteristic long tail (Song & Warren, 1996). Its systematic position is subject to a long and ongoing dispute (for a review, see Berger, 2006). Song & Warren (1996) described this species in detail and suggested its assignment to the urostylids based on its cirral pattern, which is composed of a few midventral pairs, two frontoterminal cirri, and some transverse cirri. In Berger’s (2006) review,  Psammomitra was classified as a member of Holostichidae. Berger (2006) also stated that this genus is possibly an urostylid instead of a dorsomarginalian taxon because of the absence of dorsomarginal kineties, although he suspected that P. retractilis might be an oxytrichid, based on some morphological features, e.g. it forms one, two, or three additional cirral anlagen, a process which is likely to occur several times independently in 18-cirri oxytrichids " (1,2).

"SUBCLASS STICHOTRICHIA ORDER UROSTYLIDA PSAMMOMITRIDAE STAT. NOV. Improved diagnosis:Urostylida possessing extremely contractile, elongated body that consists of three parts: head, trunk, and slender tail; midventral complex composed of midventral pairs only and restricted to about anterior 1/3 of ventral surface; frontal, frontoterminal, and transverse cirri present; one left and one right marginal row, which commence near proximal end of adoral zone and extend to near rear body end. Only one known genus " (3).

"Psammomitra (= Micromitra) brevicauda is differentiated from U. retractilis only by the possession of four longer apical membranelles and in having significantly shorter caudal cirri and dorsal bristles. However, we have observed individuals among the population of U. retractilis from Qingdao with 3-5 longer apical membranelles and with short caudal cirri and dorsal bristles. Therefore, it is likely that P. brevicauda is synonymous with U. retractilis" (3).

From Kahl 1933:  "Genus Micromitra KAHL, 1933 (for Mitra QUENNERSTEDT, 1867, nec. LAMARCK, 1799) According to our own recent observations, with its isolated ventral cirri, this genus belongs in the genus Oxytricha and forms another subgenus, which now includes two species: 
 Micromitra retractilis CLAPAREDE and LACHMANN 1858 Size160 um.  When stretched, the tail becomes thread-like and thin longer than the rest of the body, it shows bone-like myoneme strips. There are 5-6 frontal membranelles. Drsb. 10 um high.  
Micromitra brevicauda KAHL, 1933  Size 80-110 um Tail only half as long as the rest of the body. Drsb. 5 um high; 4 frontal membranelles. Sand bottom near the Heligoland dune" (4).

1. Berger H. 2006. Monograph of the Urostyloidea (Ciliophora, Hypotricha). Monographiae Biologicae 85: 1–1304.  https://www.google.com/books/edition/Monograph_of_the_Urostyloidea_Ciliophora/yl7oZtQfG8oC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=psammomitra+brevicauda&pg=PA223&printsec=frontcover

2.  Phylogenetic analyses suggest that Psammomitra (Ciliophora, Urostylida) should represent an urostylid family, based on small subunit rRNA and alpha-tubulin gene sequence information. ZHENZHEN YI, WEIBO SONG, THORSTEN STOECK, KHALED A. S. AL-RASHEID, ABDULAZIZ A. AL-KHEDHAIRY, JUN GONG, HONGWEI MA and ZIGUI CHEN. Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society, 2009, 157, 227–236

3.  A Redescription of the Marine Ciliates Uroleptus retractilis (Claparède and Lachmann, 1858) comb. n. and Epiclintes ambiguus (Müller, 1786) Biitschli, 1889 (Ciliophora, Hypotrichida) Weibo SONG and Alan WARREN. Acta Protozoologica (1996) 35: 227 - 234

4.   Kahl A. 1935. Urtiere oder Protozoa. I: Wimpertiere oder Ciliata (Infusoria), 4. Peritricha und Chonotricha. Die Tier welt Deutschlands 30: pp 838, 842.

Family: Licmophoraceae
Genus:		Licmophora (Guiry and Guiry 2023)

Holotype species, synonym(s), etc.: Licmophora argentescens C.Agardh

Summary:

Licmophora is an araphid genus. Species in the genus are cosmopolitan, found in most marine habitats including Arctic, Antarctic, and tropical regions. Cells grow in colonies, often fan shaped on branched mucilaginous stalks or pads, attached to various substrates such as seaweeds, rocks, animals or detached and found singly in the plankton. Frustules are heteropolar. They have a narrow base (sometimes slightly capitate) and broader apex and in valve and girdle view the cell is cuneate (wedge shaped). The valves have a narrow, sometimes indistinct central sternum. Septa present, distinct or indistinct (Plinski and Witkowski 2020), internally around the apical ends and tapering off down each side of the copulae.The areolae are round or elongate and externally covered by a criba. The striae are transapical, uniseriate and parallel, except at the apices where they can become radiate. A rimoportula is present on one valve at the base and on the other valve, or both valves, at the apex. External rimoportula is a circular slit like opening, whereas the internal rimoportula opening is labiate, fan shaped, sometimes stalked and flush with the frustule. Normally, there are two or three rimoportulae per cell. If 2 rimoportulae per frustule, then, one is located at the basal apex, the other at the head apex. If 3 rimoportulae, one is located at the basal apex, one at the head apex of each valve. A series of slits (multiscissura) is present around the base of both valves where mucilage for stalks and pads is secreted. Spines are present at the head apex of some species. Plastids numerous and small. There are five distinguishable girdle bands. Areolae on the copulae (girdle bands) are smaller than those on the valve. Valvocopulae open at the basal apex and maybe a septum at the apex. Relying on identification of species by light microscopy may be problematic due to fine features; SEM and TEM are utilized. AlgaeBase lists 102 accepted species and 10 varieties (Honeywill 1988, Round et al. 1990, Lobhan 2013, Lobhan et al. 2018, Plinski and Witkowski 2020: 56, Spaulding et al. 2021, Guiry and Guiry 2023).

Species Description: Licmorphora paradoxa (Lyngbye) C. Agardh 1828: 32. Due to the high striae count at both poles, it is likely this specimen is Licmophora tincta (C.Agardh) Grunow 1868: 35, syn. Licmophora_paradoxa var. tincta (Ag.) Hust. It is very similar to L. paradoxa, however the species has higher striae at 33 in 10 µm (Proshkina-Lavrenko 1950: 20, Pl. 6, fig. 11a. b.). Characteristics: distinct septa, 30-140 µm long, 7-18 µm width, sternum distinct, transapical striae fine 23-32 in 10 µm at the basal pole, 27-30 in 10 µm at the head pole. Elongate areolae
near the sternum. (Agardh 1828: 32 (no measurements given), Proshkina-Lavrenko 1950: 20, Pl. 6, fig. 11a. b., Hendey 1964: 168, Sims et. al. 1996: Pl. 123, fig. 3, Honeywill 1998: 239, Witkowski et al. 2000: 67).

near the sternum.

Previously reported by Shim (1976) as Licmophora paradoxa (Lyngbye) C. Agardh.

Methods:

Collected by brushing or scrapping the red seaweed Scagelia americana from Miners Bay Wharf, Active Pass, Mayne Island, BC., Canada., Oct. 31, 2022. Cells were cleaned with concentrated hydrogen peroxide or nitric acid at 100 C for 3-5 hours to remove organics, then rinsed multiple times in ddH20 to a neutral pH. Mounted in Naphrax on slides for light microscopy. Imaging with a Nikon E800, MU2003 20 MP camera. LM and SEM imaging, taxonomy and identifications by M. Webber.

Licmophora abbreviata C. Agardh 1831. Found on the Hydrozoan, Obelia sp. attached to Spanish Hills Wharf (SHW), Trincomali Channel, Galiano Island, B.C., Canada. Cleaned diatom frustules.

AlgaeBase lists 102 accepted species and 10 varieties (Honeywill 1988, Round et al. 1990, Lobhan 2013, Lobhan et al. 2018, Plinski and Witkowski 2020: 56, Spaulding et al. 2021, Guiry and Guiry 2023).

Species Description:
Licmorphora abbreviata C. Agardh 1831: 42. (Syn.: Podosphenia abbreviata (C. Agardh) Ehrenberg 1838: 214; Licmophora lyngbyei var. abbreviate (C.Agardh) Grunow 1881).

References:
Cupp 1943: 177, Proshkina-Lavrenko 1950: 19-20, Pl. 6, fig. 4a. b., Honeywill 1998: 231, Sims et al. 1998: 260, fig. 1, Witkowski et al. 2000: 63, Romagnoli et al. 2014: 4-7, Lopez-Fuerte et al. 2015: fig. 20, Plinksi and Witkowski 2020: 57, fig. 218.
 
In girdle view cells are wedge-shaped with rounded upper corners. Valves are narrow, spathulate with broad, acutely rounded head pole and acutely rounded rostrate foot-pole, lower part with slightly concave margins, 75.5-122.6 (20-110) µm long, 10.9-11.3 (4-13) µm wide. Sternum narrow, distinct. Transapical striae 9-10 (10-17) in 10 µm, becoming slightly finer at the head pole 9-10 (13-17) in 10 µm, 8 (9-12) in 10 µm at the foot pole. Striae density lower in the foot-pole than the head pole. 3 rimoportulae per cell, two at the foot-pole, 1 at the head pole. Elongate areolae in the apical direction, 48-50 (60) in 10 pm. Multiscissura has 9 (9-13) slits. Valvocopula has a moderately deep septum. µm 

Remarks: The morphometric characteristics of L. abbreviata so found in Galiano Island waters are within range of L. abbreviata data in the literature. Licmophora abbreviata was previously reported by Cupp (1943) North American Pacific coast; Stockner and Cliff (1975), Salish Sea and Shim (1976) from the Strait of Georgia and Chester et al. (1979) from the Strait of Juan De Fuca.
Salish Sea specimens: Licmophora abbreviata on Obelia SHW dock-Nov 3-2021 (MW)_04(x600)_4.tif; Licmophora abbreviata_#4 on Obelia SHW Oct 27-2021 Slide 3 E800(Nov 17-2024) AvA 60x oil_fs-19-25_4.tif; Licmophora abbreviata_#4 on Obelia SHW Oct 27-2021 Slide 3 E800(Nov 17-2024) AvA 100x oil_fs-28-31_4.tif; Licmophora abbreviata_#4 on Obelia SHW Oct 27-2021 Slide 3 E800(Nov 17-2024) AvA 100x oil_fs-33-36_4.tif: Licmophora abbreviata on Obelia SHW dock-Nov 3-2021 (MW)_01(x1.8k)_2.tif; Licmophora abbreviata on Obelia SHW dock-Nov 3-2021 (MW)_04(x600)_4.tif.

Methods:

Licmophora cells collected on Nov. 3, 2021 from Obelia sp. attached to Spanish Hills Wharf. Cells were cleaned with concentrated hydrogen peroxide or nitric acid at 100 C for 3-5 hours to remove organics, then rinsed multiple times in ddH20 to a neutral pH. Mounted on SEM stubs or in Naphrax on slides for light microscopy. Imaging with a Nikon TE300 and Tuscen DigiRetna16 MP camera or Nikon E800 with a Zeiss MRc5 camera and apo lenses.
Live specimens were imaged with either a Nikon TE300 or Nikon E800 with either bright-field or DIC. In-situ, environmentally prepared samples were made using minimal contact of 8-10 mm leaf section, soaked in ddH2O to remove salts and dried through an EtOH series (50%-100%) and finished off with 100% Hexamethyldisilane HMDS (Hazrin-Chong and Manefield 2012). Mounted on carbon stickies onto aluminum SEM stubs and imaged with either the Hitachi s4800 or TM4000 at AMF, at University of Victoria, B.C. My thanks to Siobhan Schenk and Laura Parfrey in the Parfrey Lab at UBC for molecular data from the eelgrass and collaboration with IMERSS. Also thanks go to Elaine Humphrey of the AMF, UVIC, imaging by Ron Read, Melanie Quenneville and Arjan van Asselt. For L. abbreviata, light microscopy by Arjan van Asselt (IMERSS) and SEM imaging, taxonomy and identifications by M. Webber (IMERSS).

316903cd-2c92-47ac-af01-d711cc072dd0.description: From the surface water of a creek through the marsh. The reducing conditions close to the bank led to formation of a surface film, which I tried to collect. The surface film which formed on the sample at home was collected on a coverslip. The first time I saw *R. nasuta*, recently, I thought it was rare. It turns out to be quite common in marsh water from all around this area. It whips its 'nose' around trying to lasso picoplanktonic algae. The food vacuoles don't contain many bacteria in this environment (evidence from staining). Cell length, 6 to 8 µm. Note that these are real time videos snippets. They really do move that fast.

1514c4c4-f5c1-4b16-8db8-0eea7e988d0d.description:
Colpoda cucullus O.F. Muller, 1773 from an infusion of moss growing on an asphalt driveway. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPLANAPO 40 0.95 objective and SPLAN 100x oil objective with slide oiled to the condenser. The cells measure from 80-100 um in length. They were difficult to image when free swimming but this became easier as water evaporated from under the coverslip and the cells were flattened and somewhat immobilized. 

" 40-110 um long; anterior keel with 8 to10 indentations; 29-34 ciliary grooves; cilia mostly paired; macro nucleus with a stellate endosome; trichocysts rod-form; usually with abundant food vacuoles; in fresh water with decaying plants" (1). 

"Body distinctly reniform in shape, dorso-ventrally flattened. Right body edge strongly convex, left body edge concave often appearing as through a bite had been taken from it. A shallow diagonal somatic groove (not easily visible) originating on the dorsal surface travels round left side to entrance of vestibulum on the flattened ventral surface. Ciliation uniform in longitudinal or oblique orientated grooves. Several notches which denote ciliary grooves often visible on preoral part of left body edge. Caudal cilia may be present on some species. There is a horse-shoe shaped arc of closely-set cilia on the right of the vestibular entrance. Single rounded macronucleus with 1, 2 or 3 micronuclei. Single terminal contractile vacuole. Division takes place in thin-walled cysts, thick-walled protective cysts also formed" (2).  

"Morphology Length 40-120 um, average about 80 um; broadly reniform, anterior keel with 8-10 indentations; uniform ciliation; buccal cavity with a deep oral funnel starting at a groove near the left side of the body, the buccal cavity leads to a diagonal groove on the dorsal surface (not evident in the figure), buccal cavity ciliated but without membranes or membranelles; 1 spherical macronucleus, exhibiting a stellate endosome; 1 micronucleus; a single terminal contractile vacuole; in the presence of a good food supply, the body is packed with food inclusions and appears very dark; fission only takes place within reproductive cysts" (3).    

" Colpoda cucullus, previously considered a "soil" protozoan, is predominantly a vegetation-associated species that is especially adapted, through its ability to encyst and excyst rapidly, to exploit the fluctuating moisture content of the terrestrial environment. Three means of distribution were discovered which explain the ubiquity of this species.  Herbivores consume Colpoda cysts while feeding on infested vegetation and deposit them with their feces; the cysts are transported by honey-bees along with pollen grains; and they are also carried through air like pollen. Dew induces excystment and contains sufficient nutritional substances to support profuse growth and reproduction" (4).

1.  PROTOZOOLOGY By RICHARD R. KUDO.  CHARLES C THOMAS • PUBLISHER Springfield, Illinois. 1954. pp 745-6. 

2.  Colin R. Curds "British and other freshwater ciliated protozoa Part I Ciliophora: Kinetofragminophora" Cambridge University Press, 1982 

3.  CILIATED PROTOZOA.  An illustrated guide to the species used as biological indicators in freshwater biology HARTMUT BICK.  WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION GENEVA 1972  pp 64-5. 
 
4.  Colpoda cucullus: A Terrestrial Aquatic.Jo Anne Mueller, Wayne P. Mueller. The American Midland Naturalist, Vol. 84, No. 1 (Jul., 1970), pp. 1-12

7b9b9ab6-7e4b-48da-b841-35a1ae758523.description:
Isthmia nervosa Kützing 1844. 

Phylum: Bacillariophyta, Subphylum: Bacillariophytina, Class: Mediophyceae, Subclass: Chaetocerotophycidae, Order: Hemiaulales, Family: Isthmiaceae, Genus: Isthmia (Guiry & Guiry,  2020). 

Light microscopic image, girdle view, of the centric diatom Isthmia nervosa. Cleaned sample from diatoms attached to the red algae Sarcodiotheca gaudichaudii collected at 1.8 m, Retreat Cove, Trincomali Channel, Galiano Island. Isthmia sp. is colonial, epiphytic on seaweeds and a coastal marine diatom. It is both highly silicified and large relative to other diatoms. 

The genus is heteropolar, where one valve is more elevated than the other. Isthmia spp. are found in both trapezoidal and rombhoidal forms (shown here is a rhomboid form). Valves are oval with no distinct transition from valve to mantle. 

The costae (rib-like thickenings) are the distinctive “nerves” of I. nervosa. The cribra (plates with pores) in I. nervosa vary over the valve face unlike I. enervis where the cribra are more regular. 

Both I. nervosa and I. enervis have only one pseudocellus per cell, a bulbous extension in which a cluster of small areolae are seen. The areolae cluster is far more pronounced in I. nervosa: the areolae being smaller in size in I. enervis, and according to Round (1984) the areolae suddenly reduce in size at the pole of the pseudocellus of I. nervosa. It is proposed that the pores behind the apex of the pseudocellus secrete a mucilage pad by which the cell attaches to the host, though areolae of the pseudocellus may also be involved (Round 1984).

Both species have a U shaped notch on the distal end of the girdle band (copula). However, it is far less obvious in I. nervosa, but usually a distinctive feature of the epivalve of trapezoidal cells of I. enervis (Round 1984). Round (1984) notes that on some cells of I. enervis the girdle band notch could not be detected. I. nervosa has very prominent struts supporting the girdle diaphragm, and less so for I. enervis.

Methods:

Sarcodiotheca gaudichaudii collected at 1.8 m depth at Retreat Cove, Trincomali Channel Galiano Island, B.C. on May 26, 2023 by the Hakai Insitute diving team as part of the 2023 Galiano BioBlitz with IMERSS and UBC and UVIC participation. Epiphytes were removed by tooth brush, pipetted and fixed in 4% formalin. Cells cleaned for 3 hrs. at 100C with 30% hydrogen peroxide, then washed with lab grade water and pipetted, air dried onto coverslips, and mounted in Naphrax. Imaged with a Nikon E800 microscope and MU2003 20 MP camera. Thank you to Arjan van Asselt and Henry McGee (IMERSS) for extracting and preserving the diatoms, Sandra Lindstrom (UBC) for identifying the red algae. Preparation of slides, imaging and taxonomy by Mark Webber (IMERSS).

Live cells brushed from Sarcodiotheca gaudichaudii collected from Retreat Cove, July 14, 2024. Diatoms imaged with a Nikon TE300 and a Tuscen 16 MP camera. Many thanks to Zeuss Cochrane and Andrew Simon for collecting the red algae. Collecting assistance by Arjan van Asselt, processing and imaging by Mark Webber (imerss.org).

6fcfa5ca-e12e-489c-8cd1-2ffc86a8b0f6.description: Abundant in reservoir outlet stream. I don't know what depth in the reservoir the outlet comes from, but the reservoir level is quite low at this time of year.  The water was crystal clear, if slightly yellow - most of the seston in the water column had fallen out when the reservoir froze over. Diagnostic features include: Middle pecten of postabdominal claw long and robust; Concave ventral head margin; Small, symmetric polygonal markings on rostrum; dorsal spines relatively close together. Length of adults, about 2.5 mm. Many of the individuals of this species were heavily colonized by epizoic diatoms, which I'll post separately. That's apparently a seasonal risk.

f9e91505-f1b9-452c-b962-7a5b65ee460e.description: In a sample of water from below the ice sheet of a frozen pond. The sample was kept warm and illuminated for two months before observation.

7809a83b-4f76-4632-859b-95b460c0c75f.description:
10-25 µm, multiple chloroplasts, red stigma, attached by a polysaccharide stalk. Attached cells are still motile, as the gif shows. There were free-living cells swimming rapidly around the sessile cells. The chlorophyll autofluorescence was brighter among the motile cells than the sessile ones. On this date, the dominant cladoceran, *Daphnia pulex*, was lightly colonized, and the dominant calanoid copepods were usually heavily colonized so they all looked green under the microscope.

I've added a photo of a first instar copepod nauplius that is already carrying two passengers.
7809a83b-4f76-4632-859b-95b460c0c75f.place_guess: Hilton Falls Reservoir outlet stream, Milton, ON, Canada

b1ab5e7d-cc78-4cf5-bf1d-e058daab2a84.description: Epizoic on especially *Daphnia pulex*, as well as the rest of the crustacean community. Arcuate and with sub-capitate ends. Most are about 90 microns long. Unfortunately the striations don't show up in the photos. Winter is the peak period for heavy epizoic loads, apparently, in part because the time between moults is extended. Also, photosythesis is not as temperature sensitive as animal metabolism is.
b1ab5e7d-cc78-4cf5-bf1d-e058daab2a84.place_guess: Hilton Falls Reservoir outlet stream, Milton, ON, Canada

Mag. 200x

- A pond-side water sample (retentate) was taken on 01/06/2024 using a 10µ dip net to enrich for microorganisms. (The shoreline had a layer of ice about 1/4" thick that needed to be breached in order to accommodate the dipnet. The retentate contained a lot of sediment due to the shallow depth and disturbance caused by the net.) Air temp 35F.

Biflagellate, phagotrophic protozoan (no chloroplasts). The flagella are anteriorly positioned and of different different lengths, one very long (>2 body lengths) and one short (about 1 body length). Both flagella are visible in the last composite image, where the specimen is rolling and tumbling, seemingly trying to decide its next direction.  In swimming mode, only the the long flagellum appears in use. I'm assume the short flagellum is tucked along the body while swimming (recurrent).  The body exhibited metabolic movement  (contorting and changing shape).  I chose the ID based on an earlier encounter with a similar specimen and the input of a number of expert iNatters, https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/74388786.
For a video of the current specimen https://youtu.be/eSA1ZPSirIA.

6bc18230-291d-4c33-92de-51073e784a6a.description:
Colpoda maupasi Enriques, 1908 from an infusion of moss collected from an asphalt driveway in an oak/hickory forest. Initially this infusion yielded a population of Colpoda cucullus ( see: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/195949464) which disappeared after a few days. I added some boiled wheat seed to the infusion in hopes of reviving the C. cucullus population but instead I found a much more vigorous and numerous population of C. maupasi. The cells range from rarely 45 to commonly 60 um in length, quite a bit smaller than the 80-100 um length of the initial C. cucullus population.  The size as well as the quite short preoral portion of the cell with the vestibule situated at 1/3-1/4 of body length, the spherical macronucleus with applied micronucleus, and the small keel with only 5 or 6 distinct notches are quite characteristic of C. maupasi.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlanapo 40 0.95 and Splan 100x oil objectives plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S9+. 

From Foissner 1993: "Morphology  and biology: Size in vivo 35-80x 20-50µm, usually about 60x 30µm. Gomez et al. (1966) and Ocam et al. (1965) showed that the size of identical clones is highly dependent on culture conditions. Size and shape rather characteristic, under certain experimental conditions specimen resembling C. inflata may occur (Biczok 1955 a). Lateral appearance reniform, preoral portion remarkably short (1/4-1/3 of body length), usually slightly ventrally inclined.  Well-nourished specimens almost globular postorally, causing tapered preoral portion. Flattened slightly to 2: I, in ventral and dorsal aspect pyriform to moderately broadly wedge-shaped; no postoral sack. Macronucleus approximately 10 um in vivo, in some populations globular, in others slightly to distinctly ellipsoid (Foissner 1980c, Kahl 1931), usually near center of cell. Data on nucleoli disparate: coarse grained (KAHL 1931), plate-like to reticulate, ramified, small and large, irregularly formed. In 6 populations I subsequently examined in this respect, a similar motley picture emerged; it is thus an unsuitable character for identification. Shape of macronucleus also varies within the same population from globular to ellipsoid and is, occasionally, even distinctly reniform. Micronucleus calotte-shaped, about 2 x 1 um, attached to macronucleus, strongly Feulgen positive. Contractile vacuole at posterior end, during diastole with small collecting vesicles, single excretory pore in centre of posterior pole. Cortex flexible, coarse, often distinctly furrowed by somatic kinetics to produce above mentioned lattice-effect in normally fed and undernourished specimens.  Extrusomes about 1 um in diameter, within somatic kinetics, do not stain with methyl green-pyronin but strongly so with protargol; prepared cells thus have most characteristic appearance.  Cytoplasm with few to many rod-shaped, yellowish crystals, especially in vicinity of contractile vacuole. Feeds on bacteria. Food vacuoles compact, often rendering cells opaque. Movement moderately rapid, usually creeps quickly among soil particles, frequently remaining immobile during feeding whereby cilia are spread, presumably with thigmotactic effect" (1).  

"Cilia approximately 7 um long, particularly closely spaced near keel, on right side usually paired, on left anterior cilium often lacking in postoral dikinetids. Number of somatic kinetics, which course distinctly spirally, conspicuously constant: in many populations  on average 15-18, with a total variability of 14-20. Keel with 4-7, usually 5 distinct notches. 3-4 postoral kinetics.  Oral apparatus in anterior third. Vestibulum remarkably small in relation to overall size, oral polykinetids protrude. Left polykinetid elliptical, occasionally slightly wedge-shaped or rectangular, distinctly broader than in other members of group, extends horizontally on bottom of vestibulum, its cilia project only slightly beyond body margin. Colpoda maupasi is readily recognizable by this distinctive shape and size of the left polykinetid. The number of kineties it consists of is also fairly constant, viz. 8-12 with an average of 9-10. Right polykinetid composed of about 7 curved kineties, strongly resembling other small Colpoda species, forms an angle of approximately 60° with left polykinetid. No vestibular kineties" (1). 

"Nomenclature, synonymy and taxonomy: Name of author often misspelled "ENRIQUEZ". I synonymize C. fastigata and C. rnarritensis with this species. Colpoda fastigata, described rather superficially by KAHL (1931), cannot be separated from C. maupasi, although both species are often found in listings, when original illustrations and descriptions are compared. A distinction is only possible due to the slightly altered redepiction by KAHL (1931) of the original illustration by ENRIQUES (1908); ENRIQUES' second drawing , largely corresponding to KAHL's illustration of C. fastigata was either not known to or ignored by Kahl!   I also redescribed C. fastigata in 1980, but was always puzzled at never having come across the so often recorded C. maupasi. The present revision, however, finally convinced me that they are synonymous. Most important characters are the short keel; the small, elliptical left polykinetid; and the fairly constant number of somatic kinetics (15-18). Kahl (1931) considers the possibility of identity with C. steinii. This may, however, be safely excluded. Biczok (1955a) found forms very similar to C. inflata under certain experimental conditions and thus suspected synonymy. This too may excluded because C. inflata has a diagonal groove and a morphometrically and morphologically different left oral polykinetid. The remaining synonymy is rather unequivocal. KLEIN (1929) obviously lumped it together with C. steinii and C. cucullus. At least some of his illustrations correspond exactly with C. maupasi; in number of somatic and postoral kineties. The description of C. matritensis may be long, but lacks important details. According to the photographs, however, there can be no doubt that this species corresponds to C. maupasi). The latticed arrangement of the left and right somatic kinetics, mentioned by the authors as a species-specific character, is found also in other species of the genus. It is actually particularly conspicuous in normally and undernourished C. maupasi, with somatic kinetics furrowing the cortex more distinctly than in most other species. The photographs also show clearly that there are only 15-20 somatic kinetics and not 26-28, as stated by the authors in their table" (1). 

Occasional individuals had large bacilliform rods in the cytoplasm and very rare food vacuoles with a fusiform shape around the same size as the bacilli.  This suggested a congener of C. maupasi: C. colpidiopsis, whose shape is very similar.  C. maupasi can be differentiated by C. colpidiopsis by the latter's defining species character, viz. the large, globular extrusomes. This species also has remarkably fusiform food vacuoles that indicate that C. colpidiopsis may possibly need to be assigned to a different (new?) genus.  C. colpidiopsis also is smaller with a length in vivo of 38-55 um, i.e. somewhat smaller than most C. maupasi populations. Also, the macronucleus of C. colpidiopsis is ellipsoid and near cell center, with "difficult to recognize nucleoli" (KAHL 1931).  Gellert (1942) illustrates a very small micronucleus.  C. colpidiopsis has a cortex notched by pearl-like extrusomes (presumably like those in C. tripartita), in single row each between somatic kineties.  Its keel has 4-5 distinct notches as opposed to C, maupasi which has 4-7 notches, usually 5 (1). 

"Body shape. Colpoda maupasi appears slightly reniform when viewed laterally. When viewed ventrally and dorsally the ciliate appears pyriform, shaped like a 'teardrop'. The short preoral keel and anteriorly placed oral cavity give this species a distinctively elongate shape. The postoral portion of the body may become swollen with densely packed food vacuoles.  C. maupasi is completely holotrichous. There are no somatic regions where kinetosomes are usually absent as described for C. steinii (Lynn 1976). The anterior ends of the left keel kineties terminate on an anterior convergence region which is almost dextral. Several kineties insert on the dorsal portion of the convergence region or keel. The kinetal counts for various body regions are quite constant within this clone.  The right and left oral polykinetids are situated, respectively, on the right and posterior walls of the oral cavity. They are oriented about 60 degrees to each other when viewed ventrally. The coniform oral cavity extends dorsad and slightly to the right. Often it is coursed by fine siver lines. The expulsion vesicle pore is located in the extreme posterior left sector. Upon it, most of the somatic kineties converge. No cytoproct was observed, although often slightly anterior to the expulsion vesicle pore, denser silver lines were sometimes present. The spherical macronucleus has a complexly ramified Feulgen-negative 'body'. Feulgen-positive material is distributed among these ramifications. A single crescentic micronucleus is closely apposed to the macronucleus" (2). 

1.   Colpodea (Ciliophora) By Wilhelm Foissner · 1993.  G. Fischer Verlag. pp 123-34. 

2.   Denis H. Lynn; Comparative ultrastructure and systematics of the Colpodida. An ultrastructural description of Colpoda maupasi Enriquez, 1908. Can.J.Zool. 54:405-420, 1976
