576485ba-37d4-4691-b8af-44e3ba4a0f3f.description:
Phacus orbicularis Hübner 1886  from a sample fed with boiled wheat seed from  the edge benthos of freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. 

The cells measure from 46 up to 52 um in length. The s[pepcies was firsts described by Hübner 1886 (1).  We can clearly see the horizontal "struts" perpendicular to the longitudinal pellicular strips first described by Lefevre in 1931 and, after much confusion see (2) felt by  Kozmala et al 2007 to be the distinguishing character for P. orbicularis (2). 

"Species. Ph. orbicularis n. spec. My illustration Fig. 1. Body is almost circular, not painted at the front. The crooked torsion is very developed, the body appears flat. The mouth fold only leads to a slight upward bulging of the dorsal ligaments. The abdominal area on the right side (back view) is visible at the top, but it does not cause any abnormal curvature of the back area. Cuticle delicately striped. Chromatophores, cell nucleus, main vacuole according to the genus character. A large granule in the shape of a disc with a central opening, resting on the ventral surface, in front of or behind the cell nucleus. Terminal spine clearly visible, 1:6 of the body length, pointed left and upwards (back view). Flagellum of body length. Size = 0.07 mm. end spine. Br. = 0.045 mm.  Occasionally, among other Euglenaceae, bird meadows" (1).

"Phacus orbicularis Hübner, Programm d. Realgymnasiums Stransund: 5, fig. 1, 1886. Emend. Zakrys´ et Kosmala. Emended diagnosis: Cells flat, 29–75 um long and 22–49 um wide, widely ovoid, ending with a more or less prominent and curved tail. Fine, numerous struts—perpendicular to the longitudinal axis—located between periplast strips" (2).  "Periplast ornamentation was recognized as a main diagnostic character, distinguishing P. orbicularis from P. pleuronectes and P. hamelii. Phacus orbicularis has struts running perpendicular to the longitudinal axis of the strips, while P. pleuronectes and P. hamelii do not" (2). Support for this morphologic character being distinctive to P. orbicularis among congeners: " On the SSU rDNA tree, obtained by the Bayesian method, P. orbicularis, P. pleuronectes, and P. hamelii belong to three distinct clades" (2).

"Our studies also point out periplast ornamentation, described as ‘‘struts’’ by Leedale (1985), which are positioned perpendicular to the longitudinal axis of the strips. The struts were present in all P. orbicularis strains surveyed by us (Fig. 1, n and u)— all SSU sequences for the P. orbicularis strains clade together on the 18S rDNA tree (Fig. 2)—but struts were not observed in P. pleuronectes or P. hamelii (Fig. 1, o and t). Lefevre (1931) was the first to notice ‘‘perpendicular stripes’’ in P. orbicularis and take them into account in his drawings. Lefevre’s drawings were used later by Pochmann (1942, fig. 78, k and n), albeit without any commentary. This action suggests that both Lefevre and Pochmann, as well as others, did not consider struts to be a diagnostic feature distinguishing P. orbicularis from P. pleuronectes. This also might be the reason for not considering struts as diagnostic in spite of their appearing on drawings of several other species (P. rostafinski [Drezepolski _ 1921 ⁄ 1922, pl. 1, fig. 3]; P. platalea [Drezepolski _ 1925, pl. 3, fig. 110]; P. caudata var. minor and var. ovalis [Drezepolski 1925, pl. 3, figs. 107 and 111]; _ P. longicauda [Lefe´vre 1931, pl. 3, fig. 32]; Phacus triqueter [Leander and Farmer 2001, fig. 3a]). The presence of perpendicular struts on the iconotype of P. platalea Drezepolski 1925 (fig. 110), as well as its _ other features, such as the size and shape of the cell and the relatively long (12–15 lm) tail, prompted us to consider P. platalea as a synonym of P. orbicularis. In our view, the presence of struts is a good diagnostic feature for distinguishing P. orbicularis from P. pleuronectes since it is not susceptible to individual, developmental, and environmental variability. Moreover, struts are clearly visible under the light microscope, even in very small cells (in which case, a brief drying out of the material facilitates observations; Fig. 1, n and u)" (2)

1.  Hübner, E.F.W. (1886). Euglenaceen-Flora von Stralsund. Programm des Realgymnasiums Stralsund 1886: 1-20, 1 pl.. 

2.  MORPHOLOGICAL AND MOLECULAR EXAMINATION OF RELATIONSHIPS AND EPITYPE ESTABLISHMENT OF PHACUS PLEURONECTES, PHACUS ORBICULARIS, AND PHACUS HAMELII.  Sylwia Kosmala, Magdalena Bereza, Rafał Milanowski, Jan Kwiatowski, and Bozena Zakrys. J. Phycol. 43, 1071–1082 (2007)

0279cf19-7f90-4f51-810e-350aa5146df0.description:
Lagynus elegans (Engelmann, 1862) Quennerstedt, 1867 from a new sampling site: Georgica Cove, a brackish (5 ppt salinity) landward offshoot of estuary Georgica Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. 

The cells measure 130-160 um in length and exhibit the classic amphora-shaped body with a flexible neck region showing four annular constrictions atop which is the oral bulge with a prominent oral basket of nematodesmata. There is an ovoid to elliposid macronucleus and for the first time I have been able to demonstrate the micronucleus. For this observation, I compare with the most recent redescription of the species, that of Jiang et al 2023 (1).  Their population was somewhat smaller than the current observation (80-125 um vs 130-160 um) but their improved diagnosis gives a range of 80-200 um based on analysis of several population reports (1).   

This population is unusual in that, like Liang et al 2023 who report the presence of two micronuclei, I also observed some cells with two micronuclei.  Liang et al 2023 note that Engelmann (1862); Sola et al. (1990); and Foissner et al. (1995)  all report a single micronucleus.  "However, only one micronucleus was recorded in all the above populations, whereas the Chinese population clearly shows two micronuclei. It is noteworthy that the size difference of the micronucleus between the two populations observed by Penard (1922) was signifcant although there was only one micronucleus per cell in each population. In addition, a variable number of micronuclei was also reported within the Chinese population of the prostomatean Pelagothrix plancticola Foissner et al., 1999 (Jiang et al. 2022). Thus, the number of micronuclei may be variable within Lagynus elegans, and could be a population-level diference" (1).

"This species was originally reported by Engelmann (1862) and was subsequently redescribed several times (Foissner et al. 1995; Kahl 1930; Liebmann 1962; Penard 1922; Quennerstedt 1867; Sola et al. 1990; Wetzel 1928). Based on new data from the Chinese population, it is redefined as follows. Improved diagnosis Cell size 80–200 × 30–60  μm in vivo; amphora-shaped; single globular to long-ellipsoidal macronucleus and one or two micronuclei; rod-shaped extrusomes, irregularly distributed beneath pellicle; contractile vacuole terminally located; three to six cervical kineties and 26–50 somatic kineties. Freshwater and brackish water habitat" (1). 

"Description Cell size in vivo about 80–125×30–55 μm, 100 × 30 μm on average (n=25), with a length to width ratio of 3–4:1 (Fig. 5A, C, E, F, H). Cell generally amphora-shaped, with an enlarged ellipsoidal main part, posterior end broadly rounded; starved individuals cylindroid, with posterior half of cell fattened and transparent (Fig. 5A, C, E, F, H). Neck-like region fexible and contractile, with four deep furrows (Fig. 5A, E, H). Oral bulge prominently projected from anterior end of cell, forming an apical plate; cytostome apical and circular; oral basket inverted trapezoidal, size about 8–11×4–6 μm after protargol staining; rod-shaped nematodesmata about 7 μm long in vivo (Fig. 5A, E, K, L, O). Cell surface with longitudinal ridges throughout cell length (Fig. 5G). Cytoplasm opaque and grayish due to being filled with multitudinous food vacuoles and light-refracting granules (Fig. 5A, F, H). Extrusomes 6–10 μm long in vivo, rod-shaped, irregularly distributed beneath pellicle (Fig. 5C). One macronucleus, globular to long-ellipsoidal, located in mid-cell, size about 18–33×8–17 μm after staining; two globular to ellipsoidal micronuclei, closely associated with macronucleus, size about 1–2 × 3–4 μm after DAPI staining (Fig. 5I, J). Single contractile vacuole, terminally located, about 11 μm in diameter (Fig. 5A, H). Locomotion by swimming moderately fast, with no obvious pattern" (1). 

"Somatic cilia about 10 μm long in vivo; in total, 26–37 somatic kineties consisting of monokinetids (Fig. 5B, N). One dikinetidal circumoral kinety encircling anterior end of cell (Fig. 5B, D, O). Brosse region composed of three rows of kineties, each of which contains two or three basal bodies (Fig. 5B, D, M). Invariably three perioral kineties, each ring-like and composed of dikinetids (Fig. 5B, D, M, O). Five or six cervical kineties around neck-like region, arranged in rings (Fig. 5B, N)" (1).


1.  Morphological and molecular examination of the ciliate family Lagynusidae (Protista, Ciliophora, Prostomatea) with descriptions of two new genera and two new species from China. Limin Jiang, Congcong Wang, Saleh A. Al‑Farraj, Hunter N. Hines and Xiaozhong Hu. Marine Life Science & Technology (2023) 5:178–195 https://doi.org/10.1007/s42995-023-00174-1

918dd96d-5a5e-4434-b770-2506017b1927.description:
Trochiliopsis opaca Penard, 1922 from a sample of freshwater Lake Agawam in the Village of Southampton, New York USA.   The cells measure from 32-40 um in length.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. 

There are two species in this microthoracid genus: the type species T. opaca and T. australis.  The cells have a dorsoventrally compressed rounded oblong body with peculiar ridging on left and right sides. There is a small anterior overhang or beak associated with the indistinct cytostome where there are two adoraal membranelles.   Augustin, Foissner and  Adam 1987 state that the cyrtos is invisible even with interference contrast and that the macronucleus is difficult to visualize in vivo. This is the type species T. opaca since T. australis has deeper ridges. It is interesting that both Penard 1922 and Augustin, Foissner and  Adam 1987 state that food vacuoles were not seen. This sample was rich in spherical small green algae and was fed with boiled wheat seed and then neglected for two weeks.  This population shows many cells distended with globular refractile food vacuoles possibly representing ingested algae. 

Penard's original 19922 description: "Trochiliopsis opaca gen. nov. sp. n. Body vaguely ellipsoidal, rounded behind, convex on the right side and with no or barely noticeable convexity on the left side, curved towards the left at its part anterior and ending in a hooked beak. The animal is strongly compressed laterally, and we can then distinguish a right flank, divided into four or five longitudinal segments or ribbons separated by deep furrows; then a divided left flank in an equal number of ribbons, but more regular, clearly arched and concaved turned towards the left side. In the furrows and on both sides arise thin and long cilia which are not very abundant; forward and under the characteristic beak, they are more tight and more vigorous, and curve downwards like a hook. Under the top of the beak, on the left flank, you can see an edge (?) or double vertical line outline, which, parallel to the edge of the animal, goes straight down to a very long distance towards the posterior part of the body. Spherical nucleus, not very bulky, central. Contractile vacuole above the  nucleus. Length 35 to 40 µ" (1).

"This is a very small organism, Fig. 103. Trochiliopsis opaca whose characters almost escape all in sight, and the study of which, which still remains very incomplete, could not be pursued only with great difficulty. Although the body is very pale, very pure, and contains only very small shiny grains scattered in a cytoplasm where coarser food boluses do not seem to be found, its cuticle rigid, colorless, is entirely opalescent, of such an opalescence that the light appears to be reflected in it; it is then very difficult to distinguish anything other than the contractile vesicle, then a core always vaguely outlined; longitudinal striations, on the other hand, are more clean, straight and equal on the right side (fig. 1), arched on the left side (fig. 2), where we still see, starting from the terminal beak, a very straight edge, the meaning of which cation remains enigmatic. But what is most characteristic in this organism, these are the trichocysts, small, very indistinct rods which escape the most often in plain sight, but which, after the explosion, appear in a curious form, a relatively short filament, and terminated at its distal end by two, three, or more generally four hooked points (fig. 4), divaricate, such that approximately we will soon see them again in another Infusoria (Pseudomicrothorax) where they were able be better studied. Fig. 3 shows the Infusoria seen from above, with the furrows on its two faces. Trochiliopsis opaca was found, still quite rare, at Ariana, in the leaves dead from Swan Pond" (1).

From the redescription of Augustin, Foissner and  Adam 1987   "Trochiliopsis Penard, 1922 Class Kinetofragminophora: Subclass Hypostomata: Order Nassulida: Suborder Microthoracina Genus TROCHILIOPSIS Penard, 1922.  Diagnosis. Microthoracidae Wrzesniowski, 1870 with cytostome in the anterior third of body. Three preoral kineties subapically on the left body side. Somatic kineties from either side terminate near the pointed beak-like region formed by the oral structures. Apex smooth. Right-most somatic kinety of the right side interrupted. Contractile vacuole located almost centrally. Freshwater, polysaprobic" (2). 

"Type-species . Trochiliopsis opaca Penard, 1922.   Freshwater. In vivo circa 30-40(-50) x 17-20 um. Body outline oval, anteriorly curved slightly to the ventral side terminating in a pointed beak-like region (peak). Body strongly compressed laterally (circa 2:1) and covered in a rigid longitudinally ribbed armour. Somatic kinetics in deep, crenelated furrows, which terminate near the oral peak. Macronucleus spherical, more or less centrally located, in vivo hardly discernible. Micronucleus closely attached to the macronucleus. Contractile vacuole centrally located above macronucleus, close to the right lateral surface, diameter about 4 um; contractile vacuole pore at the end of the paroral membrane. Cytoproct slightly posterior to the contractile vacuole pore, visible as black line in dry silvered specimen (Fig. 130). Pellicle rigid, colourless, opaque. Extrusomes about 3 um, fusiform, scattered over the whole body in the ribs between the furrows, show four anchor-like processes at the distal end in the exploded phase. Probably feeds on bacteria, but no food vacuoles were found. Slow, trembling and swaying movements. Probably only two adoral membranelles, located at the oral peak. Anterior adoral membranelle most likely built up by two rows, posterior one probably by three rows of kinetosomes. Paroral membrane with 8-9 paired basal bodies (Figs 120, 122, 124). Cyrtos invisible in life even with interference contrast, but slightly impregnated with protargol silver" (2).

1.  Penard, E. 1922. Etudes sur les infusoires d'eau douce. Georg et Cie, Geneve

2. Revision of the genera Acineria, Trimyema and Trochiliopsis (Protozoa, Ciliophora)H. Augustin, W. Foissner & H. Adam. Zoologisches Institut der Universitat Salzburg. Bulletin of the British Museum (Natural History) Zoology 52 pages 197-224 ( 24 Jun 1987 )

b530a0ac-8416-4a03-b645-0a71a989be2d.description:
Caenomorpha capucina Kahl, 1932 from the benthos of Georgica Cove, a brackish (5 ppt salinity) landward offshoot of estuary Georgica Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  The cell body length is 80 um and total length including caudal spine is 100 um.  The size (based on Kahl's illustration labelled 100 um), the quite coarse granulation, the configuration of the two spines, and the macronucleus shape (sausage-shaped with large round  micronucleus), are diagnostic.  Jankowski notes that macronucleus size and shape are quite strong characters to differentiate Caenomorpha species other than C. medusula (1). 

The species is listed in Carey 1992: "Caenomorpha capucina Kahl, 1932  Helmet-shaped or medusoid, 50-70 µm in length. There are two posterior spines. The macronucleus is large and sausage-shaped".  Kahl's original description:  "Caenomorpha capucina Size of Body 50-70 um, caudal spines just as long, secondary spines little shorter. The frontal ridge forms a strongly pronounced ectoplasmic fold to the right. The front, as a narrow cap extends over and so also forms a clearly splayed edge running parallel to it in front of the ciliated bell edge. After overlap of the right, this edge converges on the dorsal side to the main seam, and runs into the base of the tail.  Cytoplasm with coarse, dark appearing reserve bodies, which are particularly clustered at the front. Macronucleus pretty long sausage-shaped, micronucleus large, round, slightly stainable. The most complicated Caenomorpha; extremely interesting in terms of phylogenetic history as the final link in the series of developments: med., lauterborni; levanderi. Opposite of the strong development of the strongly spiral ridges with their three secondary seams the adoral zone is very reduced (less than the last half turn). On the first half are the rudimentary membranelles hidden in cilia. Not uncommon in the sapropel of the bridge bay of Schilksee (Kiel); the ventral hilltop is also very fond of stunted forms; is the secondary spine rarely rudimentary" (1). 

The congener C. lauterborni is smaller at 70 um, has an ovoid macrunculeus (vs sausage shaped in C. capucina), has a spine 2 that is curved toward the much longer caudal spine 1 while in C. capucina the two spines are roughly parallel and closer in length.  Jankowski notes that  "spine 2 is poorly developed in a majority of C.lauterborni; it looks sometimes like a short needle-like somewhat curved prominence of an armour in the contractile vacuole area" (2).  Another congener, C. levanderi,  is reported as similar in size per Kahl (80-100 um) (1) or smaller (60-70 um per Jankowski) (2), has an elongated ovoid (2) or ellipsoid short sausage-shaped (1) macronucleus, and the spine 2 never develops here unlike C. lauterborni (2).  Neither of these congeners show the coarse granular aggregate of C. capucina (1,2). .  Congeners are depicted at the end of the illustrations. 

1. A. Kahl; [Urtiere oder Protozoa I: Wimpertiere oder Ciliata (Infusoria) 3. Spirotricha]. Die Tierwelt Deutschlands und der angrenzenden Meeresteile. Germany:Verlag von Gustav Fischer. (3), 1932 

2.  Morphology and Evolution of Ciliophora. III.  Diagnoses and Phylogenesis of 53 Sapropelebionts, Mainly of the order Heterotrichida  By AXATOLY. JANKOWSKI   Arch. Protistenk. Bd. 107,pp 185-294 (1961)

a0840551-f106-4b9b-920f-89a4d70a20df.description:
Plagiopyla nasuta Stein 1860 from the northernmost edge benthos of freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. Sample was fed with boiled wheat seeds. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 objective and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  The cell measures 100 um in length. 

Plagiopyla "live in the saprobic portion of the water column of freshwater systems or in brackish and seawater habitats. They typically live in oxygen-depleted/ unoxygenated environments. These organisms bear, in their cytoplasm, hydrogenosomes and symbiotic methanogenic Archaea, prokaryotic organisms able to 
gain energy from methane production through different metabolic pathways" (1). 

Nitla et al 2019 performed a comprehensive neotypification and comparison of P. nasuta since "P. nasuta has never been redescribed up to now according to requirements of integrative taxonomy (morphology, ultrastructure and molecular characterization of a marker gene)"  by Stein and subsequent investigators (1).   They detailed many specific morphologic characters such as cell size and shape, number of types and size and shape of extrusomes, number of contractile vacuole pores, distance of cross striated band from the cytoproct, ciliature associated with the cytoprocct, number and type of micronuclei.  My observations: the ovoid cell dorsoventrally flattened measuring 100 um, the single type of extrusome- namely straight filamentous subcortically arrayed, two contractile vacuole pores, cross striated band terminating approximately 4 ciliary row thickness from the cytoproct, cytoproct with thee densely packed ciliary rows on the right side, and a single compact-type micronucleus adjacent to the ovoid macronucleus all are in agreement with the neotypification of Nitla et al 2019. 

"Ovoid body, dorso-ventrally flattened  with the peculiar slit in correspondence to the cytostome, opening on the ventral side.  Live specimens about 94.0 ± 7.1 × 57.2 ± 7.6 µm.  Length/width ratio around 1.6 for live specimens. Swimming in anticlockwise direction with respect to the longitudinal body axis when viewed from the posterior end. Somatic cilia organized in 66–84 longitudinal rows of monokinetids (35–46 dorsal rows, 31–38 ventral rows) (Fig. 14A, B). Somatic cilia terminating slightly before oral region, leaving a narrow, empty space.  All somatic cilia running to the end of the body except for 3–5 rows on the dorsal side, terminating at the cytoproct.  Oral region constituted by two lip-like structures (upper lip and lower lip), bearing denser and longer cilia than somatic ones. Striated band about 60.2 ± 4.6 µm long, commencing above oral region, running on dorsal side of the cell.  Its surface showing the peculiar striated pattern without cilia. Cell length/striated band ratio about 1.6. Cytoproct 25.4 µm long on average in silver-stained cells, located on dorsal side, commencing below cell equator toward the posterior cell end; on its left side, two or three short rows of narrowly spaced cilia. Contractile vacuole in posterior body portion, opening on dorsal side through two pores. A single, ovoid macronucleus (21.3 × 13.5 µm on average after Feulgen staining), and one roundish, compact-type, micronucleus (diameter 2.6 µm on average after Feulgen staining) located close to the macronucleus. Numerous straight, multi-layered extrusomes, uniformly distributed underneath the cortex (5.9 µm in length on average), and roundish, electron dense cortical granules (diameter around 0.3 µm) observed" (1).

1. 3dc9b58c-77de-4982-a68e-60dea8b94cf3.description:
Chaetonotus (Zonochaeta) succinctus VOIGT, 1902  belonging to the subgenus Zonochaeta, from the northernmost edge benthos of freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 objective and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Smasung Galaxy S24.   The animal measures 200 um in length. 

Thanks to Michael Müller who identifies this. He wrote: 
This is definitely Chaetonotus (Zonochaeta) succinctus VOIGT, 1902:

a pair of long bristles at the base of the toes, extending beyond the adhesive tubes
a pair of lateral long bristles somewhat in front of the toes
9 long bristles in a line in the middle of the trunk
bigger round scales behind the girdle of the long bristles, smaller scales in front of them
ventral:
no terminal plates
terminally many (18-20) rows of very small oval keeled scales
in the pharynx region rectangular braces
ciliated bands split in several branches near the mouth
pharynx with a strong terminal bulbus
length of 200µm fits perfectly (190µm - 235µm)
Ch. succinctus is a typical member of the muddy benthos. Not very rare, but I doubt, that there are many people around, who have already seen it!

Dr. Martin Kreutz has shown this species on his website: https://realmicrolife.com/chaetonotus-succinctus/

*body vigorous, stocky
*length 190–235 µm
*head weakly five-lobed, 4 lateral tufts of cilia,
*cephalion present
*two pairs of dorsal setolae at posterior end on large special scales
*toes 32–39 µm long with short base and thin adhesive tubes
*girdle of 9 curved, simple spines near mid-body on dorsal side
*11 dorsal longitudinal rows of polygonal scales with small keels in anterior half
*7 dorsal longitudinal rows of large bilobed keel scales, which medially carry a spiny tip and overlap strongly in posterior half
*laterally on posterior trunk 2 long spines
*on base of furca 2 long spines exceeding the length of toes
*ventral ciliated bands split anteriorly into several branches
*ventral side with 18–20 longitudinal rows of minute oval keel scales
*without terminal plates on ventral side

"Chaetonotus succinctus is very distinctive, due to its row of 9 long spines in the middle of the body and two further pairs of long spines in the posterior half of the body. It can be confused with Chaetonotus aemilianus and Lepidochaetus zelinkai, which also have a girdle of spines in the middle of the body. However, the spines of these species have secondary spines, whereas in Chaetonotus succinctus they are simple. Another characteristic feature of Chaetonotus succinctus is the alternation of the scale form above and below the girdle of long spines. The posterior half is covered with larger scales" (1). 

1. https://realmicrolife.com/chaetonotus-succinctus/

40af631b-aa20-4494-bf8c-86aa7d2d7c01.description:
Actinophrys sol Ehrenberg 1830 from the benthos of the freshwater Lake Agawam which polluted by runoff. The cell measures 60 um in diameter.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  

Diagnosis: Body spherical with protoplasm highly vacuolated. Usually one contractile vacuole which rises and pushes out the surface as a rounded globule before bursting. Pseudopodia extending from all parts of the body, with axial filaments arising from the membrane of the single nucleus. Cyst brown, with several layers, with a mucus layer and a layer of irregular siliceous scales. Sexual reproduction by autogamy after encystment.   
”Fressgemeinschaften”” (feeding communities) not rare. Dimensions: Main body 19-90 µm in diameter; nucleus 10-19.2 µm.

Actinophrys species belong to an informal group known as heliozoa, which are unicellular eukaryotes (or protists) that are heterotrophic (also known as protozoa) and present stiff radiating arms known as axopodia. In particular, Actinophrys species are characterized by axonemes consisting of double interlocking spirals of microtubules. Their axonemes end on a large central nucleus. They are also characterized by the siliceous material present in their cysts.
The most noticeable thing about Actinophrys and Actinophaerium are their axipodia. They are attached to the nuclear membrane surface and protrude outwards. The axopodia are supported by axial rods from within the cell. Its axopodia have a number of purposes, capturing or killing prey, and for protection from its predators, which flow along its arms. The axopodia are able to contract quickly to capture their prey. There was a presumed contractile element called contractile tubules structure that was shown to cause the axopodial cytoplasm to create beads along the length of the pseudopod. They are then able to hold onto the prey because of the protein gp40, which is stored in secretory glands called extrusomes. The protein gp40 also contributes to self recognition.

Actinophrys and Actinophaerium obtain energy heterotrophically. The axopodia will capture the prey and bring it to the body, which will then form a food vacuole to surround and digest the organism. After this the organism is lysed, the contents of the vacuole coagulate and much of the fluid is removed from the vacuole. Then the rest of the undigested food in the vacuoles is egested.
There are currently four accepted species of Actinophrys. Actinophrys was described in 1830 by German naturalist Christian Gottfried Ehrenberg, with the type species Actinophrys sol. The species originally belonged to a genus named Trichoda, described earlier by Otto Friedrich Müller and later declared obsolete. In 1824, Bory de St. Vincent transferred that species to a new genus Peritricha but, without any new observations to justify the change, it fell out of use.

53f433ed-ed5f-4a29-b06f-e3e8b6d219e6.description:
Trochiloides recta (Kahl, 1928) Kahl, 1931 from the northernmot edge benthos of Georgica Cove, a brackish (5 ppt salinity) landward offshoot of estuary Georgica Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  The cell measures 48 um in length. I the videos we can see the ciliate rotate on the coverglass pivoting on its podite which secretes mucus to help adhere. 

Foissner et al 1991 (1) provide the most complete description and note that prior descriptions Kahl 1931 (2) and Borror 1972 (3)  provide differing accounts of the ciliature (1).  My population conforms most closest to that of Foissner et al 1992.  Pan et al 2011 also provide a description though their population is somewhat smaller and more rounded anteriorly lacking the truncated anterior (2). 
 
From Foissner et al 1992:  
1) 25 - 35 um (salt water) or 30 - 50 um (fresh water) long and about half as wide (KahlL928a, 1931). According to BORROR (1972b) 43 - 60 x 23 - 31 um and t6 - 20 um thick. According to DEROUX (1976b) 45 - 75 um long.
2) Outline obovate, appearing somewhat asymmetrical rectangular. The left side almost pulls parallel with the longitudinal axis to the rear curve, where it has a very short peak on the right side peak. Right side slightly convex, slightly projecting towards the front. Anterior end almost dorsally truncated transversely. This transverse section is covered by a transparent, convex ventral plate. 
3) Slightly flattened, almost flat ventrally, more convex dorsally at the back than at the front. pellicle smooth, slightly armor-like. Rear end of the right ciliary field sunk and according to KAHL (1928a) surmounted by the roof-like rising edges of the ventral side. .
4) Macronucleus ellipsoid, left of the middle of the body, anterior part vesicular and with a small internal body, posterior part coarsely granulated. 
5) 2 contractile vacuoles on the first and last quarter in the right cilia field.
6) Podite ventrally on the edge of the right cilia field, blunt-pointed, short, does not protrude beyond the posterior end.
7) The representation of ciliation differs somewhat in KAHL (1928a, 1931), BORROR (1972b) and DEROUX (1976b), which is understandable since the older descriptions only based on live observations. 5 - 6 ciliary rows go around the podite and run along the right edge to the front. The 2 outer rows are located at the front behind the front plate and extend to the left side, the inner rows are on the right of the cyrtos. Above the oral opening 2 perioral rows of cilia. Left ciliary field with 12 -16 short, parallel rows (only clearly visible in interference contrast and after silver impregnation! 
8) Mouth in the front right quadrant of the cell. The cyrtos extends to the rear edge of the body, where it bends like a cornucopia. According to KAHL (L928a) and DEROUX (1976b), it consists of 6 rods.

Differential diagnosis from Foissner et al 1991: "See also Trochilia minuta and “Taxonomy”. The one that is very similar in infraciliature (so far the only well-described freshwater form) Trochilioides fimbriatus FOISSNER, 1984b differs from T. recta (KAHL, 1928a) in the dorsal curtain of the cyrtos, KAHL (1928a), BORROR (L972b) and DEROUX (1976b; despite silver impregnation) in their species did not mention. The review revealed that this curtain is not detectable in vivo and therefore at least could not be seen by the older authors. Therefore, T. fimbriatus and T. recta are probably synonymous. Since T. fimbriatus is not yet in saprobiological lists is recorded (FOISSNER found it at SI: 2.5), it is not described here, but for comparison shown. The similar Trochilioides artemiae lives ectoparasitically on Artemia salina (TUCOLESCO 1962b). Features 6,7 are particularly important for identification"  (1).

From Pan et al 2011:  "Description of Qingdao population: Cells about 35 × 20 μm in vivo. Body broad oval in outline with both ends bluntly rounded. Dorsoventrally flattened about 2:1, ventral side flat, in right region slightly concave where the ventral ciliary rows are located; dorsal side somewhat humped. Cytostome ventrally positioned at anterior 1/5 of body length; about six conspicuous nematodesmal rods around it. Cytoplasm colourless, containing some greasily shinning globules (2–3 μm across). Two contractile vacuoles, 5 μm in diameter, located at anterior and posterior 1/4 of cell. Podite about 6 μm long, caudally positioned. Single ellipsoid macronucleus in central region, about 15 × 10 μm in vivo. Infraciliature 17–20 somatic kineties in total, comprising six right kineties, six to nine left kineties and five postoral kineties. Two right-most kineties, almost equal in length, and extending anteriorly to anterior margin. Postoral and left kineties very short and distributed in anterior body half, the posterior ends of which are progressively shortened from right to left (Fig. 3J). Equatorial fragment  composed of 0–14 basal bodies, while terminal fragment consisting of 4–6 ones. Usually, five or six kinetosome-like granules present near the base of podite and arranged in a letter “C” pattern. Two circumoral kineties and one preoral kinety composed of dikinetids and obliquely arranged" (2). 

Kahl's original description:  Trochilioides recta KAHL, 1928 Size Gr. 40-50 um Shape short obovoid but in front not according to l. expansive, but against the stretched L. side in a blunt angle butting, i.e. without notch. Cyrtos with six rods, up to extending to the rear end where it curves to the left.  Side panel with five rows, especially placed at the back. Podite very short, almost button-like, hardly mobile; otherwise normal. hardly mobile; otherwise normal. Dorsally more arched, smooth, but with a characteristic right furrow from the hind end. This is curved ventrally. Preorally, on the ventral side, there is an ectopic plate projecting over the anterior end of the dorsal surface. Two preoral rows draw in the dorsal furrow to the beak, the other two form the mentioned membranelles. Apparently only eats Beggiatoa, which rolls up in the body with the help of the cyrtos, but is soon distributed into blackish food vacuoles. Only once abundant in shallow sapropel freshwater pool, but in Oldesloe very common to numerous in all concentrations (0.3-2.5%), i.e. halobiont, euryhaline (3). 

Borror 1972 provides this description:  "Trochilioides recta Kahl, 1928  Length 43-60 um. Width 23-31 um. Thickness about 2/3 the width (16-20 um). Cell truncate anteriorly, widest just posterior to anterior end, tapering gradually to evenly rounded but narrower posterior end. Dorsal surface evenly convex, the lateral surface converging ventrally, narrowing the ciliated portion of the ventral surface. Buccal cavity anteroventral, with cytostome at its base. Edges of cytostome raised as obvious cortical lips. A secretory papilla arises near posterior ends of ciliary rows. 
Ciliation . Cilia in four groups of rows, labelled A, B, C, and D in this discussion.  Group A: 13-16 parallel short postbuccal rows. Group B: two rows extending from cytostome posteriorly beyond secretory papilla. Group C: three rows extending from secretory papilla anteriorly along right ventral surface; left row terminating near anterior end (other two rows curving along anterodorsal edge of buccal cavity, terminating a few micrometers posterior of anterior end on left lateral surface; at this termination, two additional short rows of cilia present). Group D: two close set rows of cilia, with a unified beat, extending to animal's left and anterolateral from cytostome. Internal anatomy . Macronucleus heteromerous, approximately 26 pm long, 17 um wide consisting of anterior diffused section and posterior more granular portion (see Faure-Fremiet 1957). Water expulsion vesicle small, near secretory papilla. Cytopharynx with two sets of fibrils. Narrow, poorly refractile fibrils extend posterior from cytostome at least 1/3 cell length. In addition, 10 oral trichites more obvious, approximately 23 um in length, arranged as in Fig. 19" (4). 

"Discussion . In 1932 Kahl listed five species in this genus. Since then at least five additional species have been described (Faure-Fremiet and Guilcher 1948; Tucolesco 1962; Fenchel 1965; and Jankowski 1967). Kahl distinguished other species on the basis of body shape. In size and shape the present population most nearly resembles T. recta Kahl, 1928. According to Kahl, however, the cytopharyngeal basket contains only six nematodesmata that reach the posterior end of the cell and then bend to the left. He described it as eating Beggiatoa. Trochilioides oculata Kahl, 1933 is larger (length = 100 (im), with the ciliary rows of group A longer. Trochilioides filans Faure-Fremiet et Guilcher, 1948 is ectocommensal on planktonic copopods. Trochilioides trivialis Fenchel, 1965 has relatively long ciliary rows in group A, and a narrow unciliated vestibulum, and is ectocommensal on amphipods. T. bathybius Jankowski, 1967 has three rows of cilia in group D, each perpendicular to the long axis of the body, and five rows of cilia in group C. T. littoralis Jankowski, 1967 has two rows of cilia in group D like T. recta, but differs in arrangement of ciliary rows in group A and C, body shape, and cytopharyngeal structure" (4). 

Finally, Carey 1991:  "Trochiloides recta (Kahl, 1928) Kahl, 1931  Trochilia recta Kahl, 1928 Small, ovoid, 45-50 µm long. The edges where surfaces meet are slightly angular. The ventral ciliated area is quite conspicuous. The cytopharyngeal apparatus is reduced but the cytopharynx is long and curving, reaching almost to the posterior extremity. The anterior of the cell is ornamented by a field of long vibratile cilia. There is a single macronucleus and two contractile vacuoles" (5). 

1.  Wilhelm Foissner, Hubert Blatterer, Helmut Berger, and Fritz Kohmann; [Taxonomische und okologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobiensystems Band I: Cyrtophorida, Oligotrichida, Hypotrichia, Colpodea]. Informationsberichte des Bayerisches Landesamt fur Wasserwirtschaft. 1/91:478 pp, 1991 

2.  Taxonomic Studies on Three Marine Ciliates from China, Including a New Species (Ciliophora, Cyrtophorida) Hongbo PAN, Honggang MA, Xiaozhong HU, Khaled A. S. AL-RASHEID and Saleh A. AL-FARRAJ. Acta Protozool. (2013) 52: 25–33

3. A. Kahl; [Urtiere oder Protozoa I: Wimpertiere oder Ciliata (Infusoria) 2. Holotricha]. Die Tierwelt Deutschlands und der angrenzenden Meeresteile. Germany:Verlag von Gustav Fischer. (2)-398, 1931 (In file)

4.  Tidal marsh ciliates (Protozoa): morphology, ecology, systematics. Arthur C. Borror. ACTA PROTOZOOLOGICA WARSZAWA, Volume  X 1972  FASC. 2.  

5. Marine Interstitial Ciliates: An illustrated key (Chapman & Hall Identification Guide) by Philip G. Carey (1991) pp. 122, 26722, 267

Mesodinium pulex (Claparède & Lachmann, 1859) Stein, 1867 from the benthos of a small tidal pool at the edge of the salt marsh bordering estuary Acabonac Harbor.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  The cell measures 28 um in length and 20 um in diameter.  The cell is pyriform but divided by a waist-like furrow. Somatic ciliation reduced to two bands arising from central furrow. 

Ciliates from the genus Mesodinium are globally distributed in marine and freshwater ecosystems and may possess either heterotrophic or mixotrophic nutritional modes. M. pulex is strictly heterotrophic and does not use chloroplasts from prey. 

Mesodinium pulex has a characteristic swimming style. Between very fast jumps, the ciliate rests vertically and starts to spin. This is followed by further jumps at a very high swimming speed.  

Diagnosis: 
body pyriform, with a furrow in mid-body. length 15–35 µm
cytopharynx apical, surrounded by retractable tentacles with triangular or forked ends. pre-equatorial wreath cirri, directed anteriorly, distal ends split. 
equatorial wreath of cilia, directed posteriorly.  two spherical maconuclei in mid-body. extrusomes absent. one terminal contractile vacuole

32fa772f-c017-4342-a107-88c7c2399beb.description:
Hartmannula angustipilosa Deroux and Dragesco 1968 from the benthos of a small tidal pool at the edge of the salt marsh bordering estuary Acabonac Harbor.  Salinity is 33 o/oo.   Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objectives plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  

 I was able to image one free-swimming individual which closely resembled the population illustrated by  Agamaliev 1974, as well as several compressed individuals in varying states of obtundation.  Under the latter conditions, the cell shape became somewhat distorted- more pointed posteriorly and curled under laterally.  One feature that has not been previously described in any Hartmannula species is an apparent dense coat of rod-shaped bacteria, perhaps ectosymbionts, covering the dorsal surface which is visible also on the curled under edges in obtunded cells.   In addition, in compressed cells,  vacuoles other than the characteristic longitudinal row of contractile vacuoles on the right side were formed.  Despite these variances, the cell size, number of nematodesmata in the cyrtos, number and arrangement of contractile vacuoles all point to the diagnosis of H. angustipilosa among all species in the genus.

I sent images to Dr. Jun Gong, author of both reference papers below. The reply from him and his colleagues confirms the diagnosis. "As I do not work with ciliate taxonomy for a couple of years, I have sent your message to my ciliate colleagues who is academically active in this field and kept updated. They have responded to me that the species is highly likely Hartmannula angustipilosa, given its body shape, size, numbers of kineties and rods, CV, and your other descriptions, and pictures. My colleagues in Qingdao have found and observed this species from time to time, with almost identical morphological records as yours. Pigment in the frontal of the cell is usually present, but this feature is generally not important for species identification. The only uncertainty could be the number of right kineties, which you did not mention. However, in my experience, it should be in the recorded range of H. angustipilosa.  Hope this helps"  

In my population, the cells measure from 45- 49.6 um in length and are oval in outline with rounded anterior and posterior margins and the anterior projected to the left forming a blunt "beak" where there is a yellowish pigment spot. Gong and Song 2004 in their redescription of H. angustipilosa did not mention the yellow pigment spot in their population, however this can be a variable character among Harmannula species and has been observed before in H. angustipilosa: as Shao et 2008 (2) write:  "The yellowish pigment spot described here in H. sinica is not unique to this species; similar pigment spots have been observed also in H. derouxi and H. angustipilosa (Gong, unpublished observation)" (2).   In profile, we can see that the ventral surface is flat and the dorsal surface is vaulted but more flattened anteriorly. The anterior cytostome is surrounded by a cyrtos of 11 toothed nematodemsal rods. There is a  podite positioned subcaudally in the midline.  There are 4-6 pulsating contractile vacuoles arrayed in a longitudinal row on the right side.  The cytoplasm is greyish and ingesta are observed. The central macronucleus is oval and heteromeric. 

"Description of Qingdao population from Gong and Song 2004: "Cell size in vivo 40–60 x 20–30 um, and oval in outline shape, with anterior and posterior margins rounded, anterior ‘beak’ projected to left; dorsoventrally about 1:3 flattened. Ventral surface flat, while dorsally vaulted. Cyrtos consisting of about 10 toothed nematodesmata, 15 um long, tapering posteriorly. Endoplasm greyish, with numerous small granules (ca 1–4 mm in diameter), ingested algae also frequently observed. Macronucleus oval, centrally positioned, ca 12 um in diameter. Cilia 5 um long. Podite small, about 6 mm in length, located almost central near posterior end. Ventral surface around podite usually twisted, and probably plays a role in attachment. Four to seven contractile vacuoles, about 3 mm in diameter, longitudinally arranged on right; contractile vacuole pores can be recognized after impregnation between kinety 7 and 8.  Movement moderately fast, crawling or sliding over substrata" (1).

 "Ventral kineties in 24–28 rows. Five to six kineties extending apically, bending around and reaching left kineties at the beak-like projection; 10–12 suboral and 8–11 left kineties. Six to 11 kinetosome-like dots present near base of podite. Terminal and equatorial fragments with five to seven and zero to nine basal bodies, respectively. Macronucleus oval, about 12 x 7 mm in size.  Micronucleus not detected. Arrangement of three oral kineties typical of genus and considerably shorter than those in Hartmannula derouxi: with 14–19, seven to eight and 8–12 pairs of basal bodies in outer, inner and preoral kineties, respectively (table 1). Silverline system irregularly reticulate as in Hartmannula derouxi" (1). 

"Remarks: In the original description of Hartmannula angustipilosa, no information on the number of contractile vacuoles is given (Deroux and Dragesco, 1968). Several years later, Agamaliev (1974) redescribed a Caspian population with seven contractile vacuole pores. He stated, incorrectly however, that the contractile vacuole pores were located on the dorsal side. The Qingdao population demonstrates that the number of contractile vacuoles is not constant (ranging from four to seven; see table 2), and also that contractile vacuole pores are consistently located on the ventral side (always in a longitudinal row on the right)" (1).

1.  Morphology and infraciliature of two marine species of Hartmannula (Protozoa, Ciliophora, Cyrtophorida), from scallop-farming waters off Qingdao (Tsingtao), China.  JUN GONG and WEIBO SONG.  JOURNAL OF NATURAL HISTORY 10 JUNE 2004, 38, 1327–1337 

2.  Morphology and morphogenesis of a new marine cyrtophorid ciliate, Hartmannula sinica nov. spec. (Protozoa, Ciliophora, Cyrtophorida) from China Chen Shao, Weibo Song, Jun Gong.  European Journal of Protistology 44 (2008) 1–12

9907568e-6357-4472-8736-a5c9bc96d165.description:
Previously observed at this location (partially submerged  rock in a wooded wetland area);https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/247310700.
A sample was taken for microscopic evaluation: images 3-6 using an inexpensive stereoscope and the remainder, 7-14, using a compound microscope. Of note in the latter is the presence of brown, granular oil bodies (new to me), usually 2 to 4, in most of the cells (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35394035/#:~:text=Liverworts%20are%20known%20for%20their,compounds%20while%20limiting%20their%20cytotoxicity). The numerous chloroplasts are small, round, and congregate at the inner membrane surface. In cells at the lobe margins, the chloroplasts appear to be pulling away from the wall to form a condensed wreath-like structure (plasmolysis?). In general, the marginal cells appear more transparent (hyaline).  I've read that the distribution of oil bodies in the cells will distinguish *Riccardia multifida* from *Riccardia chamedryfolia*, but can find no images or description to help me make the distinction. Otherwise, my  ID is tenuous! (Also, my deepest apologies to the specimen - my delicate pluck took much more than intended😓. I expected a tough rocky surface to immediately underlay the green thallus, with the liverwort tightly bound. Instead, a loose, wet, spongy network of old thallus and rhizoids, of considerable depth, was under the green thallus. It tore away much too easily. A small pair of scissors would have been a more appropriate tool for procuring a suitable sample.)
9907568e-6357-4472-8736-a5c9bc96d165.place_guess: Atkinson Family Preserve - 765 Long Cove Rd, Gales Ferry, CT 06335, United States

19726062-0ed0-46c1-9757-8a9f79399b49.description:
Video: https://youtu.be/OY3TtXhhVxY

Sampling location: A water sample was collected from Srednerogatsky Pond near the shore, where the depth was about 20 cm.
Date and time of collection: September 21, 2024 at 10 AM
Date and time of observation: September 29, 2024 at 3 PM
The sample was stored in a sealed glass container at room temperature.

Parameters of the water on the day of the collection:
pH: 8.03
Conductivity: 540 µS cm–1 
TDS: 272 ppm
ORP: 159 mV
Salt: 0.02%
S.G.: 1.000

All images and video are of the same organism.

*Litonotus cygnus* (Müller, 1773) Foissner, Berger, Blatterer & Kohmann, 1995

Diagnosis of the organism observed:
•	Body slenderly lanceolate and flattened. Very contractile and flexible.
•	Length: elongated ~200 μm, contracted ~100 μm.
•	The right side is flat with seven rows of somatic cilia, the middle part of the left side is highly arched.
•	Two spherical macronuclei in the centre of the cell (∅ = 9-10 μm)
•	One spherical micronucleus between the macronuclei (∅ = 3 μm)
•	Contractile vacuole subterminal, at the end of a left-sided bulge.
•	Extrusomes rod-shaped, slightly curved (~6 µm long).
•	Extrusomes arranged mainly along oral cleft.
•	Carnivore (*Cinetochilum margaritaceum* was eaten when observed).

References:

Taxonomische und ökologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobiensystems, Band IV: Gymnostomatea, Loxodes, Suctoria (p.318) by Wilhelm Foissner, Helmut Berger, Hubert Blatterer, Fritz Kohmann (1995)

Observation by Dr. Martin Kreutz https://realmicrolife.com/litonotus-cygnus/

*Litonotus* genus observations on iNaturalist.

Related observation (prey): https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/247940084

7f8f7d07-bca6-4274-8791-74fb05f5a635.description:
Dysteria brasiliensis Faria et al., 1922  from the benthos of a channel connecting estuaries Gardiner's Bay and Three Mile Harbor.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective, SPlan 40 0.70 and SPlan 10 0.40 objectives plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. Here is a description of the features I can discern without silver stains.  There was quite a vigorous bloom of the Dysteria in the sample fed with boiled wheat seed.  Dysteria brasiliensis is reported to show remarkable phenotypic plasticity (1-3). Gong et al described three variants, normal, small-sized, and elongate (2).  Zhao et al 2022  showed 5 different populations (3).  The Springs population initially resembled the small-sized type of Gong et al (2) in body shape with absence of dorsal spine but the size was in the range of their normal type.  This initial Springs population exactly resembled the Ningbo Population-II of Zhao et al 2022 (3) both in terms of size and absence of the dorsal spine. 

After three days of the appearance of the bloom, individuals having a short dorsal spine appeared measuring 105-120 um corresponding to the  Ningbo Population-I of Zhao et al 2022 (3).   Also,  individuals with the anteriorly hooked or "hockey stick" appearance corresponding to Zhao et al's  Ningbo Population-IV  both in terms of size and absence of dorsal spine.  These were smaller than the similarly shaped but larger "elongate" hockey stick form of Gong et al (2).  All of these "emergent" types were in the range of 105-120 um. Thus, in real time I was able to observe much of the full range of phenotypic plasticity for this species emerging in a single population. 

Description of the Springs population:  Size in vivo about 110-140 x 25-40 um, body shape consistent and bilaterally flattened about 1:4. From side view, body elongate and slender in outline shape (length: width about 2.5-3:1), anterior margin slightly truncated and posteriorly more or less tapering. Anterior rounded, posterior rounded to somewhat angular in some individuals. Ventral side straight, and dorsal side slightly convex. When viewed dorsoventrally, cells always bend to the left. Podite pointed and slender, with obvious central canal, protruding subcaudally from ventral groove but not extending past cell border. One large obvious U-shaped glandule-like structure subcaudally positioned just anterior and slightly medial to the podite. Ciliary rows mostly restricted to ventral groove between left and right plates. No conspicuous grooves or ridges on lateral plates.  Surfaces of plates covered with a dense coat of drumstick-like ectosymbionts with bimodal appearance: a round refractile head and either admixed with or ?attached to rod-like portion in length 4-5 x the diameter of the head. Cytoplasm colourless to grayish, with several dark food vacuoles (4-5 um in diameter) and shining globular crystals.  Cytostome in anterior 1/5 of cell length and ventrally located. Cytopharynx slender and straight, tangentially oriented, with two relatively short pharyngeal rods which intersect and disappear where they extend dorsally and posteriorly to about the anterior 1/2 of the macronucleus. Two contractile vacuoles, ventrally located, one in anterior third the other in posterior third. Macronucleus: Ellipsoidal and elongate and characteristically heteromerous positioned in mid-body. Micronucleus not observed.  Infraciliature: Right field occupied by 5 ventral kineties (VK), among which the right-most 2 are approximately equal in length (each row consisting of 140-160 basal bodies), extend anteriorly beyond the level of cytostome and bend to the dorsal side. The left most is present only with perfect focal plane and thus appears absent in some views. Arrangement of oral kineties typical of genus: one double-rowed preoral kinety (Pr) positioned dorsally to cytostome, three single-rowed left frontal kineties (Lf) and 2 circumoral kineties (Co). 

The current population at first consistently lacked the dorsal spine but shows other characters consistent with the often noted variability of this species (1-3). Qu et al 2015 write:  "Dysteria brasiliensis, originally described by Faria et al. (1922), has been described in detail by Song and Packroff (1997) and Gong et al. (2007). The body shape of the species is quite variable, especially in the presence/absence, and the shape, of the dorsal spine (Gong et al. 2007). In contrast, the pattern of infraciliature is stable among different populations" (2).    Gong et al. (2007) wrote: "Our observations show that Dysteria brasiliensis, like D. crassipes, has considerable morphological variability in terms of the presence/absence of the dorsal spine, whereas other features, for example, the triangular or trapezoid body outline and the ciliary pattern, are relatively constant. The temporary appearance of spines and other cellular projections has been reported among other ciliates including stichotrichs, and hypotrichs, and in each case the morphological transformation was shown to be a predator-induced defense response (for review, see Wicklow, 1997). The function of the spine, and the reason for its presence in some individuals of D. brasiliensis and D. crassipes but not others, has not been determined. If it is a predator-induced defense response, it will be the first example of this phenomenon among cyrtophorids. Nevertheless, the variability of this feature indicates that spines may not be such a reliable character as previously supposed for species identification and separation in Dysteria" (1). 

Taken with the size and shape of the body and other characters, another feature of my population in common with other populations of D. brasiliensis is the dense coat of ectosymbiont bacteria on both plates.   Gong et al (2007) wrote: " To the best of our knowledge, D. brasiliensis and D. crassipes are the only species of Dysteria known to host ectosymbiotic bacteria. These bacteria are possibly sulphur-oxidizing or sulphate-reducing organisms, as found on the cell surface of other marine ciliates (Fenchel and Ramsing 1992; Rinke et al. 2006). It seems that the ectosymbiosis is species-specific, since there have been no similar reports for other known congeners, although it is possible that the presence of ectosymbiotic bacteria might be habitat-dependent. Further investigations are therefore required in order to determine the factors influencing the presence or absence of dorsal spines and ectosymbiotic bacteria in Dysteria spp., and whether there is any relationship between these features" (1).  

Apparently there can be variation in ectosymbiont shape among different populations of D. brasiliensis, and the Springs population showed yet another variation. Qu et al 2015 write regarding the ectosymbiont coat: "It was not mentioned in Faria et al. (1922) and Song and Packroff (1997). In the report of Gong et al. (2007), bar-shaped ectosymbiotic bacteria cover both plates, but these were not detected  in (Qu et al's)  Yantai population and were found to be spherical in Zhanjiang population. This difference probably indicates that the type of ectosymbiotic bacteria tends to be related to the habitat, and therefore cannot be considered to be a stable species-distinguishing character" (2). My population seem to have a different ectosymbiont morphology- a combination of bar shaped and spherical. I am uncertain if this is two ectosymbiont species or a single species having a "drumstick" morphology with bar shape and spherical head. 

1. Gong, J.; Song, W.; Warren, A.; Lin, X.; Roberts, D.M. Microscopical observations on four marine Dysteria species (Ciliophora, Cyrtophorida). Eur. J. Protistol. 2007, 43, 147–161.

2.  Taxonomic studies on seven species of Dysteria (Ciliophora, Cyrtophoria), including a description of Dysteria paraprocera sp. n.  Zhishuai Qu, Chundi Wang, Feng Gao, Jiqiu Li, Khaled A.S. Al-Rasheid, Xiaozhong Hu.  European Journal of Protistology 51 (2015) 241–258

3. A Case Study of the Morphological and Molecular Variation within a Ciliate Genus: Taxonomic Descriptions of Three Dysteria Species (Ciliophora, Cyrtophoria), with the Establishment of a New Species.  Xuetong Zhao, Hui Zhang, Qianqian Zhang, Zhishuai Qu, Alan Warren, Di Wu and Xiangrui Chen. Int. J. Mol. Sci. 2022, 23, 1764. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms23031764

ad6173e4-f88d-4a88-ac34-d6f804655b8a.description:
Urocentrum turbo (MUELLER, 1866) Nitsch, 1827 from a sample of the benthos of the Peconic River, salinity <1 o/oo, sample fed with boiled wheat seeds. The cell measures 72 um in length. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy 24. Monotypic, i.e. h. Genus consisting of only one species. A very difficult subject to image well, especially under oil- I got lucky with a compressed and trapped individual to show its very complex ciliature. We can see the cycling of the terminal contractile vacuole with the adjacent somewhat distended portions of some of the collecting canals. The goove which runs from the oral opening posteriorly to the caudal ciliary field where the twisted caudal cilia arise.

1) In vivo 40-110 um long, usually 50-80 x 30-55 um.
2) Shape champagne cork-shaped, i.e. h. front half slightly wider than back and slightly narrowed in the middle. Both ends slightly to strongly curved.
3) Macronucleus semicircular in the posterior half of the body; clearly constricted in the middle, where the micronucleus lies.
4) Contractile vacuole terminal, with 8-12 long collecting ducts
5) Numerous spindle-shaped extrusomes are located just beneath the pellicle.
6) Ciliation very complex. About 140 longitudinal rows of cilia arise from the bare frontal plate, each with about 19 basal bodies, which form a striking anterior cilia belt is interrupted in the area of ​​the oral apparatus. This is immediately followed by a thin, equatorial belt with short cilia. After a narrow unciliated area there is the posterior belt of rather irregularly arranged cilia. A groove extends from the oral apparatus to the posterior part, from which a tuft of cilia ("caudal cirrus") arises. This tuft secretes a thread of mucus with which the urocentrum attaches itself and swings back and forth rapidly rotating.
7) Oral apparatus in the equatorial groove. Oral cilia similar to Paramecium: 3 longadoral membranelles and a curved undulating membrane, which rests on a "stomatogenous" basal body field; structure of the oral cilia can only be recognized after silver impregnation, not required for the determination).

8308e953-ed44-4459-b034-bad5174c2dc2.description:
Paramecium caudatum Ehrenberg 1833 from a saprobic sample of the benthos of Peconic River, salinity 1 o/oo, fed with boiled wheat seed. The cells measure 240 um in average length.  They are cigar-shaped, posterior end bluntly pointed and with a group of long cilia, ciliation otherwise uniform; vestibulum long and slightly oblique; buccal cavity with one endoral membrane and 2 peniculi; 1 ellipsoid macronucleus and 1 compact micronucleus; 2 contractile vacuoles, each with radial canals, near the aboral surface, numerous trichocysts, which may discharge explosively, all over the body.   The current population conforms to P. caudatum with a single compact barrel- shaped micronucleus having a "cap" and the two contractile vacuoles having 7 long radiating canals and a single pore per vacuole.

Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective and SPlan 40 0.70 objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. 

Fokin has shown that Paramecium species can be differentiated by three main morphologic characters: distance of the cytoproct from the posterior end, which usually needs silver impregnation for accurate determination. The other two characters are easily documented by routine light microscopy-  number and type of micronuclei, and number and length of contractile vacuole collecting canals and number of excretory pores per vacuole.  The below discussion was taken from Fokin's excellent review (1).    Fokin writes: "The most distinctive and useful for species’ discrimination, to my mind, are type and number of the Mi as well as the structure of CV. In the Paramecium genus we can find all the possible variations of the Mi types and CV structure occurring within all the Ciliophora. Both of the features are very easy to check using living and fixed (stained by Feulgen and impregnated) cells" (1).  

"Members of the genus Paramecium look very typical and distinctive and may be characterized as follows. They are mostly elongate ciliates of cigar or slipper shape (50-300 µm) with dorsal and ventral surface, a distinct oral groove or depression running from anterior left to middle right of the body on the ventral surface. The oral groove leads into the vestibulum, which terminates in an opening, the buccal overture, leading into a buccal cavity. Buccal overture is located around the middle of the ventral surface (in most Paramecium spp.), or could be shifted forward from the cell’s equator, considerably (P. bursaria, P. putrinum and P. polycaryum) or just a little (P. schewiakoffi and Paramecium sp. from Norway). A buccal cavity has special buccal ciliature including peniculi (2 sets of ciliary structures each consisting of four converging rows), quadrulus (again four ciliary rows, but located in some distance from each other) and the endoral kinety (membrane) which is a zigzag row of cilia. This peculiar buccal ciliature is very stable in structure, but can be larger or smaller for different Paramecium spp. It gave the name to the whole subclass Peniculia" (1). 

"By the general shape of the cell, Paramecium representatives can be divided into two groups: “aurelia”, with a cigar-shaped body and “bursaria”, with the body more like a slipper with obliquely truncated anterior end. At least two species, however, deviated from those general images – P. pseudotrichium (more ellipsoidal) and the one, newly found in Norway (somehow combining cigar and slipper shape) (Fokin et al., 2006). The same division of the genus members fits for location of slit-like cytoproct on the ventral cell side. All “bursaria”- like species have it close to the posterior end of the cell, while in all the “aurelia”-like members of the genus this structure is situated at some distance from the posterior end" (1).
 
"There are four main morphological types of the Mi organization. The first, large “compact” type of the Mi can be found in P. bursaria, P. putrinum, P. caudatum. Using light microscopy, however, it is possible to discriminate only the Mi type of P. caudatum from the nucleus of other two species. P. caudatum always has the Mi with the so-called “cap”, a space without chromatin at the nuclear pole" (1).

"Structure of CV in the genus members can also be of different types (Fokin, 1987). These organelles are commonly two in number and are located close to the dorsal surface in the endoplasm, usually directly beneath the cortex. They are situated at a distance of approximately one quarter up to one third of the entire body length from the anterior and posterior ends. CV connects with the outside through pores permanently located in the cortex. There is a slightly conical, very short (except in P. putrinum) canal decorated by helically arranged microtubules. The number of pores per one CV in a species is a distinctive feature (Fokin, 1987; Fokin et al., 1999a). For example, P. caudatum and P. aurelia complex spp. always have one pore per CV, but P. bursaria and P. nephridiatum, from 2 to 5" (1). 

"In the literature two types of CV within the Paramecium genus are indicated. In one, called canal-fed type, a number of radial (collecting or nephridial) canals radiate from the vacuole and empty into it. This type is characteristic of all paramecia except P. putrinum.  In the group which has canal-fed type of CV, some variation in the number and size of canals could be recorded. For  P. caudatum there are  5-8 (more often, 7) long canals" (1).  

1.  Paramecium genus: biodiversity, some morphological features and the key to the main morphospecies discrimination. Sergei I. Fokin.  Protistology 6 (4), 227–235 (2010/11).

cb3f9686-629c-4856-9c94-9aa505b868eb.description:
A shell within a shell. This dainty *Euglypha* was attached to the inside of the messy, agglutinate shell of a large arcellinid amoeba (possibly *Cyclopyxis* sp.). See the third image for the original position of this little guy.

I've identified this as *E. crenulata* because of the shield-like shape of the body scales (a trait used by Foissner & Schiller as the basis for the genus *Scutiglypha*, in which this species is sometimes included).  It is possible that *E.crenulata* is a synonym of *E. acanthophora*.

2434485b-6261-4cbe-ad72-909566e0d54d.description:
From a rheoplankton sample collected by suspending a net in a small waterfall. I disturbed the stream bed upstream by walking in the fallen leaves (maple, beech, oak, poplar, and alder) and scraping the flat limestone bed to dislodge periphyton. The most abundant components of the plankton, by far, were the aquatic hyphomycetes, and particularly *T. elegans*. Four long tetrahedral arms spanning more than 200 µm. Individual arms of this specimen were 104 to 140 µ long by 2 - 4 µ wide. The second specimen has a vestigial 'separating cell' (Ingold 1942) that hasn't dropped off yet.
Reference: Ingold, C.T. 1942. Aquatic Hyphomycetes of decaying alder leaves. Trans. Brit. Mycol. Soc. 25, 39-4I7.
2434485b-6261-4cbe-ad72-909566e0d54d.place_guess: Silver Creek, Halton Hills, ON, Canada

*Hydra oligactis* Pallas, 1766.
 
Diagnosis of the organism observed:
•	Hydra with distinct stalk, more transparent than the body.
•	Colour of the body light brown.
•	Long six tentacles, can elongate to many times the length of the body.
•	Tentacles in fully contracted animal are not star-like, but remain curved.
•	Developing bud tentacles of unequal length.
•	Holotrichous isorhizas without transverse coils. 2.4-3.4 times as long as broad.
•	Stenoteles 1.3-1.4 times as long as broad.

References:

Tsalolikhin SYa (Ed.) (2016) Key to zooplankton and zoobenthos of fresh water in European Russia. Vol. 2: Zoobenthos. KMK Scientific Press Ltd., Saint Petersburg, Moscow, (254, Fig. 3)

217fa13b-ad01-413b-9814-d0b8b1ea263d.description:

Sampling location: A water sample was collected from Srednerogatsky Pond near the shore, where the depth was about 20 cm.
Date and time of collection: September 21, 2024 at 10 AM

The sample was stored in a sealed glass container at room temperature.

Parameters of the water on the day of the collection:
pH: 8.03
Conductivity: 540 µS cm–1 
TDS: 272 ppm
ORP: 159 mV
Salt: 0.02%
S.G.: 1.000

Figs 1-7 and video are of the same organism.

Under the influence of methylene blue, the ciliate was detached from the body of the hydra and soon disintegrated.

*Kerona pediculus* (Müller, 1773) Müller, 1786.

Diagnosis of the organism observed:
•	Found on surface of *Hydra oligactis* (on which it creeps rapidly).
•	Length 80 µm; width 80 μm.
•	Reniform. Dorsoventrally flattened.
•	AZM extends halfway down body length.
•	Six oblique, curving, subparallel rows of ventral cirri.
•	Two marginal rows of cirri joining posteriorly.
•	Macronucleus in two parts (in anterior and posterior half).
•	Feeding on algae.

References:

The identity and occurrence of Kerona pediculus (Ciliophora: Hypotrichida), a well-known epizoite of Hydra vulgaris (Cnidaria: Hydrozoa) by A. Warren & E.A. Robson (1997)

Taxonomische und ökologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobiensystems, Band I: Cyrtophorida, Oligotrichida, Hypotrichia, Colpodea (p.265) by Wilhelm Foissner, Helmut Berger, Hubert Blatterer, Fritz Kohmann (1991)

Species Identified:

Licmophora flabellata (Greville) C.Agardh 1831

Genus: Licmophora C. Agardh (1827) nom. et typ. Cons.

Taxonomic classification:

Phylum:	Heterokontophyta
Subphylum:	 Bacillariophytina
Class:	 Bacillariophyceae
Subclass:	 Fragilariophycidae
Order:	 Licmophorales
Family: Licmophoraceae
Genus:		Licmophora (Guiry and Guiry 2023)

Holotype species, synonym(s), etc.: Licmophora argentescens C.Agardh

Genus Summary:

Licmophora is an araphid genus. Species in the genus are cosmopolitan, found in most marine habitats including Arctic, Antarctic, and tropical regions. Cells grow in colonies, often fan shaped on branched mucilaginous stalks or pads, attached to various substrates such as seaweeds, rocks, animals or detached and found singly in the plankton. Frustules are heteropolar. They have a narrow base (sometimes slightly capitate) and broader apex and in valve and girdle view the cell is cuneate (wedge shaped). The valves have a narrow, sometimes indistinct central sternum. Septa present, distinct or indistinct (Plinski and Witkowski 2020), internally around the apical ends and tapering off down each side of the copulae. The areolae are round or elongate and externally covered by a criba. The striae are transapical, uniseriate and parallel, except at the apices where they can become radiate. A rimoportula is present on one valve at the base and on the other valve, or both valves, at the apex. External rimoportula is a circular slit like opening, whereas the internal rimoportula opening is labiate, fan shaped, sometimes stalked and flush with the frustule. Normally, there are two or three rimoportulae per cell. If 2 rimoportulae per frustule, then, one is located at the basal apex, the other at the head apex. If 3 rimoportulae, one is located at the basal apex, one at the head apex of each valve. A series of slits (multiscissura) is present around the base of both valves where mucilage for stalks and pads is secreted. Spines are present at the head apex of some species. Plastids numerous and small. There are five distinguishable girdle bands. Areolae on the copulae (girdle bands) are smaller than those on the valve. Valvocopulae open at the basal apex and maybe a septum at the apex. Relying on identification of species by light microscopy may be problematic due to fine features; SEM and TEM are utilized. AlgaeBase lists 102 accepted species and 10 varieties (Honeywill 1988, Round et al. 1990, Lobhan 2013, Lobhan et al. 2018, Plinski and Witkowski 2020: 56, Spaulding et al. 2021, Guiry and Guiry 2023).

From historic records, 9 species and 2 varieties of Licmophora have been previously recorded in the Salish Sea and Western Pacific waters: 

1.	Licmophora abbreviata C.Agardh 1831: 42: 20-110 µm long, 4-8 µm wide, striae at the base of valve 11-12 in 10 µm, in the upper part 14-16 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020) 
2.	L. californica Grunow 1885
3.	L. gracilis (Ehr.) Grun: 40-110 µm long, 10-16 µm wide, striae 20-22 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020)
4.	L. gracilis var. anglica (Kützing) H.Peragallo & M.Peragallo 1901
5.	L. hyalina (Kützing) Grunow 1867
6.	L. ehrenbergii (Kützing) Grunow 1867: 36: 60-180 µm long, 15-30 µm wide, striae evenly distributed throughout the valve, striae 8-11 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020)  
7.	L. ehrenbergii f. grunowii (Mereschk.) Hust.
8.	L. flabellata (Greville) C.Agardh 1831
9.	L. juergensii C.Agardh 1831: 30-100 µm long, 7-13 µm wide, striate delicate, striae at the foot pole 23-25 in 10 µm, in the head pole 27-30 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020).
10.	L. lyngbyei (Kützing) Grunow 1867
11.	L. paradoxa (Lyngb.) Agardh


Species Description:

Licmophora flabellata (Greville) C.Agardh 1831: 42 (syn: Exilaria flabellata Greville 1827: pl. 289; Echinella flabellata Carmichael, nom. inval. 2003: 78).

References:
Greville 1827: pl. 289; Hendey 1964; Honeywill 1998; Sar and Ferrario 1990; Witkowski et al. 2000: 63, Pl. 18, Fig. 2-3; Macatugal et al. 2019; Romagnoli et al. 2014: 572, Fig. 3 f-k.

Description:
Cells in girdle view, thinly cuneate with flat valve face profile. Valves long, narrow, spatulate/clavate with a round capitate foot pole. Valves 126.3-188.8 (60-300) µm long, 4.6-6.5 (4-13) µm wide at upper part, 5-6.5 (3-4) µm wide at the base pole. Striae uniseriate 30 (32-35) in 10 µm at head pole, 24-28 (29-35) at mid frustule and 32 (30) at base pole. Areolae slightly elongate in transapical direction, 45-55 (35) in 10 µm throughout the valve. A prominent transapical rimoportula (not stalked), is often at the basal pole, either in both valves of the same frustule or in only one of them. Another, smaller rimoportula is at head pole. Numerous smaller non-stalked rimoportulae 7-9 (6-9), with external openings at irregular intervals along sternum. Distinct narrow sternum, slightly curved at basal pole. Two small spines at head pole on both valves (not seen in Galiano Isl. specimens). Multiscissura has 38-43 (30-45) slits. Basal pole has a few irregularly arranged pores. Valvocopula lacking a distinguishable septum (septa shallow). Two distinctive round plastids, one near top and one in middle of cell.

Remarks:
The morphology of these Galiano Island specimens conforms well to descriptions in the listed references. The only exceptions are a greater base pole width, a higher areolae density and some slight differences in striae counts compared to published data. This may reflect normal species variation within the Salish Sea, Western Canada or indicate a new variety. Licmophora flabellata was reported in the Salish Sea by: Bailey and MacKay (1915) and Clemens 1933; no striae densities are provided.

Salish Sea specimens: Licmophora flabellata on S. gaudichaudii-RC July 14, 2024 Box 41 RC-Stb RC 14-1 Oct 16 2024-RR_m050_4.tif; Licmophora flabellata (A)on S. gaudichaudii-RC July 14, 2024 Box 41 RC-Stb RC 14-1 Oct 16 2024-RR_m050_4.tif; Licmophora flabellata (B) on S. gaudichaudii-RC July 14, 2024 Box 41 RC-Stb RC 14-1 Oct 16 2024-RR_m051_4.tif; Licmophora flabellata (B) on S. gaudichaudii-RC July 14, 2024 Box 41 RC-Stb RC 14-1 Oct 16 2024-RR_m055_4.tif; Licmophora flabellata (B) on S. gaudichaudii-RC July 14, 2024 Box 41 RC-Stb RC 14-1 Oct 16 2024-RR_m056_4.tif; Licmophora flabellata (E) on S. gaudichaudii-RC July 14, 2024 Box 41 RC-Stb RC 14-1 Oct 16 2024-RR_m053_4 copy.tif; Licmophora flabellata_#4 Licmorphora on Obelia SHW Oct 27-2021 Slide 3 E800(Nov 23-2024) AvA x60oil-fs_59-67_4.tif

Methods for Obelia sp. SHW, October 27, 2021:

Collected by brushing the Hydrozoan, Obelia sp. found attached to the dock at Spanish Hills Wharf, North Galiano Island, October 27, 2021. Cells were cleaned with 99C hot concentrated hydrogen peroxide for 3-5 hours to remove organics, then rinsed multiple times in ddH20 to a neutral pH. Mounted on SEM stubs or in Naphrax on slides for light microscopy. Imaging with a Nikon TE300 and Tuscen DigiRetna16 MP camera or Nikon E800 with apo DIC lenses and a Zeiss MRc5 camera. In-situ, environmentally prepared samples were made using minimal contact of 8-10 mm leaf section, soaked in ddH2O to remove salts and dried through an EtOH series (50%-100%) and finished off with 100% Hexamethyldisilane HMDS (Hazrin-Chong and Manefield 2012). Mounted on carbon stickies onto aluminum SEM stubs and imaged with either the Hitachi s4800 or TM4000 at AMF, at University of Victoria, B.C. Thanks go to Elaine Humphrey of the AMF, UVIC, SEM imaging by Ron Read, Arjan van Asselt and Mark Webber. Taxonomy and identifications by M. Webber.
