1.	Licmophora abbreviata C.Agardh 1831: 42: 20-110 µm long, 4-8 µm wide, striae at the base of valve 11-12 in 10 µm, in the upper part 14-16 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020) 
2.	L. californica Grunow 1885
3.	L. gracilis (Ehr.) Grun: 40-110 µm long, 10-16 µm wide, striae 20-22 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020)
4.	L. gracilis var. anglica (Kützing) H.Peragallo & M.Peragallo 1901
5.	L. hyalina (Kützing) Grunow 1867
6.	L. ehrenbergii (Kützing) Grunow 1867: 36: 60-180 µm long, 15-30 µm wide, striae evenly distributed throughout the valve, striae 8-11 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020)  
7.	L. ehrenbergii f. grunowii (Mereschk.) Hust.
8.	L. flabellata (Greville) C.Agardh 1831
9.	L. juergensii C.Agardh 1831: 30-100 µm long, 7-13 µm wide, striate delicate, striae at the foot pole 23-25 in 10 µm, in the head pole 27-30 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020).
10.	L. lyngbyei (Kützing) Grunow 1867
11.	L. paradoxa (Lyngb.) Agardh

Species Description:

Licmophora flabellata (Greville) C.Agardh 1831: 42 (syn: Exilaria flabellata Greville 1827: pl. 289; Echinella flabellata Carmichael, nom. inval. 2003: 78).

References:
Greville 1827: pl. 289; Hendey 1964; Honeywill 1998; Sar and Ferrario 1990; Witkowski et al. 2000: 63, Pl. 18, Fig. 2-3; Macatugal et al. 2019; Romagnoli et al. 2014: 572, Fig. 3 f-k.

Description:
Cells in girdle view, thinly cuneate with flat valve face profile. Valves long, narrow, spatulate/clavate with a round capitate foot pole. Valves 126.3-188.8 (60-300) µm long, 4.6-6.5 (4-13) µm wide at upper part, 5-6.5 (3-4) µm wide at the base pole. Striae uniseriate 30 (32-35) in 10 µm at head pole, 24-28 (29-35) at mid frustule and 32 (30) at base pole. Areolae slightly elongate in transapical direction, 45-55 (35) in 10 µm throughout the valve. A prominent transapical rimoportula (not stalked), is often at the basal pole, either in both valves of the same frustule or in only one of them. Another, smaller rimoportula is at head pole. Numerous smaller non-stalked rimoportulae 7-9 (6-9), with external openings at irregular intervals along sternum. Distinct narrow sternum, slightly curved at basal pole. Two small spines at head pole on both valves (not seen in Galiano Isl. specimens). Multiscissura has 38-43 (30-45) slits. Basal pole has a few irregularly arranged pores. Valvocopula lacking a distinguishable septum (septa shallow). Two distinctive round plastids, one near top and one in middle of cell.

Remarks:
The morphology of these Galiano Island specimens conforms well to descriptions in the listed references. The only exceptions are a greater base pole width, a higher areolae density and some slight differences in striae counts compared to published data. This may reflect normal species variation within the Salish Sea, Western Canada or indicate a new variety. Licmophora flabellata was reported in the Salish Sea by: Bailey and MacKay (1915) and Clemens 1933; no striae densities are provided.

Methods:

Licmophora flabellata, Retreat Cove, Galiano Island: 
Specimens on the Rhodophyta Sarcodiotheca gaudichaudii were collected by Zeuss Cochrane and Andrew Simon by scuba diving from Retreat Cove, Galiano Island on July 14, 2024. Specimens were brushed into 0.2µm filtered marine water, allowed to settle overnight, marine water decanted and washed with sterile and deionized water to remove salts. Treated with 10% hydrochloric acid. Washed again. Cells cleaned with 1:1 conc. reagent grade nitric acid and sulphuric acids at 95-100C in a water bath in a fume hood until a very faint straw colour, taking proper lab safety precautions. Frustules were further cleaned with 30% hydrogen peroxide at 95-100C in a water bath  after a prewash of distilled water to raise the pH. After settling and removing the supernatant, the frustules were washed at least 8 times to bring the pH to 6.5. SEM stubs were made by pipetting cleaned frustules onto 12mm round glass coverslips attached with double sided tape to 13 mm aluminum stubs. Stubs gold sputter coated. Slides made by pipetting sample into 10-20 drops of 10% ammonium chloride solution and air drying. Cover slips heated to 350C to sublimate ammonium chloride, cooled and Naphrax slides prepared in the usual manner. Live imaging of L. flabellata before isolating and cloning was with a Nikon TE300 inverted microscope and a Tucsen DigiRetina 16 camera. Thanks go to Ron Read and Elaine Humphrey for SEM imaging using a Hitachi S4800 SEM at the Advanced Microscope Facility at UVIC, Victoria, BC.  And thanks to Elaine Humphrey of the AMF, University of Victoria, BC, Canada. Clones were not cleaned, but dehydrated with an Ethanol series followed by 3x HMDS (Hexamethyldisilazane). Taxonomy, identifications, live imaging, cloning and adjustments by M. Webber.

Species Identified:

Licmophora gracilis (Ehrenberg) Grunow 1867: 34

Licmophora gracilis found on the Hydrozoan, Obelia sp. attached to Spanish Hills Wharf (SHW), Trincomali Channel, Galiano Island, B.C., Canada. Cleaned diatom frustules.

Genus: Licmophora C. Agardh (1827) nom. et typ. Cons.

Taxonomic classification:

Phylum:	Heterokontophyta
Subphylum:	 Bacillariophytina
Class:	 Bacillariophyceae
Subclass:	 Fragilariophycidae
Order:	 Licmophorales
Family: Licmophoraceae
Genus:		Licmophora (Guiry and Guiry 2023)

Holotype species, synonym(s), etc.: Licmophora argentescens C.Agardh



Genus Summary:

Licmophora is an araphid genus. Species in the genus are cosmopolitan, found in most marine habitats including Arctic, Antarctic, and tropical regions. Cells grow in colonies, often fan shaped on branched mucilaginous stalks or pads, attached to various substrates such as seaweeds, rocks, animals or detached and found singly in the plankton. Frustules are heteropolar. They have a narrow base (sometimes slightly capitate) and broader apex and in valve and girdle view the cell is cuneate (wedge shaped). The valves have a narrow, sometimes indistinct central sternum. Septa present, distinct or indistinct (Plinski and Witkowski 2020), internally around the apical ends and tapering off down each side of the copulae. The areolae are round or elongate and externally covered by a criba. The striae are transapical, uniseriate and parallel, except at the apices where they can become radiate. A rimoportula is present on one valve at the base and on the other valve, or both valves, at the apex. External rimoportula is a circular slit like opening, whereas the internal rimoportula opening is labiate, fan shaped, sometimes stalked and flush with the frustule. Normally, there are two or three rimoportulae per cell. If 2 rimoportulae per frustule, then, one is located at the basal apex, the other at the head apex. If 3 rimoportulae, one is located at the basal apex, one at the head apex of each valve. A series of slits (multiscissura) is present around the base of both valves where mucilage for stalks and pads is secreted. Spines are present at the head apex of some species. Plastids numerous and small. There are five distinguishable girdle bands. Areolae on the copulae (girdle bands) are smaller than those on the valve. Valvocopulae open at the basal apex and maybe a septum at the apex. Relying on identification of species by light microscopy may be problematic due to fine features; SEM and TEM are utilized. AlgaeBase lists 102 accepted species and 10 varieties (Honeywill 1988, Round et al. 1990, Lobhan 2013, Lobhan et al. 2018, Plinski and Witkowski 2020: 56, Spaulding et al. 2021, Guiry and Guiry 2023).

Species Description:

Licmophora gracilis (Ehrenberg) Grunow 1867: 34
&
Licmophora gracilis var. anglica (Kützing) H.Peragallo & M.Peragallo 1901

References:

Peragallo and Peragallo 1901 Pl. 84, fig. 10; Boyer 1927: 167; Van der Werff and Huls 1958–1975: P.A D X b. 66; Hendey 1964: 167; Siqueiros-Beltrones and Obando 1985: 48, Pl. 9, Fig. 4;  Honeywill 1998: 239, Figs 9a-9h; Witkowski et al. 2000: 65, Pl. 18 Figs 12-15, Pl. 19, Fig. 7-15, Pl. 20, Figs 11-13; Fuerte et al. 2010: 85.

Description:

Licmophora gracilis (Ehrenberg) Grunow 1867

Colonies short, fan shaped colonies with branching stalks. In girdle view cells are strongly wedge-shaped and have a slightly convex valve face profile. Valves club shaped, having a rounded foot-pole, upper part is elliptic-circular with a strongly rounded head-pole, slightly concave margins and tapering to a slender lower end. Valves 44.6-54.6 (38-110) µm long, 5.0-9.1 (7-16) µm wide with 19-24 (18-27) transapical striae in 10 µm in the mid valve, 22-26 striae in the head pole and 20-24 striae in the foot pole. 1-2 rimoportulae (2) rimoportulae per cell. Sternum fine and distinct. Both basal and head rimoportulae have short stalks, head rimoportula has a smaller labiate opening than the basal one. Slightly elongate areolae in the transapical direction, (26) in 10 pm. Virgae are unevenly silicified, i.e. some are thicker than others. Striae on opposite sides of the frustule often do not align. Multiscissura has 10-11 (9) slits. Valvocopula has a short septa, appearing in girdle view as lines in the upper part of the cell. Many evenly distributed oval plastids.

Description for the variety:

Licmophora gracilis var. anglica (Kützing) H.Peragallo & M.Peragallo 1901: 346, pl. 84: fig. 13

References:

Peragallo and Peragallo 1901; Van der Werff and Huls 1958–1975: P.A D X b. 66; Witkowski et al. 2000: 65, Pl. 20, Figs 11-13; Fuerte et al. 2010: 85

Description:

Valves 44.6-54.6 (20-120) µm long, 5.0-7.1 µm wide with 22-24 (24-27) transapical striae in 10 µm. The variety L. gracilis var. anglica is different than Licmophora gracilis in generally having a finer striae density. 

Remarks:

The morphology of these Galiano Island specimens conforms well to descriptions in the listed references for Licmophora gracilis. Licmophora gracilis var. anglica (slightly higher striae density than L. gracilis) was reported by Bailey and MacKay (1915). Licmophora gracilis was reported in the Salish Sea by: Bailey and MacKay (1915); Clemens 1933, Rao and Lewin (1977 '1976') and Roelofs (1983) and the Pacific West Coast of Mexico by Siqueiros-Beltrones and Obando (1985). 

Salish Sea specimens: Licmophora cf. gracilis var. anglica-#4 Licmorphora on Obelia SHW Oct 27-2021 Slide 3 E800(Nov 23-2024) AvA x100oil-fs 32-36_4.tif; Licmophora cf. gracilis var. anglica -#4 Licmorphora on Obelia SHW Oct 27-2021 Slide 3 E800(Nov 26-2024) AvA x100 oil-fs21-22_4.tif; Licmophora cf. gracilis var. anglica -#4 Licmorphora on Obelia SHW Oct 27-2021 Slide 3 E800(Nov 26-2024) AvA x100 oil-_36_4.tif; Licmophora gracilis- SHW-Dec 9-2024-Box 49 Stub SP-7-24-3-(RR 9 Apr 2025)_m016_4.tif

Methods:

For Obelia sp. SHW, October 27, 2021:
Collected by brushing the Hydrozoan, Obelia sp. found attached to the dock at Spanish Hills Wharf, North Galiano Island, October 27, 2021. Cells were cleaned with 99C hot concentrated hydrogen peroxide for 3-5 hours to remove organics, then rinsed multiple times in ddH20 to a neutral pH. Mounted on SEM stubs or in Naphrax on slides for light microscopy. Imaging with a Nikon E800 with apo DIC lenses and a Zeiss MRc5 camera.  Mounted on carbon stickies onto aluminum SEM stubs and imaged with either the Hitachi s4800 or TM4000 at AMF, at University of Victoria, B.C.  Also found in a plankton sample from same location, Dec. 9, 2024 (SEM images) and cleaned with 100C 37% hydrogen peroxide. Specimen collection and preparation by Arjan van Asselt (IMERSS) and Mark Webber (IMERSS, UVIC). Thanks go to Arjan van Asselt for light micrograph imaging. SEM imaging by Ron Read with the Hitachi S4800, AMF, UVIC.  Thank you Elaine Humphrey (AMF, UVIC, IMERSS) for imaging support. Taxonomy and identifications by M. Webber.

ba987769-63ac-4ed1-bd69-0b30bd3f6790.description:
Video: https://youtu.be/M-4c0SAOQdM

Sampling location: Surface soil sample containing mosses and soil algae. In the front garden of a residential property.
Date and time of collection: November 22, 2024 at 11 AM. Air temp 1 °C (33,8°F)
Date and time of observation: November 23, 2024 at 11 AM
The samples were moistened with distilled water and stored in a closed plastic container.
All images and video are of the same three organisms.

First specimen: Fig.1a, Figs.2-3
Second specimen: Fig.1b, Figs.4-5
Third specimen (bloated cell): Fig.6

*Pseudochilodonopsis* cf. *polyvacuolata / quadrivacuolata*

Diagnosis of the organisms observed (First specimen / Second specimen):
•	Length 51 µm, width 27 µm / Length 49 µm, width 27 µm.
•	Both specimens: Body oval with anterior part protruding to left. Rear shape - rounded. Dorsoventrally flattened. Body flexible but acontractile.
•	Dorsal side irregular / regular?
•	Both specimens: Contractile vacuoles = 3 (~4μm diameter).
•	Both specimens: Presence of wide glabrous region in the middle of ventral side.
•	Both specimens: Left kineties = 6, right kineties = 5 (?).
•	Both specimens: Preoral kinety segmented (composed of about 4-5 fragments).
•	Both specimens: Two circumoral kineties, the outer one longer than the inner one.
•	Both specimens: Terminal fragment (dorsal brush) apical. 
•	The terminal fragment is composed of: at least 5 cilia (length ~4μm) / at least 8 cilia (length ~4μm).
•	Cyrtos (oral basket) composed of (nematodesmal rods): about 15 / 16 / 15 in third specimen.
•	Both specimens: Macronucleus ellipsoidal.
•	All specimens: Feeds on diatoms.

References:

4270d3c7-cf64-41fd-87c6-635b4e0cc3e0.description:
Species identified: 

Berkeleya rutilans (Trentepohl ex Roth) Grunow 1880

Genus: 
The holotype of the genus is: Berkeleya fragilis Greville 1827: pl. 294 (Guiry and Guiry 2024)

Taxonomic notes on the genera:

Phylum: Bacillariophyta
Subphylum: Bacillariophytina
Class: Bacillariophyceae
Subclass: Fragilariophycidae
Order: Naviculales
Family: Berkeleyaceae
Genus: Berkeleya (Guiry and Guiry 2024)

Genus Summary:

Berkeleya cells are either solitary or form mucilage tubes or films. Valves are linear to linear-lanceolate, with bluntly rounded or slightly capitate poles. Uniseriate, consisting of simple poroids closed by hymens. External raphe endings are straight or slightly deflected towards the secondary side. The mature cingulum consists of at least five open bands, each of which bears two rows of round or oval poroids. The plastid is unique, consisting of two girdle-appressed plates connected by a narrow isthmus (Cox 1975a, Cox 1975b, Round et al. 1990, Olenici et al. 2021).


There is one previous report of Berkeleya in the Salish Sea: Berkeleya rutilans (Trentepohl ex Roth) Grunow 1880 (syn: Amphipleura rutilans (Trentepohl ex Roth) Cleve 1894: 126) by Rao & Lewin (1977 '1976') and Lobban (1985).

Species:

Berkeleya rutilans (Trentepohl ex Roth) Grunow 1880 (syn: Amphipleura rutilans (Trentepohl ex Roth) Cleve 1894: 126) .

References: Hendey 1964: 20; Rao & Lewin (1977 '1976'); Lobban (1985).; Cox 1975a; Cox 1975b; Sims (ed.) 1996: Pl. 34, Fig. 3; Witkowski et al. 2000: p. 157, plate 62, figs 14–17; Pauli Snoeijs 2012; Hamsher & Saunders 2014; Heudre et al. 2020: Figs. 48-65; Blaginina et al. 2023: Fig. 6. B.

Location: MHMPP, Galiano Island.

Habitat: On Zostera sp. leaves.

Description: Generally, a mucilage tube dwelling diatom. Cells linear to lanceolate, occasionally elliptical with rounded apices, 30.2 (17-45) µm long, 4.9 (4-6) pm wide. Axial area asymmetrical. Each raphe is approximately one-third of the valve length. Thickened silica ribs around raphe branches giving a "tuning-fork" appearance. The raphe itself is of a fairly constant length, whatever the length of valve, while the central area is variable in length. Raphe terminal ends do not extend into the apices. Transverse striae parallel in the centre of the valve to moderately radiate towards the apices, 28 (22-28) in 10 µm Two platelike chloroplasts lie along the girdle and are connected by an asymmetrical area extending around the raphe branches giving cytoplasmic bridge.

Remarks: Previously reported in the Salish Sea by: Rao & Lewin (1977 '1976') and Lobban (1985).

Berkeleya rutilans was identified in the 18S molecular data from Z. marina, Montague Harbour Marine Provincial Park (MHMPP), Galiano Isl., March 7, 2021.

Methods:

Collected by brushing or scrapping leaf sections of Zostera sp. from MHMPP, Galiano Island, B.C. Canada, July 20, 2020, Cells from brushed or scraped leaves were cleaned with concentrated hydrogen peroxide or nitric acid at 100C in a water bath for 3-5 hours to remove organics, then rinsed multiple times in ddH20 to a neutral pH. Mounted on SEM stubs or in Naphrax on slides for light microscopy. Imaging with a Nikon TE300 and Tuscen DigiRetna16 MP camera or Nikon E800. SEM imaging with a Hitachi Table Top TM4000 on loan to Elaine Humphrey, Advanced Microscopy Facility at the University of Victoria, B.C. My thanks to Siobhan Schenk, Laura Parfrey, Evan Morien and Andrea Jackman in the Parfrey Lab at UBC for molecular data from the eelgrass and collaboration with IMERSS. Also, thanks go to Elaine Humphrey of the AMF, UVIC, our SEM imaging volunteers Ron Read and Melanie Quenneville. SEM image of Berkeleya rutilans by Arjan van Asselt. Additional imaging adjustments, taxonomy and identifications by M. Webber.

Berkeleya cells are either solitary or form mucilage tubes or films. Valves are linear to linear-lanceolate, with bluntly rounded or slightly capitate poles. 406b77ee-6aa5-48c3-b1f9-481ebeb1fe6f.description:
Species Identified:

Gyrosigma arcuatum (Donkin) Sterrenburg 2005

Found on the Rhodophyta, Ceramium pacificum, Retreat Cove, Galiano Island, British Columbia, Canada. Collected during the Galiano BioBlitz, May 26, 2023.

Genus: Gyrosigma Hassall, 1845, nom. cons.

Classification:

Class: Bacillariophyceae
Subclass: Bacillariophycidae
Order: Naviculales
Suborder: Naviculineae
Family: Naviculaceae
Genus: Gyrosigma (Guiry and Guiry 2023)

Genus Summary:

Large, sigmoid shaped naviculoid diatoms. Usually solitary, occasionally in mucilage tubes, most often observed in valve view. Valves of Gyrosigma are generally slender and sigmoid, symmetrical to the apical and transapical axes. Valve face is flat with shallow mantles. Central area in Gyrosigma is longitudinally round to elliptical. Raphe system sigmoid and found midline through the valve. Central raphe endings deflected to opposite sides. Transverse and longitudinal punctate striae of Gyrosigma are equally spaced, crossing at right angles, appearing similar to squares, whereas Pleurosigma has transapical and oblique striae crossing, rows in the form of an X. In Pleurosigma The rows are arranged in 3 patterns: a trans-apical row and two opposing oblique rows. Gyrosigma has open, non-porous girdle bands (Round et al. 1990; Stidolph 1992; Stidolph 1994; Spaulding 2001; Reid 2012: 87, 136, Pl. 11; Kociolek et al. 2015: 744).

Records of Gyrosigma species reported in the Salish Sea:

1.	Gyrosigma acuminatum (Kützing) Rabenhorst 1853: 47, pl. 5: fig. 5a
2.	Gyrosigma attenuatum (Kützing) Rabenhorst 1853: 47
3.	Gyrosigma balticum (Ehrenberg) Rabenhorst 1853: 47, pl. 5: fig. 6
4.	Gyrosigma californicum (Grunow) G.Reid 2003: 133-135, fig. 3, 5, 36
5.	Gyrosigma fasciola (Ehrenberg) J.W.Griffith & Henfrey 1856: 303, pl. 11: fig. 21
6.	Gyrosigma fasciola var. sulcatum (Grunow) Cleve 1894: 116 (as 'sulcata')
7.	Gyrosigma fasciola var. tenuirostris (Grunow) Cleve 1894: 116
8.	Gyrosigma scalpriodes Rabenhorst
9.	Gyrosigma strigilis (W.Smith) J.W.Griffin & Henfrey 1856: 302,303; pl. 11, fig. 12

Species description:

Gyrosigma arcuatum (Donkin) Sterrenburg 2005: 308. (Syn: Gyrosigma fasciola var. arcuatum (Donkin) Cleve 1894: 116 (as 'arcuata') (Guiry and Guiry 2024). 

References: Donkin 1858; 25, Pl. 3, Fig. 10; Proshkina-Lavrenko 1950: 249, Pl. 82, Fig. 7; Dexing et al. 1985: 80, Pl. 24, fig. 188; Cardinal et al. 1989: 18, Fig. 7; Stidolph 1994; Sims et al.1996: Pl. 113, Fig. 4; Jahn et al. 2005: 309; 

Description:

Distinguished by long, rostrate apices curving in opposite directions, sharply turned out from the valve body. Valve distinctly sigmoid, lanceolate to elliptical-lanceolate in the central portion, narrowing to long thin extensions that are bluntly rounded or flattened. Valve face fairly flat, length 100.9-105 (60-150) µm, width 10.6-14.3 (10-24) µm. Axial area and raphe central, sigmoid, appearing slightly eccentric in the extensions of some valves. Central area quite small, orbicular or longitudinally elliptical. Central raphe endings slightly deflected to opposite sides. Longitudinal striae 25-30 (27) in 10 µm and transverse striae 24-30 in 10 µm about equal and distinct. Two marginal, thin plastids, almost exactly opposite.

Remarks:
These three specimens of Gyrosigma with long narrow apical extensions of the valve and curved in opposite directions are placed into Gyrosigma arcuatum (Donkin) Sterrenburg 2005: 308 (Guiry amd Guiry 2023), as recommended by Jahn et al. (2005). Gyrosigma arcuatum has a higher number of transverse and longitudinal striae relative to Gyrosigma fasciola (Ehrenberg) Griffith & Henfrey 1855 and varieties. Specimens found on Zostera marina at MHMPP and Retreat Cove match the G. arcuatum type material described by Jahn et al. (2005: 309): 80-110 µm long and 12-15 µm wide and 27 striae in 10 µm compared to the similar G. fasciola and varieties with an average of striae of no more than 25, most often 22-24 in 10 µm in the longitudinal direction and 20-23 in 10 µm in the transverse direction (Stidolph 1994; Jahn et al. 2005; Plinski and Witkowski 2020). Stidolph does not list any longitudinal and transverse striae above 25 in 10 µm in a comprehensive review of published data on G. fasciola (Stidolph 1994: Table 1). 

This is a first report for Gyrosigma arcuatum (Donkin) Sterrenburg 2005 in the Salish Sea and Canada’s Western marine waters (Mather et al., 2010).

Salish Sea specimens: 

Gyrosigma arcuatum on Zm MHMPP Stub 6-Zm-proximal-enviro-sections-Nov 15-20-MHHPP Gyrosigma Nov 15-2020-Dec 29-2020-(x1.2k)_3.tif; Gyrosigma_Box 9 Mar 7-2021-stb17M leaf 6 En (500x) HM (July 18-2023)_15(x1.2k)_3.tif; Gyrosigma arcuatum Sturdies Bay Dock-GBB23-May26-28_2023 Box 33-B Stub GB_001-1 (July16 2024) MW AVA_020(x1.2k)_4.tif; Gyrosigma arcuatum-on Ceramium pacificum-Retreat Cove-GBB23-May26-28_2023 Box 33-B Stub-GB_011-3 (July22 2024) MW AVA_046(x1.0k)_4.tif.

Methods:

The Rhodophyta Ceramium Pacificum was collected by Scuba as part of the 2023 BioBlitz for Galiano Island. By brushing the macroalage in 0.2 µm marine water a suspension of diatoms was obtained. This was rinsed with deionized lab water, then cleaned with hot concentrated hydrogen peroxide at 95-98C in a water bath to remove organics, then rinsed multiple times in ddH20 to a neutral pH. Mounted on SEM stubs or in Naphrax on slides for light microscopy (MW & AvA). Imaging with a Nikon E800 and Zeiss MRc5 camera. SEM imaging with a Hitachi table top TM4000 Plus, Advanced Microscopy Facility at the University of Victoria, B.C. Thanks go to Hitachi Hi Tech Canada of the loan to Elaine Humphrey of the AMF, UVIC. Also, thanks to the diving team of Hakai Institute for sampling and joint IMERSS-Hakai-UBC-UVIC BioBlitz. Sandra Lindstrom at UBC provided the macroalgae id. Molecular data was processed by the Parfrey Lab: thank you Laura Parfrey, Siobhan Schenk, Evan Morien and Andrea Jackman. SEM imaging by Arjan van Asselt and Mark Webber. Additional prep., imaging adjustments, taxonomy and identifications by M. Webber.

6187c861-939a-4cbe-a002-98077f2257df.description:
Species identified: 

Parlibellus delognei (Van Heurck) E.J.Cox 1988: 19

Genus: 
The type species (holotype) of the genus Paribellus is Parlibellus delognei (Van Heurck) E.J.Cox 1988: 19 (Guiry and Guiry 2024)

Taxonomic notes on the genera:

Phylum: Heterokontophyta
Subphylum: Bacillariophytina
Class: Bacillariophyceae
Order: Naviculales
Family: Berkeleyaceae
Genus: Paribellus (Guiry and Guiry 2024)

Genus Summary:

Valves more or less rhomboidal or bluntly lanceolate, sometimes becoming somewhat elliptical, often with a strongly convex face. The raphe is straight, terminating before the valve apices and the external polar raphe fissures curving to one side. The inner raphe fissure opens in a thickened axial raphe rib terminating in a helictoglossa at the poles. The central area is variable in shape, from a large fascia-like central area to small and oval. May have a cuniculus (one or more pores at the external central area). The stria pores are usually circular in surface view, sometimes transversely elongated, occluded on the inner face by regularly perforate ricae, and in section somewhat flask-shaped. Each frustule has a wide girdle region due to the numerous girdle bands, which are similar, each being a split ring with a double row of pores with perforate ricae. Septa are lacking. The living cells have two, often deeply lobed chloroplasts lying along the girdle region on either side of the central cytoplasm. A marine littoral species, some occurring in mucilage tubes (Cox 1988, Round et al. 1990, Spaulding et al. 2021).


Previous reports of Parlibellus species found in the Salish Sea and West Coast:

1.	Parlibellus berkeleyi (Kützing) E.J.Cox 1988: 21, figs 6-10, 16 (Lobban 1985)
2.	Parlibellus delognei (Van Heurck) E.J.Cox 1988: 19 (Lobban 1985)
3.	Parlibellus hamulifer (Grunow) E.J.Cox 1988: table 4, fig. 5 (as 'hamulifera') (Rao. & Lewin (1977 '1976')
4.	Parlibellus rhombicus (W.Gregory) E.J.Cox 1988: 25 (Lord 1866, Bailey and MacKay 1916, Clemens 1933, Rao. & Lewin (1977 '1976' and Tynni 1986)

Species Descriptions:

Parlibellus delognei (Van Heurck) E.J.Cox 1988: 19

References: Van Heurck 1880: pl. 11, figs 13, 110; Cox 1978; Lobban 1984; Lobban 1985; Cox 1988; Lobban 1990; Witkowski et al. 2000: 321-322, Pl. 104, Figs. 1-5: Vidal et al. 2017: 78.

Description:

Cells in girdle view rectangular, girdle very broad composed of numerous punctate bands. Valves lanceolate-elliptic, convex face, with acutely rounded apices, 55.0-118.0 (30-80) µm long, 15.4-33.6 (13-18) µm wide. Raphe straight, external central endings distant, somewhat expanded, apical endings terminate before apices, bent to one side in a small hook. Axial area narrow, central area small and circular with occasional puncta. Transapical striae punctate, slightly elongate, evenly spaced, parallel to slightly radiate across the valve, 20-24 (16-24) in 10 µm, areolae 23-29 (20) in 10 µm.

[Parlibellus delognei f. ellipticus (Lobban) E.J. Cox 1988: 21: Has a more elliptical-rhomboid form and lacks the occasional puncta in the central area compared to the typical form (Lobban 1984: 785; Cox 1988). 62.8 (42-50) µm long, 19.4 (13-17) µm wide, 20-21 (19-20) striae in 10 µm, 24 areolae in 10 µm.]

Remarks: 
These specimens exhibit a larger length and width than reported by Lobban (1985) and Witkowski et al. (2000), slightly radiate striae and moderately higher striae and areolae densities for the Pacific coast reports. However. Lobban observed a wider variation within Pacific west coast specimens than on the east coast of Canada, including the frequent lack of isolated puncta in the central area, an observation occasionally found in these specimens. Based on the small hooked apical external raphe endings of specimens found on Zostera marina in Montague Harbour Marine Provincial Park and Retreat Cove Rhodophyta specimens, the more elliptical-rhomboid form and 1-3 pores in the central area, compared to a similar taxa, P. hamulifer that has markedly hooked apical external raphe endings (Navarro 1987, Cox 1988, Park 2014), these specimens are placed into P. delognei (Van Heurck) E.J. Cox 1988 (Guiry and Guiry 2024).  Parlibellus delognei was previously reported in the Salish Sea by Lobban (1985). Molecular data from specimens of the eelgrass, Z. marina on March 7, 2021 identifies Paribellus delognei var. ellipticus, though Lobban (1985) did not find this variety during his sampling and from other west coast collections. It is possible that the variation in cell shape and puncta present or not in the central area is a normal species variation and not a true variety or form.

Salish Sea specimens, Parlibellus delognei: 
Parlibellus delognei on S gaudichaudii-RC-GBB23-May26-28_2023 Box 33-B Stub-GB_008-1 (July18 2024) MW AVA_65(x1.0k)_4.tif; Parlibellus delognei on Zm MHMPP-Aug 4-2020-slide 1b-H2O2_E800 100x-MU2003-Nov 20b-2021 fs_0171-184_4.tif ; Parlibellus delognei Stub 3-Zm MHMPP Nov 15-2020 NA cleaned P-M-D-S4800 Jan 20-2020_m020_4.tif; Parlibellus delognei-Diatoms on Z marina-MHMPP-H2O2-Naphrax-MU2003-Aug 4-2020_(MW-Oct 22-2020)_0010_4.tif; Parlibellus delognei GBB23-May26-28_2023 Box 33-B Stub Costaria costata-GB_006-1 (July18 2024)MW AVA_079(x1.0k)_4.tif

Methods:

Collected by brushing or scrapping leaf sections of Zostera marina from Montague Harbour Marine Provincial Park (MHMPP) November 15, 2020 and March 7, 2021. Cells were cleaned with 30% hydrogen peroxide or nitric acid/ sulfuric acids at 95-100 C, depending on volume and density of sample for 3-5 hours to remove organics, then rinsed multiple times in ddH20 to a neutral pH. Mounted on SEM stubs or in Naphrax on slides for light microscopy. Imaging with a Nikon TE300 and Tuscen DigiRetna16 MP camera or Nikon E800. Live specimens were imaged with either a Nikon TE300 or Nikon E800 with either bright-field or DIC. In-situ, environmentally prepared samples were made using minimal contact of 8-10 mm leaf section, soaked in ddH2O to remove salts and dried through an EtOH series (50%-100%) and finished off with 100% Hexamethyldisilane HMDS (Hazrin-Chong and Manefield 2012). Mounted on carbon stickies onto aluminum SEM stubs and imaged with either the Hitachi s4800 or TM4000 Plus (on loan to Elaine Humphrey by Hitachi High-Tech Canada) at AMF, at University of Victoria, B.C. Swabs of leaf material together with samples for SEM and LM were processed by the Parfrey Lab: thank you Laura Parfrey, Siobhan Schenk, Evan Morien and Andrea Jackman for molecular data from the eelgrass and collaboration with IMERSS. Also, thanks go to Elaine Humphrey of the AMF, UVIC, imaging by Ron Read, Melanie Quenneville and Arjan van Asselt (IMERSS). LM imaging, taxonomy and identifications by M. Webber (IMERSS, Salish Sea Diatom Project).

4cb8c377-75f6-446a-b68c-10e39c8de28f.description:
Mastigamoeba schizophrenia (Simpson, Bernard, Fenchel and Patterson 1997) from a benthic sample from freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. Long video is the last picture. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. The cell measures 24 um in length. The amoeboid cell glided on the substrate with a long leading flagellum that undulated at its distal 25%. After some research, I tentatively identified the organism as a mastigamoebid pelobiont based upon the combination of amoeboid movement of the cell and the presence of a single long, slow-beating flagellum (1).  The connection between the flagellar base and the anteriormost nucleus places the organism in the genus Mastigamoeba. M. schizophrenia can be distinguished from all other species in the genus by the paired nuclei (David Patterson- personal communication)  with only a single pair present in the flagellated form (1). 
 
Mastigamoeba schizophrenia is an anaerobic protist and has been encountered both in anoxic water bodies and in anoxic sediments. The life cycle of Mastigamoeba schizophrenia was established by studies of  cultures. It includes flagellated trophic cells, aflagellated trophic cells, and cysts.  The proportion of each type of cell is mainly dependent upon the age of the cultures (1).

This organism was originally described in a marine site while my observation is from a freshwater pond. Several features struck me- the paired nuclei at the base of the flagellum with one more anterior than the other, numerous pseudopods around the posterior end of the cell, and the unusual multivacuolar complex at the posterior end of the cell. Often there was a large dominant vacuole wreathed by numerous smaller vacuoles which then coalesced in the manner of some contractile vacuoles seen in some ciliates. Except for the presence of the posterior vacuolar complex (is it a contractile vacuole or some other type of organelle?) which feature was not described in the paper of Simpson et al 1997, every other feature I observed is in agreement with the light microscopic description of the flagellated trophic form of M. schizophrenia. Similar to the observations of Simspon et al 1997, there were prominent pseudopods around the posterior end of the cell. I did not observe the "small, thin, occasionally branched, conical pseudopods" they described but the "broader hyaline pseudopods which can give uncompressed cells a lumpy appearance" were quite prominent. Their detailed description follows:

"Flagellated trophic cells range from a few microns up to about 25 um (fully extended but not including fine pseudopods - see below). Flagellated forms are never observed with more than one pair of nuclei. This pair is always located at the base of the flagellum. Aflagellated cells are 10-70 um long. Aflagellated trophic cells have one to five pairs of nuclei. The larger cells tend to have the greatest number of nuclei. The flagellum is typically 50-80 um long but may be considerably shorter. The flagellated trophic cells are observed either swimming or gliding. The cell glides slowly in a monopodial configuration with the flagellum directed anteriorly. Small, thin, occasionally branched, conical pseudopods may be present around the posterior of flagellated cells. Broader hyaline pseudopods can also be extended, which can give uncompressed cells a lumpy appearance. When the cell swims, the flagellum is also directed anteriorly and draws the cell forward by generating base-to-tip waves. The cell is usually spherical during swimming. When the organism is stationary, the flagellum may be held rigidly away from the cell with only the tip moving and the flagellum is not always inserted opposite the posterior pseudopods. Aflagellated amoebae move by slow monopodial gliding but are more prone to extend hyaline pseudopodia. Gliding cells are frequently observed in clumps of several individuals" (1).

Species identified: 

Parlibellus delognei (Van Heurck) E.J.Cox 1988: 19

Genus: 
The type species (holotype) of the genus Parlibellus is Parlibellus delognei (Van Heurck) E.J.Cox 1988: 19 (Guiry and Guiry 2024)

Taxonomic notes on the genera:

Phylum: Heterokontophyta
Subphylum: Bacillariophytina
Class: Bacillariophyceae
Order: Naviculales
Family: Berkeleyaceae
Genus: Paribellus (Guiry and Guiry 2024)

Genus Summary:

Valves more or less rhomboidal or bluntly lanceolate, sometimes becoming somewhat elliptical, often with a strongly convex face. The raphe is straight, terminating before the valve apices and the external polar raphe fissures curving to one side. The inner raphe fissure opens in a thickened axial raphe rib terminating in a helictoglossa at the poles. The central area is variable in shape, from a large fascia-like central area to small and oval. May have a cuniculus (one or more pores at the external central area). The stria pores are usually circular in surface view, sometimes transversely elongated, occluded on the inner face by regularly perforate ricae, and in section somewhat flask-shaped. Each frustule has a wide girdle region due to the numerous girdle bands, which are similar, each being a split ring with a double row of pores with perforate ricae. Septa are lacking. The living cells have two, often deeply lobed chloroplasts lying along the girdle region on either side of the central cytoplasm. A marine littoral species, some occurring in mucilage tubes (Cox 1988, Round et al. 1990, Spaulding et al. 2021).


Previous reports of Paribellus species found in the Salish Sea and West Coast:

1.	Parlibellus berkeleyi (Kützing) E.J.Cox 1988: 21, figs 6-10, 16 (Lobban 1985)
2.	Parlibellus delognei (Van Heurck) E.J.Cox 1988: 19 (Lobban 1985)
3.	Parlibellus hamulifer (Grunow) E.J.Cox 1988: table 4, fig. 5 (as 'hamulifera') (Rao. & Lewin (1977 '1976')
4.	Parlibellus rhombicus (W.Gregory) E.J.Cox 1988: 25 (Lord 1866, Bailey and MacKay 1916, Clemens 1933, Rao. & Lewin (1977 '1976' and Tynni 1986)

Parlibellus delognei (Van Heurck) E.J.Cox 1988: 19
References: Van Heurck 1880: pl. 11, figs 13, 110; Cox 1978; Lobban 1984; Lobban 1985; Cox 1988; Lobban 1990; Witkowski et al. 2000: 321-322, Pl. 104, Figs. 1-5: Vidal et al. 2017: 78.

Description for Parlibellus delognei (Van Heurck) E.J.Cox 1988: 19
Cells in girdle view rectangular, girdle very broad composed of numerous punctate bands. Valves lanceolate-elliptic, convex face, with acutely rounded apices, 55.0-118.0 (30-80) µm long, 15.4-33.6 (13-18) µm wide. Raphe straight, external central endings distant, somewhat expanded, apical endings terminate before apices, bent to one side in a small hook. Axial area narrow, central area small and circular with occasional puncta. Transapical striae punctate, slightly elongate, evenly spaced, parallel to slightly radiate across the valve, 20-24 (16-24) in 10 µm, areolae 23-29 (20) in 10 µm.

Parlibellus delognei f. ellipticus (Lobban) E.J. Cox 1988: 21: Has a more elliptical-rhomboid form and lacks the occasional puncta in the central area compared to the typical form (Lobban 1984: 785; Cox 1988). 62.8 (42-50) µm long, 19.4 (13-17) µm wide, 20-21 (19-20) striae in 10 µm, 24 areolae in 10 µm.

Remarks: 
These specimens exhibit a larger length and width than reported by Lobban (1985) and Witkowski et al. (2000), slightly radiate striae and moderately higher striae and areolae densities for the Pacific coast reports. However. Lobban observed a wider variation within Pacific west coast specimens than on the east coast of Canada, including the frequent lack of isolated puncta in the central area, an observation occasionally found in these specimens. Based on the small hooked apical external raphe endings of specimens found on Zostera marina in Montague Harbour Marine Provincial Park and Retreat Cove Rhodophyta specimens, the more elliptical-rhomboid form and occasional puncta in the central area, compared to a similar taxa, P. hamulifer that has markedly hooked apical external raphe endings (Navarro 1987, Park 2014), these specimens are placed into  Parlibellus delognei (Van Heurck) E.J.Cox 1988. Parlibellus delognei was previously reported in the Salish Sea by Lobban (1985). Recent molecular data from two other Rhodophyta samples from Retreat Cove, Galiano Island, from the same day of collecting this specimen and specimens of the eelgrass, Z. marina on March 7, 2021 identifies Parlibellus delognei var. ellipticus, though Lobban (1985) did not find this variety during his sampling and from other west coast collections. It is possible that the variation in cell shape and puncta present or not in the central area is a normal species variation and not a true variety or form. 

Salish Sea specimens, Parlibellus delognei: Parlibellus delognei on S gaudichaudii-RC-GBB23-May26-28_2023 Box 33-B Stub-GB_008-1 (July18 2024) MW AVA_65(x1.0k)_4.tif; Parlibellus delognei on Zm MHMPP-Aug 4-2020-slide 1b-H2O2_E800 100x-MU2003-Nov 20b-2021 fs_0171-184_4.tif ; Parlibellus delognei Stub 3-Zm MHMPP Nov 15-2020 NA cleaned P-M-D-S4800 Jan 20-2020_m020_4.tif; Parlibellus delognei-Diatoms on Z marina-MHMPP-H2O2-Naphrax-MU2003-Aug 4-2020_(MW-Oct 22-2020)_0010_4.tif; Parlibellus delognei GBB23-May26-28_2023 Box 33-B Stub Costaria costata-GB_006-1 (July18 2024)MW AVA_079(x1.0k)_4.tif

Methods:

Retreat Cove, Galiano Island, 2023 BioBlitz:
The Rhodophyta Ceramium Pacificum and brown algae, Costaria costata were collected by Scuba as part of the 2023 BioBlitz for Galiano Island. By brushing the macroalage in 0.2 µm marine water a suspension of diatoms was obtained. This was rinsed with deionized lab water, then cleaned with hot concentrated hydrogen peroxide at 95-98C in a water bath to remove organics, then rinsed multiple times in ddH20 to a neutral pH. Mounted on SEM stubs or in Naphrax on slides for light microscopy (MW & AvA). Imaging with a Nikon E800 and Zeiss MRc5 camera. SEM imaging with a Hitachi table top TM4000 Plus, Advanced Microscopy Facility at the University of Victoria, B.C. Thanks go to Hitachi Hi Tech Canada of the loan to Elaine Humphrey of the AMF, UVIC. Thanks to Laura Parfrey, Henry Mcgee and Arjan van Asselt for initial prep of molecular and microscopy samples. Also, thanks to the diving team of Hakai Institute for sampling and joint IMERSS-Hakai-UBC-UVIC BioBlitz. Sandra Lindstrom at UBC provided the macroalgae id. Molecular data was processed by the Parfrey Lab: thank you Laura Parfrey, Siobhan Schenk, Evan Morien and Andrea Jackman. SEM imaging by Arjan van Asselt and Mark Webber. Additional prep., imaging adjustments, taxonomy and identifications by M. Webber.

Species Identified:

Licmophora flabellata (Greville) C.Agardh 1831

Genus: Licmophora C. Agardh (1827) nom. et typ. Cons.

Taxonomic classification:

Phylum: Heterokontophyta
Subphylum: Bacillariophytina
Class: Bacillariophyceae
Subclass: Fragilariophycidae
Order: Licmophorales
Family: Licmophoraceae
Genus: Licmophora (Guiry and Guiry 2023)

Holotype species, synonym(s), etc.: Licmophora argentescens C.Agardh

Genus Summary:

Licmophora is an araphid genus. Species in the genus are cosmopolitan, found in most marine habitats including Arctic, Antarctic, and tropical regions. Cells grow in colonies, often fan shaped on branched mucilaginous stalks or pads, attached to various substrates such as seaweeds, rocks, animals or detached and found singly in the plankton. Frustules are heteropolar. They have a narrow base (sometimes slightly capitate) and broader apex and in valve and girdle view the cell is cuneate (wedge shaped). The valves have a narrow, sometimes indistinct central sternum. Septa present, distinct or indistinct (Plinski and Witkowski 2020), internally around the apical ends and tapering off down each side of the copulae. The areolae are round or elongate and externally covered by a criba. The striae are transapical, uniseriate and parallel, except at the apices where they can become radiate. A rimoportula is present on one valve at the base and on the other valve, or both valves, at the apex. External rimoportula is a circular slit like opening, whereas the internal rimoportula opening is labiate, fan shaped, sometimes stalked and flush with the frustule. Normally, there are two or three rimoportulae per cell. If 2 rimoportulae per frustule, then, one is located at the basal apex, the other at the head apex. If 3 rimoportulae, one is located at the basal apex, one at the head apex of each valve. A series of slits (multiscissura) is present around the base of both valves where mucilage for stalks and pads is secreted. Spines are present at the head apex of some species. Plastids numerous and small. There are five distinguishable girdle bands. Areolae on the copulae (girdle bands) are smaller than those on the valve. Valvocopulae open at the basal apex and maybe a septum at the apex. Relying on identification of species by light microscopy may be problematic due to fine features; SEM and TEM are utilized. AlgaeBase lists 102 accepted species and 10 varieties (Honeywill 1988, Round et al. 1990, Lobhan 2013, Lobhan et al. 2018, Plinski and Witkowski 2020: 56, Spaulding et al. 2021, Guiry and Guiry 2023).

From historic records, 9 species and 2 varieties of Licmophora have been previously recorded in the Salish Sea and Western Pacific waters:

Licmophora abbreviata C.Agardh 1831: 42: 20-110 µm long, 4-8 µm wide, striae at the base of valve 11-12 in 10 µm, in the upper part 14-16 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020)
L. californica Grunow 1885
L. gracilis (Ehr.) Grun: 40-110 µm long, 10-16 µm wide, striae 20-22 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020)
L. gracilis var. anglica (Kützing) H.Peragallo & M.Peragallo 1901
L. hyalina (Kützing) Grunow 1867
L. ehrenbergii (Kützing) Grunow 1867: 36: 60-180 µm long, 15-30 µm wide, striae evenly distributed throughout the valve, striae 8-11 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020)
L. ehrenbergii f. grunowii (Mereschk.) Hust.
L. flabellata (Greville) C.Agardh 1831
L. juergensii C.Agardh 1831: 30-100 µm long, 7-13 µm wide, striate delicate, striae at the foot pole 23-25 in 10 µm, in the head pole 27-30 in 10 µm (Plinski and Witkowski 2020).
L. lyngbyei (Kützing) Grunow 1867
L. paradoxa (Lyngb.) Agardh
Species Description:

Licmophora flabellata (Greville) C.Agardh 1831: 42 (syn: Exilaria flabellata Greville 1827: pl. 289; Echinella flabellata Carmichael, nom. inval. 2003: 78).

References:
Greville 1827: pl. 289; Hendey 1964; Honeywill 1998; Sar and Ferrario 1990; Witkowski et al. 2000: 63, Pl. 18, Fig. 2-3; Macatugal et al. 2019; Romagnoli et al. 2014: 572, Fig. 3 f-k.

Description:
Cells in girdle view, thinly cuneate with flat valve face profile. Valves long, narrow, spatulate/clavate with a round capitate foot pole. Valves 126.3-188.8 (60-300) µm long, 4.6-6.5 (4-13) µm wide at upper part, 5-6.5 (3-4) µm wide at the base pole. Striae uniseriate 30 (32-35) in 10 µm at head pole, 24-28 (29-35) at mid frustule and 32 (30) at base pole. Areolae slightly elongate in transapical direction, 45-55 (35) in 10 µm throughout the valve. A prominent transapical rimoportula (not stalked), is often at the basal pole, either in both valves of the same frustule or in only one of them. Another, smaller rimoportula is at head pole. Numerous smaller non-stalked rimoportulae 7-9 (6-9), with external openings at irregular intervals along sternum. Distinct narrow sternum, slightly curved at basal pole. Two small spines at head pole on both valves (not seen in Galiano Isl. specimens). Multiscissura has 38-43 (30-45) slits. Basal pole has a few irregularly arranged pores. Valvocopula lacking a distinguishable septum (septa shallow). Two distinctive round plastids, one near top and one in middle of cell.

Remarks:
The morphology of these Galiano Island specimens conforms well to descriptions in the listed references. The only exceptions are a greater base pole width, a higher areolae density and some slight differences in striae counts compared to published data. This may reflect normal species variation within the Salish Sea, Western Canada or indicate a new variety. Licmophora flabellata was reported in the Salish Sea by: Bailey and MacKay (1915) and Clemens 1933; no striae densities are provided.

Methods:

Collected by brushing or scrapping leaf sections of Zostera marina from Montague Harbour Marine Provincial Park (MHMPP) November 15, 2020 and March 7, 2021 Cells were cleaned with 30% hydrogen peroxide or nitric acid/ sulfuric acids at 95-100 C, depending on volume and density of sample for 3-5 hours to remove organics, then rinsed multiple times in ddH20 to a neutral pH. Mounted on SEM stubs or in Naphrax on slides for light microscopy. Imaging with a Nikon TE300 and Tuscen DigiRetna16 MP camera or Nikon E800 BF or DIC with a MU2003 or Zeiss MRc5 camera. Live specimens were imaged with either a Nikon TE300 or Nikon E800 with either bright-field or DIC. In-situ, environmentally prepared samples were made using minimal contact of 8-10 mm leaf section, soaked in ddH2O to remove salts and dried through an EtOH series (50%-100%) and finished off with 100% Hexamethyldisilane HMDS (Hazrin-Chong and Manefield 2012). Mounted on carbon stickies onto aluminum SEM stubs and imaged with either the Hitachi s4800 or TM4000 Plus (on loan to Elaine Humphrey by Hitachi High-Tech Canada) at AMF, at University of Victoria, B.C. Swabs of leaf material together with samples for SEM and LM were processed by the Parfrey Lab: thank you Laura Parfrey, Siobhan Schenk, Evan Morien and Andrea Jackman for molecular data from the eelgrass and collaboration with IMERSS. Also, thanks go to Elaine Humphrey of the AMF, UVIC, imaging by Ron Read, Melanie Quenneville and Arjan van Asselt (IMERSS). LM and SEM imaging, taxonomy and identifications by M. Webber (IMERSS, Salish Sea Diatom Project).

a567059a-3f40-4d69-b887-c772d1d2c1dd.description:
Video: https://youtu.be/zI1HcNQU1XM

Sampling location: A lichen growing on the bark of a birch tree (*Betula sp.*), yard between residential buildings.
Date and time of collection: December 1, 2024 at 2 PM. Air temp 6 °C (42,8°F)
Date and time of observation: December 11, 2024 at 3 PM.
Small sample of lichen were moistened with distilled water and stored in a closed glass jar.
All images and video are of the organisms from the same population.

*Leptopharynx* Mermod, 1914.

Diagnosis of the organisms observed:
•	Length 21-34 µm, width 14-24 µm. 
•	Discoidal. Dorsoventrally flattened. Cortex rigid, with furrows accompanying rows of cilia.
•	Ventral side is more flattened than the convex dorsal side. 
•	Oblique preoral region.
•	Oral basket in anterior third, oblique to the body’s main axis.
•	Macronucleus globular or broadly ellipsoidal, with spherical nucleoli.
•	Micronucleus globular, located at ventral side of macronucleus.
•	Extrusomes fusiform, ~3 µm long.
•	About four longitudinal kinetics on left and on right side.
•	Cilia on left side widely spaced.
•	Contractile vacuole (CV) and cytopyge are located in third quarter of ventral side. CV, located near midbody, has a distinct canal (short tube). Cytopyge is underneath the CV, usually forming a blister containing food remnants.
•	Countless lipid droplets in cytoplasm.

References:

8d14b94a-9ba6-4a18-ae47-e0bc7b40a8af.description:
Acineria incurvata from a three month old benthic sample taken from a small tidal pool at the edge of the salt marsh at marine extuary Acabonac Harbor at Landing Lane.  The cells measure 72-80 um in length.  The reported variability of cell shape is evident in this sample. The rolled up apical oral slit and two spherical  macronuclei are apparent. Extrusomes are present at the oral slit and posterior end of the ciliate.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus pnone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. 

Acineria incurvata Dujardin, 1841.  About 45-200 um Abnormal, giant individuals up to 500 pm showing most organelles duplicated observed by Foissner (1977/78) and probably by Lepsi (1965). Body oblong, slightly contractile, laterally compressed, rounded posteriorly, narrowing anteriorly to a blunt point. Rather variable in shape (slender to wide and plump) depending on nutritional condition. Ventral side more or less convex, dorsal side straight or concave in the anterior, convex in the posterior region. Excavated region conspicuous, shining brightly. Anterior-most dorsal tip somewhat refractive, due to the rolled up oral slit. Cytostome more or less curved, anteriorly overlapping to the left side but not to the right as described by Lepsi (1926 a,b,1928). Macronucleus in two spherical to ovoid parts with a single micronucleus between them. 1-3 micronuclei according to Maupas (1883). Macronuclear parts fuse during bipartition and divide in the later fission stages. Single contractile vacuole at the posterior pole, diameter about 7 um, with 5-8 pores on the right lateral side which could not be seen in our slides. Cytoproct terminal, a slightly laterally located slit. Pellicle soft, flexible, with longitudinal furrows in which the cilia and bristles originate. Furrows disappear in well-fed individuals. 
Three different types of cilia: (1) normal cilia, about 10 um, (2) short bristles, about 0.5-1.0 pm. (3) club-shaped bristles, up to 2.0 um. Eleven longitudinal kineties with cilia type 1, about 8-9 of them on the right and about 3 on the left side. Extrusomes straight to slightly fusiform (arrow-shaped according to Foissner, 1977/78), thin, about 4 um long, located along the cytostome, a small accumulation of them in the ventral side of the posteriorend and even a few scattered throughout the body.  Cytoplasm of normally-fed specimens rather clear, containing some small colourless spheres.  Carnivorous, feeds on small hymenostome ciliates. Starved individuals feed even on cysts of Euglena viridis and perhaps on bacteria.

1, Revision of the genera Acineria, Trimyema and Trochiliopsis (Protozoa, Ciliophora). H. Augustin, W. Foissner & H. Adam. Bull.Br.Mus.Nat.Hist. (Zool) 1987 52(6): 197-224

f6e77f58-aa57-4076-b2b7-d29993e25fad.description:
Species identified: 

Parlibellus delognei (Van Heurck) E.J.Cox 1988: 19


Genus: 

The type species (holotype) of the genus Parlibellus is Parlibellus delognei (Van Heurck) E.J.Cox 1988: 19 (Guiry and Guiry 2024)

Taxonomic notes on the genera:

Phylum: Heterokontophyta
Subphylum: Bacillariophytina
Class: Bacillariophyceae
Order: Naviculales
Family: Berkeleyaceae
Genus: Paribellus (Guiry and Guiry 2024)

Genus Summary:

Valves more or less rhomboidal or bluntly lanceolate, sometimes becoming somewhat elliptical, often with a strongly convex face. The raphe is straight, terminating before the valve apices and the external polar raphe fissures curving to one side. The inner raphe fissure opens in a thickened axial raphe rib terminating in a helictoglossa at the poles. The central area is variable in shape, from a large fascia-like central area to small and oval. May have a cuniculus (one or more pores at the external central area). The stria pores are usually circular in surface view, sometimes transversely elongated, occluded on the inner face by regularly perforate ricae, and in section somewhat flask-shaped. Each frustule has a wide girdle region due to the numerous girdle bands, which are similar, each being a split ring with a double row of pores with perforate ricae. Septa are lacking. The living cells have two, often deeply lobed chloroplasts lying along the girdle region on either side of the central cytoplasm. A marine littoral species, some occurring in mucilage tubes (Cox 1988, Round et al. 1990, Spaulding et al. 2021).


Previous reports of Paribellus species found in the Salish Sea and West Coast:

1.	Parlibellus berkeleyi (Kützing) E.J.Cox 1988: 21, figs 6-10, 16 (Lobban 1985)
2.	Parlibellus delognei (Van Heurck) E.J.Cox 1988: 19 (Lobban 1985)
3.	Parlibellus hamulifer (Grunow) E.J.Cox 1988: table 4, fig. 5 (as 'hamulifera') (Rao. & Lewin (1977 '1976')
4.	Parlibellus rhombicus (W.Gregory) E.J.Cox 1988: 25 (Lord 1866, Bailey and MacKay 1916, Clemens 1933, Rao. & Lewin (1977 '1976' and Tynni 1986)

Species description:

Parlibellus delognei (Van Heurck) E.J.Cox 1988: 19

References: Van Heurck 1880: pl. 11, figs 13, 110; Lobban 1984; Lobban 1985; Cox 1988; Lobban 1990; Witkowski et al. 2000: 321-322, Pl. 104, Figs. 1-5: Vidal et al. 2017: 78.

Description:

Cells in girdle view rectangular, girdle very broad composed of numerous punctate bands. Valves lanceolate-elliptic, convex face, with acutely rounded apices, 55.0-118.0 (30-80) µm long, 15.4-33.6 (13-18) µm wide. Raphe straight, external central endings distant, somewhat expanded, apical endings terminate before apices, bent to one side in a small hook. Axial area narrow, central area small and circular with occasional puncta. Transapical striae punctate, slightly elongate, evenly spaced, parallel to slightly radiate across the valve, 20-24 (16-24) in 10 µm, areolae 23-29 (20) in 10 µm.


Remarks: 
These specimens exhibit a larger length and width than reported by Lobban (1985) and Witkowski et al. (2000), slightly radiate striae and moderately higher striae and areolae densities for the Pacific coast reports. However. Lobban observed a wider variation within Pacific west coast specimens than on the east coast of Canada, including the frequent lack of isolated puncta in the central area, an observation occasionally found in these specimens. Based on the small hooked apical external raphe endings of specimens found on Zostera marina in Montague Harbour Marine Provincial Park and Retreat Cove Rhodophyta specimens, the more elliptical-rhomboid form and occasional puncta in the central area, compared to a similar taxa, P. hamulifer that has markedly hooked apical external raphe endings (Navarro 1987, Park 2014), these specimens are placed into  Parlibellus delognei (Van Heurck) E.J.Cox 1988. Parlibellus delognei was previously reported in the Salish Sea by Lobban (1985). Recent molecular data from Rhodophyta samples from Retreat Cove, Galiano Island, from May 26, 2024 identifies Parlibellus delognei var. ellipticus, though Lobban (1985) did not find this variety during his sampling and from other west coast collections. It is possible that the variation in cell shape and puncta present or not in the central area is a normal species variation and not a true variety or form.

Salish Sea specimens, Parlibellus delognei: Parlibellus delognei on S gaudichaudii-RC-GBB23-May26-28_2023 Box 33-B Stub-GB_008-1 (July18 2024) MW AVA_65(x1.0k)_4.tif; Parlibellus delognei on Zm MHMPP-Aug 4-2020-slide 1b-H2O2_E800 100x-MU2003-Nov 20b-2021 fs_0171-184_4.tif ; Parlibellus delognei Stub 3-Zm MHMPP Nov 15-2020 NA cleaned P-M-D-S4800 Jan 20-2020_m020_4.tif; Parlibellus delognei-Diatoms on Z marina-MHMPP-H2O2-Naphrax-MU2003-Aug 4-2020_(MW-Oct 22-2020)_0010_4.tif; Parlibellus delongnei-Sidney Spit ECH Z marina July 2024-slide 6-E800 AvA (Jan 18-2025) x100-05_3.tif; Parlibellus delongnei-Sidney Spit ECH Z marina July 2024-slide 6-E800 AvA (Jan 18-2025) x100-65_4.tif.

Methods:

Sidney Spit, Sidney Island, ECH, July 2024:
The eelgrass, Zostera marina was collected by hand by Elaine Humphrey off a boat near the north end of Sidney Island. Diatoms were recovered by brushing the leaf into a small pool of 0.2 µm filtered marine water. This was rinsed with deionized lab water for 12 hrs. decanted and treated with 10% hydrochloric acid for 12 hrs. Frustules were cleaned with concentrated 1:1 nitric and sulfuric acids and heated for 3 hrs. at 95-98C in a water bath to remove organics. Rinsed multiple times in ddH20 to a neutral pH. Mounted on SEM stubs or in Naphrax on slides for light microscopy (MW). Imaging with a Nikon E800, DIC and Zeiss MRc5 camera. Thanks go to Elaine Humphrey (IMERSS) of the Advanced Microscope Facility at the University of Victoria who collected the sample. Imaging with the Nikon E800 LM by Arjan van Asselt (IMERSS). Mark Webber (IMERSS) did cleaning, SEM stub and slide prep., imaging adjustments and taxonomy.

8ea98164-ef21-4925-8e2d-0e5e3f00adb8.description:
From a water sample sent by Harry Mueller (@hgmueller).  This species was originally described as *Euglypha scutigera* Penard, 1911.  The species was differentiated from other *Euglypha* species by its "scutiform" (shield-shaped) scales.  In 2001, Foissner and Schiller created the genus *Scutiglypha* for euglyphids with scutiform scales, and moved *E. scutigera* to it.  Not all taxonomists accept the new genus.  Ferry Siemensma does not. See: https://arcella.nl/euglypha/ and https://arcella.nl/euglypha-scutigera/ 

Note that in this individual one scale in the third row is turned around (see the second image). This allows us to the dentate anterior which would normally be covered up.

"Belonophorus" is derived from Greek roots:

"Phorus" is derived from "phoros," meaning "bearing" or "carrying."

111d3bb4-a968-4bc0-bc41-5129c84c138b.description:
Cinetochilum margaritaceum (Ehrenberg, 1831) Perty, 1849 harvested by the floating cover glass method from benthos of the freshwater Peconic River.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. The cells  of the Peconic River population range from 30.4 up to 36 um in length.  

"Shape and dimensions: ovoid, rounded, somewhat heart-shaped; small, L: 15 to 45 um. The Ciliate shows longitudinal ridges. Somatic infiaciliature: from 19 to 21 more or less bipolar kinetics. The kinetosomes remain spaced apart and only seem to have cilia on the ventral side. The various authors include double kinetosomes in the anterior half. The top of the anterior pole is glabrous (similarly than the post-oral region). The tuft of long caudal cilia is carried by four kinetosomes (from left field). The left and right ventral kineties converge in a suture line mid-apical. There is also a post-oral suture. A segment of left kineties with tight kinetosomes runs along the oral region in its terminal region. The mouth opening is subequatorial and large. It is bordered, on the left, by three polykineties: MI quite long, made up of three rows of kinetosomes, M2 a little shorter and presenting a "beak" and a very small M3 (about twelve kinetosomes). On the right, a very undulating membrane enveloping with kinetosomes arranged in a zig-zag (haplokineties with two rows of kinetosomes). 22 to 25 oral striae adorn the oral plate. We also observe a sub-oral scutica, made up by at least 3 + 8 kinetosomes. Cytoplasmic organelles: ectoplasmic trichocysts and sometimes Zoochlorella. Cytoproct; median, terminal argyrophilic line" (1).

"Size in vivo usually 25-40 x 20-35 um, according to KAHL (1931) 15-45 um long.  Lenticular shape, strongly flattened laterally; beveled dorsally at the back and with a small but very typical notch where the contractile vacuole lies. Pellicule through the cilia rows clearly notched.  Macronucleus spherical approximately in the middle of the body, one spherical micronucleus. Contractile vacuole subterminal to the notch. Moderately numerous, approximately 3 pm long, rod-shaped extrusomes.  About 19-22 rows of cilia, arching ventrally around the oral apparatus, laterally and dorsally longitudinally lost. Cilia mostly in pairs at the front. Rear end with about 5 extended cilia (caudal cilia). Dorsal and right lateral ciliated only in front. Oral apparatus behind the middle of the body and shifted slightly to the left side. Membranelles 1 and
2 long, membrane 3 very small. Undulating membrane semicircular on the right edge of the mouth. Movement inconspicuous, mostly slowly gliding and creeping in growth and detritus" (2). 

1.  Dragesco, J. & Dragesco-Kernéis, A. (1986) Ciliés libres de l'Afrique intertropicale. Faune Tropicale, 26, 1–559

2. Taxonomische und ökologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobien Band III Hymenostomata Prostomatida, Nassulida W. Foissner, H. Berger, F. Kohmann.   Informationsberichte des Bayer. Landesamtes für Heft 1994, pp. 249-55.

11efc707-78b0-43f0-90e7-68be6ef6208f.description:
Urostomides striatus, I thought I'd share my observation this week of a free-swimming individual which shows some interesting "real world" behavior.   The ciliate is from the benthos of a three month old sample of freshwater Peconic River and is imaged in Nomarski DIC using SPlan 40 0.70 objective and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective.  
 The ciliate uses its long dorsal dome cilia to walk on the substrate. The is similar to behavior shown by another metopid genus, Caenomorpha (as well as certain hypotrichs using their cirri)  and I don't believe it has been described before. 
Also, we can see the metachronous ciliary waves of perizonal stripe cilia and the action of the undulating membrane and contractile vacuole. Besides the cortical "rind" of extrusomes,  another character of U. stiatus is that it's adoral zone of membanelles makes a sharp turn at the distal ends (the end with the mouth opening) to run parallel with the long axis of the body. We can also see the endosymbiotic bacteria in the cytoplasm at 1000x.  Finally, I caught the ciliate in the act of defecation. 
1. Morphologic and molecular characterization of seven species of the remarkably diverse and widely distributed metopid genus Urostomides Jankowski, 1964 (Armophorea, Ciliophora).  William Bourland, Johana Rotterová, Ivan  Čepička. European Journal of Protistology 61 (2017) 194–232

5098422b-f0ea-45bb-979c-194b33698354.description:
An interesting view of Spirostomum teres concentrating on its contractility viewed at 1000x oil immersion.

Spirostomum teres Claparède & Lachmann, 1859 from a benthic sample taken from freshwater Peconic River. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2 using SPlanapo 20 0.75,and Splan 100 1.25 oil objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. The cells measure from 200 um in average length, have a compact ellipsoid macronuclear nodule with two lenticular micronuclei nestled in an indentation of the macronucleus, and are pale yellow brownish in color at low power and highly spirally contractile. A single row of well-developed oral membranelles defines the left side of the long, thin peristomial field, which runs parallel to the main body axis from the anterior end to the cytostome, which is located at 45% of the body length. One stripe of packed cortical granule rows (average 3) between each kinety pair; cortical granules are of different sizes. The contractile vacuole is single and posteriorly located, with a long collecting canal extending along the dorsal side often reaching the anterior end.

"Spirostomum is a genus of ciliated protists that belongs to the class Heterotrichea. It is known for being very contractile. Having been first identified by Christian Gottfried Ehrenberg in 1834, further research has identified eight additional true morphospecies. This bacterivore genus mainly lives in the sediment deposits at the bottom of various aquatic habitats, and members possess rquA genes that could be responsible for their ability to survive in these hypoxic and anoxic environments. They are identifiable by their relatively (to other ciliates) large tubular/flat vermiform bodies. Their life cycle consists of a growth stage, in which they mature, and asexual and sexual reproduction stages. Some species are model organisms for studies on human pathogenic bacteria, while others are sensitive and accurate bioindicators for toxic substances" (1).

The name Spirostomum refers to the ability these ciliates have to contract in a spiral mode. This type of contraction is due to the presence of post-ciliary, sub-pellicular fibers that arise on the anterior end and spiral in a counterclockwise direction toward the posterior end of the body. Of the eight species that currently comprise Spirostomum, five (including S. minus) possess a moniliform macronucleus" (2). "There are currently eight accepted morphospecies in the genus: S. ambiguum, S. minus, S. teres, S. yagiui, S. dharwarensis, S. semivirescens, S. subtilis, S. caudatum" (1). Among all species of Spirostomum, only S. teres and S. caudatum have a compact macronucleus. S. caudatum is easily separated from S. caudatum by the latter's long thin tail (1). Another old species similar to S. teres is S. ephrussi but according to Repack and Isquith (1974), S. ephrussi is junior synonym of S. teres" (2).

"The giant heterotrich ciliate Spirostomum is characterized by its rod-like cell that is usually one to several millimeters in length. Upon contraction, the cell of Spirostomum typically twists and shortens its length up to 75% within 5 ms. In past decades, several studies have been carried out to elucidate the subcellular structures and biophysical features of this fascinating system" (3).

"The surface of Spirostomum contains numerous continuous spiral ciliated grooves that traverse its length. There are two types of fibrillar systems beneath the cell membrane. One comprises microtubule-based fibrillar bundles that run parallel to the base of the spiral grooves and either attach to basal bodies or lie adjacent to them. When the cell contracts, these bundles change in orientation and lie parallel to the grooves, resembling a compressed spring with high potential energy. It is hypothesized that the microtubule-based fibrillar bundles provide turgidity to the cell and may play an antagonistic role to cell contraction, thereby facilitating cell extension" (3).

"The other fibrillar system below the cell membrane of Spirostomum occurs all over the body and comprises fibrillar bundles arranged in a mesh-like pattern. This mesh-like filamentous structure was thought to be analogous to the myoneme that is found in another ultrafast contractile ciliated protozoan, Vorticella, and was thought to be the functional actuator for the ultrafast contraction of the cell. Further evidence for this is that both systems rely on Ca2+ rather than ATP for the contraction: (3).

Most  cells have a chestnut-flask shape though not all have a discernable lip (eg. https://ancientglass.wordpress.com/tag/american-chestnut-bottle/). It appears the long hair structure (with or without the lip feature) can range from straight to highly tangled. 5 cell clusters and groups were observed, each represented as a single image followed by a composite image of 4-6 photos at varying depths of field.

The water sample is from a local pond, collected about 9 months ago, and has been sitting on a windowsill since. I last collected from the Pine Swamp Wildlife Corridor so this is the likely source.
Not certain regarding the ID, though the cells appear like *G. wittrockiana* observed here:https://realmicrolife.com/gloeochaete-wittrockiana/. Two clusters were observed, easily marked by their fan of gelatinous setae radiating from the 4 and 2 cell colonies. The 4 cell cluster is documented in photos 1-3 and the 2 cell cluster in photos 4,5. Some characteristics are highlighted in photo 2.
Aside: The eukaryote *G. wittrockiana* is a member of plant phylum *Glaucophyta*, which is a sub-branch of the kingdom *Archaeplastida* (that includes land plants, red and green algae). Interestingly, *Glaucophyta* represents an evolutionary step in the assimilation of cyanobacteria as photosynthetic endosymbionts. Unlike most eukaryotic plastids, the plastids (aka muroplasts) of *Glaucophyta* retain remnants of a peptidoglycan cell wall found in bacteria (prokaryotes).  (Cool! As the JWebb Telescope lets us peer into the deep history of the universe, so our microscopes let us peer into the evolutionary history of life on earth.)

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucophyte
- https://link.springer.com/referenceworkentry/10.1007/978-3-319-32669-6_42-1

1c74f98e-c0f0-48ea-8e77-f2d70ec7f36d.description:
Coleps bicuspis NOLAND, 1925  from a benthic sample of freshwater Peconic River.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  The cells measure 56 um in length. It was difficult to get the two characteristic posterior spines in the same focal plane but we can visualize the pair using a GIF and ascertain that there are only two. 

"Coleps bicuspis . This species resembles Coleps hirtus in shape and movements, but differs from it in having sixteen instead of twenty longitudinal rows of plates, and in having two instead of three posterior spines. The cell body shows a definite dorso-ventral differentiation. At each lateral angle of the dorso-ventrally compressed mouth there are two teeth that project slightly  beyond the oral crown. These pairs of teeth occupy positions at the anterior end that correspond with those occupied by the two spines at the posterior end. Several specimens were observed from two different habitats in the shore waters of Planting Ground Lake, a soft-water lake in Oneida county, Wisconsin. Length, 55 micra" (1).


1.  A Review of the Genus Coleps with Descriptions of Two New Species. Lowell E. Noland.  Transactions of the American Microscopical Society , Jan., 1925, Vol. 44, No. 1 (Jan., 1925), pp. 3-13

2.  Morphology and Gene Sequence of Levicoleps biwae n. gen., n. sp. (Ciliophora, Prostomatida), a Proposed Endemic from the Ancient Lake Biwa, Japan. WILHELM FOISSNER, YASUSHI KUSUOK and SATOSHI SHIMANO. J. Eukaryot. Microbiol., 55(3), 2008 pp. 185–200

3. Kahl, A. 1930. Urtiere oder Protozoa I: Wimpertiere oder Ciliata (Infusoria) 1. Allgemeiner Teil und Prostomata. Tierwelt Dtl., 18: 1–180.

5d984ee4-572b-4258-b988-1a68d380db81.description:
Urocentrum turbo (MUELLER, 1866) Nitsch, 1827 from a sample of the benthos of the Peconic River, salinity <1 o/oo, sample fed with boiled wheat seeds. The cell measures 72 um in length. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy 24. Monotypic, i.e. h. Genus consisting of only one species. A very difficult subject to image well, especially under oil- I got lucky with a compressed and trapped individual to show its very complex ciliature. We can see the cycling of the terminal contractile vacuole with the adjacent somewhat distended portions of some of the collecting canals. The goove which runs from the oral opening posteriorly to the caudal ciliary field where the twisted caudal cilia arise.

1. In vivo 40-110 um long, usually 50-80 x 30-55 um.
2. Shape champagne cork-shaped, i.e. h. front half slightly wider than back and slightly narrowed in the middle. Both ends slightly to strongly curved.
3. Macronucleus semicircular in the posterior half of the body; clearly constricted in the middle, where the micronucleus lies.
4.  Contractile vacuole terminal, with 8-12 long collecting ducts
Numerous spindle-shaped extrusomes are located just beneath the pellicle.
5.Ciliation very complex. About 140 longitudinal rows of cilia arise from the bare frontal plate, each with about 19 basal bodies, which form a striking anterior cilia belt is interrupted in the area of ​​the oral apparatus. This is immediately followed by a thin, equatorial belt with short cilia. After a narrow unciliated area there is the posterior belt of rather irregularly arranged cilia. A groove extends from the oral apparatus to the posterior part, from which a tuft of cilia ("caudal cirrus") arises. This tuft secretes a thread of mucus with which the urocentrum attaches itself and swings back and forth rapidly rotating.
6. Oral apparatus in the equatorial groove. Oral cilia similar to Paramecium: 3 longadoral membranelles and a curved undulating membrane, which rests on a "stomatogenous" basal body field; structure of the oral cilia can only be recognized after silver impregnation, not required for the determination).
