dcb94fce-efed-4f4f-9a16-ade07425e7d4.description:
Vasicola parvula KAHL, 1928 from the benthos of brackish Georgica Cove (salinity 5 0/00), 4 month old sample fed with boiled wheat seed. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2SS using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.   This brackish biotope matches perfectly with the known descriptions of the species. The lorica measures 68 um in length and is saccate with a broad roomy posterior portion narrowing toward the neck which has approximately 13 characteristic corrugations.  The terminal portion of the neck at the aperture is not corrugated.  The zooid measures 44 um in length when fully extended and 32 um when fully contracted and is markedly contractile moving freely within the lorica. We can see the caudal cilium with some difficulty.  There is no terminal vacuole as seen in Metacystis. 

Vasicola is a prostomatid closely related to Metacystis. Kahl wrote about the genus in 1928:  "Ovoid Metacystidae with tail cilium.; only in a small species does a blister posterior occasionally appear at the rear end;  the other species lack this (in contrast to Metacystis). The housings are symmetrically bottle-shaped and  strongly ringed; the ringing is created by the fact that the infusorium during the excretion of the shell rotates and each transverse ciliary row creates a bulge in the housing. The mouth is typical: a lip-shaped outer edge has about  long cilia in four hort longitudinal rows; In the housing they are spread forward against the neck and form one fish trap ; Inwards there is a wreath of short, mouth-curving cilia which generate the food flow and are still at the very inner edge short bristles, perhaps effective in food selection. The receptaculum is wide and in V. ciliata is interrupted.by plasma bars, which lead to the mouth opening. Nucleus round, central, with one micronucleus. Contractile vacuole sideways, near the middle. Excreta and faeces collect in the posterior end and are expelled terminally" (1).  

Kahl found the species in weakly saline sites:  "Vasicola parvula KAHL, 1928  Length 30-50 um   Similar to V. ciliata, usually quite plump, also with a bristle, with violet food vacuoles. Builds a noticeably heavily ringed housing with broad base. Strangely enough, some can be found with the large terminal bubble of the genus Metacystis, which here is probably only  occurs temporarily. In weaker salt areas (3 -15 o/oo)  0IdesIoe, occasionally regular to frequent" (1).  

 Dragesco. J.. Dragesco-Kerneis, A. (1986) also described this species in weakly  brackish sites:  "Vasicola parvula Kahl, 1928   GEOGRAPHICAL DISTRIBUTION: described in Germany (KAHL, 1930); in Africa: water slightly  brackish (Cotonou, Benin).   MORPHOLOGY (according to protargol impregnations of only a few specimens)    Shape and dimensions: ovoid shape, fairly regular. Length: 26 um, 17 um (n = 4), on fixed animals.  Somatic infraciliature: 42 to 48 kineties constituted by 10 simple kinetosomes constituting  so many circular crowns.   Oral infraciliature:  - a crown of 4 aligned kinetosomes, very close together, as in V ciliata; - no middle crown of double kinetosomes; - no visible argyrophilic grains or traps.   Contractile vacuole: posterior.  Nuclear apparatus: 1 spherical macronucleus 6 um in diameter.   DISCUSSION  This Ciliate, thus described, corresponds well to a Vasicola and can be assimilated to the parvula species from KAHL.  This species cannot be classified in the genus Pelatractus whose oral ciliature is different nor in the genus Metacystis with a very particular caudal vesicle" (2). 

Carey 1992 also lists this species:  "Genus Vasicola Tatem, 1869 syn Pelamphora Lauterborn, 1901.   The body of this lorica-dwelling form is ovoid and transparent. Somatic ciliation is uniform,  arising from bipolar kinetosomes except around the apical cytostome where groups of cilia are arranged, and also at the rear where there is a tuft. The cytopharyngeal apparatus is simple with fine nematodesmata. The lorica is 'vase-shaped' hyaline, narrowing in the neck region with corrugated walls. The animal does not live permanently attached to the lorica. Lives in anaerobic habitats and feeds on bacteria and flagellates.    Vasicola parvula Kahl, 1928   Ovoid in shape, 25-30 µm in length, the body is deeply annulated. Cytostome is apical surrounded by long cilia. Uniform somatic dilation except at the rear where there is a single long caudal cilium. The cytoplasm has numerous large vacuoles, a large terminal contractile vacuole is present. One macronucleus centrally placed. The lorica is 'vase-shaped' with a well-developed neck. The walls of the lorica are corrugated" (3). 

1.  A. Kahl; [Urtiere oder Protozoa I: Wimpertiere oder Ciliata (Infusoria). Eine Bearbeitung der freilebenden und ectocommensalen Infusorien der Erde, unter Ausschluss der marinen Tintinnidae. 1. Allgemeiner Teil und Prostomata]. Die Tierwelt Deutschlands 18:1-180, 1930.  (ed. F. Dahl), G. Fischer, Jena. 

2.  Dragesco. J.. Dragesco-Kerneis, A. (1986) Cilies libres de l'Afrique intertropical. Introduction a la connaissance et a l'etude des Cilies.  Éditions de I'ORSTOM  INSTITUT FRANCAIS DE RECHERCHE SCIENTIFIQUE POUR LE DÉVELOPPEMENT EN COOPÉRATION  Collection Faune Tropicale no XXVI   Paris, 1986

afdaa64d-e036-49a3-9567-bf72f6964781.description:
Condylostoma curvum Burkovsky, 1970 from a benthic sample taken at a small salt marsh tide pool at the edge of estuary Acabonac Harbor at Landing Lane. The cell was harvested using the floating coverglass technique. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S25.  The cell measures 260 um in length.  This ciliate shows all of the morphologic characters for C. curvum as delineated by Chi et al 2024 in their recent revision of the genus (see description below).  The body shape and size, peristome length approximately 35% of cell length, 13 moniliform macronuclear nodules, the cortical granules: ellipsoidal and densely arranged (pattern 4 of Chi et al 2024),  the frontal membranelle kinetosomes are 7-8 blocks (pattern 1 of Chi et al 2024), approximately 32 somatic kineties (based on counting the one visible side of the cell) point to this diagnosis. 

"Condylostoma curvum Burkovsky, 1970    Improved diagnosis: Cell size variable from 120 to 505 μm, usually 150–400 μm; elongated and flattened with a rounded posterior end; peristome length to cell length variable, 20–45%; macronucleus moniliform with 5–17 nodules, 14–20 micronuclei; cortical granules large, ellipsoidal, brown to grayish green, densely arranged (Pattern 4); 60–115 adoral membranelles; 20–42 somatic kineties; frontal membranelles composed of 4–8 blocks of kinetosomes (Pattern I); brackish or marine habitat" (1).

Comparing my observation with congeners having a  elongate flattened body with rounded posterior:   C. spatiosum is larger with more somatic kineties and has a single stripe of frontal membranelle kinetosomes (Pattern II).  Condylosotoma kris is larger, has two types of cortical granules:large, ellipsoidal, grayish-green to yellowish-green, loosely arranged and  small, spherical, colorless to grayish, densely arranged (Pattern 1).   Condylostoma minutum has frontal membranelles composed of a single stripe of kinetosomes (Pattern II).  Condylostoma arenarium is larger (350–600 μm; elongated ellipsoidal with a slightly tapered posterior end; peristome length only about 1/5 of cell length; cortical granules small, ellipsoidal, green-yellowish, densely arranged (Pattern 6);  frontal membranelles composed of a single stripe of kinetosomes (Pattern II). (1,2)

Exploring the biogeography, morphology, and phylogeny of the condylostomatid ciliates (Alveolata, Ciliophora, Heterotrichea), with establishment of four new Condylostoma species and a revision including redescriptions of five species found in China. Prymnesium pigrum (Geitler) Edvardsen, Eikrem & Probert, comb. nov. BASIONYM: Platychrysis pigra Geitler. Geitler (1930). Arch. Protistenk., 69: 631, pl. 25b, c, text fig. 14a–e

Thanks to Yana Eglit for identifying this as a haptophyte belonging to the former genus Platychrysis. The Prymnesiophyta, also known as Haptophyta, is a group of autotrophic, planktonic uninucleate flagellates characterized by the presence of a haptonema (a filamentous, microtubule-supported appendage) that lies between two smooth, approximately equal flagella (Lee, 1999; Andersen, 2004). The name comes from the Greek hapsis = touch, and nema = thread. All or most of them are single-celled photosynthetic phytoplankton.

"The genus Platychrysis was characterized by two homo dynamic flagella, a short noncoiling haptonema, nonmineralized organic scales and two morphologies: a dominant phase of a flattened, nonmotile, amoeboid cell and a motile stage. Platychrysis moestrupii has two distinct morphologies, a motile swimming phase and a benthic phase. When transforming to the benthic phase, cells flatten anterio-posteriorally to become irregular discs, which adhere to the slide surface" (1).

However, Edvardsen et al. (2011) reinvestigated 37 members of the Prymnesiales using the complete nuclear-encoded SSU ribosomal gene, part of the LSU ribosomal gene and part of the plastid SSU ribosomal gene in addition to available morphological features. They found that the genus Platychrysis (Geitler) Gayral & Fresnel belonged in a new family, the Prymnesiaceae Conrad ex O.C. Schmidt emend. Edvardsen, Eikrem & Medlin. Because Platychrysis, fell within the Prymnesium clade, they reassigned all members to this genus (Edvardsen et al., 2011) (2).

"Both P. moestrupii, and the (former) type species Platychrysis (now Prymnesium) pigrum (Geitler) Edvardsen, Eikrem & Medlin , have appendages visible during the amoeboid benthic phase with both flagella coiled around the haptonema (Chretiennot 1973), whilst the other three described species lack visible flagella at the non motile stage (Norris 1967; Gayral & Fresnel 1983). Cell division was observed to commence whilst cells were benthic, with the final stages of cytokinesis being completed once the cells released" (1).

We see here the non-motile or benthic stage of Prymnesium pigrum (Geitler) Edvardsen, Eikrem & Medlin. I find many of these biflagellate cells adherent to floating coverglasses from a benthic sample taken from a small tidal pool at the edge of Acabonac Harbor estuary. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.

The cells measure 16-20 um. The cells are never moving or changing shape. They are flattened and mostly rounded with occasional small irregular extensions. There are two equal flagella which move usually very little that are tightly or loosely curled over the cell body never extending past the cell border. The haptonema is visible as a small dot between the flagella which stays in focus as you focus through the cell indicating it is adherrent to the underside of the coverglass. Visible in some cells is a round nucleus with central round nucleolus. Most cells contain 2 large golden brown plastids. The periphery of the cells has numerous refractile granules.

"Although P. moestrupii is somewhat variable in size, it is substantially larger than other (former) Platychrysis species. Of these P. pigrum is the largest; in the motile stage, cells are 12–15 x 5–9 um, and in the benthic phase cells are 12–20 mm in diameter. Other Platychrysis species range in size from 2–3 x 8–9 um to 3–4 x 12um whilst motile, and 7–12 mm whilst benthic (Gayral & Fresnel 1983; Throndsen 1997). When first collected from the field, P. moestrupii cells were typically 50–65 mm in length; however, after 6 months grown in full strength K-medium, the average cell length gradually diminished to only 25–35 um" (1).

Thus, we can infer from the work of Grant et al 2011 and their references that this population in the tidal pool is the former type species of the genus Platychrysis- P. pigra, now Prymnesium pigrum (Geitler) Edvardsen, Eikrem & Medlin 2011. Only this species and P. moestrupii Grant Waller and Wetherbee 2011 have visible flagella in the benthic stage. P. pigrum measures 12-20 um in the benthic stage while P. moestrupii is much larger as Grant et al 2011 point out.

1. Platychrysis moestrupii sp. nov. (Prymnesiophyceae): a new dimorphic, sand-dwelling haptophyte species from southeastern Australia. BRENNA GRANT,ROSS F. WALLER AND RICHARD WETHERBEE. Phycologia (2011) Volume 50 (6), 608–615

47386aa6-9bca-4c6e-bf04-b89297245ec7.description:
Homalozoon vermiculare Stokes 1867 population found using the floating coverglass method in a sample from the benthos of freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion and SPlan 40 0.70 objectives plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. 

The cells measure 300-480 um in length and have a broad flattened ribbon-shaped body which is flexible but was not seen to be contractile possibly owing to coverglass compression.  There is a well-defined thickened unciliated  ridge at the apical edge which houses the slit-like oral aperture region supported by trichites. There is an inconspicuous dorsal brush behind the oral bulge. The characteristic yellow  parapharyngeal granular mass is prominent.  There is no distinctive longitudinal ridge along its mid-line.  Filamentous extrusomes are distributed throughout body. The cytoplasm contains numeorus mitochondria.  A row of several (5-12) contractile vacuoles is present along dorsal edge. 

Two individuals are unusual in that the nuclear apparatus consists of a row of 6 roughly oblong irregular unconnected macronuclear nodules in the center of the cell along with several spherical micronuclei. It is known that cell division in Homalozoon is preceded by fusion of the segments of the macronucleus so these two individuals are likely early dividers. Interestingly, Foissner et al 1992 include an illustration from Dragesco 1966 of an H. vermiculare having 5 macronuclear nodules which is quite similar to my initial observation. 

Subsequently, I encountered normal individuals with approximately 30 moniliform macronuclear nodules with scattered micronuclei.  Foissner et al 1995 describe the nuclear apparatus of H. vermiculare:   "Macronucleus, pearl-string-shaped, consists of 13-70, usually 20-50 nodes that form a long band. Few (2) to many (50) micronuclei" (1).  

1.   Foissner W., Berger H., Blatterer H. & Kohmann F. (1995): Taxonomische und ökologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobiensystems – Band IV: Gymnostomatea, Loxodes, Suctoria. – Informationsberichte des Bayer. Landesamtes für Wasserwirtschaft, 1: 1–540.

2.  A. Kahl; [I: Wimpertiere oder Ciliata (Infusoria)]. Germany:Jena Verlag von Gustav Fishcer., 1930

2f1584a5-c666-4a67-863d-93bf46b523e9.description:
Monomorphina pyrum (Ehrenberg) Mereschkowsky harvested by the floating coverglass method from a sample of the benthos of  the freshwater kettle hole Kellis Pond.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion  objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. The cell measures 40 um including the tail.  Descriptions state that this is round in cross section but my observation is clearly broadly elliptical thus somewhat flattened  which is mentioned as a variation in some descriptions. 

From Algaebase: Monomorphina Mereschkowsky, 1877
Holotype species: Monomorphina pyrum (Ehrenberg) Mereschkowsky

Description: Marin et al. (2003: 102) provide an emended diagnosis: Cells with a single emergent flagellum; pyriform in lateral view with hyaline spine at the posterior end; in apical view not or only slightly compressed; with rigid pellicle or with slight metaboly; pellicle strips helically arranged, typically with left-handed orientation, rarely right-handed; a subset of pellicle strips elevated with conspicuous hyaline keels, resembling a screw thread; one to few large, parietal chloroplasts, not lens-shaped; pyrenoids typically absent; two (rarely 3-4) conspicuous lateral paramylon plates; nuclear- encoded SSU rRNA molecule typically with U as the third nucleotide in the terminal loop of Helix 27. Emended by Kosmala & Zakrys in Kosmala et al., 2007: 177: Cells ovoid or slightly oblate (circular or widely elliptical in cross-section) and rigid; numerous spiral stripes or a few conspicuous hyaline keels of the pellicle extending to form a pronounced tail; one parietal, spherical chloroplast (usually more or less perforated); haplopyrenoids (one or more?) present on the inner side of the chloroplast; and two or three (rarely 4) conspicuous lateral paramylon plates located between the pellicle and the chloroplast. Emended diagnosis Marin & Melkonian (in Marin et al. 2003: 102).

Monomorphina pyrum (Ehrenberg) Mereschkowsky emend. Kosmala et Zakryś 2007
= Phacus pyrum (Ehrenberg) F. Stein 1878
= Monomorphina aenigmatica (Dreźepolski) Nudelman et Triemer emend. Kosmaa et Zakryś 2007
= Monomorphina pseudopyrum Kosmala, Milanowski, BrzÓska, Pękala, Kwiatowski et Zakryś 2007
Species: About 30-50 μm long, 10-20 μm wide; circular in cross section; with caudal prolongation; pelicle obliquely ridged; flagellum as long as the body (Kudo, 19660). Cell body 28-55 μm long, 10-21 μm wide, two paramylons thick disc-shaped, parietal (An Illustrated Guide to Freshwater Zooplankton in Japan, 2000).

"The small Phacus species with an overall teardrop-shaped body and one or two chloroplasts were transferred into the little-known genus, Monomorphina Mereschkowsky. This genus had been created by Mereschkowsky in 1877 when he renamed Lepocinclis pyrum Perty as Monomorphina pyrum. When this taxon was later renamed as Phacus pyrum (Archer and Barker, 1871; Stein, 1878), the genus Monomorphina was abandoned and forgotten. It has now been rightfully restored. Second, the genus Phacus was emended to exclude those taxa now in Monomorphina making both genera monophyletic" (1).

 1. A decade of euglenoid molecular phylogenetics. Richard E. Triemer and Mark A. Farmer. Chapter 16- In: Unravelling the algae: the past, present, and future of algal systematics Edited ByJuliet Brodie, Jane Lewis 1st Edition 2007 Boca Raton CRC Press.

2.  Cryptoglena, Monomorphina and Phacus (Euglenophyceae) of a reservoir in the State of Rio Grande do Sul, southern Brazil. SANDRA MARIA ALVES-DA-SILVA and CARLOS E. DE M. BICUDO. Revista Brasil. Bot., V.32, n.2, p.253-270, abr.-jun. 2009

33399323-1856-4a0e-a554-3a86dfecf1c3.description:
Ophryoglena flavia harvested by the floating coverglass method from a benthic sample taken from freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 objective and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  Individuals of this histophagous genus (most feed on cells of dead metazoans) can be found in the sediment of almost every water sample; they never become numerous. 

The cells measure 200 um in length and are ovoid to ellipsoid. The cell is densely ciliated with numerous closely set longitudinal ciliary rows that exhibit metachronous ciliary waves.  There are small subpellicular trichocysts.   The oral aperture is situated in the anterior quarter of the body, nd is characteristically the shape of the concha of the right human ear with a small posterior projection similar to the tragus of the ear. The buccal cavity contains an undulating membrane and 3 membranelles which are arranged helically.  However, the refractile watch-glass organ of Lieberkuhn,  thought to have a photoreceptor function, was not visualized.  The oral apparatus when viewed laterally showed an interesting pedunculated structure.  The single  macronucleus is broadly ovoid and markedly flattened imparting the impression of being sausage-shaped when viewed from the side and there are two small spherical micronuclei.  There are two contractile vacuoles with associated thin collecting canals and ampullae. The anterior contractile vacuole had three excretory pores and the posterior vacuole had two. A well fed individual was packed with food vacuoles and ingesta. 

Apparently the lack or inconspicuousness of the watch glass organelle is a feature of O. flava. This and the other observed features are entirely consistent with Ophryglena flava as described by Kahl 1931, which is the only species depicted by him having two contractile vacuoles:  "Ophryoglena flava Ehrenberg,1833 (Otostoma carteri Kent, 1882).  Size: 2o0-400 um., Penard reports up to 500 um.. Metabolic slender when swimming, shortly rounded at the front, tapered at the back; more rounded when burrowing and after being heavily filled with food.  Especially at the front, the protruding anterior end has distinct trichocysts. Macronucleus short, sausage-shaped or long-elliptical. Two contractile vacuoles. one behind the other in the middle and on the last quarter, to the right of the mouth (Penard draws them approximately behind the mouth). Mouth without the grayish yellow pigment spot.  Not common; I mostly found them in weeds. The species established by Kent based on Carter's drawings and notes is a somewhat plump, ovoid Ophryoglena with two c.v. Interestingly, it encysted in Nitella internodes and divided into 2-8 individuals. Found near Bombay. (Likewise, O. ovata Stokes)" (1).

Carey 1992 also described O. flava and also notes the apparent lack of the organelle/pigment spot:  "0phryoglena flava Ehrenberg, 1833  Pyriform, rather elongate, 250--400 µm long.· The oral area is small, the pigment spot is not conspicuous. The macronucleus is ellipsoidal, and there are two contractile vacuoles. Large numbers of trichocysts are present (2). Song and Wilbert 1989 also studied the species emphasizing the two contractile vacuole and do not depict the watchglass organelle (3,4). 


1.  KAHL, A. (1931): Urtiere oder Protozoa I: Wimpertiere oder Ciliata (Infusoria) 2. Holotricha außer den im 1. Teil behandelten Prostomata. - Tierwelt Dtl., 2l: 181-398.

2. MARINE INTERSTITIAL CILIATES AN ILLUSTRATED KEY PHILIP G. CAREY Natural History Museum Publications CHAPMAN & HALL London · New York• Tokyo'. · Melbourne· Madras. 

 3. Foissner W., Berger H. & Kohmann F. (1994): Taxonomische und ökologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobiensystems – Band III: Hymenostomata, Prostomatida, Nassulida. – Informationsberichte des Bayer. Landesamtes für Wasserwirtschaft, 1/94: 1–548.

 4.  Taxonomische Untersuchungen an Aufwuchsciliaten (Protozoa, Ciliophora) im Poppelsdorfer Weiher, Bonn [Taxonomie researches on Ciiiata of perlphyton (Protozoa, Ciliophora) in the "Poppelsdorfer Weiher", Bonn (FRG)]. Weibo Song und Norbert Wilbert.   Lauterbornia H. 3: 2-221, 1989

8397ec01-0027-4614-800c-df901e0455e8.description:
Frontonia angusta KAHL, 1931 harvested by the floating coverglass method from a benthic sample taken from freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 objective and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. The cells measure 120 um in length.  This species is similar but easily distinguishable from F. acuminata which has a distinct anterior pigment spot.  Kahl initially described F. angusta as a variety of F. acuminata (2). Also similar is the soil species F. depressa (STOKES, 1886b), and the marine F. tchibisovae BURKOVSKY, 1970a, both with one (as opposed to two) excretory pore each.   My observation conforms to the characters described below from Foissner et al 1994 (1).  Characters 2 and 5 (without pigment spot) are particularly important for identification. The tuft of caudal cilia, which Foissner et al 1994 (1) point out was overlooked by Kahl and others, is present but somewhat inconsipicuous in my population.   The triangular postoral ciliary field (Kahl-behind the mouth, to the left of the postoral suture a small three-sided field of framed cilia is visible), elegantly demonstrated by Dr. Martin Kreutz (3) was also visualized with difficulty in my population. The single contractile vacuole having two excretory pores and ringed by auxiliary vacuoles but no collecting canals was nicely demonstrated as was the ellipsoid macronuclues with adjacent  spherical micronucleus in a shallow depression of the macronucleus.  Besides the large prey of diatoms and other algae in food vacules, there were tinyl round green and colorless structures in some individuals which I thought might be algal symbionts. These were often concentrated at the posterior end of the cell imparting a dark appearance at low magnification. But these are clearly variably digested and not symbionts. 

From Foissner et al 1994 (1):
1) Size, depending on the population, in vivo 80-130 x 60-100 um. In specimens, usually 115 x 60 um.
2) Shape similar to F. acuminata, but slimmer and only moderately flattened (2:1), so that the body cross-section is elliptical rather than cap-shaped
3) Macronucleus ellipsoid, usually 24 x 15 um, dorsally below the mouth. Micronucleus approximately 5 um  spherical, located in a recess of the macronucleus. 
.4) Contractile vacuole surrounded by a ring of auxiliary vacuoles, opens with 2-4, usually 3 excretory pores in the middle of the right side
5) Resting extrusomes are 6 pm long, spindle-shaped, and numerous along the cilia; they form a distinct rim beneath the pellicle. Cells are colorless and lack pigmentation.
6) 80-105, usually 94 longitudinal rows of cilia, which end ventrally at a suture (pre- and postoral suture) that extends across the poles to the dorsal side. At the posterior end, a tuft of elongated cilia, clearly visible in vivo, is present, but overlooked by previous authors. Pellicula quadrangularly lobed: cilia in the center of the lobes, extrusomes in the horizontal ridges.
7) Oral apparatus at the end of the first third of the body, ogival and moderately large (about 1/4 of the body length). On the left wall of the oral cavity, 3 membranelles (peniculi), each consisting of 4-5 long-ciliated rows of basal bodies. At the right margin of the mouth, an undulating membrane and four vestibular cilia rows consisting of closely spaced pairs of basal bodies, the exact structure of the oral cilia can only be seen after silver impregnation).

Kahl 1931 description:  "Frontonia acuminata var. angusta Size 80-100 fl. This form (from Utricularia, found by Penard in Spain)  can, according to our own investigations, be safely regarded as a stable variety of acuminata. Since it shows no transitional forms, it is listed separately here. It was recently found quite consistently in the detritus of the Outer Alster. Macronucleus with micronucleus, contractile vacuole with 2 excretory pores. Never with pigment accumulation dorsally near the anterior margin" (2).


1.  Foissner W., Berger H. & Kohmann F. (1994): Taxonomische und ökologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobiensystems – Band III: Hymenostomata, Prostomatida, Nassulida. – Informationsberichte des Bayer. Landesamtes für Wasserwirtschaft, 1/94: 1–548.

2. KAHL, A. (1931): Urtiere oder Protozoa I: Wimpertiere oder Ciliata (Infusoria) 2. Holotricha außer den im 1. Teil behandelten Prostomata. - Tierwelt Dtl., 2l: 181-398.

3.  https://realmicrolife.com/frontonia-angusta/

cfccbe00-34bd-4a22-adf8-4740629d7429.description:
A tiny lynchellid cyrtophorian, with features of Wilbertella distyla (Wilbert, 1971) Gong & Song, 2006  harvested using floating coverglass method from the freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective. The cells measure 20 to 22 um in length. The cells are slightly kidney-shaped to ovoid, broadly rounded anteriorly and posteriorly, slightly bluntly protruding on the left anterior side with a relatively straight to slightly convex left border and a markedly convex right border. The ventral surface is flattened and ciliated and has two club-shaped protuberances at the posterior 1/3 of the cell. The dorsum not ciliated and is moderately vaulted and flattened forming a lip at the anterior pole. Macronucleus is heteromeric and ovoid, approximately in the middle of the body, with peripherally located, plate-shaped nucleoli. No micronucleus could be discerned. The cytostome is at the right anterior 1/4 of the cell, surrounded by a cyrtos of 12 toothed nematodesmal rods which converge distally to form a slightly curled cornucopia pointed slightly towards the macronucleus. Usually 2 contractile vacuoles each to the left anterior and right posterior (less often seen) of the median in the ciliated field. Ventrally, a total of 12 somatic kineties slightly C-shaped, four of which were frontoventral kineties. Oral kineties Y-shaped. Notably, the left ventral kineties are shortened creating a barren patch at the left posterior ventral portion of the cell. 

These characters seemed to conform exactly to decriptions (1-3) of Chlamydonella derouxi Song 2003, a marine form. However, I overlooked the shortened left ventral kineties and barren left posterior patch.  I am grateful to Dr. Martin Kreutz who kindly pointed out to me this important generic character of the genus WIlbertella. 

I had briefly considered Wilbertella distyla based on the single illustration in Gong and Song  2006 (2) but was put off by the shaped of the two ventral protuberance- pointed and stylus shaped unlike the club-shaped ones of my ciliate. With regards to this apparent deviation, Professor Weibo Song wrote to me:  "A brief note on Wilbertella distyla:  It is reasonable to classify your form as a population of this species. The shape of the protuberances is clearly observation-dependent—you may mention this in your redescription, but it should not be overemphasized. Norbert’s (Wilbert) definition was primarily based on stained specimens, which may have led to a minor misinterpretation". I also overlooked the clearly shortened left ventral kineties in that illustration.  However, as Dr. Kreutz points out, such features as the shape of the protuberances can be variable in many species and the number and location of the protuberances are a perfect match to my observation as are the number of nematodesmata and ventral kineties and the location of the two contractile vacuoles. Also, the used of fixed versus live cells and other technical factors could account for this difference. It is also important to note that my observation is a freshwater form and, as Gong and Song 2006 point out, so is Wilbertella distyla. 

Wilbert 1971 (4) first described Wilbertella distyla as Parachilonodella distyla.  Gong and Song 2006 placed it in the new Genus Wilbertella (2).  "The genus Parachilodonella was erected by  Dragesco (1966) to include a single marine species, P. lygiae Dragesco, 1966. Main generic characteristics of this taxon are: (1) Chilodonella-like infraciliature and  (2) possessing a typical podite on ventral side (Dragesco  1966, Fig. 5G). According to these two points, the nominal species P. distyla, a freshwater form, is likely misplaced because it has a different ciliature-pattern and two ventral cytoplasmic protuberances (Wilbert 1971).  Nevertheless, although similar to the well-known  Chlamydonella  regarding the general ciliature, P. distyla can be clearly distinguished from Chlamydonella  (including C. derouxi described above) in the presence (vs. absence) of a distinct non-ciliated zone in left posterior of ventral surface, which should be considered as a feature at the generic level" (2).  

Gong and Song's 2006 erection of the genus Wilbertella:  "Wilbertella nov. gen.  Diagnosis: Lynchellidae with a distinct blank zone in left posterior portion of cell because left kineties distinctly shortened, right kineties extending to posterior end; perioral kineties in flattened Y-shaped; no distinct gap between left and right ciliary fields. Type species: Parachilodonella distyla Wilbert,1971" (2).   

"Comparison with related genera: Both the genera  Chlamydonella Deroux in Petz Song et Wilbert, 1995  and Atopochilodon Deroux, 1976 resemble Wilbertella  nov. gen. with respect to the flattened Y-shaped perioral  kineties (Deroux 1970, 1976; Petz et al. 1995; this paper; fig. 5D). However, the new genus can be distinguished from the former two in the structure of the left kineties which are distinctly shortened posteriorly (vs. extending to cell end in Chlamydonella and Atopochilodon). In addition, the left and right ciliary fields are distinctly separated in Atopochilodon (vs. continuous in Wilbertella). Compared with Wilbertella, another similar taxon, Parachilodonella Dragesco, 1966 can be recognized by having a podite (vs. ventral club-shaped protuberances or absent in Wilbertella) and Chilodonella-like infraciliature (Dragesco 1966, Fig. 5F), that is, left and right ciliary fields are separated as parenthesis marks (vs. continuous in Wilbertella)" (2).

"The posterior ends of left kineties in Brooklynella Lom et Nigrelli, 1970 are also greatly shortened relative to right ones, leaving a blank area in posterior left of ventral surface (Lom and Nigrelli 1970, Gong and Song 2006; Figs 5H, I). Nevertheless, Brooklynella differs from Wilbertella in: (1) arrangement of oral structure (one preoral and two circumoral kineties vs. flattened Y-shaped perioral kinety); (2) absence (vs. presence) of the interruption between frontoventral and oral kineties; and (3) presence (vs. absence) of a typical podite" (2).

a10874fe-9b75-4044-a68b-a16bbeafd137.description:
Gastronauta membanaceus Bütschli, 1889 harvested using floating coverglass method from the freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective.  Two moribund individuals were found at first on March 9, 2025. Subsequently I found several healthy moving individuals on April 11, 2025 and added some imaging from those.   The cells measure 50-63.5 um um in length.  

 Size in vivo 45 -70 x 30 -45 um (Blochmann 1895, Gong Xunju and Shen  Yunfen 1989,Vuxanovici 1962, Wilbert 1972; Table 2). Elliptical to broadly elliptical, left margin less curved than right. Strongly flattened, ventral side slightly concave causing broad, bulge-like fringe, which surrounds dorsal, wrinkled hump containing a refractive structure right of midline which lies between the anterior vacuole and the macronucleus. The macronucleus is ellipsoid, with a vesicle in its center, containing a nucleolus in its center, with many peripheral nucleoli. Macronucleus located approximately midway below the mouth, that is, under barren postoral stripe, with up to three distinct lobes, nearby a single large, globular micronucleus. Two contractile vacuoles and excretory pores, which are easily recognisable even in live specimens, in constant, characteristic position: anterior vacuole slightly right of midline underneath oral cleft with excretory pore between anterior portion of kineties 1 and 2 of right ciliary field, contracts every 10s at 22 deg C; posterior vacuole in left posterior quadrant of cell with excretory pore between kineties 3 and 4 of left ciliary field, contracts rarely or not at all (Vuxanovici 1962). Extrusomes possibly lacking (Schneider 1930). Cytoplasm hyaline, cells thus colourless and transparent. Glides slowly on ventral surface (1,2). 

"Somatic and oral ciliary pattern: 15 - 16 ciliary rows on postoral surface, postorally separated by a narrow, barren stripe. Left ciliary field composed of six kineties gradually shortened from right to left posteriorly, straight anteriorly, leftmost row almost continuous with vertical kinety fragment 1. Right ciliary field composed of nine to ten rows, of which four to six are postoral, while the others extend anteriorly forming wide arcs on anterior body margin; anterior portion of kinety 1 (innermost ciliary row) sharply curved to left almost touching anterior end of left ciliary field. Four to six slightly convex, widely spaced preoral ciliary rows between curved anterior portion of right ciliary field and circumoral kinety, shorten gradually from right to left at right end of oral cleft. Left above circumoral kinety three short, vertically extending kinety fragments" (1).  

"So far, it has been found mainly in flowing waters, ponds, and roadside ditches; only Deroux & Dragesco (1968) reported it from the estuary of a river on the French Atlantic coast (brackish water). Rare and mostly isolated. Blatterer (1989) found it in abundance in the surface cuticle of a fresh, detritus-rich soil sample from the hypertrophic Salzburg Uniteich. Distribution probably cosmopolitan" (2).

1. Revision of the Genera Gastronauta Engelmann Bütschli, 1889 and Paragastronauta nov. gen. (CiIiophora : Gastronautidae).   Wilhelm Foissner.  Protozoological Monographs, Vol. 1, 63 - 101 @ Shaker-Publishers 2000

 2.  Foissner W., Blatterer H., Berger H. & Kohmann F. (1991): Taxonomische und ökologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobiensystems - Band I: Cyrtophorida, Oligotrichida, Hypotrichia, Colpodea. – Informationsberichte Bayer. Landesamt für Wasserwirtschaft, München, 1/91:  pp  106-109

7b698367-34bb-4221-8419-fd0c7e5b634a.description:
WACT-004
Collected by:
Toni Sardelis and Casey Ledford

Locality:
collected from an exposed rocky outcrop just north of Trinidad Head, near the mid-beach access trail. 41.05634° N, -124.14648° W (±8 m). The area is a rugged rocky shoreline with broad, elevated benches and shallow tide pools. The rock surface was slick, wet, and partly shaded, with visible green, red, and brown algal growth. A freshwater seep was present nearby, flowing down from the bluff and keeping the rock face damp.

Tide Level:
Tide was rising at the time of collection.The tide was estimated to be around +2 to +2.5 feet. The alga was collected from the upper mid intertidal zone, moist but not submerged at the time.

Substrate:
growing directly on Fucus and small filamentous red algae. The area retained moisture due to wave splash and runoff.

Habitat:
Exposed rocky intertidal bench, The specimen was found in a microhabitat that stayed moist longer, due to shade and freshwater seepage from the bluff. The surrounding area was coated in slick biofilm .

Specimen Measurements:
n/a

Microscopic Features:
• Filaments  unbranched, consisting of a single row of cells
• Cell walls are thick and clearly defined
• Chloroplasts were lining the cell wall, forming a diffuse, net-like pattern
• No spiral chloroplasts or filament branching observed
• No pyrenoids clearly visible, though cell content was granular

Herbarium voucher:
N/A

d8b9ea93-28a6-4006-b1bb-5f3f8427eba9.description:
Bicosoeca petiolata (F.Stein) E.G.Pringsheim 1946 harvested using floating coverglass method from the freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective.

Bicosoeca are stramenopile flagellates surrounded by an organic lorica, to which the smooth flagellum is attached by its tip. No chloroplast. When cells are disturbed, the recurrent flagellum contracts and the anterior flagellum is rolled up in a tight coil; this behaviour is diagnostic. Lorica morphology is used to distinguish between species. Unicells and colonies.  Each cell forms a goblet-shaped lorica or envelope (Pringsheim 1946), open at the top and pointed at the bottom, that often remain attached to each other.   When bacteria as food are plentiful, the loricas are not formed – presumably because of rapid cell division and growth.

Bicosoeca petiolata-  Flagellates ovoid, with rudimentary collar, length 5-10 µm. Cells form branching colonies of vase-shaped loricas. Loricas 10–20 µm long, stem of colonies 10–100 µm long. Cells are attached to the bottom of lorica with the short, posterior flagellum. Anterior flagellum about 40 µm long. Nucleus spherical, in center of cell. 1–2 contractile vacuoles in posterior third.  The cell are anchored in the lorica with the short, posterior flagellum. The longer, anterior flagellum catches food (bacteria) and performs sine wave movements. When disturbed, the flagellate retracts in the lorica and the long flagellum  retracts in a spiral pattern. The flagella do not emerge apically, but both emerge subapically behind the rudimentary snout-like projecting collar.

3f8b9b56-5e73-4eae-b6c6-788394850eca.description:
Goniomonas truncata (Fresenius, 1858) Stein, 1878  harvested using floating coverglass method from the freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective. The cells measure 8-9.6 um in  length.  They tended to drag the cell apex across the substrate.  I observed one individual in the process of division. 

Goniomonas truncata (Fresenius, 1858) Stein, 1878  (Basionym: Monas truncata) Observations: Cryptomonad. Cell oval in profile but
 with a flattened anterior margin, cell body 8-14 µm long and very compressed. Cells often have 4 faint longitudinal striations following a curving path across both faces of the cell - some cells may have 3 or 5 striations, and in other cells (especially smaller ones) it was not possible to observe striations. Striations may appear granular. A single lateral row of extrusomes (ejectisomes) runs across the cell just behind the anterior face. Two equal length flagella are roughly two-thirds cell length and insert in a small pocket near the dorsal margin of the anterior face. Nucleus is located near the middle of the body behind the flagellar pocket. Contractile vacuole anterior. Some cells with food vacuoles. Cell swims either with one face against the substrate, or through the fluid with rotation.

 Remarks: Goniomonas truncata (previously also referred to as Cyathomonas truncata - see Larsen and Patterson 1990) has not previously had a clear identity. It was originally described from freshwater, and descriptions from freshwater refer to organisms ranging in size from 3 to 25 µm (Vørs 1992a) and having no-to-many ridges (Vørs 1992a, Skuja 1939). The uncertainty of the identity of the species G. truncata and the poor qualityof the original account are now being resolved along the lines indicated by Vørs (1992a), that is to use the name G. truncata for a cell that is generally larger than G. amphinema and G. pacifica, the only other species in the genus and typically with more than 3 ridges per side, but not with many finely separated ridges. The presence of food vacuoles confirms the case presented by Kugrens and Lee (1991) that this species is  phagotrophic. This species has been reported widely in  the Northern Hemisphere but not previously from Australia.


 Free-living Heterotrophic Flagellates from Freshwater Sites in Tasmania  (Australia), a Field Survey. Won J. LEE, Alastair G. B. SIMPSON and David J. PATTERSON. Acta Protozool. (2005) 44: 321 - 350

4f195d07-1379-40af-8e8d-d38b9bd3370f.description:
Anthophysa vegetans (Müller, 1773) Stein, 1878 harvested using floating coverglass method from the freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective. Colonies measured 24 um in average diameter while individual cells measured 8 um in length. The colonies tended to be floating and detached from the brown thick stalks which were also abundantly present oin the floating coverglass preparations but were almost always devoid of cell colonies.  

"Anthophysa vegetans (Müller, 1773) Stein, 1878   (Basionym: Volvox vegetans)  Observations: This heterotrophic stramenopile occurs in spherical colonies of cells, 8-10 µm long, borne on the end of irregular branching brown stalk which tends to be paler near unattached end of the stalk. Cells with one long and short flagella emerging apically. The cells are usually in clusters of 20-30 cells, and are borne at the end of branched stalk. 

 Remarks: The genus is most usually interpreted as being monospecific (Starmach 1985, Preisig et al. 1991, but see Hänel 1979 for differing point of view), and the organisms observed here correspond well with previous accounts of A. vegetans. This species has been widely reported from the Northern hemisphere, and has previously been reported in Australia by several workers" (1). 

1.  Free-living Heterotrophic Flagellates from Freshwater Sites in Tasmania  (Australia), a Field Survey. Won J. LEE, Alastair G. B. SIMPSON and David J. PATTERSON. Acta Protozool. (2005) 44: 321 - 350

a60f6d58-d5d7-43fa-9030-90ac3fb70d95.description:
Astasia tortuosa (Stokes) Popova, 1951  harvested using floating coverglass method from the freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective.   The cells measure 60-70 um in length and are strongly elongated and flattened, sometimes C- or S-shaped and  metabolic.  The cell narrows and tapers posteriorly to a rounded tip.  The anterior end with neck-like tapering. The mouth opening with distinct "bottle lip" appearance transversely truncated. One flagellum, about a third of body length. Reservoir is elongate oval. Nucleus central, oval. Paramylon grains uniform. Periplast with fine striation.  At first I thought I was looking at a Menoidium since the cells did not show the shape-shifting metaboly of euglenids but rather a flexilibility rarely bending into various shapes.

Bruce Taylor writes: "This is a rare euglenoid, according to David Angeler.  This organism has gone by many names, over the years. It was first identified by A. Stokes, in 1885, and described under the name Atractonema tortuosa. The species was later moved to Menoidium (Senn, 1900), and to this day is most widely known under the name Menoidium tortuosum.  In 1942, E. G. Pringsheim introduced Astasia harrisii, which appears to be a form of the same organism. In 1998, David Angeler addressed the taxonomical confusion, following Popova in moving the species to Astasia, under the name A. tortuosa. Variants resembling Pringsheim's are referred to as A. tortuosa var. harrisii. The move to Astasia was justified on structural / morphological grounds. Intuitively, the move makes sense: species in Menoidium are typically stiff and banana-shaped, whereas this one is remarkably lithe (although, like other Astasia it seems able to stiffen its body, at times, and tends to straighten out in death). However, genetic analysis may require the species to be moved yet again. It has already been predicted that Astasia tortuosa, along with several other members of that genus, will group more closely with Distigma than Astasia. (Leander, 2001) Evidently, the organism is an osmotroph, feeding by absorption. It seems to enjoy bacteria-rich conditions, and tolerates low oxygen levels fairly well (although, after a half hour under the coverslip, they become stiff and lethargic)" (1).

"The observations on A. tortuosa (Euglenaceae) are essentially consistent with the data of Popova 1951, Popova & Safonova 1976, Pringsheim 1963, Skuja 1956, and Wolowski 1991. Habit (Fig. 1): The cells are elongated and flattened. Sometimes they are bent in an S-shape. The widest point is just below the reservoir. The posterior aspect of the cell narrows.  Flagellate increases and tapers to a rounded tip. The distinctly transversely truncated mouth opening is located apically at the neck-like, extended anterior end. A short flagellum (approximately 1/16 to 1/2 the length of the body) protrudes from it. The reservoir is elongated oval. The cell dimensions are 74-95 μm (length) x 4.5-9 μm (width). The periplast (pellicula) has fine spiral striation, which can be seen under a light microscope. The nucleus is oval and located more or less in the center of the cell. The paramylon granules are uniformly small and usually found in the anterior half of the cell. Sometimes they can also be loosely distributed throughout the cell. Swimming movement: The monad rotates along its longitudinal axis while swimming. Due to its body shape, swimming resembles a corkscrew movement, which is particularly evident at high swimming speeds. Euglenoid movement: During free swimming, the flagellate appears almost rigid. Upon irritation, especially in methylcellulose preparations, violent metabolic movements begin. Helical, twisting movements can be observed" (2).  

"Systematic position in Astasia or Menoidium? The assignment of A. tortuosa to the genus Menoidium was based on morphological criteria. The dorsiventral flattening of the cells was apparently used by Senn in 1900 as the most important criterion for the renaming. The ability for euglenoid movement was disregarded, especially since it can only be seen under certain conditions, such as irritation. Literature data on the performance of metabolic movements are controversial. While Lemmermann (1910, 1913), and Senn (1900) consider A. tortuosa to be completely rigid, Huber-Pestalozzi (1955) and Skuja (1948) mention a certain capacity for metabolism. Popova (1951) observed that the posterior end became slightly curved during fixation and placed A. tortuosa in the genus Astasia. By comparing A. tortuosa with cultures of the species M. bibacillatum (E. G. Pringsheim) and M. cultellus (E. G. Pringsheim), it was clearly demonstrated that in methylcellulose preparations, A. tortuosa can be forced into violent euglenoid movements, whereas these never occur in M. bibacillatum and M. cultellus" (2).

1.  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VxLs2gMmCjw

2.   Zur systematischen Stellung von Astasia tortuosa  (STOKES) POPOVA, inkl. A. tortuosa var. harrisii (E. G. PRINGSHEIM) ANGELER stat. nov. (Euglenophyta). On the systematic position of Astasia tortuosa (STOKES) POPOVA, including A. tortuosa var. harrisii (E. G. PRINGSHEIM) ANGELER stat. nov. (Euglenophyta).   David G. ANGELER.   Phyton (Horn, Austria)  Vol. 39  Fase. 1  27-35 20. 8. 1999

6d7ea694-052a-4229-804c-4c0ce8e067c7.description:
Phialina pupula (Müller, 1773) Foissner, 1983 harvested using floating coverglass method from a benthic sample of the freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. 

The individuals measure from 90 up to 120 um in length when fully extended and show contractility becoming much more plump and rounded but never showing an extensible neck like Lacrymaria. The head is always attached directly on the trunk and is quite mobile rotating in all directions. The cytoplasm is filled with refractive dumbbell-shaped inclusions making observation of the central ellipsoid macroncleus difficult. There is a terminal contractile vacuole.

"Phialina pupula (Müller, 1773) Foissner, 1983 represents a free-living, predatory ciliate belonging to the subclass Haptoria Corliss, 1974 of the highly diverse class Litostomatea Small and Lynn, 1981. Müller (1773) described this species for the first time as a cone-shaped microorganism with an apical head-like structure. Later on, Bory de Saint-Vincent (1824) classified all ciliates with an apical head into the genera Phialina Bory de Saint-Vincent, 1824 and Lacrymaria Bory de Saint-Vincent, 1824. He distinguished the two genera by the localization of the cell mouth: Phialina has a lateral while Lacrymaria possesses a terminal cytostome. These generic characters were, however, revealed to be problematic and consequently most species were assigned to Lacrymaria (Ehrenberg 1838, Dujardin 1841, Claparède and Lachmann 1859, Fromentel 1874, Bütschli 1887–89, Penard 1922)" (1).

"Kahl (1930) noticed that all species with an apical head have only a terminal cell mouth. This showed the main diagnostic feature of the genus Phialina to be incorrect. Therefore, Kahl (1930) abandoned the genus name Phialina and used only the generic name Lacrymaria. In spite of this, Phialina was resurrected and both genera were redefined as follows (Foissner 1983, Foissner et al. 1995): (i) Lacrymaria is highly contractile and has a conspicuously long, highly extensible, swan-like neck while (ii) Phialina is less contractile and does not have a distinct extensible neck but, instead, the head is attached directly to the trunk" (1).

Rajter et al write: " Size in vivo 60–130 × 20–50 µm, usually about 85 × 30 µm. Body shape highly variable depending on state of contraction, ranging from clavate in extended condition through fusiform, obpyriform, elliptical to almost globular in semi-contracted and contracted state. Head barrel-shaped, distinct from trunk but without neck-like region, sometimes retracted into trunk creating an impression of shoulders. Oral apparatus occupies apical end of head. Oral bulge contains tip of extrusomes, posteriorly delimited by circumoral kinety as usual in congeners. Head kineties helical and narrowly spaced, extend between circumoral kinety and dorsal brush, composed of densely arranged monokinetids bearing about 10 µm long cilia in vivo and almost completely covering head" (1).

"Posterior body end tapered and tail-like in extended condition, narrowly to broadly rounded in semi-contracted and contracted state. Contraction occurs slowly. Nuclear apparatus located in or slightly posterior to mid-body, usually slightly lateral of cell center. Macronucleus elliptical, micronucleus adjacent to macronucleus, usually attached to anterior pole of macronucleus, elliptical and about 2 µm long in vivo. Contractile vacuole subterminal in extended specimens while terminal in semi-contracted and contracted cells, excretory pore(s) not recognizable in vivo or after protargol impregnation. Only one type of extrusomes, rod-shaped, about 10 × 0.5 µm in size in vivo, attached to oral bulge and in bundles scattered throughout cytoplasm. Cytoplasm colorless, packed with few to many lipid droplets, some extrusome bundles, and many highly refractive inclusions. Individual inclusions dumbbell-shaped, about 2 µm long and usually numerous in anterior body half, rendering the cell dark in appearance at low magnifications. Swims fast along helical trajectory by rotation about main body axis"
 1.  Morpho-molecular Characterization of the Litostomatean Predatory Ciliate Phialina pupula (Müller, 1773) Foissner, 1983 (Haptoria,Lacrymariidae). Ľubomír RAJTER, William BOURLAND, Peter VĎAČNÝ. Acta Protozoologica · July 2019. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/334965520

134cb891-2082-4883-ae1f-ad96f412db4c.description:
Chilodontopsis depressa (Perty, 1852) Blochmann, 1895 harvested using floating coverglass method from a benthic sample of the freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  The cell measures 92 um in length. This ciliate conforms with all characters described by the three studies below. Imaging the synhemnium was quite difficult with this actively swimming specimen. This feature along with the quite large terminal contractile vacuole and the slightly ellipsoid to rounded macronucleus are characteristic. The contractile vacuole often appeared multilocular during stages of systole but coalesced at diastole into the characteristic large terminal vacuole sometimes extending anteriorly up the left side of the ciliate. 

From Foissner, Berger and Kohmann. 1994 (1): 
1) Size in vivo 50-80 x 20-35 um.
2) Ellipsoid shape, very similar to large specimens of -+ Chilodonella uncinata or small forms of -+ Trithigmostoma (-+ Vol. I); dorso-ventrally also distinctly flattened, right margin convex, left margin straight to slightly sigmoid and slightly projecting at the hypostomial cilia  (synhymenium), forming a short, rounded beak. 
3) Ellipsoid macronucleus approximately midbody. 1 ellipsoid micronucleus.
4) Contractile vacuole strikingly large, filling the entire posterior end.
5) Extrusomes inconspicuous in vivo.
6) 20-30 ventral and approximately 7-12 dorsal rows of cilia. The rows of the right half arcuately surround the mouth entrance and meet the hypostomial cilia on the left.  The silver line system is lattice-like, with silver lines undulating in a puzzle-like pattern.
7) Oral funnel (cyrtos) in the anterior quarter in the median, consisting of 12-15 tough rods. Hypostomial cilia (synhymenium) is delicate and difficult to identify, extending slightly obliquely from the tip of the beak to the right body edge, consisting of 20-32 cilia.  (1)

"It is best distinguished from the often quite similar Chilodonella spp. and Trithigmostoma spp. (Vol. I) by its large, terminal contractile vacuole. The rare and perhaps exclusively terrestrial Chilodontopsis rhinuscorum has its contractile vacuole located somewhat behind the midbody (redescription in Foissner 1984a). The limnic records of this species are probably based on confusion with C. planicaudara SONG WEIBO & WILBERT, in which the contractile vacuole is also located approximately in the midbody, but is somewhat smaller (25-40 um) and has a distinct, flat, and therefore light-colored posterior end. -) Zosterodasys transversa is considerably larger (130-250 um), has many small contractile vacuoles, and the hypostomial ciliated band encompasses almost the entire body. Characters 4 and 6 (fully ciliated) are particularly important for identification" (1).

From Kahl 1931 (2): 
Chilodontopsis (Chilodon) depressa (PERTY, 1852) (Chilodon propellens GRUBER?). Size 50-80 um. · Shape somewhat variable, with the concave left side sometimes sharp, mostly rounded, abutting the rounded anterior end, which is slightly bent forward. Sometimes somewhat broadened posteriorly. It can hardly be called a beak. From this point, a weakly curved chain of strengthened and elongated cilia, the synhemnium, extends to the posterior edge of the mouth.  The remaining cilia are very delicate, dense, and in narrower rows. Cyrtos with about 12-15 rods (rectangular in cross-section) on the anterior fifth of the cell. Macronucleus ellipsoid, evenly granulated, with micronucleus. Contractile vacuole very large, terminal; It often expands considerably, especially on the left side towards the front. Swims with a bent anterior end, rotating, or burrows metabolically, feeding on small diatoms. Distributed in ditches, in the weeds of shallow pools, never numerous (freshwater) (2). 

From Omar, Choi and Jung 2023:
"Diagnosis. Size about 100 × 45 μm in vivo and 65 80 × 25-30 μm after protargol impregnation (n=7); body ellipsoidal, length:width ratio about 3 :1, dorsoventrally flattened; cortex studded with cortical granules between ciliary rows both in vivo and after protargol impregnation; macronucleus in mid-body and sometimes in posterior third of body, globular about 15 μm in diameter; contractile vacuole very large in posterior ventral portion of body; cyrtos in anterior third of body and consists of about 14 nematodesmal rods; synhymenium running 
obliquely on ventral side, composed of about 30 dikinetids; 30-40 somatic ciliary rows" (3).

"Up to date, 11 species are assigned to the genus Chilodontopsis, only five of them with known morphology (Wang et al., 2012), i.e., C.
Depressa; C. kurensis Alekperov, 1985; C. muscorum Kahl, 1931; C. simplex Ozaki and Yagiu, 1941; and C. vermiformis Deroux, 1978 (Kahl, 1931; Ozaki and Yagiu, 1941; Deroux, 1978; Alekperov, 1985). Chilodontopsis depressa is most similar to C. muscorum but they differ 
mainly in the body shape (ellipsoidal vs. oval), the size of macronucleus (~15 μm vs. 10×5 μm), and the number of  somatic kineties (30-40 vs. ~21) (Foissner, 1984). Also, C. depressa differs from C. simplex, which was described in details by Wang et al. (2012), in the smaller body size (65-80×25-30 μm vs. 90-160×45-95 μm), the body shape (ellipdoidal vs. oval), the smaller macronucleus (15×15 μm vs. 25-55×20-40 μm), the lower number of somatic kineties (30-40 vs. 59-78), and the dikinetids in the synhymenium (~30 vs. 45-90) (Wang et al., 2012)" (3). 

1.  Foissner, W., H. Berger and F. Kohmann. 1994. Taxonomische und ökologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobiensystems - Band III: Hymenostomata, Prostomatida, Nassulida. Informationsberichte des Bayer Landesamtes für Wasserwirtschaft 1/94:1-548.

2.   Kahl, A. (1931) Urtiere oder Protozoa I: Wimpertiere oder Ciliata (Infusoria), 2. Holotricha (ausser den im I. Teil behandelten 
Prostomata). Die Tierwelt Deutschlands, 21, 181–398.

 3.  New record of ten ciliate species (Protozoa, Ciliophora) from South Korea.  Atef Omar, Ji Hye Choi and Jae-Ho Jung.  Journal of Species Research  12(1):95-108, 2023

925cbb67-7a7f-4f0b-a6c7-57835b21eb87.description:
An unusual Lacrymariidae, cf Lacrymaria pumilio Vuxanovici, 1962,  harvested by floating coverglass method from a benthic sample of the freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. The sample was fed with boiled wheat seed.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective.  The cell measures 80 um in length and the body divided into oral dome, head, and an acontractile flexible neck and a trunk. The posterior end is tapered and rounded not pointed.  There are three slightly spiralized somatic kineties visible on one side making a total of 6 or perhaps at most 7 somatic kineties. The macronucleus is centrally located and an elongate ellipsoid with an abutting ellipsoid micronucleus.  There is a terminal contractile vacuole which is surrounded by yellowish refractive crystals. A few rod-shaped extrusomes are present in the head and very few shorter rod-shaped extrusomes are widely scattered in the cytoplasm. 

The characteristic oral dome and head readily allows recognition of this ciliate as belonging to the Lacrymariidae. There is a distinct neck region which is quite flexible but was not seen to be at all extensible over more than 2 hours of observation, thus likely ruling out the genus Phialina. Looking at Kahl 1930 an illustration of Lacrymaria coronata Claparede & Lachmann, 1859  (comb form Phialina coronata (Claparède & Lachmann, 1859) Buitkamp, 1977), this ciliate appeared quite similar but Foissner et al state this species is only found in saltwater and it is larger at 200 um. 

Tang et al 2023 (1) compared all species of Lacrymaria with a compact macronucleus. According to their table 10, the species which is the closest match of my observation was Lacrymaria pumilio Vuxanovici, 1962 (1,2).  Foissner  1983 redescribed this species (2). The size, shape, and number of somatic kineties are quite similar, though based on observation of 3-4 kineties on one side of my observation inferring a total of 6-7, this is slightly less that L. pumilio. In addition, extrusomes are not described. In this same paper, Foissner 1983 also describes Lacrymaria filiformis Maskell 1886 which appears to resemble my observation, however it is larger (120-160 um) and has many rows of extrusomes, a highly extensible neck and a strikingly small head. Other congeners are L. vaginifera which has a similar number of somatic kineties (7-8) but is quite a bit smaller at 30-40 um, lives in a shell, and looks remarkably like L. olor with a highly extensible neck up to 200 um in length (1,2).  Lacrymaria nana (VUXANOVICI, 1961) is smaller (40-60um) with 13 kineties and an acutely pointed posterior end (1,3).  


"Lacrymaria pumilio Vuxanovici, 1962 Morphology: Elongated 40-80 μm, club-shaped, contracted about 30-50 μm, ovate and strongly spirally striated. Pharyngeal cone cuboidal; head about 4x5 μm; neck relatively broad; bulbous pouch-shaped and rounded posteriorly, rarely pointed. Head separated from the neck by a ciliated zone, but in contracted individuals it is attached to the neck. Pharyngeal cone and head about 10 straight to slightly curved 5-7 μm long rods. Macronucleus about 5x8 μm, with large nucleoli and a 4-5 μm long, bean-shaped micronucleus, the honed side of which is closely apposed to the macronucleus. Pellicula strongly notched by the ciliary rows, especially on the neck and in contracted individuals. Contractile vacuole terminal, surrounded by many small, slightly yellowish granules. Entoplasm clearly clouded by 1-5 μm large, colorless, spherical inclusions. Burrows in the detritus, twitches rapidly back and forth. Approximately 12 kineties, each with approximately 35 basal bodies. Above, all kinetes have 4-5 pairs of basal bodies. The head has about 14 strongly obliquely positioned kineties.  Discussion: Kahl (1926) identified a very similar freshwater species with the marine Lacrymaria lagenula (Claparede et al., 1868). With the exception of habitat, no significant differences can be found between L. pumilio and L. lagenula.  They could therefore be synonymous" (2).

1.  Tang J, Zhang G, Guo J, Luo L, Jiang J and Pan H (2023) A new contribution to the raptorial ciliate genus Lacrymaria (Protista: Ciliophora): a brief review and comprehensive descriptions of two new species from Changjiang Estuary. Front. Microbiol. 14:1259653.
 doi: 10.3389/fmicb.2023.125965
   
2.  Taxonomische Studien uber die Ciliaten des Grossglocknergebiete (Hohe Tauern, Osterreich I. Familien Holophryidae, Prorodontidae, Plagiocampidae, Colepidae, Enchelyidae und Lacrymariidae nov. fam. Von WILHELM FOISSNER.  Ann. Naturhist. Mus.Wien  84/B  49-85 ZOOLOGIE  Wien, Mai 1983 

3.  Song, W., and Wilbert, N. (1989). Taxonomische Untersuchungen an Aufwuchsciliaten (Protozoa, Ciliophora) im Poppelsdorfer Weiher, Bonn. Lauterbornia 3, 2–221.

18271cb7-3b75-43fb-8e0c-8886a57978bf.description:
Dileptus margaritifer (Ehrenberg, 1833) Dujardin, 1841  in a very busy neighborhood harvested by the floating coverglass method from a benthic sample taken from freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlanapo 20 0.70,  SPlan 40 0.70,  and SPlan 100 1.25 oil objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.

The ciliate measures 480 um in length.  Shape very narrowly to cylindroidally dileptid with distinct tail, proboscis usually 1/3 of body length. Innumerable scattered macronuclear nodules and several globular micronuclei. Individual nodules highly variable in size and shape. A dorsal row of contractile vacuoles. Two types of extrusomes attached to proboscis oral bulge: the longer type I rod-shaped with slightly narrowed ends, about 10 × 0.7 μm in size; and the shorter more numerous type II oblong, about 3 μm long.  The oral bulge runs down the ventral side of the flexible proboscis and with the mouth forms a keyhole shape.

 I believe this is Dileptus margaritifer.  The size matches,  size of environmental specimens about 400 × 50 μm (range of North American specimens 200-600).  Most importantly, the extrusomes of the proboscis match perfectly, numerous type II oblong, about 3 μm long with fewer scattered type I rod-shaped extrusomes with slightly narrowed ends, about 10 × 0.7 μm in size.  Interestingly, there are quite large macronuclei among the more numerous smaller ones.  Macrocuclear nodules may divide in vegetative specimens (Hayes 1938), first increasing in size and becoming dumbbell-shaped before separating into two oblong pieces.  These larger macronuclei match the illustrations of this phenomenon shown by Vďačný & Foissner 2012. 

Among congeners belonging to the D. margaritifer group,  D. jonesi is perhaps the most similar. It has the ability to form a mucous thread at the tail which serves to anchor the cell to the substrate which is, however, a difficult feature possibly not present all the time.  I did not observe the mucus thread formation. The size of 480 um, the number of macronuclei less than 100. There are two size-types of extrusomes- (5 μm and 2–3 μm) of rod-shaped extrusomes. This differs from the pattern seen in D. margaritifer. 

 D. beersi is a large (450-900 um) species that was found in a slightly brackish (3‰) pond on an island off the North Carolina coast and also in vey sand soil from a savannah in Venezuela.  It has dorsal contractile vacuoles in a wider band straddling either side of the dorsal edge sometimes in pairs rather than a single row. The extrusomes are very narrowly ovate as opposed to thin and rod-like. It also has 127-336 macronuclear nodules. 

Apodileptus visscheri is a freshwater species that has a similar number of macronuclei but is smaller (183-269 um) and has two types of extrusomes that differ from the thin rod-like extrusomes of my species-  type I very narrowly ovate, about 6 × 0.5–0.8 μm in size; type II oblong with rounded ends. 

1. Monograph of the Dileptids (Protista, Ciliophora, Rhynchostomatia).  Peter Vďačný & Wilhelm Foissner.   Denisia 31 1-529 13. 7. 2012

62039227-d212-4d2b-a12e-0f8c0eb20a5e.description:
Holophrya ovum EHRENBERG, 1831, t4he type species of the genus,   harvested by the floating coverglass method from a benthic sample taken from freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. Sample fed with boiled wheat seed.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 and SPlan 100 1.25 oil objectives plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  The cells range from 80- 160 um in length and are mostly ovoid to elliptical. Inactive cysts are present which can be seen to become active. The tuft of caudal cilia is very hard to demonstrate as is the dorsal brush in these moving cells.  As Foissner et al 1994 point out, H. discolor and H. teres can ingest green algae and appear green, but in the Kellis Pond population the algal cells are uniformly viable with no degeneration or digestions and are not resident in food vacuoles. 

1) Size in vivo 100-160 x 70-90 um.
2) Shape quite variable due to the life cycle, usually broadly ellipsoid and slightly constricted in the middle, almost transversely truncated anteriorly and posteriorly; rarely ovoid or cylindrical.
3) Ellipsoid macronucleus approximately in the middle of the body. 1 ellipsoid micronucleus.
4) Contractile vacuole at the posterior end.
5) Extrusomes (mucocysts and trichocysts) very delicate and therefore difficult to identify. Cells green and/or colorful due to many 5 μm zoochlorelles (Chlorella faginea; SUD 1969) and consumed algae.
6) 52-80, usually 66 longitudinal cilia. Several distinctly elongated cilia at the posterior end.
7) Mouth at the anterior end, oral funnel strong, consisting of 24-34 brace-shaped rods. Undulating membrane circular, 3 longitudinal adoral organelles ("brush") in enclitolophore-dexiotropic position.

Easily confused in size and shape with H. teres and H. discolor, from which it differs but in its long, delicate trichocysts and symbiotic algae (Caution! H. discolor and -+ H. teres also often feed on green algae and then appear as green as -+ H. ovum). Prorodon species have a sausage- or rope-shaped macronucleus (-+ P. niveus, -+ P. ellipticus). Characteristics 3 and 5 are particularly important for identification.


1.  Foissner, W., Berger, H., Kohmann, F., 1994. Taxonomische und ökologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobiensystems – Band III: Hymenostomata, Prostomatida, Nassulida. Informationsberichte des Bayer. Landesamtes für Wasserwirtschaft 1/94, pp 322=327.

28910cfb-e01c-4d86-908a-8348679ec28a.description:
Here is an interesting flagellate, a retortamonad. The retortamonads are a small group of flagellates, most commonly found in the intestines of animals as commensals, although a free-living species called the Chilomastix cuspidata exists. This is the species I show here. They are grouped under the taxon Archezoa. They are usually around 5-20 μm in length, and all of their small subunit ribosomal RNA gene sequences are very similar to each other. There are two genera: Retortamonas with two flagella, and Chilomastix with four. These organisms lack the usual mitochondria but instead possess highly modified mitochondria known as mitochondrion-related organelles (MROs). The best-studied of these are the hydrogenosomes of Trichomonas vaginalis and Spironucleus salmonicida, which produce ATP anaerobically through substrate-level phosphorylation with concomitant hydrogen production (Leger et al 2017).

Chilomastix cuspidata (Larsen & Patterson, 1990) from the sulfidic superficial benthos of a small tidal pool at the edge of the salt marsh bordering estuary Acabonac Harbor. The salinity is 33 o/oo. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. Thanks to Jeffrey Silberman of the Biology Center CAS Institute of Parasitology České Budějovice, Czechia for confirming the diagnosis. 

This species was described by Larsen and Patterson 1990 as Percolomonas cuspidata. Brugerolle 1991 assigned an organism isolated from a salt marsh by Farmer (unpublished), and indistinguishable from P. cuspidata, to Chilomastix. Bernard, Simpson, and Patterson 1997 formally moved the species Percolomonas cuspidata to Chilomastix on the basis of ultrastructural analysis (2).

The cell measures 17.5 um in length and conforms to the original description by Larsen and Patterson 1990: "Percolomonas cuspidata Larsen and Patterson sp. nov. Diagnosis. Cell 14-28 um long, drop-shaped, with long posterior spike with which the cell attaches to the substrate, and a cusp on the right-hand margin of the groove. All flagella of approximately the same length as the cell body. Description. Drop-shaped cell body with posterior end always drawn out into a spike the end of which adheres to the substrate, 14-28 um long (mostly 15-16 um), 6-12µm wide; with a groove extending from immediately below the apex to the posterior of the untapered part of the body; right margin of groove with cusp. Four flagella inserting at head of groove; two extending laterally away from the cell—one almost perpendicular to the axis of the cell; two lying within the groove; the flagella create a current of water and bacteria are trapped within the groove. The groove continues as a narrow curved channel extending into the cell and trapped bacteria pass along this channel until enclosed within a food vacuole. The cell normally spins when feeding, with one flagellum extending almost parallel to the substratum. Encountered in large numbers in organically enriched culture which was smelling of hydrogen sulphide (1).

The redescription from From Bernard, Simpson and Patterson 1997 (2): "The cell is lute- shaped. There is a posterior spike with which they may temporarily attach to the substrate. Attached cells usually appear to be feeding. The spike can be as long as the body. The length of the cell, including the spike, ranges from 14 to 33 um. Cells are ventrally flattened and dorsally convex. The cell has a deep groove on its ventral face extending from near the apex anteriorly to just above the spike posteriorly. The right wall of the groove (G) is more strongly developed than the left one and has a cusp about one third along its length. The cell bulges out ward just anterior to the cusp. Posteriorly the groove becomes a tube which twists to the left and into the cell. Food is ingested at the inner end of the groove. Food vacuoles are numerous and scattered throughout the cell. The four flagella insert subapically at the head of the groove. Three flagella of similar length and width extend antero-laterally from the cell . Their beating causes the cells to swim in a spiral path. The shortest flagellum is recurrent and lies in the groove" (2).

"The genus Percolomonas was created by Fenchel and Patterson [17] for P. cosmopolitus, a quadriflagellated protist originally assigned to Tetramitus by Ruinen [32]. Percolomonas was originally distinguished by a suite of largely ultrastructural features and assigned to the Heterolobosea [17]. Larsen and Patterson [23] used the following criteria to assign flagellates to Percolomonas on the basis of light microscopical characteristics: free-living flagellates with four flagella, flagella inserting at the head of a well-developed groove, and flagella used to draw bacteria into the groove where the bacteria are ingested. They transferred six nominal species previously assigned to Tetramitus and one species originally described in the genus Choanogaster to Percolomonas. Two new species were added: P. membranifera (since transferred to Carpediemonas [16])and P. cuspidata [23]" (2).

"The generic assignment of Percolomonas cuspidata has been the subject of dispute. Brugerolle [8] assigned an organism isolated from a salt marsh by Farmer (unpublished), and indistinguishable from P. cuspidata, to Chilomastix. This is one of the two genera of retortamonads. Patterson and Zolffel [29] also noted a close resemblance between P. cuspidata and Chilomastix caulleryi Alexeief], Electron-microscopical observations of retortamonads have revealed a distinctive cellular architecture but have not shown the presence of mitochondria [5, 6]. The retortamonads have been usually regarded as primitively amitochondriate [10, 15,27,28, 35]. All nominal species of retortamonads have been reported as intestinal endocommensals [22] with the exception of four records of free-living species [8,20,34] none of which we regard as unambiguously of retortamonads " (2).

1.  Some flagellates (Protista) from tropical marine sediments. Larsen J. and Patterson D. J. (1990). J. Nat. Hist., 24, 801-937.

2. An Ultrastructural Study of a Free-living Retortamonad, Chilomastix cuspidata (Larsen & Patterson, 1990) n. comb. (Retortamonadida, Protista) Catherine Bernard, Alastair G. B. Simpson, and David J. Patterson. Europ. J. Protistol. 33, 254-265 (1997)
