4fa6c1e5-9df1-45fc-8a1e-2862f0722875.description:
Polykrikos herdmanae Hoppenrath and Leander 2007 harvested using the floating coverglass method from a sample of the benthos of a small salt marsh tidal pool at the edge of estuary Acabonac Harbor. imaged in Nomrski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. the cells measure up to 70 up to 90 um in length. The pseudocolonies invariably contain eight integrated zooids and two nuclei but some individuals had just one visible nucleus with the other likely obscured by food bodies.  The population is clearly heterotrophic with a diverse array of ingested flagellates and contains complex extrusomes or taeniocyst—nematocyst complexes.  The only benthic species of this athecate marine dinoflagellate was thought to be Polykrikos lebourae which was originally thought to have both photosynthetic and heterotrophic forms. The heterotrophic form was later designated Polykrikos herdmanae by Hoppenrath and Leander (1).  "The "molecular phylogenetic data using small subunit rDNA demonstrated that the photosynthetic and heterotrophic forms of P. lebourae represent two distinct clades. The more inclusive clade containing both forms of P. lebourae was most closely related to heterotrophic polykrikoids, namely P. kofoidii. These results led us to conclude that the photosynthetic and heterotrophic forms of P. lebourae are in fact two distinct lineages, and the heterotrophic form is described here as Polykrikos herdmanae n. sp."(1). 

"Pseudocolonies of the heterotrophic form of  ‘P. lebourae’ (from Canadian and German sites)  almost always consisted of eight zooids and two nuclei. In Canada reduced pseudocolonies consisting of five or four zooids and one  nucleus, containing nematocysts were also observed.  Specimens with eight zooids were 40.0—80.0mm long and 30.0—50.0mm wide in Canada, and 45.0—90.0mm long and 32.5— 55.0mm wide in Germany, and lacked visible  borders between zooids (Fig. 8A). The cells were ovate in shape, with the terminal zooids being about half as wide as the central ones and the apical zooid  having a pointing shape. The acrobase was loop-shaped. The pseudocolonies were obliquely flattened, and fused sulci were positioned laterally on the right-hand side of the cell. The cinguli were descending, displaced about one cingular width. Eight sets of longitudinal and transverse flagella were present. The two nuclei were  nearly spherical and were distributed within the anterior and posterior halves of the pseudocolony" (1).

 "The heterotrophic form of ‘P. lebourae’ possessed taeniocyst-nematocyst-complexes typical for Polykrikos species. A taeniocyst, associated with a nematocyst, anchored beneath the sulcus near each flagellar insertion zone. These complex extrusomes were also present in other parts of the pseudocolony. Specimens contained yellow, orange, red and colorless food bodies of variable number and size, and positioned in different areas of the pseudocolony. Many colorless  granules were also present in the cytoplasm. Pseudocolonies of the heterotrophic form of ‘P. lebourae’ swam in a straight line and rotated around its longitudinal axis" (1). 

"Polykrikos (from Greek “poly” - many, and “krikos” – ring or circle) is one of the genera of family Polykrikaceae that includes athecate pseudocolony-forming dinoflagellates. Polykrikos are characterized by a sophisticated ballistic apparatus named the nematocyst-taeniocyst complex, which allows species to prey on a variety of organisms. Polykrikos have been found to regulate algal blooms as they feed on toxic dinoflagellates. However, there is also some data available on Polykrikos being toxic to fish (1). Polykrikos was first seen in 1868 by Uljanin and was mistakenly considered as a metazoan larva of a turbellarian flatworms. In 1873 Butschili re-examined the specimen and concluded that the cell was an unusual ciliate, and Bergh later, in 1881, clarified Polykrikos dinoflagellate affinities" (2).

1. Morphology and Phylogeny of the Pseudocolonial Dinoflagellates Polykrikos lebourae and Polykrikos herdmanae n. sp. Mona Hoppenrath and Brian S. Leander. Protist, Vol. 158, 209—227, April 2007

2.  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polykrikos

*Pseudochilodonopsis* cf. *quadrivacuolata* Qu, Pan, Hu, Gao & Al-Rasheid, 2015.

All images and video are of the organism.
Diagnosis of the organism observed:
•	 Length 45 µm, width 25 µm. 
•	Body oval with anterior part protruding to left. Rear shape - rounded. Dorsoventrally flattened. Body flexible but acontractile.
•	Dorsal side regular.
•	Contractile vacuoles = 3 (~4μm diameter).
•	Presence of wide glabrous region in the middle of ventral side.
•	Left kineties = 6, right kineties = 5.
•	Preoral kinety segmented (composed of about 4-5 fragments).
•	Two circumoral kineties, the outer one longer than the inner one.
•	Terminal fragment (dorsal brush) apical.
•	The terminal fragment is composed of at least 5 cilia (length ~5μm).
•	Cyrtos (oral basket) composed of (nematodesmal rods): 14.
•	Macronucleus ellipsoidal.
•	Feeds on diatoms.

References:

My previous observation of the species: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/254607983

Morphological and phylogenetic studies on three members of the genus Pseudochilodonopsis (Ciliophora, Cyrtophoria) isolated from brackish waters in China, including a novel species, Pseudochilodonopsis quadrivacuolata sp. Nov (2015)

Microhabitat: Found in a dock scrub of the boardwalk at Sea Brim National Park. 
Morphological Information:  Asexual Reproduction, nonmotile, individual cells from a flat colony from 4-120 cells, creating a ring like structure. Identifiable by the "spikey" outer ring, and multiple layers of cells in a circle shape. 
Autecology: Found in lakes, ponds, and along shore lines. Do better in nitrogen rich habitats. 

Refrences: Guiry, M.D. and G.M. Guiry  2013.  AlgaeBase. World-wide electronic publication, National University of Ireland, Galway. http://www.algaebase.org; searched on 28 September 2013.

•	Contractile vacuole in anterior body half.

Mag. 400x
- Sample collected on  4/17/2025 using a plastic film canister dragged over moss growing on a completely submerged rock in Lee Brook.

Live, testate, lobose amoeba: 98µ long x ~45µ wide in broad lateral profile; aperture ~17µ.  The test appears to be a fine latticework of bio-cement and transparent silica grains. The test has a thick keel-band that proceeds from aboral region to the top of the neck region. Near the ends of the keel are small, lateral notches that may be the pores noted by Siemensma here: https://arcella.nl/gibbocarina-galeata/. In general,  characterlistics, fit Siemensma's description of *G. galeata* cited above, however, the smaller size of this specimen may correspond better with *G. gracilis* https://arcella.nl/gibbocarina-gracilis/. I could not uncover if this smaller species also has the lateral neck "pores" observed in the current specimen and reported in *G. galeata.*

c7e500be-9c9d-4bd4-94a3-4a57bd8f1f22.description:
A haptophyte belonging to the Coccolithophyceae.  Most likely genus Hymenomonas, very possibly Hymenomonas roseola F.Stein, 1878 (3). It was found using the floating coverglass method from a benthic sample taken from a small salt marsh tidal pool salinity 29 o/oo  at the edge of estuary Acabonac Harbor.  When I first noticed them they were motile with two roughly equal flagella emerging from one end. I could not appreciate a haptonema.   They measured 12-18 um in length and were somewhat globoid to ellipsoid. The most striking feature is a thick exoskeleton or coccosphere covered with tiny scales: these were narrowly elliptical ring shaped structures with open central area. The cell contains two golden brown plastids.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. 

H. roseola is the only known freshwater species. Various references state that it can be found as well in slightly brackish estuaries.  World Register of Marine Species has it in marine, brackish, and freshwater sites. Lefort 1975 describes Hymenomonas roseola Stein var. marina var. nov. which is entirely consistent with this observation. Lefort writes regarding this variety of H. roseola: " These characteristics were consistently observed on a large number of cells belonging to strains originating from very different sites (Villefranche-sur-Mer, Saint-Malo, Roscoff). The geographical range occupied by the species H. roseola Stein is therefore considerably expanded, since the marine domain is added to fresh and brackish waters" (1).  His description of the new variety   "Hymenomonas roseola Stein var. marina var. nov.  Species collected in seawater. Cell diameters globose: 12-16. Two anterior flagella slightly unequal (16-18 µ and 16-22 µ) and thinner than flagella of other Hymenomonas species. Each chromatophore wall contains one pyrenoid. Coccolith: diameters 0.8-1.6 µ; height 0.6-0.7 µ. Badis forms an arch. They are raised from the base of the crystal (usually 14), which give the coccoliths the appearance of a dentate crown. Crystal: 0.7 µ in length, 0.1 µ in width. The base is narrow. The crystal tapers and terminates symmetrically at the apex. The coccolith tapers steadily from the base and gradually tapers towards the apex" (1).
 
"The living coccolithophores are marine, unicellular, flagellate phytoplankton, belonging to the phylum Haptophyta and division Prymnesiophyceae. Haptophyte algae have golden-brown chloroplasts, an exoskeleton of scales and a unique flagella-like structure, known as the haptonema. Within the Haptophyta, only the coccolithophores produce calcified scales know as coccoliths. Coccolithophores produce two types of disc-like coccoliths, heterococcoliths and holococcoliths, which are distinguished by their morphology, mode of formation, and life-cycle stage during which they are produced.  These organisms have a complex life cycle. 

Heterococcoliths are typically circular to elliptical discs or rings constructed from one or more radial arrays (cycles) of elaborate and variably shaped crystal units. This disc or ring is termed the rim and encloses a central area, which may be open, virtually closed or spanned by a variety of structures. Heterococcoliths are formed within the cell (in Golgi vesicles) and then extruded to form a composite exoskeleton, the coccosphere.  Holococcoliths are typically disc- or dome-shaped and formed of numerous, minute (~0.1µm), equidimensional calcite crystallites of simple, usually rhombic, shape. Compared to heterococcoliths, holococcolith morphologies are relatively similar through time, and there is a less well-defined distinction between rim and central-area structures. Holococcolith formation is not well understood but they tend to form in the motile, life-cycle stage and calcification appears to be extracellular. The fossil record of holococcoliths is sporadic and sparse, because their structure is weaker than the heterococcoliths and the small, modern forms rarely survive in sea floor sediments. 

Our knowledge of haptophytes life cycles is limited to the few species that survive in laboratories, and even these species rarely give up their secrets easily. Like many algae, haptophytes can reproduce asexually or sexually, and can switch between haploid (half the normal DNA compliment) and diploid (complete DNA compliment) phases. Haptophytes are unusual, however, in that they can maintain reproducing populations in both haploid and diploid states and survive this way for many years in laboratories. They obviously switch from one phase to another in the natural environment but we know little of why and how this happens, although it may allow them to resist viral attack or respond to detrimental environmental changes. In some coccolithophores this switch is also accompanied by production of a completely different coccosphere, most commonly haploid motile phases producing holococcoliths and motile and non-motile diploid phases producing heterococcoliths. They do not always conform to this pattern, however, and additional phases may occur, such as benthic stages in near-shore species, and non-coccolith structures or naked stages may also occur.

Living coccolithophores have a widespread oceanic distribution, living in the photic zone and being most diverse at low latitudes. Generally speaking, they are rare or absent at latitudes higher than 70° and flourish in warm, stratified, oligotrophic, mid-ocean environments. A number of species have very broad ecological tolerances but only one freshwater coccolithophore has been well documented.

Taxonomy is the description, naming and classification of organisms, and the taxonomy of coccolithophores is based largely upon the structure of the coccoliths. The production of coccoliths requires complex biochemical processes, which have been programmed into the group since their origination, and so they provide an apparently faithful record of evolutionary history. The coccolith-based taxonomy has stood up well to the introduction of detailed biological and DNA-based molecular genetic studies on living taxa and in most case the different approaches agree well.  

All heterococcolith formation observed to date, begins with the formation of a ring of calcite crystals (the proto-coccolith ring) on an organic base-plate scale within the cell. The proto-coccolith ring is formed of calcite crystals with alternating sub-vertical and sub-radial c-axis orientations, known as the V- and R-units. Their subsequent growth into complex coccolith structures forms the basis for coccolithophore taxonomy" (4).

ed56b237-7057-439d-af6d-04bbcd038cec.description:
Frontonia mengi Fan, Chen, Song, Al-Rasheed, and Warren 2011 from a small salt marsh tidal pool at the edge of Acabonac Harbor at Landing Lane. I had previously observed this ciliate at the same site but that sample was from the main intertidal benthos of the harbor, not a tidal pool (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/177168374). Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2 using SPlan 40 0.70 objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  I am grateful to Professor Weibo Song of the Laboratory of Protozoology, Institute of Evolution and Marine Biodiversity, Ocean University of  China,Qingdao PR China for solving this mystery for me and making the correct diagnosis. I originally thought this was a species of Cardiostomatella. 

The ciliate is found only in samples taken directly from the sand and not using the floating coverglass method. I have found this ciliate several times before in benthic samples taken from the same nearby estuary. The cells range from 120-200 um in length and their diet is diatoms. The shape is narrow, worm-like and elongate with the anterior 1/5 slightly bent to the right. At the level of the bend or slightly anterior to it there is a penniculid oral apparatus which is fusiform in shape with penniculi on the left and the undulating membrane on the right.  The postoral or pharyngeal field region is prominent and complex.  Depending on the plane of focus, we can see the vestibular kineties and postoral kineties on the surface. Deeper optical sections show a striking parallel array of structures that represent the two types of cytopharyngeal rods.  The mid-anterior macronucleus is elongate, narrow and fusiform to ellipsoid. There is a lenticular micronucleus nestled in a recess of the macronuclues. The macronucleus is sometimes markedly displaced anteriorly by the ciliates meals of diatoms. There is a left midposterior contractile vacuole. There are subcortical spindle-shaped extrusomes.  These features are those of Frontonia mengi Fan et al 2011. 


From Fan et al 2011:  Cell in vivo distinctly elongate, usually about 250 x 45 um,(range 150-242 x 40- 60 um) with ratio of length to width about 5:1,  Anterior region slightly curved to right. Dorsoventrally flattened about 3:2. Buccal field small and slightly depressed, about 20u m long. Cilia of peniculi  about 10 um long. Buccal and pharyngeal fields about one-third of body length. Two kinds of cytopharyngeal rods detectible). Cell colourless under low magnification, with small granules sparsely distributed within transparent cytoplasm. One contractile vacuole (CV), about 15 um in diameter, located dorsal-left in posterior one-third of cell; single CV pore on dorsal surface. Several non contractile vacuoles (probably food vacuoles) often present in middle and/or posterior regions of cell. Macronucleus elliptical, about 45 x10 mm; single micronucleus closely associated with macronucleus. Extrusomes spindle-shaped, 5–6 um long; when extruded, about 30 um long. Somatic cilia mostly about 8–10 um long, those at caudal end about 12 um long.  Locomotion mainly by swimming moderately fast along substrate such as bottom of Petri dish or detritus.

Buccal apparatus with peniculi 1–3 about equal length, peniculi 1 and 2 each with  five kinety rows, peniculus 3 with two rows. Paroral membrane double-rowed, located on right side of buccal  cavity. Forty-eight to 60 somatic kineties, which form sutures in ventral midline and at both ends of cell . Three vestibular kineties extending along the  paroral membrane. Five postoral kineties, four of which terminate posterior of the three peniculi, the fifth one terminating posterior of the paroral membrane to the right of the cytopyge.  Argyrome typical of genus (Fig. 1e, g). One CV pore  positioned on dorsal side at about level of posterior one third of body.

1.  Two novel marine Frontonia species, Frontonia mengi spec.nov.and Frontonia magna spec.nov. (Protozoa;Ciliophora),with notes on their phylogeny based on small-subunit rRNA gene sequence data.  Xinpeng Fan, Xiangrui Chen, Weibo Song, Khaled A.S.Al-Rasheid and Alan Warren.  International Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary Microbiology( 2011),61,1476–1486.

a276b9a0-abe3-4ec7-8770-f21df757e44e.description:
Several specimens of *Heleopera sphagni*, from the edge of a small fen that was just beginning to thaw out. In life, the amoebae encased within these shells were bright green from algal endosymbionts ("zoochlorellae"), so there is no doubt about the identification.

At the time they were collected, the amoebae were all encysted, with their apertures blocked by plugs, as shown in the fourth image.  As the water warmed up, the plugs were expelled and the amoebae began to extend their pseudopods. 

The shells are mostly composed of jagged siliceous plates, neatly glued together. The source of these plates is not clear to me. *Heleopera* species sometimes incorporate the scales of prey organisms in their own tests, but I don't recognize these. Could they be self-generated? I have no idea!

c3fa2518-1ef8-458f-a11c-262840b1b60e.description:
Video: https://youtu.be/2Z2LQZKqTjE

Sampling location: Top layer of soil in a lawn in a residential area.
Date and time of collection: 23 April 2025 at 12:12. Air temp 9 °C (48,2°F)
Time of observation: at 15:29.
The soil sample containing the top layer of soil was stored in a plastic container at room temperature for the duration of the experiment. The sample contained *Vaucheria* sp. filaments and an abundance of diatoms, chlamydomonadid algae, cyanobacteria filaments were also observed.

*Thecamoeba* cf. *quadrilineata* (Carter, 1856) Lepşi, 1960.

Diagnosis of the organism observed:
•	Stationary amoeba knobby but very little or not at all wrinkled.
•	In locomotion flattened, oblong or elongate elliptical in outline, with broadest point usually just anterior to middle of amoeba and with posterior end usually broadly rounded.
•	Frontal hyaline area lasted posteriorly along the lateral sides of the cell, forming an anterio-lateral hyaline crescent.
•	Several parallel dorsal folds (usually 4) extending far anteriorly common in locomotive form.
•	Length about 36 µm, breadth about 22 µm. Length: breadth ratio appr. 1.6.
•	Nucleus with a single central nucleolus of homogeneous texture. Both are highly deformable. Nucleolus with one or a few visible lacunae. Nucleus ∅=7 μm appr. Nucleolus ∅=4 μm appr.
•	Contractile vacuole ∅=7 μm appr. Highly deformable.
•	The granuloplasm contained, besides the nucleus and a large CV, food vacuoles (filled with chlamydomonad algae and small diatoms), numerous small spherical granules.

References:
https://arcella.nl/thecamoeba-quadrilineata/

Observation by Dr. Martin Kreutz https://realmicrolife.com/thecamoeba-quadrilineata/

Observation by Jeffry Silverman (@peptolab) https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/190579726

*Thecamoeba cosmophorea* n. sp. (Amoebozoa, Discosea, Thecamoebida) — Anexample of sibling species within the genus *Thecamoeba* by Y.S. Mesentsev, A.V. Smirnov (2018)
doi.org/10.1016/j.ejop.2018.12.003

d9037457-918a-48c2-a12b-4e6e4be3102c.description:
A Microthoracid ciliate harvested using the floating coverglass method from a benthic sample of freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DI using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. Thanks to Dr. Atef Omar for pointing out that this is Trichiliopsis opaca Penard 1922. The cells average 34 um in length. It is interesting that in this population, I was able to easily identify a tube connecting the contractile vacuole with the slit-like cytoproct.  Succh a tube is a feature of the genus Drepanomonas which caused me to think this might be a species of Drepanomonas. This contractile vacuole tube has not been described in published accounts  of  T. opaca, however Dr. Martin Kreutz has demonstrated the tube in his specimen https://realmicrolife.com/trochiliopsis-opaca/. 

There are two species in this microthoracid genus: the type species T. opaca and T. australis. The cells have a dorsoventrally compressed rounded oblong body with peculiar ridging on left and right sides. There is a small anterior overhang or beak associated with the indistinct cytostome where there are two adoral membranelles. Augustin, Foissner and Adam 1987 state that the cyrtos is invisible even with interference contrast and that the macronucleus is difficult to visualize in vivo and indeed this has been my experience with this species.  This is the type species since T. australis has deeper ridges.

Penard's original 1922 description: "Trochiliopsis opaca gen. nov. sp. n. Body vaguely ellipsoidal, rounded behind, convex on the right side and with no or barely noticeable convexity on the left side, curved towards the left at its part anterior and ending in a hooked beak. The animal is strongly compressed laterally, and we can then distinguish a right flank, divided into four or five longitudinal segments or ribbons separated by deep furrows; then a divided left flank in an equal number of ribbons, but more regular, clearly arched and concaved turned towards the left side. In the furrows and on both sides arise thin and long cilia which are not very abundant; forward and under the characteristic beak, they are more tight and more vigorous, and curve downwards like a hook. Under the top of the beak, on the left flank, you can see an edge (?) or double vertical line outline, which, parallel to the edge of the animal, goes straight down to a very long distance towards the posterior part of the body. Spherical nucleus, not very bulky, central. Contractile vacuole above the nucleus. Length 35 to 40 µm (1).

"This is a very small organism,  Trochiliopsis opaca whose characters almost escape all in sight, and the study of which, which still remains very incomplete, could not be pursued only with great difficulty. Although the body is very pale, very pure, and contains only very small shiny grains scattered in a cytoplasm where coarser food boluses do not seem to be found, its cuticle rigid, colorless, is entirely opalescent, of such an opalescence that the light appears to be reflected in it; it is then very difficult to distinguish anything other than the contractile vesicle, then a nucleus always vaguely outlined; longitudinal striations, on the other hand, are more clean, straight and equal on the right side (fig. 1), arched on the left side (fig. 2), where we still see, starting from the terminal beak, a very straight edge, the meaning of which cation remains enigmatic. But what is most characteristic in this organism, these are the trichocysts, small, very indistinct rods which escape the most often in plain sight, but which, after the explosion, appear in a curious form, a relatively short filament, and terminated at its distal end by two, three, or more generally four hooked points (fig. 4), divaricate, such that approximately we will soon see them again in another Infusoria (Pseudomicrothorax) where they were able be better studied. Fig. 3 shows the Infusoria seen from above, with the furrows on its two faces. Trochiliopsis opaca was found, still quite rare, at Ariana, in the leaves dead from Swan Pond" (1).

From Augustin, Foissner, and Adam:  "Type-species . Trochiliopsis opaca Penard, 1922. Freshwater. In vivo circa 30-40(-50) x 17-20 um. Body outline oval, anteriorly curved slightly to the ventral side terminating in a pointed beak-like region (peak). Body strongly compressed laterally (circa 2:1) and covered in a rigid longitudinally ribbed armour. Somatic kinetics in deep, crenelated furrows, which terminate near the oral peak. Macronucleus spherical, more or less centrally located, in vivo hardly discernible. Micronucleus closely attached to the macronucleus. Contractile vacuole centrally located above macronucleus, close to the right lateral surface, diameter about 4 um; contractile vacuole pore at the end of the paroral membrane. Cytoproct slightly posterior to the contractile vacuole pore, visible as black line in dry silvered specimen (Fig. 130). Pellicle rigid, colourless, opaque. Extrusomes about 3 um, fusiform, scattered over the whole body in the ribs between the furrows, show four anchor-like processes at the distal end in the exploded phase. Probably feeds on bacteria, but no food vacuoles were found. Slow, trembling and swaying movements. Probably only two adoral membranelles, located at the oral peak. Anterior adoral membranelle most likely built up by two rows, posterior one probably by three rows of kinetosomes. Paroral membrane with 8-9 paired basal bodies (Figs 120, 122, 124). Cyrtos invisible in life even with interference contrast, but slightly impregnated with protargol silver" (2).

1.  Penard, E. 1922. Etudes sur les infusoires d'eau douce. Georg et Cie, Geneve

2.  Revision of the genera Acineria, Trimyema and Trochiliopsis (Protozoa, Ciliophora)H. Augustin, W. Foissner & H. Adam. Zoologisches Institut der Universitat Salzburg. Bulletin of the British Museum (Natural History) Zoology 52 pages 197-224 ( 24 Jun 1987 )

406cef89-83c1-4ef1-9f2a-5f3b22933f09.description:
A most interesting freely reproducing population of CHILODONELLA UNCINATA Ehrenberg (Kahl 1931) from the freshwater glacial kettle hole Kellis Pond which divulged some morphologic features I had not seen before. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2 using SPlan 100 1.25 oil objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S9+.  This population provides insight into the process of nuclear morphogeneis in dividing cells. 

There are numerous conjugating pairs as well as dividers. Normal vegetative individuals measured 40 um and show the concentric coarsely granular heteromeric macronucleus with a posterior spherical micronucleus. However, I noticed a population of larger individuals measuring around 60 um in length which show a massively enlarged nuclear structure accompanied by a second smaller coarsely granular nuclear structure situated anterior to it which looks more like a normal macronucleus. I had not seen this before and, after consulting Foissner et al 1991,  I believe these enlarged cell are post conjugation dividers with mid to late stages of macronuclear morphogenesis. Indeed, Foissner et al 1991 depict such an individual (1, page 48-figure eight) with a similar large posterior nuclear body which they label "macronucleus primordium" accompanied by a the normal-appearing macrocucleus anterior to it.

Recent work by  Ahsan et al 2025 (2) show that this occurs after conjugation where the new somatic  macronucleus develops as the old parental macronucleus degenerates (2).  What I saw in my slides was the late stage of macronucleuar morphogenesis. "During Chilodonella’s early development, the old MAC retains its “typical” morphology 
while the newly developing MACs appear attached to them.
We found a consistent positioning of the old and new (developing) MACs during the 
early and late developing stages: the old MACs tend to be on “top” (toward the anterior 
portion of the cell), and the newly developing (new) MACs position on the “bottom” 
(toward the posterior portion of the cell—under the old MACs) of the old MACs. During the late developmental stage, the old MACs lose their typical morphology and degrade as the new MACs develop with the new MIC attached 
or almost attached. After going through all of these stages, they return to their vegetative stage" (2).

The normal cells measure 40 um in length, a bit smaller than Kahl's described range of 50-90 um. Foissner (1981) gives a range of 28-36 um, Song (1997) around 30 um, and Song et al. (2009) a range of 30-50 um. The infraciliature is perfect for C. unicnata- there are 4 left and 4 right kineties as well as two circumoral kineties and a single preoral kinety. The postoral region is devoid of cilia. The anterior dorsal brush row of bristles is only visualized when the indivdual is viewed from the dorsal surface which was not seen since the population was crawling on the underside of the coveglass.  Interphase macronucleus spherical to ellipsoid, usually near the posterior end, hyaline, with numerous chromatin globules at the periphery and a central inner body usually with a spherical micronucleus posterior to the macronucleus. Post dividers showed an array of nuclear morphology often with solid chromatin bodies or with a ring-shaped solid peripheral chromatin body rather than the coarsely granular peripheral morphology of non-dividers. The cyrtos forms a distally coiled cornucopia-like basket and in this population consists of 11 rods surrounding the circular cytostome. My previous population from the same site sampled exactly one year prior showed 10 rods: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/206970264 . The two contractile vacuoles are diagonally opposed in the anterior right and posterior left quadrants of the cell and can be seen cycling quite frequently.

1. Foissner W., Blatterer H., Berger H. & Kohmann F. (1991): Taxonomische und ökologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobiensystems - Band I: Cyrtophorida, Oligotrichida, Hypotrichia, Colpodea. – Informationsberichte Bayer. Landesamt für Wasserwirtschaft, München, 1/91: pp 45-51.

2.  Genome content reorganization in the non-model ciliate Chilodonella uncinata: insights into nuclear achitecture, 
DNA content, and chromosome fragmentation during 
macronuclear development
 Ragib Ahsan, Xyrus X. Maurer-Alcalá, Laura A. Katz.  https://doi.org/10.1128/msphere.00075-25

70a26fee-fc86-4440-bf29-58ce82f2e5de.description:
Salpingoeca gracilis James-Clark 1868 harvested by the floating cover glass method from a benthic sample of the freshwater glacial kettle pond Kellis Pond. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. The lorica measures from 35-41 um in length including the elongate stem. The zooids measure 14-16 um in length. James-Clark first described the species in New England USA in 1868. He described the lorica as resembling a champagne glass with subdivision of the lorica into three sections: a central cylindrical part encasing the zooid, a posterior stalk of varying length, and a flared anterior end.   Stein published the first European sighting in 1878.  Thomson showed in 1977 using electron microscopy that the lorica has dense minute proteinaceous non-silicaceous longitudinal striations not visible with light microscopy. 

I believe I have observed some novel morphologic findings in the Kellis Pond population. In my material, we can appreciate a knobby foot-like structure at the attachment point which has not been described before. Rather, James-Clark 1867, in describing the stalk, says: "(it) thence tapers gradually into a slender posterior third, but expands again slightly as it terminates upon its place of attachment" (1). Also, in some exquisitely focused individuals, I visualized minute fibrils at the posterior end of the zooid which appeared to be attached to the lorica and may represent the means of retraction of the zooid within the lorica. Such a structure has not been described before.  James-Clark describes two contractile vacuoles which can sometimes be observed one behind the other temporarily- a phenomenon I also observed (1).   The species is obviously plaktonic since it had to swim to reach the floating coverglass where it then attached by this knobby foot plate. The planktonic nature of S. gracilis is discussed by Thomsen 1977 (2). 

 The original description by James-Clark 1867:  "Salpingoeca gracilis was found upon only one occasion, and then in an old aquarium, which could not be said to be in a perfectly healthy condition, although its contents were by no means putrid. The body is yellow, and has a cylindrical shape, about four times as long as broad, narrowed and rounded behind, and rounded-truncate in front. Like Codosiga it bears a filmy, membranous, colourless collar which is attached to the extreme edge of the frontal area, and rises to a height which is equal to two-thirds of the length of the body. The outline of the collar is generally cylindrical, and truncate at the distal end, but still is subjected to various degrees of momentary change. Unless it be by means of the vibrations of the flagellum, there is no other immediate agent which can be supposed to move the body up and down in its sheath. These is no visible movement in itself, like creeping, to be observed; and moreover the body progresses so quickly, when changing its place in the calyx, that it becomes evident that it is not due to any reptant mode of transposition. When withdrawn into the basal tapering portion of its calyx, the collar does not extend beyond the rim of the latter, but, on the other hand, the body occasionally moves so far in the opposite direction that nearly the whole of the collar (b) projects outside of the dormitory. The flagellum is a delicate filament which arises from the axial point of the front, and projects a short distance beyond the edge of the collar. It presents a constantly undulating aspect, and vibrates from base to tip. The mouth, we are obliged to presume lies somewhere about the base of the flagellum. Abundant digestive vacuoles were observed, as well as loose particles of food, in various parts of the body; but at no time were we so fortunate as to see the introception of nutritive material or the ejection of fecal matter" (1). 

"The contractile vesicles are two in number. They lie between the second and posterior thirds of the body, usually on opposite sides, and close to the surface. In aspect and rate of systole they resemble those of Cadosigna pulchereima, but they are a little smaller in proportion to the size of the animalcule. Sometimes the protean changes of the body are so extensive as to throw the two vesicles into a line with each other in an antero-posterior direction; but they hold this position only temporarily, and soon return to their normal relations. The calyx (lorica) has the general shape and proportions of a champagne-glass, and appears to be hollow to the very bottom of its pedicel-like inferior third. Anteriorly it is truncate, smooth, and flares quite strongly. About the middle it bulges very sensibly, and thence tapers gradually into a slender posterior third, but expands again slightly as it terminates upon its place of attachment. It is colourless; excessively transparent and exhibits considerable flexibility under the movements of the body, apparently having the consistency of a mere film (1). 

The discussion from Thomsen's 1977 study of the lorica's ultrastructure:  "The lorica of S. gracilis falls into three distinct regions : (1) an apparently hollow stalk, in length approximately one third to half of the total lorica length, (2) a cylindrical central part surrounding the protoplast, and (3) an anterior funnel-shaped part. At low magnification the lorica appears completely amorphous. However, high magnification of the S. gracilis lorica discloses a distinct longitudinal striation with a periodicity of 13-19 nm. In certain areas of the lorica the longitudinal striation is crossed by much less conspicuous transversely oriented structural elements. The angle between the two directions is approximately 9o°. Tiny fibrils apparently constitute an important part of the lorica. Scrutinizing the five loricae observed it appears that the regular striation is confined to the anterior part of the lorica. The cylindrical central part appears amorphous even at high magnification. The stalk displays an irregular pattern of coarse longitudinally oriented wrinkles. At the very mouth of the lorica a structureless rim is just observable. This may be a kind of matrix underlying the fibrillar material. The protoplast fills up the central part of the lorica almost completely. At the posterior end it is drawn out into a finger-like extension. Approximately forty tentacles make up the collar. When the protoplast is at the bottom of the lorica, the collar is completely sheathed by the funnel-shaped anterior part" (2). 

"Specific characteristics of S. gracilis are not to be found in exact lorica measurements, rather in the ratios between dimensions of different parts of the lorica. To put it differently, the most prominent characteristic of this species seems to be the obvious subdivision of the lorica into three sections: a central cylindrical part encasing the protoplast, a posterior stalk, and an anterior part shaped as an inverted cone-stub. James-Clark (1867) described the lorica of S. gracilis by stating that it had the general shape and proportions of a "champagne glass'.  The Danish material corresponds in every detail with that examined by Willen (1963). The agreement is not restricted to morphological data, but also applies to ecological aspects. In contradiction to the majority of previous observations claiming the species to be attached by the stipe, Willen (1963) observed S. gracilis as a true planktonic species appearing in great quantities (20000-20000o cells/l). As the cells from Aalsgaarde were found in a water sample, they too, must be considered true planktonic organisms. The lorica, described by James-Clark (1867) as having `the consistency of a mere film is shown by the present study — based on electron microscopy of whole mounts — to be delicately striated in the anterior third. Microfibrils appear to form part of the lorica of this species, perhaps as in Salpingoeca pelagica Laval, where the presence of fine fibrillar material was demonstrated by sectioning (Laval, 1971). In the two additional non-silicified Salpingoeca species investigated by shadowcast whole mounts, S. frequentissima (Kristiansen, 1972) and Salpingoeca sp. (Thomsen, 1973), no fibrils have been observed" (2). 


 1.  James-Clark, H., 1867. On the Spongiae Ciliatae as Infusoria Flagellata: or  observations on the structure, animality and relationship of Leucosolenia
 botryoides Bowerbank. Mem. Boston Soc. Nat. History 1, pp. 199-200. 

 2.  Thomsen, H.A., 1977. External morphology of the choanoflagellate Salpingoeca  gracilis James-Clark. J. Mar. Biol. Assoc. UK 57, 629–634.

3.  THE ORGANISM OF THE INFUSION ANIMALS BASED ON MY OWN RESEARCH PREPARED IN SYSTEMATIC ORDER BY DR. FRIEDRICH RITTER v. STEIN, IMPERIAL AND ROYAL KINGDOM COUNCIL AND OÖ PROFESSOR OF ZOOLOGY AT THE IMPERIAL AND ROYAL KINGDOM UNIVERSITY IN PRAGUE. DEPARTMENT III. THE NATURAL HISTORY OF FLAGELLATES OR FLAGILLA INFUSORIE. WITH 24 COPPER PLATES. 1ST HALF,
CONTAINING THE NOT-YET-COMPLETE GENERAL PART AND EXPLANATIONS OF ALL ILLUSTRATIONS. LEIPZIG, PUBLISHED BY WILHELM ENGELMANN. 1878.

405ad2e5-f83d-4f1c-8245-6f740bcf7408.description:
Peranema trichophorum (Ehrenberg, 1832) Stein, 1878 harvested by the floating coverglass method from a benthic sample taken from freshwater Town Pond in East Hampton Village. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. The cells measure 44-48 um in length.  This population conforms to the genus Peranema. The genus Peranema Dujardin, 1841 "is distinguished as being a metabolic gliding euglenid, with an ingestion apparatus, and with two flagella emerging from the reservoir. A longer, thicker flagellum is directed anteriorly during gliding, and flagellar movements are greatest at its tip. The recurrent flagellum is about as long as the cell or longer than the cell, and is attached to the cell surface. The flagellar canal opens as a slit extending from the apex to slightly subapical. The genus is also characterised by having an ingestion apparatus with two rods. The pellicle has fine spiral or longitudinal ridges" (1).  The presence of longitudinal extrusomes is diagnostic of P. trichophoum. The cells were observed ingesting detritus as described by Schroeckh et al 2003 where we can observe the back and forth motion of the the rods of the ingestion apparatus. The longitudinally arrayed rod-like extrusomes are apparent, they are densest in the subapical or neck region. The anterior flagellum is quite thick and about the same length of the cell. The recurrent flagellum emerges from the posterior end of the slit- like flagellar canal opening and is tightly adpressed to cell surface, lying in a longitudinal groove and is equal to or slightly less than the cell length.  


"Peranema trichophorum (Ehrenberg, 1832) Stein, 1878.  Description: Gliding, metabolic euglenid, 30–110 µm, mostly 50–75 µm long and 8–20 µm wide. Cell cylindrical, apically narrowed. The posterior end of the cell is sac-shaped and may have a short point. Cells contain many refractile paramylon grains. The pellicle has delicate, longitudinal ridges with small rod-like bodies (extrusomes). The cell is very metabolic. The anterior flagellum is strongly developed and is about the same length as the cell. The recurrent flagellum is hard to see. It lies in a flagellar canal, which defines the ventral surface of the cell and is 0.75–0.95 CL. The ingestion apparatus is well developed, with two rods. The reservoir is located in the first sixth of cell on the right side with an associated contractile vacuole. A spherical nucleus is located in the posterior of the cell. This species eats algae and detritus and two cells observed contained 5–8 other euglenids (Trachelomonas) in food vacuoles. The description is based on observations of 115 cells" (1).


"Peranema trichophorum has been reported with lengths from 22 to 81 µm (Huber-Pestalozzi, 1955), as a taxon with or without extrusomes, and as a taxon with or without a pointed posterior end. We have found variation with extrusomes, posterior end, and storage materials in populations of this species. There is considerable overlap with other species assigned to the genus (P. pleururum, P. inflexum) such that it is probable that descriptions of more than one species have been included under the name P. trichophorum. In an attempt to establish an identity for this species we have compared our organism with Peranema trichophorum 1260/1b from the Culture Collection for Algae and Protozoa (CCAP, The Ferry House, Ambleside, Cumbria LA22 0LP, England). We reestablished new cultures from clonal isolates of 1260/1b and cells in these varied in size from 45 to 80 µm, but mostly were 55-65µm. The clonal isolates initially lacked extrusomes, but extrusomes became numerous as populations aged.  The CCAP strain and the individuals reported here as P. trichophorum have a similar aspect, similar variation in paramylon granules, extrusomes and profile of the posterior end. For the purposes of this paper, we regard this strain and the organisms described above as being of Peranema trichophorum. Peranema trichophorum may be difficult to distinguish from some other species of Peranema. There is considerable overlap in size between P. trichophorum and P. pleurururm or P. inflexum. The appearance of the cytoplasm of all of these species can vary because of variable amounts of food vacuoles or paramylon inclusions. In mixed populations, cell length, the longitudinal alignment of extrusomes and the dense collection of extrusomes located subapically (the neck), the relatively wide body and often rounded posterior end of the cell– when used together– are useful in distinguishing this species. We distinguish P. trichophorum from P. inflexum Skuja, 1939 because P. inflexum is smaller, usually has a more curved body, a pointed posterior end and no extrusomes; and 
from P. pleururum Skuja, 1948 which typically has a flattened body, a long pointed posterior end, well- marked pellicular ridges and no extrusomes" (1).

1.  Free-living heterotrophic euglenids from freshwater sites in mainland Australia. Sabrina Schroeckh, WonJeLee & David J. Patterson. Hydrobiologia 493: 131–166, 2003.

260f9c1f-e5ef-4ee3-94d9-5cfc594b124c.description:
Dexiostoma campylum (Stokes, 1886) Jankowski,1961 harvested by the floating coverglass method from a benthic sample taken from freshwater Town Pond in East Hampton Village. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 and 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. The cells measure 56-64 um in length. The cells were narrowly reniform to plump and ovoid when well fed with an indented mouth region and with rounded posterior but sometimes with narrowed posterior all in accordance with shape variants depicted by Ganner and Foissner 1989.  Cells show pronounce ribbing at the anterior right side as noted by Ganner and Foissner 1989 (1).  Cells show usually from 8 up to 10 occasionally up to 16 (in plump well-fed cells) ciliary rows on one side consistent with the range of 16-33, usually 20-25 longitudinal rows of cilia given by Ganner and Foissner 1989 (1) and Foissner et al 1994 (2).  There are a few short caudal cilia. The contractile vacuole is located in the posterior third of the body and sometimes shows accessory vacuoles as depicted by Kahl.  The large round macronucleus is located centrally. A micronucleus over the macronucleus was rarely observed. Besides the dot-like mucocysts arranged in rows between the ciliary rows, haphazardly arranged rods were sometimes present that are probably ectosymbiont prokaryotes which have not been described before. These features served to distinguish this population of  Dexiostoma campylum from its closest congeners (see Foissner et al 1994 below). 


 "In vivo 35-90 x 15-35 um, a size of about 60 x 20 um is common. Body form a slender, sometimes a broad oval, about three times as long as it is broad. Anterior pole round, preoral section ventrally slightly truncated and markedly indented by ciliary rows, resulting in a rather conspicuous ribbing of the anterior nonciliated area of the left side. Posterior pole round, occasionally weakly tapered. Laterally slightly compressed, gradually becoming broader from anterior to posterior. Mucocysts arranged in a single row between two kineties and between the cilia of each kinety.  Macronucleus approximately round, in vivo 12-20 um in diameter. Contractile vacuole in vivo 6-12 um in diameter, located at the posterior third of body, its pore in vivo 1 um in diameter.
The pore interrupts kinety number 5-7.  Cilia in vivo 8-10 um- long, caudal cilia 12-15 um. Movement fast with permanent rotation around the long axis of the body. 16-33 somatic kineties. Bending of kineties of the right side much less pronounced than in Colpidium and Paracolpidium. Preorally, kineties of the right side do not (or only very slightly) overlap to the left side. Thus, preoral suture straight, nearly median, slightly inclined to the left. Kineties of the right side reach nearer to the anterior pole than those of the left side, therefore, oval non-ciliated apical pole field somewhat shifted to the left. Anteriorly, bipolar kineties between kinety number 5-6 and 20 possess paired basal bodies, which is not mentioned by Dragesco 8L Dragesco-Kerneis (1986). Distance between kinety number 2 and 3 slightly enlarged preorally. Likewise, distance between  the kinety fragment and the kinety to the left of this fragment slightly larger compared to the distance of the other kineties of this side" (1).


"1. Size in vivo 35-90 μm, usually 50-70 x 20-30 um.
2. Shape in lateral view slender, kidney-shaped, slightly depressed at the oral apparatus; somewhat narrower pre-orally than post-orally, ovoid when well fed. Not flattened.
3. Macronucleus spherical in the center of the cell. 1 spherical micronucleus.
4. Contractile vacuole in the posterior third of the body to the right of the median.
5) Extrusomes (mucocysts) inconspicuous (only visible in interference contrast).
6) 16-33, usually 20-25 longitudinal rows of cilia, forming a short, straight suture preorally. At the posterior end, there are a few slightly elongated cilia that are difficult to identify.
7) Oral apparatus in the anterior third of the body, oriented obliquely to the longitudinal axis of the body. Mouth opening is approximately triangular. The exact structure of the oral cilia can only be identified after silver impregnation" (2).

" Colpidium colpoda and -s Colpidium kleini are over 80 um in size and usually plumper.  Paracolpidium truncatum usually has a pointed anterior end and a pronounced dorsal "hump"; furthermore, this species lacks the second-order silver line meridians. Dexiostoma campylum is easily confused in vivo with the frequently associated species of the  Tetrahymena pyriformis complex (shape more pronouncedly ovoid because the mouth is not indented, oral apparatus parallel to the body's longitudinal axis; no caudal cilia) and with Glaucoma species (ellipsoidal shape, adoral membranelles visible as beating plates even at low magnification); in atypical populations, check the silver line system, which can easily separate the three species. For identification, the characteristics 1, 2, 6 are particularly important" (2). 


 1.  Taxonomy and ecology of some ciliates (Protozoa, Ciliophora) of the saprobic system. III. Revision of the genera Colpidium and Dexiostoma and establishment of a new genus, Paracolpidium nov. gen. B. Ganner & W. Foissner.  Hydrobiologia 182:181-218, 1989.

 2.  Foissner W., Berger H. & Kohmann F. (1994): Taxonomische und ökologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobiensystems – Band III: Hymenostomata, Prostomatida, Nassulida. – Informationsberichte des Bayer. Landesamtes für Wasserwirtschaft, 1/94: pp 33-42.

575e3ae2-2ca9-4235-bbf3-50eeab76c2bf.description:
Trithigmostoma cucullulus (MUELLER, 1786) Jankowski, 1967 harvested by the floating coverglass method from a benthic sample taken from freshwater Town Pond in East Hampton Village. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 and 100 1.25 oil immersion objectives plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. The cells measure 100 um in average length.  I was happy to find several individuals that were browsing the detritus using their cyrtos to vacuum up various meals. 

I was able to focus on 6 contractile vacuoles with demonstrable excretory pores- two anteriorly on either side of the mouth and several others scattered more posteriorly.  I counted usually 17 ventral ciliary rows, two of which ended behind the mouth (postoral kineties). The three populations described by Qu et al 2021 (2) had from 16-21 somatic kineties with two of them post oral (as opposed to three for Foissner et al). I found 7 right (frontoventral) kineties and 8 left kineties.  These numbers are congruent with those of Qu et al 2021 (2) and with Foissner et al (1) for the right side but less than the 9-11 reported by Foissner et al on the left. Foissner et al 1994 (1) called the dorsal kinety structure a dorsal brush while Qu et al 2021 (2) called it the terminal fragment with a range of from 15-36 basal bodies.  I counted from 17 up to 23 basal bodies and/or bristles in the dorsal brush (terminal fragment of Qu et al) in the Town Pond population- the latter figure is in keeping with many reports including Qu et al 2021 (2) but Foissner et al (1) showed 29–40 (median : 33). The alveolar structure of the dorsal pellicle was visible as well.     

From Foissner et al 1991
"1. Size in vivo 80 - 160 x 30 - 70 μm, usually around 90 - 110 x 40 - 50 μm.
2. Shape narrow to broadly ellipsoid, often slightly more broadly rounded anteriorly than posteriorly. Right margin convex, left slightly sigmoid, slightly retracted at the level of the snout, forming a somewhat protruding, usually gently rounded beak preorally.
3. About 2-3:1  flattened. Ventrally flat. Dorsal body convex, does not project beyond the ventral side.
4) Macronucleus ellipsoid, slightly below the middle. Coarsely granulated at the ends, hyaline in the middle and with a central inner body.
5) 2-11, usually 3-7 regularly distributed contractile vacuoles. 
6) Pellicula covered by a mucous layer about 1 μm thick, which can be shed as in T. steini.
7) According to FOISSNER (1988b) 19 - 22  (median = 20.5) ventral rows of cilia, according to SOLTYNSKA (1971) and KOWALSKA & KACZANOWSKA (1970) 16 - 21, according to RADZIKOWSKI (1966) 18 - 21. On the right, 7 - 8 pass the mouth and abut at a very acute angle against the preoral cilia row, which runs slightly sigmoidally from the snout to the tip of the beak. 3 cilia rows end behind the mouth. On the left, 9 - 11 rows abut the preoral cilia row. The outer, longer of the 2 circumoral cilia rows is curved around the snout on the right- only clearly visible in interference contrast and after silver impregnation! 
8) Dorsal brush straight to slightly curved, runs subapically to the left of the median across the beak. In the population studied by Foissner (1988b), it consists of 29–40 (median : 33) cilia. In other populations, it only consists of 20–30 cilia.
9) Mouth in the anterior third slightly to the right of the median. The cyrtos is inclined dorsally, funnel-shaped. According to Foissner (1988b), it consists of 11–17 (median : 13.8). According to RADZIKOWSKI (1966) from 10-14 rods" (1). 

"Trithigmostoma steini has 25–33 (usually n–30) ventral cilia, more contractile vacuoles (10–40), and a mostly arched dorsal brush composed of more cilia (usually around 50). + T. srameki and Z. bavariensis (KAHL, 1931) have fewer ventral cilia, and the distance between the postoral cilia is increased. Trithigmostoma bavariensis also appears to be restricted to terrestrial biotopes. Characters 1,7 (number of cilia), 8 are particularly important for identification" (1). 

" Presumably, T. cucullulus was often confused with T. steini (BLOCHMANN, 1895), since KAHL (1931) wrongly synonymized these two species. Trithigmostoma alpestris FOISSNER, 1979c is identical to T. cucullulus. The smaller T. hunanensis GONG & SHEN, 1989 has only two contractile vacuoles and is definitely synonymous with Chlamydonellopsis polonica (FOISSNER et al., 1981). Further verifications would be necessary: ​​Chilodon spiralidentis BHATIA & MULLICK 1930 has a spirally curved cyrtos; Chilodon schewiakoffi SCHOUTEDEN, 1906 has only one contractile vacuole; Chilodonella plicata TUCOLESCO, 1962a has folds at the front and, in our opinion, is synonymous with T. cucullulus" (1).

"Jankowski (1967) established the genus Trithigmostoma from Chilodonella, mainly based on the lack of a barren gap between right and left kineties. The type is Trithigmostoma cucullulus. Foissner (1987, 1988) then summarized and made new combinations for some Chilodonella species. So far, the
 genus is comprised of five species, namely: T. bavariensis (Kahl, 1931) Foissner, 1987; T. chattoni (MacDougall, 1936) Foissner, 1988; T. cucullulus (Müller, 1786) Jankowski, 1967; T. srameki (Sramek-Husek, 1952) Foissner, 1988; and T. steini (Blochmann, 1895) Foissner, 1988. Details about the species identification refer to Foissner (1987,1988) and Blatterer & Foissner (1992). Three other genera, Odontochlamys Certes (1891), Thigmogaster Deroux, 1976 and Pseudochilodonopsis Foissner,1979 were also separated from Chilodonella Qu etal., 2015), and together with Trithigmostoma, are now assigned to the family Chilodonellidae. However, characteristics such as a lack of barren gap between right and left kineties, almost all right kineties reaching posterior cell end, and many irregularly distributed contractile vacuoles, make Trithigmostoma very special in Chilodonellidae" (2).

"Trithigmostoma cucullulus is one of the earliest identified ciliates. It was originally reported by Müller (1786), using the name Kolpoda cucullulus (Aescht, 2001). Because of its wide distribution and relatively high abundance, Trithigmostoma cucullulus has been recorded worldwide and its morphology is well studied. Since the original report, the generic assignment of this species (species name) has been changed several times, for example to Chilodon cucullulus (Müller, 1786) Klein, 1927, Chilodonella cucullulus (Müller, 1786) Kahl,1931 and Trithigmostoma cucullus (Müller, 1786) Foissner (1988)  Jankowski, 1967 (spelling mistake was corrected by Foissner, 1988). Foissner et al., 1991 summarized the morphology of the species in detail. Our populations correspond well with the previous populations as well as with a recent estuarine population from China (salinity 4.3; Chen et al., 2018). Although reported many times in history, T. cucullulus demonstrates very stable morphological features.  In addition, considering its worldwide distribution, it might be a cosmopolitan species" (2).


1.  Foissner W., Blatterer H., Berger H. & Kohmann F. (1991): Taxonomische und ökologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobiensystems - Band I: Cyrtophorida, Oligotrichida, Hypotrichia, Colpodea. – Informationsberichte Bayer. Landesamt für Wasserwirtschaft, München, 1/91: 478 pp

 2.  Qu Z, Pan H, Wang C, Ma H, Stoeck T and Hu X (2021) Gastronautidae Deroux, 1994 and Trithigmostoma Jankowski, 1967: Evolutionary Links Among
 Cyrtophorian Ciliates (Protista, Ciliophora, and Phyllopharyngea). Front. Mar. Sci. 8:625644. doi: 10.3389/fmars.2021.625644

82111ab9-779b-4104-833f-df44df655a51.description:
Urotricha agilis (STOKES, 1886) KAHL, 1930 harvested by making touch preparations from boiled wheat seeds used to feed a benthic sample taken from freshwater Town Pond in East Hampton Village. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 and 100 1.25 oil immersion objectives plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  The cells measure 18  um in length and have a roughly triangular sometimes ovoid (in well-fed individuals) shape.  We can count 7 ciliary rows on one side pointing to a total of 14 or 15 in total which is diagnostic of Urotricha agilis-the only species with so few ciliary rows.  The population showed the characteristic movement of spinning and wide jumps. 

 1) Size in vivo about 10-20 x 7-14 um.
 2) Body roughly cone-shaped, that is, outline triangular with unciliated posterior portion not set off plug-like from body proper. 
 3) Macronucleus globular, near mid-body.
 4) Contractile vacuole in posterior end, slightly eccentric.
 5) Extrusomes sparse and inconspicuous because short, thin, and rod-shaped.
 6) 12-14 meridional ciliary rows shortened posteriorly by about 30 %.Invariably one caudal cilium of body length. 
 7) Oral opening at anterior end of cell, oral basket inconspicuous in vivo. Undulating membrane circular, consists of short, paired cilia forming digitate processes (oral flaps) around oral opening; details of oral ciliature not yet known and not necessary for identification.
 8) Movement conspicuous, that is, periods of very fast spinning interrupted by wide jumps at irregular intervals.

In spite of its small size, easy to recognize as Urotricha because of the spinning and jumping movement (note that small Cyclidium species show a similar behaviour) and the single caudal cilium. It is also easy to identify in silver slides because it is the sole species with a single caudal cilium having <15 somatic ciliary rows; all other small urotrichs, except for U. nais mentioned above, have >20 ciliary rows. In vivo, however, the characteristic body shape must serve as main character because the number of ciliary rows is difficult to recognize. -+ Urotricha furcata is slightly longer (20-30 pm) and invariably has 2 caudal cilia. Urotricha matthesi tristicha, which is rather similar in shape, is distinctly larger (35-45 pm) and has 4 caudal cilia. -+ Balanion planctonicum, which is
similar in size, is bursiform and has very long and thus conspicuous oral flaps. 1,2,6,7 (oral flaps short) are key characters for identification.

1. ldentification and Ecology of Limnetic Plankton Ciliates.  W. Foissner, H. Berger, J. Schaumburg. Informationsberichte des Bayerischen Landesamtes für Wasserwirtschaft-ISSN ot76-4217 Issue 3/99  Munich, November 1999 - ISBN 3-930253-79-8

b286d0c8-e73c-487e-b71f-2ea40d6a2073.description:
Metopus species, cf the unnamed putative variant form of M. rostratus described but not specifically named by Kahl 1932 in his figure of page 406 no.19 (1) which seems identical. The species was harvested by making touch preparations from boiled wheat seeds used to feed a saprobic benthic sample taken from freshwater Town Pond in East Hampton Village. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 and 100 1.25 oil immersion objectives plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. I show five individuals under varying degrees of compression under the coverglass found on two different days in the same sample. 

The cells measure 120 um in length.  The shaped closely matches M. rostratus- more flattened, but more long-oval in outline, widened in the middle.  The most striking feature is the type 1 preoral dome which is extremely narrow and compressed and twisted terminally, overhanging the left margin, tapered into a beak-like structure terminally, occupying about 30% of body length. The perizonal stripe is best seen en face at the beak where we can appreciate the tuft of its cilia.  The macronucleus is quite distinctive taking the form of a long finely granular sausage shape, occasionally curling up due to the cell's contortions and coverglass compression,  but in time returning to its straight quite elongate form. The macronucleus is associated with an adherent spherical micronucleus at its midpoint. There are no caudal cilia or anterior granular cytoplasmic mass.  There are 7 somatic kineties visible on one side so 14-15 in total can be inferred. They are widely set as mentioned by Kahl.  I found what might be possible ectosymbionts in some individuals.  

Kahl's description of M. rostratus: "Metopus rostratus KAHL,1927 (Fig. 18). Size 100 um. Shape more flattened, not left-sided, but more long-oval in outline, widened in the middle. Cervical plate so sharply bent over that an (apparent) beak protrudes far to the left.  Widely streaked, colorless, loosely and rather coarsely ciliate. Marginal zone distinct, forming a whorl on the beak. Membranelles narrow, half as long as the zone. Macronucleus short ellipsoid, not sausage-shaped like the previous species- hyalinus" (1).   

In a separate paragraph of his description of M. rostratus, Kahl's describes an occasionally observed variant which he informally considered to be a variant of M. rostratus with a somewhat larger size and with a long nucleus: " Only once, but in larger numbers, in a collecting jar with decaying material; thus, it appears to be more saprobic. Floats gliding. Similar is the occasionally seen form (Fig. 19), but with a longer nucleus and also larger (160 um), probably a modification of this species; likewise, the one drawn in Fig. 20 is perhaps a modification of hyalinus, from which it differs in its shorter nucleus and more strongly twisted head plate" (1).  I have been unable to find any further descriptions of this putative M. rostratus variant. 

The validity of M. rostratus as a species was questioned by  Esteban et al  who synonymized M. rostratus as well as the similar appearing (though lacking a defined beak) M. hyalinus (Kahl, 1927) Kahl, 1935 with the variable species M. palaeformis Kahl, 1927 (2).   Foissner et al 2003 discuss this and state: "Based on the data available, ESTEBAN et al. (1995) suggest the following synonymy, with which we largely agree: M. hyalinus KAHL, 1927a (Fig. 192j); M. rostratus KAHL, 1927a (Fig. 192l) (3).  However, Foissner 2016 (4) later placed H. palaeformis into the new genus Heterometopus and stated that M. rostratus likely belongs in a different genus (Metopus?):  "(Fig. 4I-  Metopus rostratus from Botswana (Africa). The asterisk denotes the narrow side-stripe. This species, which has a similar size as H. meisterfeldi and H. palaeformis, looks quite different, showing that both very likely belong to different genera" (4).

Very few metopid species possess this pronounced preoral dome terminal beak.  Zhuang et al 2022 described Metopus spiculatus, a marine form with a beak, a long tail-like posterior and endocymbionts (5). They compared it to other species with the preoral beak and include M. rostratus as a valid species in their comparison with the other markedly different beak-bearing metopids:   "Tropidoatractus acuminatus and Tropidoatractus spinosus are medium-sized, and have an oblong body and one acute tail, but all of them lack ectosymbionts, which are considered as an important feature for species identification (Esteban et al.1995; Rotterova et al 2018; Li et al2021a). In addition, M. rostratus Kahl,1932 and Tropidoatractus levanderi Rotterova et al 2018 also possess a beak-like preoral dome end, but both lack a long tail and conspicuous ectosymbionts as shown in our form (Kahl, 1932; Foissner,2016a; Rotterovaetal 2018)" (5). I am uncertain whether my population of this putative M. rostratus variant form has symbionts. 

So then, is M. rostratus still a valid Metopus species? Is this variant with a long nucleus really a variant of M. rostratus or an as yet undescribed separate species?  For now, based on the current literature going all the way back to Kahl, whose depiction of the variant form seems to perfectly match my population, I am calling this Metopus cf rostratus variant Kahl 1927. 

1.  A. Kahl; [Urtiere oder Protozoa I: Wimpertiere oder Ciliata (Infusoria) 3. Spirotricha]. Die Tierwelt Deutschlands und der angrenzenden Meeresteile. Germany:Verlag von Gustav Fischer. (3), 1932 

2.  Genoveva Esteban, Tom Fenchel, and Bland J. Finlay; Diversity of Free-Living Morphospecies in the Ciliate Genus Metopus. Arch.Protistenkd. 146:137-164, 1995

3.  Foissner W., Agatha S. & Berger H. (2002): Soil ciliates (Protozoa, Ciliophora) from Namibia (Southwest Africa), with emphasis on two contrasting environments, the Etosha region and the Namib Desert. – Denisia, 5: 1–1459.

4.   Heterometopus meisterfeldi nov. gen., nov. spec. (Protozoa, Ciliophora), a new metopid from Australia Wilhelm Foissner.  European Journal of Protistology 55 (2016) 118–127. 

5.  New Contribution to the Diversity of the Anaerobic Genus Metopus (Ciliophora, Armophorea),

41240494-caac-4191-9ba8-fcd30787883e.description:
Rhinothrix porculus (Penard, 1922) a curious apertospathid ciliate with a snout-like dorsal elongation of the oral bulge, harvested by the floating coverglass method from a benthic sample taken from freshwater Town Pond in East Hampton Village. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 and 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  The cell measures 110 um in length. Unfortunately, I  encountered the ciliate on a slide thick with debris and matted cyanobacteria preventing optimal imaging.  However, we can clearly see the characteristic palpus oralis leaving no doubt as to the diagnosis. 

Size 80–130 x 25–40mm, usually about 100 30mm in vivo.  Length: width ratio moderately variable, that is, about 2.5–4.5:1 in vivo, usually 3–4:1. Very flexible but not contractile and only slightly flattened laterally, mainly in narrowed posterior half. Shape dominated by the dorsally projecting oral bulge, forming a distinct process (nose or snout), for which we suggest the term palpus oralis; usually more or less narrowly obovate (3–4:1), especially when seen ventrally and dorsally, while narrowly ellipsoidal or oblong in lateral view, becoming cylindroidal (4–5:1) in starved specimens. Macronucleus in or near mid-body, oblong ( 3:1), rarely globular or reniform; chromatin granules in vivo up to 3mm across and distinct. Micronucleus in minute depression of mid macronucleus, conspicuous in vivo because about 6 x 4mmin size, broadly ellipsoidal to almost hemispherical. Contractile vacuole in posterior end, large, forms from several smaller vacuoles; some excretory pores in pole area. Cytopyge in posterior pole area, fecal mass globular and compact, migrates through the contractile vacuole. Cortex very flexible, of ordinary appearance, contains about eight rows of narrowly spaced, minute (c 0.5mm), colorless granules between two kineties.  

Extrusome apparatus highly developed, composed of three types of specifically arranged and located toxicysts; inconspicuous in vivo because individual extrusomes thin and/or short and/or hidden by cytoplasmic inclusions. Type I (body) toxicysts within or slightly left of ciliary rows, about as widely spaced as cilia, extend transversely into body proper, basically rod-shaped with narrowed ends, distinctly curved when attached to cortex and becoming straight when detached, in vivo about 7 x 0.5mm in size, circa 15mm long when exploded. Type II and III toxicysts associated with oral bulge. Type II extrusomes about 50 x 0.5mm in size, rod-shaped and slightly curved, attached to inner margin of anterior loop of circumoral kinety, extend obliquely backwards; in vivo distinct in flattened cells and very conspicuous. Type III oral bulge extrusomes oblong and about 1.5 x 0.3mm in size, arranged in many oblique rows, each consisting of 5–10 toxicysts; extrusome rows in both halves of oral bulge, including palpus oralis, form ladder-like pattern extending to posterior end underneath left branch of circumoral kinety; fairly distinct also in vivo because individual extrusomes rather refractive;  scattered and numerous in cytoplasm, where they are about 2mm long and often flask-shaped. 

Cytoplasm colorless, contains some lipid droplets up to 10mm across and numerous highly refractive inclusions up to 6 4mm in size in anterior, rarely also in posterior half of body. Specimens thus dark under low(</= 100x ) bright field magnification and details of oral apparatus and dorsal brush difficult to analyze. Inclusions globular to ellipsoidal, rarely ring-shaped, the larger ones often with a central cleft, do not dissolve when specimens are squashed but disappear in starving cells. Food vacuoles up to15mm across, in some specimens contain oral baskets of microthoracid ciliates or euglenids, suggesting that the refractive inclusions described above are paramylon grains; one specimen contained a small desmid. Swims slowly to rather rapidly by rotation about main body axis; highly flexible under slight coverslip pressure.

 Oral bulge, except for palpus oralis, inconspicuous invivo when viewed laterally because merely 3–4mm high and clearly recognizable only in anterior quarter of cell; conspicuous when viewed ventrally because sigmoidally curved,extending spirally the whole length of body, and cuneate with width decreasing from 7–10mm anteriorly to about 4mm posteriorly; inflated anterior portion with distinct central cleft dividing bulge in a right half extending to the posterior end and a left half restricted to the anterior third of the body. Palpus oralis conspicuous because 5–12mm long in vivo and distinctly projecting from dorsal anterior end of cell; cylindroidal and slightly contractile,belongs to the oral bulge because studded with type III extrusomes.Circumoral kinety of same
shape as oral bulge, that is, lasso-like and widely open ventrally ( 4mm); right branch extends full body length, left branch restricted to anterior 37% of body on average and not continuing posteriorly as ordinary somatic kinety; composed of dikinetids very narrowly spaced inanterior third,where faintly impregnated nematodesmata originate from the right and left branch of the  circumoral kinety, forming a rather conspicuous oral basket. 


The Apertospathulidae, a New Family of Haptorid Ciliates (Protozoa, Ciliophora).  WILHELM FOISSNER, KUIDONG XU and MARTIN KREUTZ. J. Eukaryot. Microbiol., 52(4), 2005 pp. 360–373.   DOI: 10.1111/j.1550-7408.2005.00049.x

d87b3f9f-189c-4a7f-bf6d-de1ff8d0077c.description:
Atopospira galeata (Kahl, 1927) Bourland & Wendell, 2014 from a benthic sample of the brackish (salinity 3.5 o/oo) estuarine cove Georgica Cove. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 objective and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsing Galaxy S24.  

The cells measure 45 um in length. The body is pyriform with a helmet-shaped apical dome with a prominent brim. This brim margin of the helmet-shaped dome has very long cilia of the perizonal stripe kineties. The adoral zone encirles the body completely and is hard to see other than four of the quite long downward- projecting buccal membranelles.  The macronucleus is spherical to broadly oval, variously located in apical dome or sometimes in the mid-portion of the cell. The spherical micronucleus is variously positioned adjacent to the macronucleus but sometimes distant from it in the cell posterior.  The cytoplasm filled with ingested dark gray sulfur- and pinkish rhodobacteria. There is a large terminal contractile vacuole. The posterior end is truncate with loose long caudal cilia.  I identified some rod-shaped endosymbionts which Bourland and Wendell state can be seen transiently in some populations (1). 

Atopospira galeata was first described in 1927 by Kahl as Metopus galeatus. In 2014 the species was redescribed by Bourland & Wendell who transferred the species to the genus Atopospira (which was erected by Jankowski in 1964) and renamed in Atopospira galeata. Atopospira galeata inhabits sulfidic bottom sediments in lentic habitats. Although found in anoxic/hypoxic habitats, A. galeata exhibits notable aerotolerance since it survives unscathed for up to seven days in open jars. Indeed, my population swam happily under the coverglass for three hours. Bourland and Wendell report that " movement slow, often appears suspended motionless".  My population was often quite animated swimming briskly, but on the second day I found individuals moving slowly and so was able to image them under oil.  The most striking feature of this species is the dark cytoplasm filled with its meals of sulfur and rhodobacteria. I observed one cell in the process of defecation and one fissioning pair. 

 "Size in vivo 46–59 44–54 μm length:total width ratio 1:1, dorsoventrally compressed approximately 2:1. Cells dark under low magnification and violet under higher power due to contents of food vacuoles. Outline broadly pyriform; preoral dome with prominent brim spirals leftward 360° from mid-body to merge with body slightly anteriorly, dome brim overhangs postoral body; postoral half of body obconical, rounded to truncate depending on status of contractile vacuole. Macronucleus broadly ellipsoidal, in preoral dome, chromatin finely granular in vivo. Micronucleus difficult to see in vivo, ellipsoidal, often distant from macronucleus. Contractile vacuole in posterior end. Neither cytopyge nor excretory pore identified. Cortex inconspicuously furrowed, without granules. Extrusomes absent. Cytoplasm colorless, contains scattered shiny approximately 2 μm globules, without crystals. Food vacuoles numerous, up to 15 μm across, invariably contain coccoid purple sulfur bacteria. Anterior accumulation of cytoplasmic granules absent. Endosymbionts usually absent (see occurrence and ecology section below). Movement slow, often appears suspended motionless" (1). 

 "Ordinary somatic cilia about 12 μm long in vivo, 10–15 approximately 20 μm long lank posterior cilia sparsely distributed over posterior end, immotile, never stiffen. Somatic cilia fragile, thus many often missing in fixed specimens. About 16 somatic kineties on average (including dome kineties). Six dome kineties, crowded to right of buccal vertex, spiral leftward onto dome in widely spaced furrows, small glabrous area right dorsal dome since dome kineties shortened anteriorly. Perizonal ciliary stripe on preoral dome brim, approximately same length as adoral zone, composed of five kineties. Perizonal stripe kinety 5 unciliated.  Adoral zone of membranelles parallels dome brim thus nearly equatorial; extends from cytostome to distal end of preoral dome brim. Bipartite, buccal part with five to seven membranelles composed of four long rows of basal bodies with approximately 8 μm long cilia in buccal cavity, five longest membranelles in center of buccal part; distal part of adoral zone on postoral somatic cortex, made up of about 19 (range 17–24) membranelles having four rows of only two basal bodies each, slightly oblique to long axis, only distal basal body of right row ciliated. Paroral membrane diplostichomonad (i.e. composed of parallel files of ciliated, nonzigzagging monokinetids); files separated by approximately 0.6 μm-wide cortical strip, inner file sometimes slightly longer, files extend from distal portion of buccal cavity on undersurface of preoral dome, curve toward cytostome under buccal lip proximally, usually one or both files with a few unciliated basal bodies distally; about 5 μm long cilia" (1).
