95fcaf14-d793-4bf0-9b5c-6c0958dee7ea.description:
Monodinium balbiani FABRE-DOMERGUE, 1888 from a benthic sample taken from freshwater Lily Pond in the village of East Hampton. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 objective and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  The cell measures 50 um in length. 

Description from Foissner et al 1995 (1) 
1) Size in vivo 50-120 x 30-80 μm, usually 50-80 μm long.
2) Shape slender to broadly cup-shaped, anterior end with a conical mouth bulge (nose, beak).
3) Macronucleus kidney- to horseshoe-shaped in the middle of the body. A spherical micronucleus.
4) Contractile vacuole in the posterior end.
5) Many 5-10 μm long toxicysts are found in the mouth cone and plasma, and countless granular mucocysts are found in the cortex.
6) 54-80 (according to SONG WEIBO & WILBERT about 100) longitudinal rows of basal bodies, which are ciliated only at the anterior end and therefore form a conspicuous ciliated belt (pectinella, cilia).  Behind the ciliated belt, usually five rows of dorsal brushes; only visible in interference contrast or after silver impregnation, not necessary for identification).
7) Oral bulge formed as a conical peg at the anterior end, can expand considerably during feeding. Circumoral row of cilia at the anterior end of the ciliated belt, only visible in the electron microscope.
8) Usually swims back and forth extremely quickly

"There are several varieties and several similar species that still require confirmation: M. perrieri DELPHY, 1925 (50-60 um, ciliated girdle in a groove about 5 um deep, macronucleus ellipsoid), M. vorax FAURE-FREMIET, 1945 (presumably a younger synonym), Didinium armatum PENARD, 1922 (with distinct extrusome rim), D. alveolatum KAHL, 1930 (hemispherical, transversely arranged extrusomes in small vesicles beneath the pellicle). Occasionally associated with Didinium nasutum (B. GULATI 1925), which, however, always has two ciliated girdles visible, during division M. balbianii also has two ciliated girdles and is significantly larger (usually 120-150 μm long). Due to its very rapid movement, it may be confused by the untrained with Peritrich swarmers (no appendage, usually strongly contractile) and larger -+ Oligotrichs(Strombidium, Strobilidium), apical ring of membranelles much more distinct). Characters 2 and 6 are particularly important for identification" (1).

 1.  Foissner W., Berger H., Blatterer H. & Kohmann F. (1995): Taxonomische und ökologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobiensystems – Band IV: Gymnostomatea, Loxodes, Suctoria. – Informationsberichte des Bayer. Landesamtes für Wasserwirtschaft, 1: pp 235-42.

*Cyclidium* cf. *glaucoma* Müller, 1773

Diagnosis of the organism observed:
•	Body ovoid, sometime barrel- or spindle-shaped.
•	Distinct frontal plate.
•	Length, μm 19-25
•	Width, μm 11-15
•	Oral apparatus half body length.
•	L-shaped undulating membrane.
•	Somatic cilia are paired in anterior half.
•	One spherical macronucleus in anterior third.
•	Contractile vacuole terminal.
•	Caudal cilium, bent at distal end.
•	Movement jumping and sliding; During the often long breaks the cilia are spread apart undulating membrane is set up like a sail and food is swirled in.

211bd745-93ac-4a26-8ff9-3bb24baa924a.description:
Urostomides bacillatus (Levander, 1894) comb. nov. (original combination Metopus bacillatus Levander, 1894) from a benthic sample of the brackish (salinity 3.5 o/oo) estuarine cove Georgica Cove. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 objective and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsing Galaxy S24.  The cells measure 80-100 um in length.  This size range (up to 100 um) along with the absence of an elongated tail-like posterior end serve to distinguish this species from its close congener U. striatus which also has a refractive fringe of extrusomes but measures 80-90 um and the posterior end tapers into an elongated tail. This is my first observation of a Urostomides species in a brackish biotope. 

"Foissner (2016) established the family Apometopidae to include Apometopus (a junior synonym of Urostomides) and Cirranter Jankowski, 1964. These two genera differ from all other metopid genera in having a four-rowed perizonal ciliary stripe, the only currently recognizable morphologic synapomorphy for the family. The members of Urostomides show remarkable morphologic diversity. The genus has a broad geographic distribution, occurring on six continents. Urostomides species form a strongly supported clade in phylogenetic analyses" (1).
. 
"Size in vivo 84–98 × 50–64 m.  Shape obpyriform, variable dorsoventral flattening from minimal to 1.4:1. Length:width ratio including preoral dome. Preoral dome broadly rounded, right margin convex, left anterior margin projects beyond left margin, dome occupies about two-thirds of body length, dome brim broad, glabrous, overhangs entire adoral zone. Body posterior to preoral dome obconical, more or less triangular in cross-section, posterior end rounded to obliquely truncate, not tail-like, right margin slightly concave, left margin slightly convex. Macronucleus 15–27 m in length, globular to reniform, located in anterior half of body, chromatin finely granular, many nucleoli of 1.5–3.0 m in diameter. Micronucleus ellipsoidal, relatively large, about 6 m long in vivo. Contractile vacuole subterminal, excretory pore not observed, may empty via cytopyge. Cytopyge subterminal, on ventral surface. Extrusomes narrowly ellipsoidal to oblong, 2–3 m long, colorless in vivo but form distinct refractive peripheral fringe in vivo, ejection with mucus coat formation not observed. Cortex slightly flexible, kinetal furrows conspicuous in dome, very shallow in posterior body, cortical granules absent. Cytoplasm colorless, contains scattered refractive 2 m diameter globules, anterior granule aggregate absent. Food vacuoles up to 20 m diameter. Swims at moderate pace, rotates on long axis. Twenty-three somatic kineties on average (range 21–25); about 15 kineties converge at posterior body end, posteriormost dikinetids usually bear about 12 elongated caudal cilia, invariably eight widely-spaced dome kineties, none obviously specialized" (1). 

1.  Morphologic and molecular characterization of seven species of the remarkably diverse and widely distributed metopid genus Urostomides Jankowski, 1964 (Armophorea, Ciliophora). William Bourland, Johana Rotterová, Ivan Čepička. European Journal of Protistology 61 (2017) 194–232

49dbc133-74aa-4744-b6ec-71cefc94cf35.description:
Sonderiella scandens (Kahl, 1926) from the benthos of a small salt marsh tidal pool at the edge of marine estuary Acabonac Harbor at Landing Lane. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2 using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. The cells measure 28 um. The anterior vestibule with sickle-shaped buccal lip, the contractile vacuole at the mid right side, the posterior round macronucleus, large rod-shaped subpellicular extrusomes and ventral kineties are diagnostic. 

From Carey 1992 Interstitial Marine Cilates An Illustrated Guide: Genus Sonderiella Kahl, 1928 Detritus-dwelling ciliates, ellipsoidal in shape with the ventral region flattened. The dorsal side is domed. An oval vestibulum lies in the anterioventral region. There is no caudal tuft of cilia and no gelatinous investment. No transversely striated ribbon has been observed.

Sonderiella scandens (Kahl, 1926) Kahl, 1928 syn Saprophilus scandens Kahl, 1926 Small, ovoid to ellipsoidal in shape, 15-20 um in length. The ventral side is flattened with longitudinal kineties, the dorsal surface is domed. The vestibule is oval in the anterioventral region. There is a single macronucleus and single contractile vacuole. Large extrusomes (trichocysts sic.) lie beneath the pellicle.

From Kahl 1931: Sonderiella (Saprophilus) scandens (KAHL, 1926) . size 20-25 um· in shape it is very reminiscent of the previous three (small) Sonderia species (S. mira, vestita, cyclostoma) , the sickle-shaped lip protrudes strongly over the anterior side and forms a membranoid lip with a chimney-like projection adjoining it in which the cilia that are probably present were not recognized. The 0Idsloe specimens showed long (trichocysts sic) extrusomes which have not been observed in the freshwater sapropel. The CV lies strikingly on the first third on the right side. Cilia are long and sparse, only ventral side ciliated. Movement clumsy, climbing or jerking on detritus. The last observed Oldesloer specimen showed a clear jelly cover, that might otherwise have been overlooked. The freshwater forms are mostly shorter oval and seem ventrally. to be more tightly striped; Maybe it is an independent form. Very isolated in the sapropel of the sweet and salt water; difficult to observe.

713d96f7-63c1-404c-97a1-325cdc93697b.description:
Disematostoma  minor Kahl, 1931 from a benthic sample taken from freshwater Lily Pond in the village of East Hampton. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 objective and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. The cells vary in shape from pyriform with a tapered posterior to more ovoid and measure mostly from 60-70 and occasionally 75-80 um in length. 

"This species was originally described as D. buetschlii var. minor by Kahl (1926), and subsequently identified as a separate species, D. minor by Kahl (1931). Michiels & Wilbert (1973) redescribed it and updated the information on general morphology and details of the oral apparatus" (1). The appearance of the Lily Pond population is essentially identical to Disematostoma buetschlii Lauterborn, 1894 except for the much smaller size. D. buetschlii measures 110–200 µm (2,3). For D. minor, various populations are similar and "have relatively smaller body size in vivo (<100 um in length) compared to other Disematostoma species, though they differ slightly from each other (85 to 90 x 65 to 70 um in the population of Xu et al 2017 (1), 50 to 60 x 31 to 37 um in Kahl 1931 population and 78 x 57um  in Michiels & Wilbert 1973  population)" (1). 

It is interesting that none of these reported D. minor populations describe algal symbionts that are known to be present in D. buetschlii (2,3). The Lily Pond population has varying numbers of algal forms in the cytoplasm in clumps that differ in appearance from the single cell algal symbionts depicted by Kreutz (2).  Indeed, Foissner states that D. buetschlii can be differentiated from D. minor by this feature: "Disematostoma minor KAHL, 1926 (65-80 um, Fig. 15) and D. bengalensis NAIR, 1971 can be distinguished from D. buetschlii by the lack of zoochlorella" (3). So the presence of algal forms in the cytoplasm of my population is puzzling- perhaps they are not symbionts. I did observe cells with few or no algal elements in the cytoplasm. 

The body is obovoidal or pyriform with ventral surface flat and dorsal surface curved. The oral aperture is roughlly one third down from anterior end. I visualized the preoral suture with difficulty since the cells swim fast while rotating around the caudal end and never stand still. The postoral suture was even harder to image.  The dorsal polar band could be seen with compressed cells at 1000x oil immersion which also be seen at 400x on occasion.  It runs on the dorsal surface beginning at the posterior pole and terminates at the level of the contractile vacuole pore.  The dorsal polar band is associated with long cilia while the surrounding area is devoid of cilia. The contractile vacuole is subequatorial and at 1000x in compressed cells I could visualize the 7 collecting canals which tended to dilate greatly with increasing coverglass pressure as well as the dorsal excretion pore. The macronucleus is sausage-shaped with blunt rounded ends and is often curved. It had a variable position sometimes lying in a transverse or in other cells in longitudinal orientation.  I did not visualize micronuclei. There is a fringe of distinct extrusomes (about 10 µm) beneath pellicle. The cytoplasm contains varying numbers of clumped algal cells.  I observed division by transverse fission but no conjugation. 

Among penniculids, Disematoastoma was previously thought to belong to the Frontoniidae. However, Xu et al 2017 reassigned the genus to the Stokesiidae: " The family Stokesiidae Roque, 1961, was expanded to include the genera Disematostoma and Marituja in addition to its type genus Stokesia, since the three genera formed a well-supported clade in the phylogenetic analyses. The diagnosis of Stokesiidae was improved to include the newly recognized synapomorphies, i.e., barren kinetosomes on the dorsal side, a ciliated dorsal suture, and the somatic ciliature that can be recognized as transversely oriented circles" (1). 

1.  Reconsideration of the systematics of Peniculida (Protista, Ciliophora) based on SSU rRNA gene sequences and new morphological features of Marituja and Disematostoma Yuan Xu . Feng Gao . Xinpeng Fan.  Hydrobiologia  DOI 10.1007/s10750-017-3371-4

2.  https://realmicrolife.com/disematostoma-buetschlii/

3.  Foissner W., Berger H. & Kohmann F. (1994): Taxonomische und ökologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobiensystems – Band III: Hymenostomata, Prostomatida, Nassulida. – Informationsberichte des Bayer. Landesamtes für Wasserwirtschaft, 1/94: pp 178-84.

e93e96cd-909b-40ad-b17e-a87aa027736a.description:
Trachelius ovum EHRENBERG, 1831 EHRENBERG, 1838 from the benthos of freshwater Tuthill Pond which is situated only 100 feet from the marine Fort Pond Bay in Montauk New York. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using Splan 40 0.70 and SPlan 100 1.25 oil  objectives plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. The cells measure 280 um in length.  

The macronucleus consists of two closely set nodules, in some cells roughly identical ovals and in others asymmetrical or unequal ovoid to somewhat irregular nodules consistent with the dumbbell shape described for this species.  Currently, Trachelius is officially a monotypic genus though a putative second species, Trachelius subtilis PENARD, 1922, a species which Vďačný & Foissner (2) synonymized with T. ovum, is stated to have two oval macronuclear nodules with an intervening micronucleus. I was able to visualize a micronucleus between the two nodules in some cells and the uneven irregular shape of the two closely set macronuclear nodules in the Tuthill Pond population is more in keeping with the dumbbell shape though I could not demonstrate a connection.  Dr. Martin Kreutz (3) has a well illustrated observation of T. subtilis but this is not an official taxonomic event.  

From Foissner et al (1): 
Size in vivo 200-600 x 75-350 um, usually 250-350 um long.
Shape sac-shaped to almost spherical, starving specimens clearly flattened on one side. Proboscis often only about 1/4-, rarely up to 1/2-length, usually curved dorsally. In well fed specimens it becomes a short, stalk-shaped extension. Ventro-laterally a small, difficult to recognize pit that serves as a suction cup.
Macronucleus dumbbell-shaped, often disintegrates into a few spherical parts in postconjugates. Several micronuclei.
Many small contractile vacuoles scattered throughout the cell. Plasma very strongly vacuolated, the strands form a coarse network.
Short, rod-shaped extrusomes in the proboscis along the ridge of the mouth. Cortex thick, with many ellipsoid granules.
About 80-120 longitudinal rows of cilia, some of which extend into the ventro-lateral fossa, where there are several specializations, which are explained in the figure legends. Brush 3-4 rows, on the dorsal side of the trunk, a row extending almost to the end of the body; only clearly visible after silver impregnation and in the scanning electron microscope.
Mouth entrance at the base of the proboscis, surrounded by many very delicate bars that form a club-shaped, thick-walled funnel. To the right of the circumoral row of eyelashes there is a longitudinal row of cilia, on the left there are many short oblique rows of perioral cilia; more precise structure of the oral cilia can only be recognized after silver impregnation.

1.  FOISSNER W., BERGER H., BLATTERER H. & KOHMANN F. (1995): Taxonomische und ökologische Revision der Ciliaten des Saprobiensystems – Band IV: Gymnostomatea, Loxodes, Suctoria. – Informationsberichte des Bayer. Landesamtes für Wasserwirtschaft, 1: pp. 208-18

2. VĎAČNÝ P. & FOISSNER W. (2012): Monograph of the dileptids (Protista, Ciliophora, Rhynchostomatia). – Denisia, 31: 1–529.

3. https://realmicrolife.com/trachelius-subtilis/

Trachelocerca conifera Kahl 1930 harvested by the floating coverglass method from a sample of the benthos of a small salt marsh tidal pool at the edge of estuary Acabonac Harbor.  Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  This species was fairly abundant on the slides along with the closely related (by Kahl) vermiform psammophile species Paraspathidium fusca (syn Trachelocerca fusca) and Pseudotrachelocerca trepida (syn Trachelocerca trepida).  In fact, at first I thought this species were forms of P. trepida until I noticed the quite unusual strongly backswept cilia of the oral cone. It was then that I searched in Kahl and found his illustration of T. conifera  which is identical to the tidal pool population. However, this population is smaller than Kahl's reported 140 um extended and 90 um contracted. While I did notice slight contractility, my population measured only 70 um in length.  Here is a link to a full length video:  https://youtu.be/MRAIWc7Ahts

Kahl's description described perfectly (except for size)  the tidal pool population:  "Trachelocerca conifera spec. n.  Size 140 um, contracted 90 um.  Not noticeably flattened. Neck tapered to 1/3-1/4 of the body width, the anterior cone (7 x 3 um) very densely, the rest of the body very loosely ciliated; a fine central fibril between each row of filaments. The strong, saber-shaped, curved cilia of the special row are only found on the cone, extending slightly forward to one side of the oral margin; the mouth is somewhat cleft after this row; the anterior margin appears beveled here.  Nucleus circular to slightly oval (with large micronucleus), ciliary rows (10-12) very wide. Neck with a conical, non-contractile extension at the anterior end. Special ciliary row of the neck consisting of strikingly strong, backward-curved cilia" (1).  

"Only during printing did I succeed in observing these two outwardly quite similar species in unmixed populations, whereas I had confused them in 1927.  Hence my erroneous perception of the great variability of the species trepida. I have often seen a third, somewhat larger Oldesloe species with strong trichocysts but have never been able to observe it carefully enough" (1).

So, by his own admission, Kahl confused Pseudo)trachelocerca trepida, which has a distinctly un-karyorelectid type of nuclear apparatus being of a compact curved long sausage shape, and my current observation Trachelocerca conifera, which also has a compact nuclear apparatus again distinctly different to the nuclear groups of karyrelectids.  I had initially confused them as well since both species were abundant on the same slides.  Interestingly, Foissner 1991 (2) in his paper transferring yet another so-called trachelocercid species- Trachelocerca entzi Kahl, 1921 to the gymnostomatids, mentions that Trachelocerca conifera is likely misplaced in the tracheloceridae and coincidently mentions it with T. conifera's  two companions in my sample : "The present paper describes in detail the morphology and infraciliature of T. entzi and shows that it does not belong to the karyorelictid trachelocercids but to an entirely different group, the gymnostomatid helicoprorodontids. The same previously happened to Trachelocerca fusca Kahl, 1928, which became type of the (gymnostomatid or trichostomatid) genus Paraspathidium Noland, 1937, and Trachelocerca trepida Kahl, 1928, which became type of another gymnostomatid genus, Pseudotrachelocerca Song, 1990. Very likely, several other trachelocercids are also misplaced, e.g. Trachelocerca conifera Kahl, 1930 and T. minor Gruber, 1888" (2). 


1.  Kahl A. (1930) Urtiere oder Protozoa I: Wimpertiere oder Ciliata (Infusoria) 1. Allgemeiner Teil und Prostomata. Tierwelt Dtl. 18: p. 121. 

2. Updating the Trachelocercids (Ciliophora, Karyorelictea). IV. Transfer  of Trachelocerca entzi Kahl, 1927 to the Gymnostomatea as a New Genus,  Trachelotractus gen. n. (Helicoprorodontidae). Wilhelm FOISSNER.  Acta Protozoologica (1991) 36: 63 - 74

9c18d50d-6599-4251-812c-5f73224fd156.description:
Cohnilembus verminus (O. F. Müller, 1786)  from a nearly two month old putrifying sample of the benthos of a channel connecting Fresh Pond to Napeague Bay, salinity 24o/oo. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  As mentioned by Song (2000), C. verminus shows great variation in size and this is reflected in my sample with individuals ranging from 30 um up to 75 um. 

Genus Cohnilembus Kahl, 1931; Cohnilembus verminus (O. F. Müller, 1786) Syn. Lembus punctatus Kahl, 1928; Lembus reesi Kahl, 1931.

"Description. Size highly variable, in vivo 40-130 x 6-20 µm, depending evidently on population rather than nutrition state: in one population mostly more than 100 µm in length, while in others seldom over 80 µm. Length: width in slender population about 7-10:1, in thick populations ca 5-6:1. Outline basically very slender, spindle-shaped or fusiform with anterior portion considerably narrowed and tapering, both ends pointed. Cross section circular, yet in starved (?) specimens much flattened (likely bilaterally) so that the cells sometimes make a fold-up or twisted appearance. Buccal field narrow, about 2/5 to over 1/2 of body length. Pellicle smooth. Extrusomes spindle-like, about 1 µm long, sparsely arranged beneath pellicle, which are recognized from life only at high magnification" (1).

"Cytoplasm colorless and hyaline, always containing several to many large (2-4 µm across), shining greenish granules. Food vacuoles large and few in number, containing possibly bacterial. Contractile vacuole small, located caudally or slightly subcaudally near ventral margin of cell with frequent pulsation (about several seconds intervals). Macronucleus large, elongate to oval in shape, centrally located with many to numerous nucleoli, which are often irregular-shaped after protargol impregnation. Single micronucleus close to macronucleus" (1).

"Cilia more or less sparsely arranged, 7 to 10 µm in length, single caudal cilium about 15 µm long. Cilia of membrane/ membranelles about 12-15 µm in length. Movement not very active, swimming snake-like or slightly zig-zag, moderately fast; in culture usually motionless for a long time or gathered together on sediment (food) as shown in Fig. 4 B. When disturbed, swimming for a short distance and then motionless again" (1).

"Somatic kineties longitudinal, extending over entire length of body. Unlike in most other scuticociliates, among these “mixed” kineties each composed of often only a few to several dikinetids at anterior end, while in most portion with monokinetids. Along buccal field, kinety left of oral area (SKn) membranelle-like, consisting of densely arranged paired basal bodies, adjacent to membranelle" (1).

"Buccal apparatus highly specialized. Membranelle 1 (M1) occupying about 4/5 of buccal length, one-rowed in most portion; its posterior portion splitting into 3 groups, each with 3 basal bodies. Most part of M1 adjacent to densely-ciliated kinety n (SKn), both of which form together the prominent “undulating membranes”. Membranelle 2 and 3 close to M1, relatively small and each with about 5-8 basal bodies. Paroral membrane (PM) on right of shallow buccal cavity, short and gently curved, extending anteriorly to about level of M2; its anterior half one-rowed, posterior with zig-zag structure. Scutica (Sc) Y-shaped, consisting of about 3 pairs of basal bodies" (1).

"As revealed in previous work, this species appear very much size- and shape-variable and may exhibit rather different appearances in vivo, but after impregnation, all share the same patterns of the silverline system and infraciliature (Kahl 1931; Borror 1963; Thompson 1964, 1968; Jones 1974; Foissner 1976; Foissner et al. 1982; Ströder 1991, master thesis; Hu et al. 1996). Based on the body shape and the general appearance from life, two marine slender Lembus-species described by Kahl, L. punctatus Kahl, 1928 and L. reesi Kahl, 1931 should be compared. The former has a narrowed posterior end (similar to the thicker form of the Qingdao population) with relatively shorter buccal field. Considering the fact that the body shape of Cohnilembus verminus is highly population-dependent, it is reasonable to come to the conclusion that Kahl’s L. punctatus represents only a form-variation and should be thus conspecific with the former. Lembus reesi is characterized by the distinctly smaller cell size (ca 30 µm long) as described originally (Kahl 1931). However, the minimum size of some starving cells of the Qingdao-population could be-during culture-only 30-40 µm long, therefore, Lembus reesi should be possibly synonymized with Cohnilembus verminus" (1).

1.  Morphological and Taxonomical Studies on Some Marine Scuticociliates from China Sea, with Description of Two New Species, Philasterides armatalis sp. n. and Cyclidium varibonneti sp. n. (Protozoa: Ciliophora: Scuticociliatida) Weibo SONG. Acta Protozool. (2000) 39: 295 - 322

57466bee-38b4-4d33-9c90-2dd16b9a4468.description:
Mesodinium cinctum, Calkins 1902  harvested by floating coverglass method from a benthic sample taken from a small salt marsh tidal pool at the edge of estuary Acabonac Harbor. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  The cells measure 32-35 um in length.  The size, the large number of anterior directed cirri and the anterior oral portion being flexible sometimes slightly invaginated other times evaginated with one or two capitate tentacles visible barely protruding over the edge are characteristic.  

From Calkins 1901:  "Body spherical to pyriform, constricted near the middle, the constriction dividing the body into dissimilar parts. The anterior part is broadly pyriform, somewhat plastic and hyaline, with an oral extremity which is sometimes hollow, sometimes evaginated and convex. Upon this flexible anterior part there are four short but distensible tentacles. The posterior part is granular and usually filled with food particles; it is well rounded and holds the nucleus and contractile vacuole. The entire body is surrounded by a fine cuticle. The nucleus is elongate and extends through the greater part of the posterior half. The contractile vacuole Iies on one side, near the girdle. The mouth is on the anterior pole in the tentacle region. The motile organs are cirri and cilia, all inserted in the constriction. There are two sets of cirri and one of cilia; the latter stand out radially from the girdle and are usually in motion. The cirri of one set, the anterior, extend forward about twice the length of the anterior half; those of the posterior set closely englrdle the lower half, reaching not quite to the posterior  extremity. These are somewhat hyaline and are closely approximated, giving the impression of a tight-fitting crenulate casing about the lower half. The cirri are sharply pointed, much broader at the base, and the two sets are so placed that, looked at from above, they have the appearance of a twisted cord. Movement erratic; sometimes the animal swims steadily forward with mouth in front; again it shoots across the field of the microscope, either backward or forward or sideways, through the action of its powerful cirri. It is often quiet, usually mouth downward, and is held in place by adhesion of the tentacles. Length 35 um; greatest width 30 um. Not uncommon" (1).

"The chief features by which this species is distinguished from the frequently described M. pulex of Europe are the number of anterior cirri and the ring of true cilia in place of the central girdle of cirri. The European form is described with four anterior bristles; the present form has from 28 to 32. The radial cilia differ decidedly from the more powerful cirri and they are not in one plane, so that counting is difficult; they are not closely set.  (1).

From Carey 1992 (2): "Mesodinium cinctum Calkins, 1902 Body anteriorly conical but with the cytostome invaginated. Anterior globose. Organism 35 µm in length. Nematodesmata are projected clear of the body. The macronucleus is large and ovoid. Two bands of cilia emerge from the anterior groove together with some cilia which emerge radially" (2). 


1.  MARINE PROTOZOA FROM WOODS HOLE. BY GARY N. CALKINS  Contributions from the Biological Laboratory of the U. S. Fish Commission, Woods Hole, Massachusetts.  Bulletin of the United States Fish Commission 21:415-468, 1901

2. MARINE INTERSTITIAL CILIATES AN ILLUSTRATED KEY PHILIP G. CAREY. Chapman and Hall 1992 London. pp64, 234.

715bc86a-bbdc-4435-bc5a-404767ca9dc1.description:
Stephanopogon apogon Borror 1965  harvested by the floating coverglass method from a benthic sample taken from a small salt marsh tidal pool at the edge of estuary Acabonac Harbor. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24.  The cells measure 20-40 um in length. The cells rarely swim in a rotational; manner but usually crawl on the substrate sometimes struggling with their anterior unciliated Iips or ridge to dislodge a meal. I observed ingestion of a meal and defecation. 

Here is a link to a full length viideo of a perfectly a Stephanopogon cell perfectly  compressed  under the coverglass. https://youtu.be/ofP9C2kEgRI

The enigmatic marine protozoan Stephanopogon was first classified with ciliate protozoa because its pellicle also has rows of cilia. As ciliates have nuclear dimorphism with separate germline and somatic nuclei, Stephanopogon with several identical nuclei was regarded as a model for a hypothetical homokaryotic ancestor of ciliates. When electron microscopy revealed radical differences from ciliates (2) this idea was abandoned" (3).  Stephanopogon closely resembles certain ciliates and was originally classified with them but is now considered related to heterolobosean flagellates (2,3). The cell is somewhat flattened, with multiple smooth flagella arranged in rows running from the front to the back, and has an anterior mouth supported by rods. They feed on bacteria, diatoms, and other smaller organisms. There are 2-16 nuclei depending on the species and cell size, but they are not differentiated into macronuclei and micronuclei as occurs in ciliates. They have a cosmopolitan distribution.

"The average size of the trophic cells was about 40 um but cells with lengths from 20 to 70 um were encountered, the variation apparently reflecting the recent feeding history of the individuals. The organism has an anterior mouth which is situated at the end of a flattened prominence (neck). Behind the neck the body is sac-like, slightly twisted or humped. The ventral surface is defined as that applied to the substrate. The number of rows of flagella depends on the size of the cell, and the following details refer to most but not all, cells. Seven rows of flagella extend from mouth on the ventral face of the cell. Six run parallel to the left ventral margin, the one closest to the left margin being longest. One long ventral row follows the right margin. The dorsal surface supports only five short rows of flagella. The dorsal
rows lie in grooves, and between and to the right of them run 10 to 15 rows of refractile granules.  The mouth lies at the anterior end of the cell, and is bordered by hyaline, non-ciliated lips. A flat channel runs into the body from between the lips.  There are two similar nuclei in most cells, but larger cells may have as many as 10 nuclei. The nuclei typically contain a central nucleolus" (1). 

"Individuals swim in tight spirals if disturbed but will normally settle on a surface and glide across it. They may sometimes attach to the substrate by their posterior ends and slowly rotate. They have catholic feeding preferences, consuming bacteria, diatoms, flagellates, yeast cells, and organic detritus. Flagella bend stiffly at their base, and not with a sine wave or helical pattern. They appear to be widely spaced in living cells and the behavior of crawling cells is very reminiscent of small hypostome Ciliophora.  The flagella create a thrust parallel to the cell surface and we regard them from a behavioral point of view as cilia" (1). 


 1. The Ultrastructural Identity of Stephanopogon apogon and the Relatedness of the Genus to Other Kinds of Protists.  David J. Patterson
 and Guy Brugerolle. Europ.J.Protistol. 23, 279-290 (1988)
 
2. Stephanopogon, a Phylogenetically Important ``Ciliate,'' Shown by Ultrastructural Studies to be a Flagellate.  Diana L. Lipscomb and John O. Corliss.  Science, New Series, Vol. 215, No. 4530 (Jan. 15, 1982), pp. 303-304

3.   The Zooflagellates Stephanopogon and Percolomonas are a Clade (Class Percolatea: Phylum Percolozoa. THOMAS CAVALIER-SMITH and SERGEY NIKOLAEV.   J. Eukaryot. Microbiol., 55(6), 2008 pp. 501–509

fb05cfd8-2179-421f-bd38-499bb21c2f4a.description:
Chlamydodon wilberti   QU, LI, LIN, STOECK, PAN, AL-RASHEID and SONG 2018, a marine psammophilic cyrtophorid ciliate, harvested both by floating coverglass method and aspiration from sand layer of a benthic sample taken from a small salt marsh tidal pool at the edge of Acabonac Harbor. I show both well fed  cells swimming in the substrate at 400x  to show the 3 dimensional structure and compressed cell  crawling on the coverglass at 1000x  to show ciliature and details. The major characters for species identifiction in the genus Chlamydodon are cell size and shape, cross-striated band, number of somatic kineties, and number of nematodesmal rods in the cyrtos. The morphometric data given by Qu et al 2018:   C. wilberti   Cross-striated band complete Cell size 65–105 um   somatic kineties  38–49,  right kineties 19–25,  left kineties15–20,  postoral kineties 4–5,   nematodesmal rods 10–13    contractile vacuoles  5–11. 


 This species has a complete cross-striated band with no interruption.  All morphometric parameters (n=4) are those of C. wilberti: size 100 um, somatic kineties 44-46, left kineties 17-18, right kineties 21-22, postoral kineties 4, nematodesmal cyrtos rods 13, contractile vacuoles 9-14 randomly distributed.  There are miltiple contractile vacuole excretory pores.  The macronucleus is ovoid and heteromeric. This population is different only in the nature of the pigment spot. The left anterior pigment spot was described by Qu et al as "One small reddish pigment spot positioned at anterior left of cell". However, in the tidal pool population the pigment spot is yellow and is usually obvious and discrete but is sometimes diffuse and widespread over the left anterior quadrant of some cells. This might be due to coverglass compression since I observed cells with the discrete pigment spot which after some time under the ever- more compressive coverglass had a more diffuse and spread out yellow pigmentation. There are two circumoral kineties and a single preoral kinety to the left anterior of the circumoral kineties. 

I reviewed a number of papers and compared differential diagnostic morphometry which confirms the diagnosis. The major part of my investigation was the discussion of  Qu et al 2018 who also compared their new species with congeners: "The new species is very similar to Chlamydodon mnemosyne in body shape and cell size. Nonetheless, the present species can be distinguished from the latter by having more somatic kineties (38–49, 43.0 on average vs. 25-40), especially the right kineties (19–25 vs. 11–18) (Gong et al., 2005; Kurth & Bardele, 2001). Chlamydodon roseus comprises more somatic kineties (54–58 vs. 38–49) and fewer nematodesmal rods (8–9 vs. 10–13), and thus can be separated from the new species (Dragesco, 1966). Chlamydodon minutus differs from C. wilberti sp. nov. in having a smaller cell size (40–50 mm vs. 65–105 mm), fewer somatic kineties (30–32 vs. 38–49), and more nematodesmal rods (16–18 vs. 10–13) (Dragesco, 1965). Chlamydodon paramnemosyne and C. similis also have fewer somatic kineties (16–18 and 22–28, respectively vs. 38–49) (Pan et al., 2013; Quetal.,2018)" (1).

 "Both Chlamydodon obliquus and C. exocellatus are much larger (120–180 mm and 150–230 mm, respectively vs. 65–105 mminC. wilberti sp. nov.), and have much more somatic kineties (66–72 and 83–97, respectively vs. 38–49) than C. wilberti sp. nov. (Gong et al., 2005; Kahl, 1931; Ozaki & Yagiu, 1941; Snoeyenbos-West et al., 2004). The new species can be separated from C. rectus since it has fewer nematodesmal rods (10–13 vs. 16–22) and comparatively more somatic kineties (38–49 vs. 3138) (Ozaki & Yagiu, 1941; Pan et al., 2017). Chlamydodon caudatus has a similar number of somatic kineties as the new species (34–40 vs. 38–49), but it can be distinguished from the latter by obviously caudal posterior (vs. rounded) (Pan et al., 2013)" (1). 


 
 1.  Diversity of the cyrtophorid genus Chlamydodon (Protista, Ciliophora): its systematics and geographic distribution, with taxonomic descriptions of three species.  ZHISHUAI QU, LIFANG LI, XIAOFENG LIN, THORSTEN STOECK, HONGBO PAN,  KHALEDA.S.AL- RASHEID  & WEIBO SONG.  Systematics and Biodiversity (2018), 1–15

49d3553a-2e4a-46c9-b841-f60a3b46469f.description:
An unusual metopid with many morphologic features suggestive of the slender morphotype of Palmarella salina (Gajewskaia, 1925) from the benthos of small salt marsh tidal pool at the edge of Acabonac Harbor.  It was found only in aspirations of the sand at the bottom of the container, not in floating coverglass preparations. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S using SPlan 40 0.70 objective plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. I examined three individuals before they disappeared from the sample. Ivan Cepicka and Ondrej Pomahac confirm this is Palmarella salina-swimming form.  

Size 50 um, dorsoventrally flattened body curved ventrally (convex dorsally concave ventrally), ventral side with a posterior keel, rectangular outline but with variably tapered posterior due to obliquely truncate posterior right and left ends. Small flattened very thin preoral dome with abruptly downturned ventrally recurved very thin preoral dome brim. Coarse yellowish granular accumulation at the base of  preoral dome extending into dome.  Cell surface with dense coat of bacilliform ectobionts. Macronucleus ovoid centrally located, micronucleus identified with difficulty at 400x. AZM entirely on ventral side short and non-spiraling  small and relatively straight, 6 or 7 membranelles visible, cytostome at anterior 1/3 of cell length. Prominent round food vacuole just posterior to proximal end of  oral cavity adjacent to or sometimes deforming macronucleus, several small vacuoles in a row posterior to this large food vacuole at mid body, very small posterior contractile vacuole occasionally seen.  Ciliature sparse. Cilia of perizonal stripe prominent beating with metachronous waves.  Terminal tuft of 2-4 stiff caudal cilia. Swims in moderately fast in straight line while rotating back and forth over 180 degrees, or darts back and forth in all directions. 

This ciliate seems to have many morphologic affinities to a slender morphotype of Palmarella salina- the  (see above description) with the notable exception of the coarse anterior granular aggregate which is absent in Palmarella salina (1) and the ventrally curved body with ventral keel.  Also, this ciliate swam moderately fast and rarely stopped thus was difficult to image whereas Rotterová et al state that  "Palmarella salina tend to swim very slowly, often attaching to detritus by thigmotactic posterior or perizonal stripe cilia while feeding" (1).  "Gajewskaia (1925) stated that Palmarella salina lacked a contractile vacuole but, rather, had multiple noncontractile vacuoles (“vacuolae aquilegiae”), the number of which varied directly with the salinity of the media. Our observations indicate that a single terminal contractile vacuole is present, albeit with a rather long cycle (≥5 min), possibly explaining Gajewskaia’s impression of non-contractility" (1). I too initially thought that there was no contractile vacuole and noted a variable number of vacuoles in mid-body before I noted a small terminal contractile vacuole.  

Jankowski delineated the characteristics of the genus Palmarella (Palmarium): Characterization of the genus: body flattened, with distinct dorsal and ventral surface, unarmoured; buccal cavity wide, anterior, rhomboid or triangular, with relatively short, right, not spiraling AZM; the left-side anterior body torsion is insignificant; the perizonal cilia are located on a peculiar hoop, anteriorly, like in Tropidoatratus" (2).

Kahl's description: "Palmarium salinum GAJEVSKAIA, 1925 Size 30 to 40 μm; slender ovoid, slightly curved to the right anteriorly; narrowly rounded anteriorly, broader posteriorly, with a small projection at the posterior end with a long cilium (40 fL). Cilia long (12 μm), sparse; rows not recognizable. Peristome in the anterior third, one zone on the left; slightly dorsally anteriorly, 7 tufts of body-length membranelles which in my opinion probably correspond to the marginal zone of the Metopus, after which this species is added here.  If, however, they are modified membranelles, the animal would have to be placed close to the genus Condylostoma. On the right peristome margin, there is a narrow, umbrella-like protruding ridge (reminiscent of Condylostoma).The shape, however, is more reminiscent of the small Metopus species (mucicola, Iatus KAHL). The anus is terminal, Macronucleus round, central. The c.v. is absent, but the number of non-contractile v. in the plasma increases with the salinity of the water in which it lives. Polyhaline in 9-30% salt water. Southern Russia" (3). 


 1. Tropidoatractidae fam. nov., a Deep Branching Lineage of Metopida (Armophorea, Ciliophora) Found in Diverse Habitats and Possessing Prokaryotic Symbionts.  Johana Rotterová, William Bourland and Ivan  Čepička.  Protist, Vol. 169, 362–405, July 2018. 

 2.  Jankowski AW (1964b) Morphology and evolution of Ciliophora III. Diagnoses and phylogenesis of 53 sapropelebionts, mainly of the oder Heterotrichida. Arch Protistenkd 107:185–330

3.   Kahl A (1932) Urtiere oder rotozoa I: Wimpertiere oder Ciliata Infusoria) 3. Spirotricha. Tierwelt Dtl 25:399–650

bf4ba928-d9cb-4152-9e45-36feafe973a6.description:
*Arcella spectabilis* is common in the Mer Bleue bog. However, the shells in most populations I've found have been quite large (107-136 μm).  Recently, I encountered a population with smaller shells (similar in size to those originally described by Joseph Leidy, later classified as *A. mitrata* var *spectabilis*).

I collected a bunch of them for measurements and gene sequencing. Some, like this specimen, had encystment plugs over the aperture. The composition of these plugs is interesting. Unlike the shell itself, which is composed of discrete hexagonal building units, the encystment plug is a smooth, continuous sheet of material.

869047ce-1fde-47aa-9859-daf000b46e93.description:
A broken shell gives us a chance to see the internal structure of an *Arcella* shell.  

Members of the family Arcellidae make their shells from secreted vesicles of organic material, which become hexagonal when pressed together. Images 2-4 show cross-sections of the stiff-walled "areoles" that give the shell its strength and durability.

This specimen also has a partial "encystment plug" over the aperture.

Mag.: 400x.

- Water sample collected on 7/18/2025 using a 10µ dip net to enrich for microbes. (Air temp. ~80F) The sample was stored on a windowsill and reexamined on 8/15/2025.

Freshwater cyanobacterium. Spectacular blue/green color. Small, spherical cells; approx. diameter range 3-5µ (images 1,2). This relatively large colony (longest dimesion,130µ) of tightly packed cells appears hollow. The 3rd image presents a series of photos with the focal plane starting at the surface in panel 1, then slicing down through the colony in panels 2-6. Panels 5-6 predominantly resolve the edge cells, while the interior of the colony appears devoid cells. A smaller colony (perhaps 50µ wide), with similar color, cells and coenobium, was previously observed from a different local waterbody, https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/135865808. There are few references and images available online for *Coelosphaerium aerugineum*. 2 references are cited in the earlier observation noted above. The current specimen is the largest colony I've seen and I'm uncertain that it is consistent with *C. aerugineum*

5a06c7ad-b42e-4b37-bb79-dafc8a41d0b0.description:
Pseudotrachelocerca trepida (Kahl, 1928) Song, 1990 harvested by floating coverglass method from a small salt marsh tidal pool at the edge of estuary Acabonac Harbor. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S under SPlanapo 40 0.95 and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objectives plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. The species was first reported by Kahl 1928 as Trachelocerca trepida (1).  The species was redescribed by Song 1990 who erected the genus Pseudotrachelocerca with P. trepida as the type species by monotypy. 

Various reports differ somewhat in their descriptions of certain characteristics. The cells of the tidal pool population are highly flexible and markedly contractile particularly in the anterior half. This population moved rather slowly with only moderate coverglass pressure.  The fully extended cells measure up to178 um in length showing a spindle shape while contracted cells assume a more club-shaped or bottle-shaped contour measuring 80 um.  I found that individuals are variably dorso-ventrally flattened but well fed  cells are more rounded in cross-section.  It is interesting to note that observed the population on one slide ingesting small hypotrichs from the genus Aspidisca.  The pellicle is textured with pits from which cilia emerge as first depicted by Kahl 1928 (Trachelocerca trepida) (1).  I could not appreciate This feature was later described as grooved by Petz et al 1995 (2) and depicted in live photos of Hu, Lin and Song 2019 (3), though Song 1990 (4) in his redescription describes a smooth pellicle. The macronucleus is elongate and variably S-shaped or U-shaped  (horseshoe-shaped) as shown by all observers. Postoral kineties as depicted by Song (1990) (4) are plainly visible subapically. I could occasionally visualize extrusomes in the anterior of the cell.   The dorsal brush (or adoral organelle of Petz et al 1995), whose irregular arrangement rather than in rows, is plainly seen when the cells orientation is correct but can be very difficult to visualize in vivo as noted by Song 1990.  There was a small terminal contractile vacuole. The cell cytoplasm was filled with shiny globules of various sizes.  I counted 9 longitudinal somatic kineties on one side which infers a total of 18-20 while Song 1990 (4) reported 26-33 and Petz, Song and Wilbert 1995 (2) report 19-27 in their population from the Weddel Sea. Song 1990 also mentions the results of Wilbert and Kahan 1981 in a population from Solar Lake on the Red Sea shore: "their animals possess less somatic kineties (18 only)" (4).   This constellation of features points to a diagnosis of Pseudotrachelocerca trepida (Kahl, 1928) Song, 1990.

 I shall present all available descriptions and end with a discussion of the current thinking with regards to placement of the genus.

Kahl's initial description of Trachelocerca trepida: "Trachelocerca trepida KAHL, 1928 Size stretched 140 um, contracted (ovoid) 70 um; Body flattened (2:1). Neck tapered about half the width, contractile to the anterior end. core sausage-shaped, medium wide (20-24 heights). Neck to front end contractile. Special decoration row (dorsal brush) of the neck is not very noticeable. Near the left edge of a broad side of the neck a hyaline stripe on which a very dense series of long, backward curved cilia pulls, which can be seen towards the back of the body until about the middle which is (not easily recognizable). Cilia long and quite dense and inserted in pits. Trichocysts difficult to visualize in the throat (or at least very indistinct). Distributed in stronger 0Idesloe salt sites, oligosapropel, never numerous; occasionally in Sylt seawater ditch (160 um); but not examined in more detail here" (1).

Song's 1990 redescription: "New diagnosis. In vivo about 80-160 x 30 um; neck region somewhat contractile; body bottle-shaped, sometimes slightly flattened dorsoventrally. Macronucleus U or S-shaped; single contractile vacuole posteriorly; Extrusomes (toxicysts) genus-specific, mostly around the cytostome; 28 meridional somatic kineties on average. Redescription. Body shape in vivo moderately variable, anterior third neck-like narrowed, can be slightly curved in all directions. Anterior end more or less coned but not truncated as depicted by Kahl, posteriorly rounded, sometimes bag-like. Oral opening oval to long elliptic, lies polar on small, indistinct oral bulge, hardly recognizable in vivo. Nematodesmata not recognizable in vivo. Cilia ca. 5-8 um long, which at the oral end (circumoral ciliation) increase to ca. 10 um and, like that of Phialina, form a tuft with 5 girdles of cilia and beat anteriorly when feeding. Cilia of dorsal brush about 4-5 um, very difficult to recognize in living cells. Pellicle thin and smooth, not indented by ciliary rows as described by Kahl; beneath pellicle no special granules recognisable. Extrusomes occur both around cytostome and within cytoplasm,short rod-or spindle-shaped, often heavily stained with protargol. Cytoplasm very hyaline, colorless, usually densely filled with numerous dark grey, ca. 2 um particles. Macronucleus usually horseshoe-shaped, centrally located, with numerous nucleoli; micronucleus not found, presumably too near to macronucleus. Movement moderately rapid, usually swimming ahead in straight line while rotating around longitudinal body axis. Feeds possibly mainly on bacteria both in nature and in culture.

Somatic kineties course longitudinally, composed of monokinetids; distance between basal bodies smaller anteriorly than posteriorly. At base of oral bulge a circumoral kinety composed of dikinetids is present; the number of the basal body pairs of this kinety is smaller than that of somatic kinetics. After protargol impregnation the rhabdos is composed of, very probably, only one component: the nematodesmal bundles which originate from the anterior kinetosomes of the oral dikinetids. Dorsal brush very characteristic: made up of many basal body pairs which are "piled up" irregularly, unlike those in other haptorid families, where it forms regular rows. Brush extends posteriorly to about one sixth of the body length and, in addition, is connected with only one somatic kinety" (4).

Petz, Song and Wilbert described a population from icy waters of the Weddell Sea: " Pseudotrachelocerca trepida (KAHL, 1928a) SONG, 1990: In vivo 90-110 x 30-37 um. Body elongate club- to spindle-shaped, anteriorly narrowed, widest at or behind mid-body, frontal end straight, posteriorly rounded; contractile. Cross section elliptical to circular. Cytostome apical, not protruding, very likely circular. Pellicle thin, slightly grooved by kineties. Cortical granules colourless. Single macronucleus sausage- to U-shaped, located in mid-body, contains spherical (up to 3 urn across) and, rarely, elongate nucleoli. Once 3 micronuclei, globular, in indentation of macronucleus, usually not impregnated with protargol. Single contractile vacuole terminally. Cortical granules in rows along somatic kineties. Cytoplasm colourless, contains many greenish shining globules (1.5-4 um across) and food vacuoles with unidentified contents; specimens usually appear rather dark. Movement slow. Somatic kineties meridional, extending over entire length of body, especially anterior portions composed of very densely spaced monokinetids, cilia about 10 um long; parasomal sac adjacent to each basal body in silver nitrate slides (cf. FOISSNER 1983). Argentophilic structure (fibres?) immediately beneath each kinety. Somatic kineties terminate anteriorly with single dikinetid forming circumoral kinety. Adoral organelle (FOISSNER et al. 1994; formerly brosse) parallel to somatic kineties, i.e. aklitolophic (HILLER & BARDELE 1988), 28-51% of body length (x = 41%, n = 7), composed of numerous irregularly arranged dikinetids, distally indistinctly 2- to 3-rowed, proximally single-rowed, continued posteriad in 1 row of monokinetids (short somatic kinety); cilia about 10 um long. Extrusomes spindle-shaped, usually slightly bent, about 0.5 um thick, sometimes with thread-like process, scattered in body, not found surrounding cytostome (not impregnated?), once, however, observed outside cytostome (preparation artifact?); in protargol slides, extruded extrusomes very fine, ca. 20 um long. Nematodesmata fine, about 23 um long. Occurrence and ecology: Infrequently found in the endopagial of pancake and multiyear sea ice of the Weddell Sea, between latitude 69° 07-70° 30' S and longitude 07° 19'-12° 08' W. Occurs together with diatoms, autotrophic and heterotrophic flagellates and ciliates "(4).

Discussion from Petz et al 1995: " Comparison with related species and systematic considerations: The irregularly arranged adoral organelle is a main character of the monotypic genus Pseudotrachelocerca (SONG 1990). The Antarctic specimens are quite similar to P. trepida (AGAMALIEV 1983; BORROR 1965; KAHL 1928a; SONG 1990; WILBERT & KAHAN 1981). They differ slightly in the possession of cortical granules (perhaps a variable character) and a longer adoral organelle (1/3 1/2 vs. 1/6-1/4 of body length; AGAMALIEV 1983; KAHL 1928a, 1932; SONG 1990; WILBERT & KAHAN 1981). The latter depends, however, on the contraction of the specimens. The population studied by BORROR (1965) also has a long adoral organelle, thus we identify the present organisms with P. trepida. The adoral organelle arrangement and the meridional somatic kineties suggest that Pseudotrachelocerca is related to holophryids (FOISSNER et al. 1994; HILLER & BARDELE 1988). This genus is thus transferred from the Spathidiida to the Prostomatida. The family Holophryidae PERTY, 1852 is, however, distinguished from Pseudotrachelocercidae SONG, 1990 in the 3-rowed adoral organelle (FOISSNER et al. 1994; HILLER & BARDELE 1988). [Due to the rather complicated nomenclature and taxonomy in prostomatids, Prorodontidae of HILLER & BARDELE (1988) are Holophryidae (FOISSNER et al. 1994)]" (4).

Finally, Huang et al 2019 analyzed 14 small subunit ribosomal RNA gene sequences, 13 large subunit ribosomal RNA gene sequences and 13 ITS1- 5.8S- ITS2 gene sequences of various haptorians including the first molecular data from Pseudotrachelocerca Song, 1990: "The historical assignment of Pseudotrachelocerca trepida to the class Litostomatea is rejected by our analyses; rather, it clusters with Cyclotrichium cyclokaryon (a planktonic Mesodiunium-like organism) with high or full support and shows close relationships to classes Colpodea, Prostomatea and Plagiopylea, in all our single- gene and concentrated trees. Hitherto, Pseudotrachelocerca trepida has been assigned to the monogeneric family Pseudotrachelocercidae. Pseudotrachelocercica is similar to other litostomateans in having a dorsal brush (DB), apical extrusomes and a mesh- like silver line system (Song, 1990). Among these characters, the DB is an important feature for the classification of litostomateans, and a three- rowed DB is considered as an apomorphy of the last common ancestor (Vd’ačný et al., 2011). However, Pseudotrachelocerca is divergent in that its DB is composed of irregularly arranged kinetids and is connected to only one somatic kinety (vs. to several somatic kineties in most other litostomateans; Song, 1990). Both the divergent phylogenetic position and the heterogeneities in the DB appearance imply that the DB structure of Pseudotrachelocerca might be a homoplasy of the typical litostomatean dorsal brush. In addition, the topology testing results strongly reject the grouping of Pseudotrachelocerca to either Haptoria or Litostomatea (AU test, ρ< .05; Table 2). Accordingly, we suggest an exclusion of Pseudotrachelocercidae from the class Litostomatea" (5).

"Although Pseudotrachelocera grouped with Cyclotrichium with moderate- to- high support in all the phylogenetic analyses, there is no distinct morphological evidence to support this phylogenetic affiliation. Morphologically, Pseudotrachelocerca is similar to Cyclotrichium in possessing both oralized somatic monokinetids and circumoral dikinetids, characters that are also commonly present in some typical haptorians, for example Chaenea (Kwon, Vďačný, Shazib, & Shin, 2014; Xu, Song, & Hu, 2005). Other genera that cluster with Pseudotrachelocerca and Cyclotrichium and which are systematically ambiguous include Askenasia, Paraspathidium and the prostomatean genus Plagiocampa. Previous studies have placed these taxa in the class Plagiopylea, which was not well supported by our results (Gao, Warren, et al., 2016; Zhang, Yi, Song, Al- Rasheid, & Warren, 2010; Zhang et al., 2012). Relationships between these genera remain unresolved pending enrichment of taxa and genes. Based on the current knowledge, we propose that Pseudotrachelocercidae should be regarded as incertae sedis within the Prostomeatea + Plagiopylea + Colpodea complex" (5). 

Finally, it is interesting that in this study, Pseudotrachelocerca clusters with Paraspathidium, another ciliate which I also identified in this benthic sample of a saprobic estuarine salt marsh tidal pool.

1. Kahl A. (1930): Urtiere oder Protozoa. I. Wimpertiere oder Ciliata (Infusoria). I. Allgemeiner Teil und Prostornata. Tierwelt Dtl., 18, 1-180.

2. Taxonomy and ecology of the ciliate fauna (Protozoa, Ciliophora) in the endopagial and pelagial of the Weddell Sea, Antarctica Wolfgang PETZ, Weibo SONG & Norbert WILBERT. Stapfia 40, 1995  pp 15-17.

3. Ciliate Atlas: Species Found in the South China Sea. Xiaozhong Hu • Xiaofeng Lin • Weibo Song Editors. Science Press Beijing, Springer. 2019. ISBN 978-981-13-5900-2 College of Life Science South China Normal University Guangzhou, Guangdong, China ISBN 978-981-13-5901-9 (eBook) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-13-5901-9, pp 84-5.

4. Infraciliature and Silverline System of the Ciliate Pseudotrachelocerca trepida (Kahl, 1928), nov. gen., nov comb., and Establishment of a New Family, the Pseudotrachelocercidae nov fam. (Ciliophora, Haptoria). Weibo Song. Europ.J.Protistol. 26, 160-166 (1990)

d071b3d4-a438-43fb-98f2-c10ffcf95ea1.description:
Chlamydonella derouxi Song 2003 harvested harvested by floating coverglass method from a small salt marsh tidal pool at the edge of estuary Acabonac Harbor. Imaged in Nomarski DIC on Olympus BH2S under SPlan 40 0.70 and SPlan 100 1.25 oil immersion objectives plus variable phone camera cropping on Samsung Galaxy S24. 

The cells measure 22-30 um in length and are oval in outline with a flattened ventral surface and a vaulted dorsum. Ciliation is limited to the ventral surface where there are 12 somatic kineties, four of which are frontoventral.  The preoral kinety is Y-shaped and difficult to visualize. The ventral surface has seven club-shaped protuberances irregularly arranged in 3 rows.  There is a terminal fragment at the apical end of the dorsal surface consisting of 5 basal bodies. The dorsum show scattered irregularly positioned cortical granules.  The cytostome is in the anterior third of the cell left of the midline and is surrounded by a cyrtos consisting of 14 nematodesmal rods. The macronucleus is oval and heteromeric and difficult to visualize clearly.  Micronuclei were not seen, nor were the equatorial fragments. There are two contractile vacuoles diagonally opposed on the right anterior and left posterior of the cell.  Movement by gliding on the coverglass or climbing on debris, occasionally swimming while rotating. These features correspond well with the redescription of C. derouxi by Qu et al 2015 (1).  Gong and Song 2006 (2) also redescribed the species. Their population had only three club-hsped protuberances and the terminal fragment had 4 basal bodies. 

The redescription of the species by Qu et al  2015:  "Cell size16–45 x 15–30 um in vivo. Body oval in outline, with anterior end slightly protruding to left. Cytoplasm colourless to greyish at low magnifications (40X). Cytostome located in anterior fourth, elliptical in shape with a width of 4–6 um. Cyrtos composed of 12–14 nematodesmal rods measuring about 12um in length. Seven to 14 club shaped protuberances, about 3–4 um long, distributed in 3–4 longitudinal rows on ventral side. Two contractile vacuoles, each about 3 um in diameter diagonally located in anterior and posterior third, contracting at an interval of about 5–8s. Single macronucleus juxtaposed heteromerously, about 10 x6 um in vivo. Colourless cortical granules (about 0.5 um across) irregularly distributed on dorsal side. Cilia about 7 um in length. Movement by gliding on substrate or on interface between air and water. A total of 12–15 somatic kineties, four of which were frontoventral kineties. The left and right equatorial fragments composed of 2–9 and 1–8 basal bodies respectively. The terminal fragment apically positioned on dorsal side, consisting of 4–9 basal bodies). One to two micronuclei.  Oral kineties Y-shaped, with a fragment of 3–6 pairs of basal bodies usually separated from main part on right" (1).

37a0c814-858b-464f-bea5-ee0267d50346.description:
Species Identified: 

Fogedia krammeri Witkowski, Lange-Bertalot, Kociolek & M.Kulikovskiy 2010

Taxonomic classification:

Phylum: Bacillariophyta
Subphylum: Bacillariophytina
Class: Bacillariophyceae
Subclass: Bacillariophyceae
Order: Naviculales
Family: Naviculales incertae
Genus: Fogedia (Guiry and Guiry 2025)

Type species, synonym(s), etc.: Holotype species  is Fogedia giffeniana (Foged) Witkowski, Lange-Bertalot, Metzeltin & Bafana 1997

Main genus characteristics (see Witkowski et al. 1997):

1.	the presence of short, simple apical external raphe endings (they are strongly hooked on the same side in Navicula s.str.)
2.	the internal raphe slit being straight (it is strongly oblique in Navicula)
3.	the valve face of most Fogedia species bears a lateral area differing from those observed either Fallacia or Lyrella
4.	The valve face is flat
5.	Apical striae, which are missing in Fogedia.

Species Descriptions:

Fogedia krammeri Witkowski, Lange-Bertalot, Kociolek & M.Kulikovskiy 2010: 50, figs 1, 2

References: Witkowski et al. 2010; Kim et al. 2022. 

Description:
Valves moderately variable in outline from broad-elliptic or broadly elliptic-lanceolate to linear-elliptic, the ends cuneate and at the terminus shortly-protracted subrostrate. Length 23.5-28.2 (20–30) μm, width 11.7-12.0 (9.5–12.0) μm. Raphe slightly lateral, two minor undulations in the raphe ¼ distance away from the central endings and ¼ from the terminal endings. Expanded external central raphe endings and short, slightly bent terminal raphe endings in same direction. Axial area narrow, linear throughout. Central area forming a shortened, almost rectangular fascia connected to the lateral area and in the marginal part on either side the transapical striae are interrupted. Striae subparallel to slightly radiate proximally, becoming more strongly radiate distally up to the ends, where they are very slightly denser, 11-12 (10–12) in 10 μm. Lineolae of the striae comparatively coarse, discernible by LM, 27-30 (26–29) in 10 μm.

Remarks: This specimen has similarities to both Fogedia krammeri and F. finmarchica Cleve 1895: 28 (Van der Werff & Huls 1958–1975: P.D G XVI. 109; Hendey 1964: 198, Pl. 30, Fig. 5; Riznyk 1973: 126, Pl. 11, Fig. 7; Sims 1996: Pl. 141, Fig. 12; Witkowski et al, 1997). As noted in Witkowski et al. (2010), F. finmarchica has a more lanceolate outline and higher lineolae density of 35-40 in 10 μm, which is very difficult to resolve by LM. For the MHMPP specimens observed with LM, the valve outline is more broadly elliptic than drawings in the literature for F. finmarchica and the lineolae can be resolved and are 27 in 10 µm matching the data for F. krammeri and the SEM image from SHW shows an areolae density of 30 in 10 µm. Also, the undulations in the raphe of the SHW specimen (SEM) match the undulation in the San Francisco Bay specimens. Further, the expansion of the raphe endings are more pronounced in F. krammeri, matching our specimens. Lastly, most images of F. finmarchica show a pronounced lanceolate outline. For these criteria, we place these specimens in F. krammeri. Fogedia krammeri was previously reported and first described in San Francisco Bay by Witkowski et al. (2010) and as far as can be ascertained it was, before this report its only known locality. 

Fogedia krammeri is a first record for the Salish Sea, a second report for the East Pacific Coast and a second recording of the species.

Methods: 

All samples were nitric acid cleaned (Jackman et al. 2025) and either mounted on SEM stubs or made into slides with Naphrax using standard procedures. Our thanks to the late Andrzej Witkowski for observing Fogedia sp. in our MHMPP LM images and his suggestion to examine the data in the 2010 paper on Fogedia found in San Francisco Bay (Witkowski et al. 2010). Thanks also go to Melanie Quenneville for the SEM image of a specimen from the eelgrass at Montague Harbour Marine Provincial Park (MHMPP). Collection and prep. of samples by Arjan van Asselt (IMERSS) and Mark Webber (IMERSS & UVIC). LM imaging and taxonomy by M. Webber. Many thanks to Elaine Humphrey (UVIC & IMERSS) for SEM and image support.

References:

Cleve, P.T. (1895). Synopsis of the naviculoid diatoms. Part II. Kongliga Svenska Vetenskapsak Akademiens Handlingar 27(3): 1-219, 4 pls.

Guiry, M.D. & Guiry, G.M. 08 July 2022. AlgaeBase. World-wide electronic publication, National University of Ireland, Galway. https://www.algaebase.org; searched on 05 Sept. 2025.

**THE SPECIMEN WAS INCORRECTLY MEASURED. IT WAS ACTUALLY ONLY ~363µ LONG, NOT 700µ.  THE IMAGES ARE NOW CORRECTED**
Large (~363µ x ~210µ) broken shell of a testate amoeba. Still filled with zoochorellae. Based on size alone, the specimen is on the boaderline between *D. pyroformis* and *D. gigantea*. Siemensma records 380µ *D. pyroformis* specimens here, https://arcella.nl/difflugia-cf-pyriformis-2/.  Both *pyroformis* and *gigantea* have coarse, agglutinated, pyriform tests and both can have zoochlora symbionts. One of my 2 previous observations of similar specimens may need to be reidentified as *D. gigantea*, because of its exceptional size (475µ long), https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=1105303&user_id=mnold1&verifiable=any.  See comments by curator bdstaylor below.
